LO 001Substance Use & Tox✓ In your notes

Apply the appropriate pharmacologic intervention for the management of a substance use disorder

Answer

For alcohol use disorder, naltrexone (oral or long-acting injectable) manages craving and can be started while the patient is still drinking, while acamprosate (an NMDA-receptor antagonist plus GABA-A agonist) supports relapse prevention; disulfiram acts through a one-step enzymatic block, with baclofen, nalmefene, gabapentin, and topiramate as recognized off-label options. Long-acting benzodiazepines (diazepam, lorazepam, chlordiazepoxide) are preferred for alcohol detoxification because their GABA-A cross-reactivity and active metabolites smooth the taper and lower seizure/recurrent-withdrawal risk. For opioid use disorder, medications for opioid use disorder (MOUD) target the mu-opioid receptor either as agonists (methadone, buprenorphine) or an antagonist (naltrexone). Across substances, the detox strategy (cold turkey, taper, or MOUD) depends on the substance and danger of its withdrawal, and pharmacology alone has little effect on long-term outcomes unless paired with psychosocial interventions such as CBT and mutual support programs (AA/NA).

🧠
Memory hook · N-A-D for alcohol use disorderNaltrexone kills the Need (craving — can start while still drinking) · Acamprosate keeps Abstinence (NMDA antagonist + GABA-A agonist, 3×/day) · Disulfiram is the Deterrent (blocks aldehyde dehydrogenase → instant hangover).

Pulled from: Addiction & Non-Clinical Drug Use

Naltrexone

Oral or long-acting injectable

Can start while the patient is still drinking (unlike opioid use disorder). Avoid in patients taking opioids for pain or with hepatic insufficiency. Used mainly for craving management.

Acamprosate

Oral, 3×/day

NMDA-receptor antagonist + GABA-A agonist — mirrors alcohol's own mechanism. Effective, but 3×/day dosing hurts adherence.

Disulfiram ⭐ HY — Aversive Therapy

Aldehyde dehydrogenase inhibitor

Blocks acetaldehyde → acetate, letting acetaldehyde bioaccumulate → intense hangover (flushing, headache, nausea, vomiting, weakness, orthostatic hypotension, respiratory difficulty) if alcohol is consumed. This is negative reinforcement by design — requires informed patient buy-in, since the reaction itself can warrant an ED visit. Rare AE: hepatitis, optic neuritis, peripheral neuropathy.

Two pharmacologic strategies, both targeting the μ-opioid receptor — agonist-based (methadone, buprenorphine) or antagonist-based (naltrexone). All are most effective paired with psychotherapy/counseling; accessibility remains a major real-world barrier (accreditation hurdles, enrollment hurdles, inconsistent insurance coverage, social stigma).

Long-acting benzodiazepines (diazepam, lorazepam, chlordiazepoxide) are preferred — their cross-reactivity at GABA-A smooths the taper and their active metabolites give a lower chance of recurrent withdrawal or seizures. Two dosing strategies: symptom-triggered (dose only once significant symptoms appear) vs. front-loaded (proactively substitute sedation regardless of symptoms, then taper).

Disulfiram's one-step block is the entire mechanism — worth being able to draw from memory

Off-label options you should recognize but aren't held accountable for in depth: baclofen (GABA-B agonist), nalmefene (opioid antagonist), gabapentin, topiramate.

🩹

Detoxification

Cold turkey vs. taper vs. MOUD — the approach depends entirely on which substance and how dangerous its withdrawal is.

🧩

Treatment

Pharmacologic — aversive therapies (block desired effects/cause hangover), replacement therapy (manage dysphoria/reward), treat comorbid psychiatric disease. Psychosocial — CBT, mutual support (AA/NA), moderation management as early intervention.

⚠️ Pharmacology Alone Is a Drop in the Bucket

Pharmacologic interventions mostly target detoxification and relief of withdrawal — they have little effect on long-term addiction or outcomes by themselves. Psychosocial interventions (CBT, mutual support programs) are what actually move outcomes, and addiction is very often a comorbid condition that complicates diagnosis in its own right.

Q3: How can mutual support programs (AA/NA) help treat addiction, and how should they be complemented by medical oversight?

Answer

They build relapse-prevention skills and social learning that combats stigma; mutual support and psychosocial intervention alongside medical management together increase positive outcomes more than either alone.

LO 002Psychotherapy & Theory✓ In your notes

Appropriately select a form of psychotherapy to apply to a patient presentation based on a case

Answer

Selecting a first-line psychotherapy is driven by the case's diagnosis: for borderline personality disorder, choose DBT (dialectical behavioral therapy, built around emotion regulation, mindfulness, distress tolerance, and interpersonal effectiveness modules) — the exam rule is to pick DBT whenever it's an option, otherwise choose CBT, since CBT is the mainstay for the other nine personality disorders. Interpersonal Therapy (IPT) fits a patient whose central problem is current relationships and communication, while EMDR is chosen for trauma-focused presentations where reminders of the trauma trigger a misattributed fight-or-flight response. Supportive therapy (listening, encouragement, stability) is the right choice during acute crises or acute medical comorbidity. For acute stress disorder or adjustment disorders, CBT or psychodynamic psychotherapy plus supportive psychotherapy is used to improve coping skills and strengthen defense mechanisms. As a founder shortcut: Rogers → humanistic, Freud → psychodynamic, Beck & Ellis → cognitive, Skinner → behavioral.

🧠
Memory hook · The 10-second therapy pickerBPD → DBT · trauma → EMDR · relationship problems → IPT · acute crisis / medically ill → supportive · everything else → CBT. Dr. Smith's rule: if DBT is an answer choice and the vignette is borderline, pick DBT; otherwise CBT.

Pulled from: Personality Disorders · Introduction to Therapy · Anxiety, OCD & Trauma-Related Disorders · Introduction & History of Psychiatry

🧠
The exam shortcut: DBT (dialectical behavioral therapy) is specifically for borderline PD; CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) is the mainstay for the other 9 personality disorders. Dr. Smith's exact framing: "DBT is a form of CBT, so if the exam has DBT as an option, choose it; if not, choose CBT." In other words, DBT beats CBT as an answer choice only when the vignette is specifically about BPD — otherwise, default to CBT.
Question 12
A 24-year-old woman meets full criteria for borderline personality disorder, including recurrent self-harm and highly unstable relationships. Which specific psychotherapy modality is most appropriate as first-line treatment?
A. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT)
B. Dialectical behavioral therapy (DBT)
C. Psychoanalysis
D. Exposure and response prevention
Answer: B. DBT was developed specifically for BPD and is the only personality disorder with a dedicated first-line psychotherapy (Section 13). Remember the exam shortcut: DBT is technically a form of CBT — "if DBT is an option, choose it; if not, choose CBT" — but when both are listed and the vignette is BPD, DBT is the more specific and correct answer.

Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) ⭐ HY

Created by Marsha Linehan, PhD — for borderline personality disorder
StructureA skills-based, manualized treatment built around 4 modules: emotion regulation, mindfulness, distress tolerance, and interpersonal effectiveness.
OriginLinehan developed DBT partly from her own lived experience with BPD — she has spoken publicly (including in a well-known New York Times profile) about how the treatment reflects what helped her.
Also used forAdapted well beyond BPD to many other conditions, but the BPD connection is the one to remember for exams.

Interpersonal Therapy (IPT)

Focused squarely on relationships
ApproachA structured, time-limited therapy focused on improving current interpersonal relationships and communication skills — less exploratory than psychodynamic work, more here-and-now than CBT's focus on thought content.
Worth knowingDistinct from the humanistic modalities above — IPT is manualized and diagnosis-focused (often depression), not a general relational philosophy.

EMDR (Eye Movement Desensitization & Reprocessing)

Trauma-focused; closely related to systematic desensitization
ConceptTrauma creates a fight-or-flight response that becomes misattributed to non-threatening reminders of the traumatic event. EMDR uses an external stimulus (classically a light bar moving back and forth) while the patient discusses the traumatic material, pausing before it becomes unmanageable and shifting attention to a neutral stimulus — aiming to decouple the trauma from its physiologic response.
YieldTesting on EMDR has increased somewhat in recent years, though it's still not top-tier yield.

Supportive Therapy

"You're going to feel better"
ApproachListening, encouragement, and stability — filling in a supportive presence that may be missing elsewhere in the patient's life. Sometimes called (a bit dismissively) a "professional friend."
Best fitAcute crises, medical comorbidity, or acute stressors — this is essentially what's delivered on psychiatric consult-liaison services.
LimitationDoesn't always account for the limits of a relationship built mainly on support.

Remove the etiologic stressor where possible, plus CBT or psychodynamic psychotherapy; supportive psychotherapy also helps. Focus is on improving coping skills, strengthening defense mechanisms, or changing how the person relates to the stressor. Medication can help adjunctively (anxiety, secondary insomnia, depressive symptoms).

🧠
Founder pairs worth locking in: Rogers → Humanistic. Freud → Psychodynamic. Beck & Ellis → Cognitive. Skinner → Behavioral. If a board question names a founder, work backward to the family, then to the matching technique list.
LO 003Substance Use & Tox◐ Partly covered

Based on a clinical scenario; apply the appropriate intervention in the context of recreational drug use

Answer

For an acute LSD 'bad trip,' the most effective intervention is non-pharmacologic talk-down/reality-grounding, with benzodiazepines as an option and antipsychotics used more controversially. For acute psychotic or drug-induced agitation more broadly, the go-to PRN is the 'B-52' cocktail — Haldol 5 mg + Ativan 2 mg + Benadryl 50 mg IM — which combines an antipsychotic and benzodiazepine for the fastest effect, with the Benadryl/Cogentin component pre-empting acute dystonia; watch for repeated dosing producing neuroleptic malignant syndrome (rigidity, diaphoresis, hyperthermia), which requires stopping the antipsychotic. Beyond the acute encounter, detoxification is tailored to the agent, usually via a taper rather than abrupt cessation, with clonidine (an alpha-2 agonist) blunting the sympathetic surge of opioid or nicotine withdrawal, though it is not sufficient monotherapy for CNS-depressant withdrawal because it does not prevent withdrawal seizures. When working up new psychosis or delirium, recreational drugs to consider include marijuana, cocaine/amphetamines, LSD/PCP/psilocybin, and bath salts/Spice/K2/Flakka, and a negative urine drug screen does not rule out use since kratom, synthetic bath salts, and novel psychoactive substances are often missed on standard screens. Naloxone (Narcan) is the opioid receptor antagonist that reverses opioid overdose via IN/IM/IV routes; because its half-life is shorter than most opioids, redosing or auto-redosing may be needed.

🧠
Memory hook · The B-52 bomberAgitation cocktail = Benadryl 50 mg + Haldol 5 mg + Ativan 2 mg IM. The Benadryl on board is what pre-empts acute dystonia. Repeated dosing → watch for NMS (rigid + sweaty + hot → STOP the antipsychotic).
◐
Missing from your notesDrug-specific management of acute stimulant (cocaine/amphetamine) agitation/intoxication is still not addressed by any source, including the two new lectures, which cover pediatric psychiatry and basic limbic/monoamine neuroanatomy rather than acute toxicology management.

Pulled from: Psychotic Disorders & Antipsychotic Pharmacology · Addiction & Non-Clinical Drug Use · Psychiatry Key Drug List 2026

What Is a "B-52"? ⭐ HY

A PRN IM "cocktail" for acute psychotic agitation
RecipeBenadryl 50 mg + Haldol 5 mg + Ativan 2 mg, given IM.
RationaleCombining a benzodiazepine + antipsychotic works fastest for decreasing psychotic aggression and acute manic symptoms; the Benadryl/Cogentin component pre-empts acute dystonia from the Haldol.
UsePRN only — not a scheduled/standing combination.
🟢 The Most Effective Acute Intervention Isn't a Drug

Talk-down / reality-grounding — simply staying with the patient and talking — is the most effective acute intervention for a bad trip. Benzodiazepines are an option; antipsychotics are sometimes used, though their indication here is debated in the literature.

📌
Watch for this vignette pattern: a patient given repeated "B-52" doses who develops rigidity, diaphoresis, and hyperthermia is showing neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS), not simple dystonia or parkinsonism — the fever and diaphoresis are the tip-off. First step is to stop the antipsychotic and provide supportive care/cooling; dantrolene or bromocriptine may be added in severe cases. This exact scenario is Case D in Section 28.

Other acute-agitation options

  • ▸ Chlorpromazine / diphenhydramine combination
  • ▸ Olanzapine IM — effective monotherapy alternative (note: avoid combining IM olanzapine with a benzodiazepine within 2 hours, per Section 18, due to additive cardiorespiratory depression risk)
  • ▸ Other de-escalation and pharmacologic strategies per clinical context

Clonidine ⭐ HY

α2-adrenergic agonist

Inhibits noradrenergic outflow, blunting the sympathetic surge common to withdrawal from most drugs of abuse — including partially blocking opioid withdrawal symptoms and easing nicotine withdrawal. Not a monotherapy: does not adequately prevent withdrawal seizures, so it is not recommended alone for CNS depressant (alcohol/benzo/barbiturate) withdrawal.

  1. Taper — gradually decrease the dose to ease withdrawal symptoms; often used as a harm-reduction bridge in patients not yet ready for full treatment (nicotine patches/lozenges, methadone for opioids, cross-tolerant benzodiazepines for alcohol).
  2. Long-acting, cross-tolerant substitutes — a drug in the same class with a longer half-life smooths the withdrawal course (e.g., long-acting benzodiazepines for alcohol withdrawal).
  3. Symptomatic support — an α2-adrenergic agonist (clonidine) blunts the sympathetic hyperactivity common to nearly every withdrawal syndrome.
CategoryExamples
Recreational / drugs of abuseMarijuana, cocaine/amphetamines, LSD/PCP/psilocybin/other hallucinogens, bath salts/Spice/K2/Flakka
Prescribed medicationsParkinson's medications, corticosteroids, benzodiazepines/Z-drugs, leukotriene inhibitors (montelukast, zafirlukast, zileuton), opiates, antibiotics, clonidine, varenicline (Chantix)
Endocrine/metabolicMyxedema (severe hypothyroidism, 5–15% present with psychosis), dehydration
InfectiousSyphilis, UTIs/URIs, advanced HIV, Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis
Neurodegenerative / structuralParkinson's disease, Huntington's disease, Lewy body dementia, Alzheimer's disease, frontotemporal lobar degeneration, CVA/stroke, traumatic brain injury, pituitary tumor
RheumatologicLupus
🧪
A negative urine tox screen does NOT rule out drug use. Common substances that don't reliably show up on a standard urine drug screen: kratom, synthetic bath salts, and many novel psychoactive substances (Spice/K2). Dr. Smith's real case from Dartmouth: two patients were found having sex on the ground in front of a Dunkin' Donuts drive-through window and brought in as a psychiatry consult for "new-onset schizophrenia — in two people, simultaneously." Tox screen was negative; only searching their clothes turned up a synthetic-marijuana packet (K2/Spice) — the real cause.
🩹

Detoxification

Cold turkey vs. taper vs. MOUD — the approach depends entirely on which substance and how dangerous its withdrawal is.

🧩

Treatment

Pharmacologic — aversive therapies (block desired effects/cause hangover), replacement therapy (manage dysphoria/reward), treat comorbid psychiatric disease. Psychosocial — CBT, mutual support (AA/NA), moderation management as early intervention.

  • Harm reduction — any reduction in use, or a patient simply returning after being told you're concerned, is a genuine win.
  • Abstinence — considered by some literature to itself be a behavioral intervention; not functional for every SUD.
  • Psychosocial — CBT, mutual support programs (note: some are faith-based and may not fit every patient).

Q5: Why did buprenorphine/naloxone relieve Mr. A's symptoms and long-term craving, and how long should maintenance continue?

Answer

As a partial agonist, buprenorphine prevents withdrawal symptoms and reduces craving by increasing mesolimbic dopaminergic neurotransmission just enough to relieve dependence without a full-agonist high. It can be used for both detox and long-term maintenance — and because addiction is considered permanent, maintenance is often continued for years, with tapering (as Mr. A begins to consider) approached cautiously and individually.

Memory Hook — the alcohol trio & the opioid trio
ETOH: Disulfiram punishes, Naltrexone un-craves, Acamprosate re-balances (and A-camprosate = A-fter detox, TID, diarrhea, liver-safe). Opioids: Naloxone rescues (short!), Buprenorphine plateaus (partial agonist ceiling), Methadone replaces (full agonist, QTc).
LO 004Substance Use & Tox✓ In your notes

Based on a clinical scenario; identify the appropriate pharmacologic intervention to manage a patient in withdrawal

Answer

Alcohol withdrawal — the most dangerous withdrawal syndrome covered, given its seizure and delirium tremens risk — is managed with long-acting benzodiazepines (diazepam, lorazepam, chlordiazepoxide), dosed either symptom-triggered or on a fixed taper; their GABA-A cross-reactivity and active metabolites smooth the taper and lower the chance of recurrent withdrawal or seizures. Clonidine, an alpha-2 agonist, blunts the sympathetic surge of withdrawal and partially blocks opioid and nicotine withdrawal symptoms, but is not adequate monotherapy for CNS-depressant (alcohol/benzodiazepine/barbiturate) withdrawal because it does not prevent withdrawal seizures. Withdrawal from short-half-life SSRIs such as paroxetine is managed simply by resuming the same medication, which abates the withdrawal anxiety.

🧠
Memory hook · Shakes by breakfast, seizures by tomorrow, DTs by day 2Alcohol withdrawal timeline: tremor/anxiety first → hallucinosis & seizures at 24–48 h → delirium tremens peaks around day 2 (can last a week). It's the only withdrawal that kills — treat with long-acting benzos (diazepam, chlordiazepoxide); clonidine alone never prevents the seizures.

Pulled from: Addiction & Non-Clinical Drug Use · Anxiety, OCD & Trauma-Related Disorders

Long-acting benzodiazepines (diazepam, lorazepam, chlordiazepoxide) are preferred — their cross-reactivity at GABA-A smooths the taper and their active metabolites give a lower chance of recurrent withdrawal or seizures. Two dosing strategies: symptom-triggered (dose only once significant symptoms appear) vs. front-loaded (proactively substitute sedation regardless of symptoms, then taper).

Clonidine ⭐ HY

α2-adrenergic agonist

Inhibits noradrenergic outflow, blunting the sympathetic surge common to withdrawal from most drugs of abuse — including partially blocking opioid withdrawal symptoms and easing nicotine withdrawal. Not a monotherapy: does not adequately prevent withdrawal seizures, so it is not recommended alone for CNS depressant (alcohol/benzo/barbiturate) withdrawal.

Q: Why is clonidine not recommended as monotherapy for withdrawal from CNS depressants (alcohol, benzodiazepines, barbiturates)?

Answer

Clonidine blunts sympathetic outflow but does not adequately prevent withdrawal seizures — a life-threatening feature specific to depressant withdrawal (via GABA-A/NMDA rebound) that an α2-agonist doesn't address.

⚠️ Alcohol Withdrawal Is the Most Dangerous Withdrawal in This Lecture

Relative to opioids, stimulants, or nicotine, alcohol withdrawal carries the highest risk of death — via seizures and delirium tremens. This is why alcohol detox is managed so much more aggressively than, say, opioid withdrawal.

🍷

Intoxication

  • Emotional lability, slurred speech
  • Ataxia, blackouts, coma
🚨

Withdrawal

  • Anxiety, tremor, insomnia
  • Severe: autonomic hyperactivity, seizures, delirium tremens
⚠️
Short half-life SSRI withdrawal: withdrawal from short-t½ drugs like paroxetine can produce an anxiety state worse than the anxiety the drug was originally prescribed for. If withdrawal occurs, the fix is straightforward: have the patient take another dose of the same medication, which abates the withdrawal.
LO 005Substance Use & Tox✓ In your notes

Based on a clinical scenario; identify the pharmacologic intervention employed in the management of a substance use disorder

Answer

For alcohol use disorder, naltrexone (oral or long-acting injectable) manages craving and can be started while the patient is still drinking, while acamprosate (an NMDA-receptor antagonist plus GABA-A agonist) supports relapse prevention; disulfiram acts through a one-step enzymatic block, with baclofen, nalmefene, gabapentin, and topiramate as recognized off-label options. Long-acting benzodiazepines (diazepam, lorazepam, chlordiazepoxide) are the preferred agents for alcohol detoxification, smoothing the taper and lowering seizure risk via GABA-A cross-reactivity and active metabolites. For opioid use disorder, MOUD targets the mu-opioid receptor either as agonist-based treatment (methadone, buprenorphine) or antagonist-based treatment (naltrexone), most effective when paired with psychotherapy/counseling. Overall, the detox strategy (cold turkey, taper, or MOUD) depends on the substance involved, and pharmacology alone has little effect on long-term outcomes without accompanying psychosocial treatment.

🧠
Memory hook · N-A-D for alcohol use disorderNaltrexone kills the Need (craving — can start while still drinking) · Acamprosate keeps Abstinence (NMDA antagonist + GABA-A agonist, 3×/day) · Disulfiram is the Deterrent (blocks aldehyde dehydrogenase → instant hangover).

Pulled from: Addiction & Non-Clinical Drug Use

Naltrexone

Oral or long-acting injectable

Can start while the patient is still drinking (unlike opioid use disorder). Avoid in patients taking opioids for pain or with hepatic insufficiency. Used mainly for craving management.

Acamprosate

Oral, 3×/day

NMDA-receptor antagonist + GABA-A agonist — mirrors alcohol's own mechanism. Effective, but 3×/day dosing hurts adherence.

Disulfiram ⭐ HY — Aversive Therapy

Aldehyde dehydrogenase inhibitor

Blocks acetaldehyde → acetate, letting acetaldehyde bioaccumulate → intense hangover (flushing, headache, nausea, vomiting, weakness, orthostatic hypotension, respiratory difficulty) if alcohol is consumed. This is negative reinforcement by design — requires informed patient buy-in, since the reaction itself can warrant an ED visit. Rare AE: hepatitis, optic neuritis, peripheral neuropathy.

Two pharmacologic strategies, both targeting the μ-opioid receptor — agonist-based (methadone, buprenorphine) or antagonist-based (naltrexone). All are most effective paired with psychotherapy/counseling; accessibility remains a major real-world barrier (accreditation hurdles, enrollment hurdles, inconsistent insurance coverage, social stigma).

Long-acting benzodiazepines (diazepam, lorazepam, chlordiazepoxide) are preferred — their cross-reactivity at GABA-A smooths the taper and their active metabolites give a lower chance of recurrent withdrawal or seizures. Two dosing strategies: symptom-triggered (dose only once significant symptoms appear) vs. front-loaded (proactively substitute sedation regardless of symptoms, then taper).

Disulfiram's one-step block is the entire mechanism — worth being able to draw from memory

Off-label options you should recognize but aren't held accountable for in depth: baclofen (GABA-B agonist), nalmefene (opioid antagonist), gabapentin, topiramate.

🩹

Detoxification

Cold turkey vs. taper vs. MOUD — the approach depends entirely on which substance and how dangerous its withdrawal is.

🧩

Treatment

Pharmacologic — aversive therapies (block desired effects/cause hangover), replacement therapy (manage dysphoria/reward), treat comorbid psychiatric disease. Psychosocial — CBT, mutual support (AA/NA), moderation management as early intervention.

⚠️ Pharmacology Alone Is a Drop in the Bucket

Pharmacologic interventions mostly target detoxification and relief of withdrawal — they have little effect on long-term addiction or outcomes by themselves. Psychosocial interventions (CBT, mutual support programs) are what actually move outcomes, and addiction is very often a comorbid condition that complicates diagnosis in its own right.

LO 007Psychotherapy & Theory✓ In your notes

Be able to identify concepts that serve as the basis for choosing a first-line psychotherapeutic intervention

Answer

Choosing a first-line psychotherapy rests less on which theory is 'correct' than on two things both being true: the therapist must believe in the approach and the patient must accept it as something that can help them, alongside the strength of the therapeutic relationship — the alliance between patient and treater is one of the strongest predictors of outcome, even outperforming the specific modality (the 'dodo bird verdict,' where research repeatedly fails to show any single modality is clearly superior overall). Where evidence does point toward a specific match, it is diagnosis-specific: CBT is the usual go-to for depression on exams, with little difference found between CBT and psychodynamic approaches for anxiety. Theory itself matters because it provides the therapist a roadmap for treatment, a lens for case formulation, and a way to explain the approach to the patient, so therapist-theory compatibility factors into selection as well.

🧠
Memory hook · Founder → school, in one breathRogers → humanistic (unconditional positive regard) · Freud → psychodynamic (free association, transference) · Beck & Ellis → cognitive · Skinner → behavioral · Linehan → DBT.

Pulled from: Introduction to Therapy

Beyond the relationship itself, fit matters: the patient has to believe in and accept the chosen modality (much like a patient who won't take a medication with a side effect they can't tolerate). Selecting a theory really requires two things to both be true — the therapist must understand and believe in it, and the patient must also believe it can help them.

DiagnosisWhat the evidence shows
DepressionCBT is the usual go-to on exams; psychoanalytic approaches are also used. If a question doesn't name a specific evidence-based match, CBT is a reasonable default guess given how broadly it's now indicated.
AnxietyLittle difference found between CBT and psychodynamic treatment.
Alcohol use disorderCBT, motivational interviewing, 12-step programs, and social skills training are all efficacious — no single winner.
Personality disorders (esp. BPD)Most personality disorders lack strong evidence-based treatments; BPD is the best-studied. Some research favors transference-focused therapy over DBT specifically for impulsivity, anger, aggressiveness, and irritability — though DBT remains the most widely taught/tested BPD treatment.

Across theories, research repeatedly fails to show that any single modality is clearly superior overall — a phenomenon sometimes called the "dodo bird verdict" (everybody wins, in Alice in Wonderland). What matters, according to several researchers:

🤝
The therapeutic relationship ⭐ HY: the alliance between patient and treater consistently shows up as one of the strongest predictors of outcome — even in pharmacotherapy. In the TDCRP study, psychiatrists with a strong alliance giving placebo got better results than psychiatrists with a weak alliance giving actual medication. Social skills and simple interpersonal connection between provider and patient measurably move outcomes.
  • Provides a roadmap for the treatment
  • Gives the therapist a lens for formulating the case
  • Therapist and theory need to be compatible
  • Gives the therapist a way to explain the approach to the patient
Extra detail: what even counts as "scientific"?
  • Gain a basic understanding of the history of psychotherapy.
  • Understand the theoretical basis for the major therapies.
  • Compare the different approaches to therapy and the patient populations each is best suited for.

History, theory, and the major psychotherapeutic modalities — from Freud's couch to DBT skills groups.

Lee Wolfrum, DO MHBH at Spring Harbor Medical UNECOM · Psychiatry Discipline Director Yield check: Therapy itself is not the highest-yield topic for the psych systems exam or boards — but the underlying concepts (conditioning, defense mechanisms, DBT↔BPD, CBT triangle) are recurring test favorites, and the material is clinically essential. Facts flagged ⭐ HY throughout are the ones most likely to show up on an exam.

Definitions shift depending on a theory's origins, but most converge on the same core idea: an interpersonal, principle-based treatment delivered by a trained therapist to a patient with a disorder, problem, or complaint, individualized to that patient — using talk, rather than a physical or pharmacologic intervention, to work through emotional distress.

LO 008Eating Disorders✓ In your notes

Be able to identify each of the eating disorders, their modifiers and severity

Answer

Anorexia Nervosa is subtyped as restricting type (restriction of intake/exercise without binge-eating or purging in the past 3 months) or binge-eating/purging type (some binge/purge behavior in the past 3 months), with severity specifiers that are BMI-based — a lower BMI signaling greater severity — plus partial/full remission specifiers. Bulimia Nervosa requires binge eating with recurrent inappropriate compensatory behavior (vomiting, laxatives, fasting, excessive exercise), has its severity specified by how often that compensatory behavior occurs weekly, and typically presents at a normal-to-high BMI rather than the low BMI of anorexia. Binge Eating Disorder is defined by binge eating with no compensatory behavior at all — the key differentiator from bulimia — is often associated with obesity, and has a more equal 2:1 F:M ratio versus the 10:1 ratio seen in anorexia and bulimia. Presentations that don't cleanly fit these criteria (e.g., a near-normal-BMI restriction-driven pattern) may be diagnosed as an unspecified/atypical feeding or eating disorder. BMI is the fastest way to narrow the eating-disorder differential, and identifying the driving behavior (ongoing weight loss vs. correcting a binge vs. no correction) is the key discriminator.

🧠
Memory hook · BMI first, behavior secondLow BMI (<18.5) → anorexia. Normal/high BMI → is there compensation? Yes → bulimia, no → binge eating disorder. Anorexia severity is graded by BMI; bulimia severity by compensations per week.

Pulled from: Eating Disorders

SpecifierDefinition
Restricting typeRestriction of intake or use of exercise, without binge-eating or purging, in the past 3 months.
Binge-eating/purging typeSome binge-eating and/or purging behavior present in the past 3 months.
Partial remissionCriteria previously met; symptoms improved for a shorter recent period (roughly <1 year, as a general DSM pattern).
Full remissionSymptoms improved and sustained long enough (roughly >1 year) that relapse risk is considered lower.

Q — Case Revisited (Bulimia Variant): Same opening presentation, but vitals now show BP 110/60, Pulse 60, BMI 24. She binges on a half-gallon of ice cream weekly (or more) after a full meal, feels out of control during the episode, and afterward sprints ½ mile 4 times per week. Diagnosis?

Answer

Bulimia Nervosa, Moderate. BMI 24 is normal-to-high, which excludes anorexia. The weekly ice-cream episodes with a subjective loss of control meet binge-eating criteria, and the compensatory exercise (sprinting) occurring 4×/week places this in the moderate specifier range (4–7 compensatory behaviors/week).

FeatureAnorexia NervosaBulimia NervosaBinge Eating Disorder
F:M ratio10:110:12:1
Typical onset12–14, and again ~18Often after 18, into 20sNot specified in lecture
Typical BMILow (defines severity)Normal to highOften associated with obesity risk factors
Core behaviorRestriction ± binge/purgeBinge → compensatory behaviorBinge, no compensatory behavior
MortalityHighest of all psychiatric disordersHigh, but lower than anorexiaNot specified in lecture
First-line treatmentMedical stabilization, then CBTCBT (+ interpersonal therapy, Maudsley model, DBT)CBT, interpersonal therapy, DBT
Medication noteNone FDA-approved; appetite stimulants used off-labelSSRI/SNRI; avoid bupropion & lithiumVyvanse (FDA-approved), sertraline, topiramate
📉

Anorexia — Restrict to Lose

Driving factor is ongoing weight loss. Expect a low-to-very-low BMI. Core behavior is restriction, sometimes layered with binge/purge episodes — but the goal underneath is always further weight loss.

  • BMI: low (specifiers are BMI-defined)
  • Self-view: "I am overweight," despite objective evidence otherwise
🔁

Bulimia — Binge, Then Correct

Driving factor is avoiding weight gain after a binge episode. Expect a normal-to-high BMI. Core behavior is binge → compensate, in a repeating cycle.

  • BMI: normal to elevated
  • Self-worth tied to body shape/weight, without the same degree of "I am overweight" distortion seen in anorexia

Bulimia Nervosa

Epidemiology

  • F:M ratio 10:1 (same as anorexia)
  • Onset typically later than anorexia — often not diagnosed before 18, sometimes not until the 20s
  • High mortality, but lower than anorexia
  • Risk factors: history of physical/sexual abuse, family connection to eating disorders

Diagnostic Criteria

  • Recurring episodes of binge eating
  • Recurrent inappropriate compensatory behaviors to prevent weight gain (laxatives, enemas, other meds, fasting, exercise, vomiting)
  • Occurring ≥1×/week for 3 months
  • Self-worth heavily tied to body shape and weight
  • Cannot be a presentation better explained exclusively by Anorexia — anorexia must be excluded first

Binge Eating Disorder

Epidemiology

  • Prevalence assessed as a 12-month prevalence rate (measurement window, per lecture)
  • F:M ratio 2:1 — notably more equal than anorexia/bulimia's 10:1
  • Medical associations: Prader-Willi syndrome (chromosome 15 deletion), Kluver-Bucy syndrome (bilateral temporal lobe lesions)
  • Risk factors: childhood obesity, weight-based bullying

Diagnostic Criteria

Recurring episodes of binge eating, with specified associated symptoms:

  • Eating rapidly
  • Eating past the point of fullness
  • Embarrassment around eating
  • Feelings of depression, disgust, or guilt afterward
  • Eating until uncomfortably full
🔎 The Key Differentiator from Bulimia

BED's criteria list has no requirement for compensatory behavior — no purging, fasting, or excessive exercise afterward. This is exactly what separates it from Bulimia, whose diagnosis specifically requires recurrent inappropriate compensatory behaviors.

🧩 "Unspecified" Eating Disorder

Real presentations don't always fit neatly. A person might show a clear anorexia-pattern (restriction, fear of weight gain, body image distortion) at a BMI of 19 — technically above the anorexia cutoff — or have a binge/purge pattern where it's unclear if the driving factor is more anorexia-like or bulimia-like. Clinically, these get labeled an unspecified feeding/eating disorder rather than forced into a diagnosis that doesn't fully fit.

LO 009Psychotherapy & Theory✓ In your notes

Be able to identify psychotherapeutic modalities of choice indicated by patient presentations; provide rationale for populations best suited for CBT, CBT-P, EMDR, DBT, and IPT

Answer

CBT teaches skills to identify and change unhelpful thoughts and behaviors via a thoughts-behaviors-emotions triangle, and is broadly indicated — it's the exam default for depression, is used across the eating disorders (anorexia, bulimia, BED), and is the mainstay for personality disorders other than borderline. DBT, created by Marsha Linehan around four modules (emotion regulation, mindfulness, distress tolerance, interpersonal effectiveness), is specifically indicated for borderline personality disorder — the rule of thumb is to choose DBT over CBT whenever BPD is the presentation and DBT is an answer choice. IPT is a structured, time-limited therapy for patients whose primary problem is current interpersonal relationships and communication, and is also used as an alternative in bulimia and BED. EMDR is trauma-focused, indicated when a traumatic fight-or-flight response has become misattributed to non-threatening reminders, using an external stimulus (classically a light bar) to reprocess the trauma. CBT-P (CBT for anorexia) specifically challenges the belief that thinness defines self-worth while behaviorally targeting restriction, such as gradually reintroducing feared foods.

🧠
Memory hook · The 10-second therapy pickerBPD → DBT · trauma → EMDR · relationship problems → IPT · acute crisis / medically ill → supportive · everything else → CBT. Dr. Smith's rule: if DBT is an answer choice and the vignette is borderline, pick DBT; otherwise CBT.

Pulled from: Personality Disorders · Introduction to Therapy · Eating Disorders

🧠
The exam shortcut: DBT (dialectical behavioral therapy) is specifically for borderline PD; CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) is the mainstay for the other 9 personality disorders. Dr. Smith's exact framing: "DBT is a form of CBT, so if the exam has DBT as an option, choose it; if not, choose CBT." In other words, DBT beats CBT as an answer choice only when the vignette is specifically about BPD — otherwise, default to CBT.

Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT)

Thoughts, behaviors, and emotions feed into each other in a loop
ApproachTeaches skills to identify and change unhelpful thoughts and/or behaviors, which then shifts emotion. Any corner of the triangle can be the entry point.
Types / subtypesNumerous adaptations targeting specific symptoms — CBT-P (psychosis), CBT-I (insomnia), CBT for eating disorders, and more.
Worth knowingDepression example: low energy/interest makes it hard to get out of bed → forcing the behavior (get up, shower, walk the dog) can itself shift the thoughts and emotions, even before "feeling better" arrives on its own.

Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) ⭐ HY

Created by Marsha Linehan, PhD — for borderline personality disorder
StructureA skills-based, manualized treatment built around 4 modules: emotion regulation, mindfulness, distress tolerance, and interpersonal effectiveness.
OriginLinehan developed DBT partly from her own lived experience with BPD — she has spoken publicly (including in a well-known New York Times profile) about how the treatment reflects what helped her.
Also used forAdapted well beyond BPD to many other conditions, but the BPD connection is the one to remember for exams.

Interpersonal Therapy (IPT)

Focused squarely on relationships
ApproachA structured, time-limited therapy focused on improving current interpersonal relationships and communication skills — less exploratory than psychodynamic work, more here-and-now than CBT's focus on thought content.
Worth knowingDistinct from the humanistic modalities above — IPT is manualized and diagnosis-focused (often depression), not a general relational philosophy.

EMDR (Eye Movement Desensitization & Reprocessing)

Trauma-focused; closely related to systematic desensitization
ConceptTrauma creates a fight-or-flight response that becomes misattributed to non-threatening reminders of the traumatic event. EMDR uses an external stimulus (classically a light bar moving back and forth) while the patient discusses the traumatic material, pausing before it becomes unmanageable and shifting attention to a neutral stimulus — aiming to decouple the trauma from its physiologic response.
YieldTesting on EMDR has increased somewhat in recent years, though it's still not top-tier yield.

CBT for Anorexia ⭐ HY

A tie-in from the eating disorders lecture
Cognitive focusChallenges the thought that thinness defines the person's whole worth/identity, and works on the cognitive distortions tying self-worth to weight.
Behavioral focusTargets the restriction itself — e.g., gradually reintroducing higher-fat, higher-calorie foods that had been mentally recategorized as "unhealthy," after medical stabilization.
Question 12
A 24-year-old woman meets full criteria for borderline personality disorder, including recurrent self-harm and highly unstable relationships. Which specific psychotherapy modality is most appropriate as first-line treatment?
A. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT)
B. Dialectical behavioral therapy (DBT)
C. Psychoanalysis
D. Exposure and response prevention
Answer: B. DBT was developed specifically for BPD and is the only personality disorder with a dedicated first-line psychotherapy (Section 13). Remember the exam shortcut: DBT is technically a form of CBT — "if DBT is an option, choose it; if not, choose CBT" — but when both are listed and the vignette is BPD, DBT is the more specific and correct answer.
DiagnosisWhat the evidence shows
DepressionCBT is the usual go-to on exams; psychoanalytic approaches are also used. If a question doesn't name a specific evidence-based match, CBT is a reasonable default guess given how broadly it's now indicated.
AnxietyLittle difference found between CBT and psychodynamic treatment.
Alcohol use disorderCBT, motivational interviewing, 12-step programs, and social skills training are all efficacious — no single winner.
Personality disorders (esp. BPD)Most personality disorders lack strong evidence-based treatments; BPD is the best-studied. Some research favors transference-focused therapy over DBT specifically for impulsivity, anger, aggressiveness, and irritability — though DBT remains the most widely taught/tested BPD treatment.

Treat medical abnormalities, reduce binge/purge frequency, treat comorbid diagnoses. Therapy is first-line — CBT primarily, with interpersonal therapy, the Maudsley model, and DBT also used.

LO 010Substance Use & Tox✓ In your notes

Be able to identify the intoxication or withdrawal toxidrome present in a patient case of substance misuse

Answer

The core organizing rule is that 'uppers' cause psychosis in intoxication while 'downers' cause psychosis in withdrawal: amphetamine intoxication produces psychosis but amphetamine withdrawal does not, whereas alcohol, benzodiazepine, and opioid withdrawal can cause psychosis (e.g., delirium tremens) while their intoxication generally does not. Opioid intoxication shows euphoria, CNS depression, decreased gag reflex, and pinpoint pupils (progressing to poisoning with respiratory depression/apnea), while opioid withdrawal is the mirror image — dilated pupils, goosebumps, lacrimation/rhinorrhea, and GI cramping/diarrhea/vomiting, described as 'the worst flu ever.' Cocaine and amphetamine intoxication both cause pupillary dilation, paranoia, and cardiovascular stimulation (cocaine also causes tactile hallucinations), while amphetamine withdrawal causes anhedonia and hypersomnolence; PCP intoxication causes belligerence, agitation, and analgesia that can mask serious injury, with its withdrawal marked by fever, tachycardia, and seizures. Alcohol withdrawal is the most dangerous of the group, following a timeline from minor symptoms to hallucinosis/seizures at 24–48 hours and delirium tremens peaking around day 2.

🧠
Memory hook · Uppers freak you ON the drug; downers freak you OFF itPsychosis with stimulant intoxication (amphetamines, cocaine) but with depressant withdrawal (alcohol/benzo/opioid — think DTs). Opioids: intox = dry & pinpoint; withdrawal = wet & wide (tearing, runny nose, diarrhea, dilated pupils — 'worst flu ever', miserable but not lethal).

Pulled from: Psychotic Disorders & Antipsychotic Pharmacology · Addiction & Non-Clinical Drug Use · Anxiety, OCD & Trauma-Related Disorders

🧠
One-line summary for substance-induced psychosis: uppers in intoxication, or downers in withdrawal. Amphetamine intoxication → psychosis; amphetamine withdrawal → no psychosis. Alcohol/benzo/opiate withdrawal (downers) → psychosis (e.g., delirium tremens); their intoxication generally doesn't. Apply it in both directions on an exam question.

Pinpoint pupils = intoxication; dilated pupils = withdrawal

Track marks — a physical exam clue to IV opioid use

🧠 Memory Hook — Opiate Withdrawal, Head to Toe

A patient described it as "the worst flu you've ever had" — and that head-to-toe picture is the mnemonic: goosebumps/chills, lacrimation & rhinorrhea, dilated pupils (mydriasis — opposite of intoxication's pinpoint pupils), GI cramping/diarrhea/vomiting, muscle aches, tachycardia. None of it is life-threatening the way depressant withdrawal is — but the fear of going through it again is a major driver of return to use.

😌

Intoxication

  • Euphoria
  • Light-to-moderate CNS depression
  • Decreased gag reflex
  • Pupillary constriction (pinpoint)
☠️

Poisoning

  • Altered level of consciousness
  • Decreased respiratory drive → apnea — this is what actually kills the patient
⚡

Cocaine Intoxication

  • Impaired judgment, pupillary dilation
  • Hallucinations — including tactile ("bugs crawling")
  • Paranoid ideation; angina; sudden cardiac death (Na-channel block + NE flood)
😔

Cocaine Withdrawal

  • Hypersomnolence, bradycardia, malaise
  • Severe psychological craving
  • Depression, suicidal ideation
⚡

Intoxication

Euphoria, grandiosity, pupillary dilation, prolonged wakefulness/attention, hypertension, tachycardia, anorexia, paranoia, fever.

😔

Withdrawal

Anhedonia, increased appetite, hypersomnolence, and — a distinctive one — existential crisis.

😡

Intoxication

Belligerence, impulsivity, psychomotor agitation, homicidality, psychosis, delirium. Significant analgesia means patients can sustain severe, unnoticed injuries while acting impulsively.

🌀

Withdrawal

Fever, tachycardia, seizures, depression, anxiety, irritability, restlessness, disturbed thought/sleep.

⚠️ Alcohol Withdrawal Is the Most Dangerous Withdrawal in This Lecture

Relative to opioids, stimulants, or nicotine, alcohol withdrawal carries the highest risk of death — via seizures and delirium tremens. This is why alcohol detox is managed so much more aggressively than, say, opioid withdrawal.

🍷

Intoxication

  • Emotional lability, slurred speech
  • Ataxia, blackouts, coma
🚨

Withdrawal

  • Anxiety, tremor, insomnia
  • Severe: autonomic hyperactivity, seizures, delirium tremens
🧠
Withdrawal from a downer produces upper effects — and vice versa (this exact logic reappears in the antipsychotic pharmacology unit). Benzo withdrawal syndrome: anxiety, insomnia, tremulousness, nausea/vomiting, transient hallucinations, and — critically — seizures are possible with acute withdrawal, so taper slowly. Adverse cognitive effects of ongoing use include difficulty focusing attention, memory impairment, and confusion.

LO 011Psychotherapy & Theory◐ Partly covered

Be able to identify therapeutic modalities best suited to employ with a patient based on a patient presentation (focus on EMDR, CBT, Gestalt, supportive and psychodynamic)

Answer

EMDR is trauma-focused and closely related to systematic desensitization: it targets a fight-or-flight response that has become misattributed to non-threatening trauma reminders, using an external stimulus (classically a light bar) to reprocess the memory. CBT works the thoughts-behaviors-emotions triangle, teaching patients skills to identify and change unhelpful thoughts and/or behaviors, with any corner of the triangle serving as an entry point. Supportive therapy — listening, encouragement, and stability, sometimes dismissively called a 'professional friend' — best fits patients in acute crises or with acute medical comorbidity. Psychodynamic therapy, founded by Freud, uses free association, dream analysis, and transference, in contrast to Humanistic therapy, founded by Carl Rogers, which uses unconditional positive regard and reflection.

🧠
Memory hook · The 10-second therapy pickerBPD → DBT · trauma → EMDR · relationship problems → IPT · acute crisis / medically ill → supportive · everything else → CBT. Dr. Smith's rule: if DBT is an answer choice and the vignette is borderline, pick DBT; otherwise CBT.
◐
Missing from your notesGestalt therapy remains absent from every source, including the new child psychiatry and neuroanatomy lectures, neither of which describes psychotherapy modalities in this way.

Pulled from: Introduction to Therapy · Introduction & History of Psychiatry · Anxiety, OCD & Trauma-Related Disorders · Personality Disorders

EMDR (Eye Movement Desensitization & Reprocessing)

Trauma-focused; closely related to systematic desensitization
ConceptTrauma creates a fight-or-flight response that becomes misattributed to non-threatening reminders of the traumatic event. EMDR uses an external stimulus (classically a light bar moving back and forth) while the patient discusses the traumatic material, pausing before it becomes unmanageable and shifting attention to a neutral stimulus — aiming to decouple the trauma from its physiologic response.
YieldTesting on EMDR has increased somewhat in recent years, though it's still not top-tier yield.

Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT)

Thoughts, behaviors, and emotions feed into each other in a loop
ApproachTeaches skills to identify and change unhelpful thoughts and/or behaviors, which then shifts emotion. Any corner of the triangle can be the entry point.
Types / subtypesNumerous adaptations targeting specific symptoms — CBT-P (psychosis), CBT-I (insomnia), CBT for eating disorders, and more.
Worth knowingDepression example: low energy/interest makes it hard to get out of bed → forcing the behavior (get up, shower, walk the dog) can itself shift the thoughts and emotions, even before "feeling better" arrives on its own.

Supportive Therapy

"You're going to feel better"
ApproachListening, encouragement, and stability — filling in a supportive presence that may be missing elsewhere in the patient's life. Sometimes called (a bit dismissively) a "professional friend."
Best fitAcute crises, medical comorbidity, or acute stressors — this is essentially what's delivered on psychiatric consult-liaison services.
LimitationDoesn't always account for the limits of a relationship built mainly on support.

Humanistic

Founded by Carl Rogers
TechniquesUnconditional positive regard; reflection.

Psychodynamic

Founded by Sigmund Freud
TechniquesFree association; dream analysis; transference.

Biological

Somatic / medication-based interventions
ModalitiesTranquilizers, antipsychotics, lithium, antidepressants, psychosurgery, ECT.

Cognitive

Founded by Aaron Beck & Albert Ellis
BranchesBeck's Cognitive Therapy; Ellis's Rational Emotive Therapy (RET).

Behavioral

Founded by B. F. Skinner
TechniquesSystematic desensitization; behavior modification; aversion therapy; exposure; flooding.

Other

Modality-agnostic formats
ExamplesGroup & family therapy; Gestalt therapy.
🧠
Founder pairs worth locking in: Rogers → Humanistic. Freud → Psychodynamic. Beck & Ellis → Cognitive. Skinner → Behavioral. If a board question names a founder, work backward to the family, then to the matching technique list.

By the mid-20th century there were dozens of therapy "brands." Research eventually showed that what mattered most wasn't necessarily which theory a therapist used, but whether the therapist believed in it and the patient accepted it as something that could help them — plus the strength of the relationship carrying the work (see Efficacy below). Here are the modalities most likely to come up clinically and on exams.

Humanistic (modern)

"How the person interacts in relationships"
Core ideaDysfunctional relationships and environment drive distress; therapy helps the person understand themselves in relation to others and the world.
Key figuresCarl Rogers (person-centered — unconditional positive regard, reflection); Fritz Perls (Gestalt — intense role-play to safely express relational dynamics); Viktor Frankl (existential approaches). This wave grew after World War II, as the field leaned back toward meaning and away from pure science for a time.
LimitationThe approach can be shaped by the very relational/environmental patterns it's trying to correct.
Exploration vs. skill-building: Psychoanalytic/psychodynamic work is fundamentally exploratory — there's no fixed roadmap, which is part of why it tends to run longer. Behavioral, cognitive, and CBT-family therapies are much more skills-based, often with an established goal and a defined path to get there — some (like CBT and DBT) are so manualized that nearly every session is scripted.

Remove the etiologic stressor where possible, plus CBT or psychodynamic psychotherapy; supportive psychotherapy also helps. Focus is on improving coping skills, strengthening defense mechanisms, or changing how the person relates to the stressor. Medication can help adjunctively (anxiety, secondary insomnia, depressive symptoms).

🧠
The exam shortcut: DBT (dialectical behavioral therapy) is specifically for borderline PD; CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) is the mainstay for the other 9 personality disorders. Dr. Smith's exact framing: "DBT is a form of CBT, so if the exam has DBT as an option, choose it; if not, choose CBT." In other words, DBT beats CBT as an answer choice only when the vignette is specifically about BPD — otherwise, default to CBT.
LO 012Psychotherapy & Theory✓ In your notes

Be able to identify therapeutic modalities indicated by patient presentations

Answer

Presentation-driven modality selection follows the same rules across the therapy lecture: DBT is chosen specifically for borderline personality disorder (four modules — emotion regulation, mindfulness, distress tolerance, interpersonal effectiveness), while CBT is the default for the other personality disorders and a reasonable go-to for depression generally. IPT suits patients whose central issue is current interpersonal relationships and communication, and EMDR is chosen for trauma-focused presentations where reminders of the trauma trigger a misattributed fight-or-flight response. Supportive therapy is best for acute crises or acute medical comorbidity, where listening, encouragement, and stability are the goal. For acute stress disorder and adjustment disorders, CBT or psychodynamic psychotherapy plus supportive psychotherapy is used to build coping skills and strengthen defense mechanisms.

🧠
Memory hook · The 10-second therapy pickerBPD → DBT · trauma → EMDR · relationship problems → IPT · acute crisis / medically ill → supportive · everything else → CBT. Dr. Smith's rule: if DBT is an answer choice and the vignette is borderline, pick DBT; otherwise CBT.

Pulled from: Personality Disorders · Introduction to Therapy · Anxiety, OCD & Trauma-Related Disorders

🧠
The exam shortcut: DBT (dialectical behavioral therapy) is specifically for borderline PD; CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) is the mainstay for the other 9 personality disorders. Dr. Smith's exact framing: "DBT is a form of CBT, so if the exam has DBT as an option, choose it; if not, choose CBT." In other words, DBT beats CBT as an answer choice only when the vignette is specifically about BPD — otherwise, default to CBT.

Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) ⭐ HY

Created by Marsha Linehan, PhD — for borderline personality disorder
StructureA skills-based, manualized treatment built around 4 modules: emotion regulation, mindfulness, distress tolerance, and interpersonal effectiveness.
OriginLinehan developed DBT partly from her own lived experience with BPD — she has spoken publicly (including in a well-known New York Times profile) about how the treatment reflects what helped her.
Also used forAdapted well beyond BPD to many other conditions, but the BPD connection is the one to remember for exams.

Interpersonal Therapy (IPT)

Focused squarely on relationships
ApproachA structured, time-limited therapy focused on improving current interpersonal relationships and communication skills — less exploratory than psychodynamic work, more here-and-now than CBT's focus on thought content.
Worth knowingDistinct from the humanistic modalities above — IPT is manualized and diagnosis-focused (often depression), not a general relational philosophy.

EMDR (Eye Movement Desensitization & Reprocessing)

Trauma-focused; closely related to systematic desensitization
ConceptTrauma creates a fight-or-flight response that becomes misattributed to non-threatening reminders of the traumatic event. EMDR uses an external stimulus (classically a light bar moving back and forth) while the patient discusses the traumatic material, pausing before it becomes unmanageable and shifting attention to a neutral stimulus — aiming to decouple the trauma from its physiologic response.
YieldTesting on EMDR has increased somewhat in recent years, though it's still not top-tier yield.

Supportive Therapy

"You're going to feel better"
ApproachListening, encouragement, and stability — filling in a supportive presence that may be missing elsewhere in the patient's life. Sometimes called (a bit dismissively) a "professional friend."
Best fitAcute crises, medical comorbidity, or acute stressors — this is essentially what's delivered on psychiatric consult-liaison services.
LimitationDoesn't always account for the limits of a relationship built mainly on support.

Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT)

Thoughts, behaviors, and emotions feed into each other in a loop
ApproachTeaches skills to identify and change unhelpful thoughts and/or behaviors, which then shifts emotion. Any corner of the triangle can be the entry point.
Types / subtypesNumerous adaptations targeting specific symptoms — CBT-P (psychosis), CBT-I (insomnia), CBT for eating disorders, and more.
Worth knowingDepression example: low energy/interest makes it hard to get out of bed → forcing the behavior (get up, shower, walk the dog) can itself shift the thoughts and emotions, even before "feeling better" arrives on its own.

Remove the etiologic stressor where possible, plus CBT or psychodynamic psychotherapy; supportive psychotherapy also helps. Focus is on improving coping skills, strengthening defense mechanisms, or changing how the person relates to the stressor. Medication can help adjunctively (anxiety, secondary insomnia, depressive symptoms).

LO 013Substance Use & Tox◐ Partly covered

Characterize the adverse effects of commonly administered antidotes to poisonings

Answer

Naloxone, a competitive mu-opioid receptor antagonist used to reverse opioid overdose, rapidly restores respiratory drive without requiring ventilation, but a key adverse effect is that it can precipitate acute opioid withdrawal. For serotonin syndrome, benzodiazepines and supportive care are first-line, with cyproheptadine, a 5-HT2 receptor antagonist, added if there is no improvement. Flumazenil is used as the antidote for benzodiazepine and Z-drug (zolpidem/eszopiclone/zaleplon) overdose, though its own adverse effects are not detailed in available sources.

🧠
Memory hook · Narcan wears off before the opioid doesNaloxone's half-life is shorter than most opioids → redose or watch for re-sedation. Its main adverse effect: it precipitates acute withdrawal. Serotonin syndrome antidote ladder: benzos + supportive care → add cyproheptadine (5-HT2 antagonist) if no improvement.
◐
Missing from your notesN-acetylcysteine, atropine/pralidoxime, and physostigmine (and their adverse effects), and flumazenil's own adverse effects, are still not covered; the new child psychiatry and neuroanatomy lectures do not address toxicology antidotes.

Pulled from: Addiction & Non-Clinical Drug Use · Mood Disorders · Psychiatry Key Drug List 2026

Naloxone ⭐ HY

IV, IM, intranasal spray (auto-injectors discontinued)

μ-opioid receptor competitive antagonist — rapidly reverses opioid activity, restoring respiratory drive without requiring ventilation. Adverse effects: precipitates withdrawal (a real complication, not just a side effect — it should be dosed to restore respiratory drive, not to "wake the patient up" or as punishment); cardiac arrhythmia with rapid IV push; rare flash pulmonary edema from catecholamine-surge-driven adrenergic crisis, which rapid ventilation alongside naloxone can worsen.

🩺 Treatment

Benzodiazepines and supportive care first; cyproheptadine (a 5-HT2 receptor antagonist) if there's no improvement. Prevention: avoid combining serotonergic drugs and observe a proper washout period between them (2 weeks after stopping an MAOI before starting another serotonergic drug).

BZ1-selective — the "Z-drugs"
Zolpidem (Ambien) · esZopiclone (Lunesta) · Zaleplon (Sonata)
  • Short-term insomnia: rapid onset, little morning hangover; tolerance develops → use intermittently. Abuse potential at high doses.
  • Benzo-like SEs incl. rare anterograde amnesia, plus the famous ones: parasomnias — sleep-eating, sleep-sex, sleep-DRIVING (zolpidem especially; real crashes), daytime dream-like states.
  • OD antidote: flumazenil (same receptor).
benzos↑FREQUENCY Cl⁻ opening; acute anxiety/panic/status (lorazepam)/ETOH detox (chlordiazepoxide); flumazenil antidote; LOT (lorazepam-oxazepam-temazepam) in liver disease; alprazolam=panic/abuse, midazolam=procedures
Z-drugsBZ1: sleep only; parasomnias (sleep-driving); flumazenil works
barbiturates↑DURATION; resp depression OD; porphyria CI; CYP inducers; thiopental=ECT
buspirone5-HT1A partial agonist; no sedation/addiction; 4–6 wk (useless acutely); 60 mg OK
othershydroxyzine=antihistamine PRN no abuse · ramelteon=melatonin-R · suvorexant=orexin antagonist
LO 014Somatoform, Dissoc. & Sexual✓ In your notes

Construct a differential diagnosis listing of the somatoform disorders

Answer

The somatoform differential starts by asking whether symptom production is unconscious (somatic symptom disorder, illness anxiety disorder, conversion disorder) or consciously produced (malingering, factitious disorder). Somatic symptom disorder presents as multi-system complaints lasting months to years with excessive/persistent thoughts about the symptoms; illness anxiety disorder is fear of serious illness despite reassurance with minimal actual somatic symptoms; conversion disorder presents with neurological-type symptoms (e.g., sudden blindness or paralysis) with a normal workup, classically with 'la belle indifférence' — an odd lack of concern about the deficit. Among consciously produced conditions, malingering is driven by external secondary gain (financial compensation, avoiding work or legal consequences, obtaining drugs) and is not itself a psychiatric diagnosis, whereas factitious disorder is driven by internal/primary gain — wanting the sick role. Vignette clues pointing to the somatoform spectrum include a thick chart, multiple specialists already seen, normal or inconsistent workups, and dramatic or peculiar complaints out of proportion to any organic disease found.

🧠
Memory hook · The three-branch deception treeSymptoms unconscious → somatoform spectrum. Conscious, to live the sick role (internal gain) → factitious. Conscious, for money/court/drugs (external gain) → malingering (not a psychiatric diagnosis). Vignette tells: thick chart, many specialists, normal workups.

Pulled from: Sexual, Somatoform & Dissociative Disorders

Master split
Unconscious production (somatic symptom, illness anxiety, conversion) vs. conscious production (malingering, factitious).
Somatic symptom disorder
Multi-system complaints, months-years, excessive/persistent thoughts about symptoms.
Illness anxiety disorder
Fear of serious illness despite reassurance; minimal actual symptoms.
Conversion disorder
Sudden sensory/motor loss after a stressor; la belle indifférence; F > M, young.
Malingering
External gain; complaints STOP once gain achieved; avoids invasive workups.
Factitious disorder
Sick role = primary gain; WELCOMES invasive procedures; Munchausen = chronic physical form.
Munchausen by proxy
Illness caused in a child/elder by caregiver; mandatory reporting, = abuse.
DID criteria
≥2 distinct personality states + recurrent amnesia gaps; early childhood trauma.
DID alter patterns
Mutually aware / mutually unaware / one aware, not reciprocated.
DID vs. PTSD
Ongoing field debate: is DID distinct, or severe/chronic PTSD with dissociative features?
Dissociative amnesia
Localized/selective vs. generalized; info not permanently lost, just unretrievable.
Dissociative fugue
A SPECIFIER of dissociative amnesia (not separate dx) — purposeful travel/wandering + identity amnesia.
Amnesia/fugue course
Usually adult-onset, rapid onset/resolution, F > M; most recover spontaneously.
Depersonalization
Altered perception of SELF (detachment, out-of-body).
Derealization
Altered perception of ENVIRONMENT (foggy, dreamlike, unreal).
Depersonalization/derealization key
Reality testing INTACT — this is what separates it from psychosis.
Sexual dysfunction classification
DSM-5 lists alphabetically (no agreed sexual-response model) — replaced Masters & Johnson's 4-stage cycle.
Psychogenic vs. physiologic ED
Preserved nocturnal/morning erections → psychogenic. Absent → physiologic.
Paraphilia vs. paraphilic disorder
Paraphilia = atypical interest (ascertained). Disorder = + distress/impairment/harm to others (diagnosed).
8 named paraphilic disorders
Fetishistic, transvestic, pedohebephilic, voyeuristic, exhibitionistic, frotteuristic, sexual sadism, sexual masochism.
Non-consent paraphilias
Voyeuristic, exhibitionistic, frotteuristic — inherently involve a non-consenting party.
Paraphilia treatment
Incorporation therapy, psychotherapy, orgasmic reconditioning, drug therapy (antiandrogens/SSRIs).
Hypersexuality red flags
Brain injury, Klüver-Bucy, Kleine-Levin, dopamine agonists (mesolimbic overactivity) — rule out before assuming psychiatric.
🧠
One clean decision tree, memorized: (1) Is there a conscious attempt to deceive? If no → somatoform disorder (somatic symptom, illness anxiety, or conversion, depending on presentation). If yes → (2) is the goal psychological/internal (wanting to be sick, cared for, the center of medical attention) or external (money, work avoidance, drugs, legal advantage)? Internal/psychological → factitious disorder. External → malingering.
Unconsciously-ProducedConsciously-Produced
DisordersSomatic symptom disorder, illness anxiety disorder, conversion disorderMalingering, factitious disorder
IntentSymptoms and illness motivation are NOT intentionally producedIntentional production or feigning of symptoms
EpidemiologyMore common in womenVaries by specific disorder (Section 04)

Somatic Symptom Disorder

PictureA variety of complaints across one or more organ systems, lasting months to years, associated with excessive and persistent thoughts about the symptoms. May genuinely co-occur with real medical conditions — the psychological preoccupation is disproportionate to whatever organic pathology is (or isn't) present.
VideoNone available for this one per the handout.

Illness Anxiety Disorder (Hypochondriasis)

PicturePreoccupation with and fear of having a serious medical illness, despite medical evidence and reassurance to the contrary. Unlike somatic symptom disorder, the somatic symptoms themselves may be minimal or absent — it's the fear/preoccupation that's the disorder.
▶ Illness anxiety disorder case 🔒 UNE

Conversion Disorder

Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder
PictureSudden loss of sensory or motor function — paralysis, blindness, mutism — often following an acute stressor. Classically more common in females, young adults, and adolescents.
Signature findingLa belle indifférence — the patient is aware of the symptom but shows a striking, disproportionate lack of concern about it.
▶ Conversion disorder case 🔒 UNE
📌
La belle indifférence, translated: "the beautiful indifference." It's the single most quotable, most testable finding in this section — a patient who has just gone functionally blind or paralyzed, but who seems almost unbothered by it. Note it's a classic association, not a required or universal criterion for conversion disorder — plenty of real patients with conversion disorder are appropriately distressed.

Malingering

Not itself a psychiatric diagnosis — a V-code / behavior
MotivationDriven by external incentives — the classic "secondary gain": financial compensation, disability payments, avoiding work, avoiding legal consequences, obtaining drugs.
PatternPoor compliance with treatment, follow-up, or diagnostic testing (since genuine treatment isn't actually the goal). The complaints cease once the gain is achieved — a key differentiator from factitious disorder.
▶ Malingering case 🔒 UNE

Factitious Disorder

A true psychiatric diagnosis
MotivationDriven by a desire to assume the sick role and receive medical attention itself — this is primary gain, not an external reward.
Munchausen syndromeThe chronic form, predominantly physical signs/symptoms — a history of multiple hospital stays and a striking willingness to undergo invasive procedures.
Munchausen syndrome by proxyIllness is caused in a child or elderly dependent by their caregiver, so the caregiver can occupy the sick role by proxy. This is a form of child/elder abuse and must be reported to authorities.
▶ "Rebecca" — factitious disorder case 🔒 UNE
🩺
Reading this pattern as a vignette: a patient with a thick chart, a long list of specialists already seen, normal or inconsistent workups, and a symptom picture that doesn't fit any single organic disease process is the classic setup for a somatoform-spectrum diagnosis. The specific disorder then comes down to what kind of complaint dominates (diffuse multi-system complaints → somatic symptom disorder; fear of illness despite reassurance → illness anxiety disorder; a discrete neurological deficit → conversion disorder).
LO 015Substance Use & Tox✓ In your notes

Describe and appropriately apply the pharmacologic and non-pharmacologic management of substance use disorder to a clinical scenario

Answer

Management of substance use disorder combines pharmacologic and non-pharmacologic approaches, with detoxification strategy (cold turkey, taper, or MOUD) tailored to the substance and how dangerous its withdrawal is. Pharmacologically, alcohol use disorder is treated with naltrexone (craving management, can start while still drinking) and acamprosate (NMDA antagonist/GABA-A agonist) for relapse prevention, long-acting benzodiazepines (diazepam, lorazepam, chlordiazepoxide) for detox, and disulfiram as a one-step aversive block; opioid use disorder uses MOUD targeting the mu-opioid receptor, either agonist-based (methadone, buprenorphine) or antagonist-based (naltrexone). Non-pharmacologically, harm reduction (any reduction in use is a genuine win), abstinence, and psychosocial interventions such as CBT and mutual support programs (AA/NA) are used. Pharmacology alone has little effect on long-term outcomes, so it should be paired with psychosocial treatment for the best result in a given clinical scenario.

🧠
Memory hook · N-A-D for alcohol use disorderNaltrexone kills the Need (craving — can start while still drinking) · Acamprosate keeps Abstinence (NMDA antagonist + GABA-A agonist, 3×/day) · Disulfiram is the Deterrent (blocks aldehyde dehydrogenase → instant hangover).

Pulled from: Addiction & Non-Clinical Drug Use

🩹

Detoxification

Cold turkey vs. taper vs. MOUD — the approach depends entirely on which substance and how dangerous its withdrawal is.

🧩

Treatment

Pharmacologic — aversive therapies (block desired effects/cause hangover), replacement therapy (manage dysphoria/reward), treat comorbid psychiatric disease. Psychosocial — CBT, mutual support (AA/NA), moderation management as early intervention.

  • Harm reduction — any reduction in use, or a patient simply returning after being told you're concerned, is a genuine win.
  • Abstinence — considered by some literature to itself be a behavioral intervention; not functional for every SUD.
  • Psychosocial — CBT, mutual support programs (note: some are faith-based and may not fit every patient).

Naltrexone

Oral or long-acting injectable

Can start while the patient is still drinking (unlike opioid use disorder). Avoid in patients taking opioids for pain or with hepatic insufficiency. Used mainly for craving management.

Acamprosate

Oral, 3×/day

NMDA-receptor antagonist + GABA-A agonist — mirrors alcohol's own mechanism. Effective, but 3×/day dosing hurts adherence.

Disulfiram ⭐ HY — Aversive Therapy

Aldehyde dehydrogenase inhibitor

Blocks acetaldehyde → acetate, letting acetaldehyde bioaccumulate → intense hangover (flushing, headache, nausea, vomiting, weakness, orthostatic hypotension, respiratory difficulty) if alcohol is consumed. This is negative reinforcement by design — requires informed patient buy-in, since the reaction itself can warrant an ED visit. Rare AE: hepatitis, optic neuritis, peripheral neuropathy.

Long-acting benzodiazepines (diazepam, lorazepam, chlordiazepoxide) are preferred — their cross-reactivity at GABA-A smooths the taper and their active metabolites give a lower chance of recurrent withdrawal or seizures. Two dosing strategies: symptom-triggered (dose only once significant symptoms appear) vs. front-loaded (proactively substitute sedation regardless of symptoms, then taper).

Disulfiram's one-step block is the entire mechanism — worth being able to draw from memory

Off-label options you should recognize but aren't held accountable for in depth: baclofen (GABA-B agonist), nalmefene (opioid antagonist), gabapentin, topiramate.

Two pharmacologic strategies, both targeting the μ-opioid receptor — agonist-based (methadone, buprenorphine) or antagonist-based (naltrexone). All are most effective paired with psychotherapy/counseling; accessibility remains a major real-world barrier (accreditation hurdles, enrollment hurdles, inconsistent insurance coverage, social stigma).

⚠️ Pharmacology Alone Is a Drop in the Bucket

Pharmacologic interventions mostly target detoxification and relief of withdrawal — they have little effect on long-term addiction or outcomes by themselves. Psychosocial interventions (CBT, mutual support programs) are what actually move outcomes, and addiction is very often a comorbid condition that complicates diagnosis in its own right.
