LO 016Assessment & MSE✓ In your notes

Discuss the Mental Status Exam and Mini Mental State Exam and be able to demonstrate the ability to administer it in the appropriate clinical setting, understanding what information is obtained in each MSE domain

Answer

The MSE is the full narrative description of a patient's mental functioning, distinct from the MMSE (a scored 0-30 cognitive screening test) and the MoCA — a very common source of confusion on exams. It is performed as part of the psychiatric SOAP note, substituting for (or supplementing) the physical exam, and forms section XI of the initial psychiatric interview, following identifying data, the various histories, and review of systems. Its components include physical appearance (dress/grooming), arousal and attention (e.g., serial sevens), and psychomotor activity, among other domains, each with example bedside tests. A key testable pitfall: the MSE itself is not a scored instrument — a numeric score out of 30 describes the MMSE (or MoCA), which is only one piece of the full MSE.

🧠
Memory hook · MSE describes; MMSE scoresThe MSE is the narrative exam (appearance, attention, thought process/content…) inside the psych SOAP note. A number out of 30 means MMSE/MoCA — a single cognitive screen, never the whole MSE. Classic exam trap.

Pulled from: Introduction & History of Psychiatry

🧩
MSE vs. MMSE vs. MoCA — a very common source of confusion:
  • MSE (Mental Status Exam): the whole written narrative described above — a full description of the patient's mental functioning.
  • MMSE (Mini-Mental State Exam): just one piece of the MSE — a scored (0–30) cognitive screening test.
  • MoCA (Montreal Cognitive Assessment): a specific type of MMSE-style instrument, testing visuospatial/executive function, naming, memory, attention, language, abstraction, delayed recall, and orientation — also scored out of 30.
ComponentWhat you're observingExample bedside tests
Physical appearancePhysical signs of illness, manner of dress, grooming—
Arousal & attentionLevel of arousal; ability to focus/sustain attentionSerial sevens
Psychomotor activityAppropriateness, focal deficits, incoordination, abnormal movementsHandshake
SpeechRate, rhythm, articulation, coherency, vocabularySentence repetition
MoodLevel of psychomotor activity, patient's self-report—
AffectFacial expression, quality, range, intensity—
Memory & other cognitive fxAbility to relate history, understand/communicate, recognize people/objects, plan & execute tasksDigit span; orientation; three objects at 5 min; demographic recall; sentence repetition; comprehension of instructions
Thought processResponding to hallucinations, overly suspicious/grandiose/guilty/bizarre presentation, coherency of historyQuestions about persecutory, referential, or grandiose ideation; proverb interpretation; similarities & differences
Thought contentInformation-related themes, suicidal/homicidal ideation, judgment—

Guiding question: Comment on the psychiatric diagnostic interview — what is the MSE and what are its parts?

Psychiatry documents in a SOAP-note structure, just like every other specialty — but with one substitution: the Mental Status Exam (MSE) is done either alongside or in place of the physical exam. It's a written description detailed enough that another clinician reading only your note can understand the patient's mental state at the time you saw them.

  1. I–IV. Identifying data, source/reliability, chief complaint, present illnessSame as any H&P.
  2. V–IX. Psychiatric, substance use, medical, family, developmental/social historyStandard background — but substance use history carries extra weight here.
  3. X. Review of systems
  4. XI. Mental Status ExaminationThe psychiatry-specific substitution for (or complement to) the physical exam.
  5. XII. Physical examination
  6. XIII–XV. Formulation, DSM-5 diagnoses, treatment planFormulation is where the biopsychosocial synthesis happens (below).
Practice Question
A colleague says a patient "scored 24 on her MSE." What's wrong with this statement?
A. Nothing — the MSE is scored out of 30, and 24 is a valid score.
B. The MSE itself isn't a scored instrument — a numeric score out of 30 describes the MMSE (or a MoCA), which is only one component of the full MSE.
C. The MSE is scored out of 100, so 24 would indicate severe impairment.
D. MSE scores only apply to inpatient settings.
Answer: B. The full MSE is a written narrative, not a single number. The 0–30 scored instruments (MMSE, MoCA) are cognitive-screening subcomponents that sometimes get colloquially (and incorrectly) referred to as "the MSE."
LO 017Mood & Mood Stabilizers✓ In your notes

Given a clinical vignette, differentiate mood disorders based upon clinical presentations, DSM criteria, severity and functioning and psychotic features

Answer

Mood disorders are built from combinations of episodes: MDD requires 1+ major depressive episode (5+ of SIG E CAPS for 2+ weeks); persistent depressive disorder is milder depression lasting 2+ years; Bipolar I requires 1+ manic episode (a depressive episode is not even required); Bipolar II requires 1+ hypomanic episode plus 1+ major depressive episode and never a manic episode. Severity/functioning discriminates manic (7+ days, or any duration if hospitalized or psychotic, with significant impairment) from hypomanic (4+ days, no psychosis, no marked impairment). Psychotic features are allowed only during the mood episode itself — in an MDE with psychotic features, psychosis appears only during the depressive episode, and in Bipolar I it can appear during the manic or depressive episode but never during euthymia. Schizoaffective disorder is the key differential once psychosis and mood symptoms co-occur: it requires at least a 2-week period of psychosis with an absence of mood symptoms, which never happens in a mood disorder with psychotic features (where psychosis is confined entirely to the mood episode).

🧠
Memory hook · Mania is a 7-day week; hypomania a 4-day workweekDIGFAST ≥3 (4 if only irritable): ≥7 days OR hospital OR psychosis + impairment = mania → Bipolar I (depression not required). ≥4 days, fully functional, no psychosis = hypomania; + ≥1 MDE and never mania = Bipolar II. One manic episode ever → converts to Bipolar I forever.

Pulled from: Mood Disorders · Psychotic Disorders & Antipsychotic Pharmacology

DisorderBuilt from
Major Depressive Disorder1+ major depressive episode
Persistent Depressive DisorderDepression "light" but long — mild depressive symptoms ≥2 years
Bipolar I1+ manic episode, +/− a depressive episode (depression isn't even required!)
Bipolar II1+ hypomanic episode + 1+ major depressive episode (never a full manic episode)
Cyclothymic disorderHypomania "light" + depression "light," fluctuating for ≥2 years, never meeting full episode criteria
EpisodeDefinitionDuration
Manic episode3+ of DIGFAST (4+ if mood is only irritable)≥1 week, OR any duration if hospitalization required
Hypomanic episodeSame symptom list as mania, less severe — no psychosis, doesn't wreck functioning≥4 consecutive days
Major depressive episode (MDE)5+ of SIG E CAPS — must include depressed mood or anhedonia≥2 weeks

Axis shows labeled thresholds only (not strictly linear) — bars extend right because DSM-5 sets no upper duration limit.

ConditionWhere Psychosis Is Allowed to Appear
MDE with psychotic featuresOnly during the depressive episode itself
Bipolar I (with psychotic features)Requires 1 episode of mania; psychosis possible during manic or depressive episodes — never during euthymia
Bipolar II (with psychotic features)Requires 1 hypomanic episode + 1 MDE; psychosis possible during the MDE, but does not occur with hypomania (hypomania is by definition non-impairing)
Schizoaffective disorderPsychosis is the baseline — always present — with mood episodes overlapping it; but psychosis must also occur by itself for >2 weeks at some point (Section 06)

This is the single most useful picture for keeping MDE-with-psychotic-features, bipolar I, bipolar II, and schizoaffective disorder straight — it plots mood state (mania → euthymia → depression) over time and shades in exactly when psychotic features (pink bands) are allowed to appear.

Psychosis (pink) only ever appears layered on top of a mood episode in MDE/Bipolar I/Bipolar II — but sits at baseline in schizoaffective disorder, with mood episodes layered on top of it (detailed in Section 06)

🧠
The discriminator vs. mood disorder with psychotic features: in MDD/bipolar with psychotic features, psychosis occurs only during the mood episode — ask "what's the baseline symptom?" In MDD-with-psychosis, baseline = depression, with psychosis layered on top at its worst. In bipolar I with psychosis, psychosis can appear at the peak (mania) or valley (depression) but never during euthymia. In schizoaffective disorder, psychosis outlasts the mood episode — there's a real stretch (≥2 weeks) of pure psychosis with no mood symptoms at all. That "psychosis alone" window is the diagnostic key.
DisorderRequired episodes
Bipolar I≥1 manic episode (may be preceded/followed by hypomanic or MDEs — not required)
Bipolar II≥1 hypomanic episode + ≥1 MDE, never a manic or mixed episode
Cyclothymic disorder≥2 years of numerous hypomanic-symptom periods + numerous depressive-symptom periods, never meeting full episode criteria, symptom-free gaps never >2 months
⚡

Major Depression

  • 5 criteria required
  • ≥2 weeks
  • Lower functioning
🌫️

Persistent Depression

  • 3 criteria required
  • ≥2 years (1 year in youth)
  • Milder, higher functioning
  • ▸ Cognitive disorders — delirium, and later-stage dementia (early dementia does not typically present with psychosis)
  • ▸ Mood disorders — major depressive disorder, severe, with psychotic features; bipolar I disorder, with psychotic features (psychosis occurs only at the peaks/valleys — the manic or depressive episodes — never during euthymia, "the middle part"); psychotic features are either mood-congruent or mood-incongruent
  • ▸ Autistic disorder — disorganized speech/behavior can be mistaken for psychosis
  • ▸ Primary psychotic disorders (Sections 05–07)
  • ▸ Personality disorders — mainly Cluster A, with Cluster C to a lesser degree (and Cluster B least so) can show psychotic-flavored presentations, though it's a manifestation of the personality pathology rather than pure psychosis

LO 018Mood & Mood Stabilizers◐ Partly covered

Given a clinical vignette, distinguish antidepressant-associated mood switching from persistent major depressive disorder and serotonin toxicity

Answer

A patient started on an antidepressant for depression who returns looking manic roughly 3-6 weeks later is displaying an 'unmasking' of bipolar disorder rather than persistent depression, since a true switch requires meeting full manic (or hypomanic) episode criteria: 3+ DIGFAST symptoms (distractibility, impulsivity, grandiosity, flight of ideas, increased activity, decreased sleep, talkativeness) lasting at least 7 days, or any duration with hospitalization or psychosis, versus 4+ days with no impairment for hypomania. Persistent, non-remitting major depressive disorder, by contrast, continues to meet major depressive episode criteria — 5+ of 9 SIG E CAPS symptoms for at least 2 weeks — without any new DIGFAST symptoms emerging. Serotonin toxicity is distinguished by its timeline and exam findings rather than mood change: it develops rapidly, within 24 hours of starting or combining a serotonergic drug (not just MAOIs), with hyperreflexia, clonus, and autonomic instability such as hyperthermia, diaphoresis, and diarrhea, and is treated with benzodiazepines and supportive care, adding cyproheptadine if there's no improvement.

🧠
Memory hook · Manic at week 3–6? You unmasked bipolarAntidepressant started → returns manic ~3–6 weeks later = unmasking, needs full DIGFAST episode criteria. Serotonin toxicity instead shows up in <24 h with clonus + hyperreflexia + autonomic storm — a neuro exam, not a mood change.
◐
Missing from your notesAn explicit passage naming persistent/non-remitting MDD as a labeled third differential option is still absent; the new pediatric and neuroanatomy lectures do not address mood-switching or serotonin toxicity.

Pulled from: Mood Disorders

"Unmasking" a Bipolar Disorder with an Antidepressant

Presentation: A patient presents with a depressive episode and is started on an antidepressant, as is standard practice. Several weeks later (roughly 3–6 weeks), they return looking manic.

What happened? This is a classic "unmasking" scenario — the patient likely had an underlying, not-yet-diagnosed bipolar disorder the whole time. Since <5% of bipolar patients present with mania as their very first episode, a first depressive episode can't rule bipolar disorder out, and an antidepressant can push a susceptible patient into their first manic (or hypomanic) episode.

Bipolar I or Bipolar II? Judge by extremity, not just presence of symptoms. Example given in lecture: if the patient is shopping more than usual and can comfortably afford it, that impulsivity looks more like hypomania. If the patient buys three cars and a Lamborghini and bankrupts themselves, that degree of impaired judgment and consequence is mania — pushing the diagnosis to Bipolar I.

How do you know it's "real" bipolar and not just a substance-induced mood disorder? There's no perfect test — it's a clinical judgment call. The strongest supporting clue is the typical pattern: most people with bipolar disorder present with a depressive episode first, and the age of first manic-episode onset for that small subset clusters in the 18–20 range, consistent with the overall epidemiology of the disorder.

If a manic episode ever occurs, the diagnosis is Bipolar I regardless of prior hypomanic/depressive history.

5+ of 9 SIG E CAPS symptoms for ≥2 weeks, including depressed mood or anhedonia, causing clinically significant distress or impairment. Lifetime prevalence up to 15% (up to 25% in women); annual prevalence ~10%; female:male ratio 2:1. Formally, diagnosis technically requires ruling out that symptoms represent a single vs. recurrent presentation (2+ episodes separated by ≥2 months of normal mood) — but in practice, most people are diagnosed off a single qualifying episode without getting hung up on that technicality.

⚠️ Antidepressant Caution in Bipolar

Fluoxetine's own bipolar-context side effect profile flags worsening of depression and manic episodes in bipolar patients, plus increased suicidality in children — antidepressants in bipolar disorder are generally used cautiously and typically alongside a mood stabilizer, never as unopposed monotherapy. The one FDA-approved exception is a fluoxetine + olanzapine combination — but that's a maintenance-phase indication, not a treatment for acute mania. You would not start an acutely manic patient on fluoxetine.

Q: How do you distinguish serotonin syndrome from neuroleptic malignant syndrome at the bedside?

Answer

Serotonin syndrome develops rapidly (hours) with hyperreflexia and clonus, and follows a serotonergic drug/combination. NMS develops over days with "lead-pipe" rigidity and hyporeflexia, and follows antipsychotic (dopamine-blocking) exposure. Both can cause hyperthermia and autonomic instability, but the reflex findings and time course are the key differentiators.

Can be triggered by any serotonergic medication or combination — not just MAOIs. Onset is typically rapid (within 24 hours of a new drug/dose/interaction).

Severity roughly tracks degree of CNS serotonin excess — mild, moderate, or severe toxicity, each with a typical trigger:

🩺 Treatment

Benzodiazepines and supportive care first; cyproheptadine (a 5-HT2 receptor antagonist) if there's no improvement. Prevention: avoid combining serotonergic drugs and observe a proper washout period between them (2 weeks after stopping an MAOI before starting another serotonergic drug).

🔑 First Aid Mnemonic — DIGFAST (Mania)

Distractibility · Impulsivity/Indiscretion (hedonistic) · Grandiosity · Flight of ideas · goal-directed Activity/psychomotor agitation · ↓need for Sleep · Talkativeness/pressured speech

🔑 First Aid Mnemonic — SIG E CAPS (Depression)

Sleep disturbance · ↓Interest (anhedonia) · Guilt/worthlessness · ↓Energy · ↓Concentration · Appetite/weight change · Psychomotor retardation/agitation · Suicidal ideation

DisorderBuilt from
Major Depressive Disorder1+ major depressive episode
Persistent Depressive DisorderDepression "light" but long — mild depressive symptoms ≥2 years
Bipolar I1+ manic episode, +/− a depressive episode (depression isn't even required!)
Bipolar II1+ hypomanic episode + 1+ major depressive episode (never a full manic episode)
Cyclothymic disorderHypomania "light" + depression "light," fluctuating for ≥2 years, never meeting full episode criteria
LO 019Mood & Mood Stabilizers✓ In your notes

Given a clinical vignette, distinguish the unique considerations for each of the medications designated as mood stabilizers

Answer

Lithium requires renal-handling considerations captured by the LiTHIUM mnemonic (hypothyroidism, Ebstein anomaly, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, tremor); toxicity above a level of 1.2 causes nausea, ataxia, hyperreflexia, and seizure, treated with stopping the drug, hydration, and possibly dialysis; and prescreening labs (renal and thyroid function, ECG, HCG) plus caution with thiazides, NSAIDs, and ACE-inhibitors that raise lithium levels, making it the default exam answer for bipolar disorder unless pregnancy, renal impairment, or another exception applies. Valproic acid modulates GABA and can cause hyperammonemic delirium — an altered patient on valproate warrants an ammonia level regardless of dose — plus weight gain, hair loss, thrombocytopenia, and neural tube teratogenicity, requiring CBC/platelet and liver-function prescreening. Carbamazepine's hallmark trap is autoinduction of its own hepatic metabolism (and that of oral contraceptives), so a level checked as therapeutic early on can fall as the patient becomes manic again weeks later; it can also cause SIADH and is the second most common cause of rash among mood stabilizers. Lamotrigine is the best-tolerated mood stabilizer (nausea most common, weight neutral) but carries a Stevens-Johnson syndrome/TEN risk requiring slow titration, with its target dose cut by about 50% when combined with valproate because valproate inhibits its glucuronidation clearance.

🧠
Memory hook · Each stabilizer has one signature trapValproate → hyperammonemic delirium (check ammonia at ANY dose) + neural tube defects. Carbamazepine → the cannibal: autoinduces its own metabolism (early 'therapeutic' level, manic again weeks later) + SIADH. Lamotrigine → best tolerated, but titrate slowly or SJS; halve the dose with valproate on board.

Pulled from: Mood Disorders

🔑 First Aid Mnemonic — LiTHIUM

Low Thyroid (hypothyroidism) · Heart (Ebstein anomaly — right atrial enlargement, displaced tricuspid valve) · Insipidus (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus) · Unwanted Movements (tremor)

☐ Lithium Toxicity — level >1.2

Nausea, diarrhea, altered mental status, severe tremor, ataxia, slurred speech, hyperreflexia, polyuria, seizure. Treatment: stop lithium, hydrate; consider dialysis in severe cases.

🔑 Default Answer, With Four Exceptions

On an exam, if a stem describes bipolar disorder and gives you a plain drug list with no other clues, lithium is the default first-line answer. Four things should make you look elsewhere: (1) pregnancy (Ebstein anomaly), (2) significant renal impairment (lithium is a salt excreted essentially unchanged by the kidney, so impaired renal clearance is a direct problem), (3) cardiac conduction disease such as an existing heart block (lithium can further affect cardiac conduction), and (4) difficult-to-manage thyroid disease (lithium can push a patient hypo- or hyperthyroid).

MOA: Modulates GABA. Side effects: weight gain (can contribute to PCOS), hair loss, sedation, thrombocytopenia, elevated ammonia, rash (less common than lamotrigine), neural tube teratogenicity. Supratherapeutic above 100–125.

🩺 Clinical Pearl — Check an Ammonia Level

Valproate can cause a hyperammonemic delirium — a confused, altered patient on valproate should prompt an ammonia level, regardless of whether the dose "seems low." This isn't strictly dose-dependent, and it can happen at any point in treatment. Catching this is a small detail that reads as genuine clinical fluency. (Weight gain and hair loss are also worth knowing as the reasons patients often stop taking valproate on their own.)

Key feature: CYP autoinduction — induces its own metabolism (and that of oral contraceptives). Generally well tolerated: nausea, dizziness, drowsiness. Can cause SIADH (hyponatremia via increased ADH sensitivity). Rash is the second most common cause among mood stabilizers. Teratogenic (neural tube defects). Can help treat certain pain syndromes.

⚠️ Autoinduction — a Classic Trap

Autoinduction means the drug ramps up its own breakdown over time via the CYP system. Clinical trap: start carbamazepine, check a level a week later — it looks great, therapeutic, everything's going well. Come back two weeks later and the patient looks more manic again, even though nothing about the prescription changed. Check the level and it's dropped significantly — carbamazepine induced its own metabolism faster than expected, and the same dose no longer produces the same blood level. The fix isn't "the drug stopped working" — it's recognizing that carbamazepine levels need to be rechecked periodically even on a stable dose, especially early in treatment.

Thought to be the best tolerated mood stabilizer. Nausea is the most common side effect. Weight neutral.

☐ Rash Risk

Stevens-Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis. Risk rises with fast titration — always titrate slowly, and cut the target dose by 50% if combined with valproate (valproate slows lamotrigine clearance).

Notice the flip: lithium/valproate/carbamazepine lead for mania but fall back for depression — lamotrigine does the opposite.

  • Lithium: Ebstein anomaly risk is trimester-specific — cardiac formation happens early, so risk is highest in the first trimester. Many clinicians minimize or hold lithium during the first trimester, then resume or increase the dose later in pregnancy once heart formation is complete and risk drops substantially.
  • Valproate, carbamazepine, lamotrigine: neural tube defect risk; folic acid supplementation (typically more than a standard prenatal vitamin provides) can help mitigate this risk.
  • Antipsychotics: most have little to no pregnancy safety data — the exception is clozapine, which actually has accumulated outcome data. Because of this data gap (not necessarily proven danger), antipsychotics are often the preferred bipolar treatment in pregnancy when a mood stabilizer's teratogenic risk is a bigger concern.
  • Antidepressants: no strong teratogenic signal either way. The main concern is neonatal discontinuation/serotonin syndrome in the newborn after birth, from placental transfer — but most patients are kept on their antidepressant throughout pregnancy regardless, because untreated depression carries its own fetal risk.

Q: A woman with bipolar I disorder is starting lamotrigine and is also on valproate for seizure control. What special dosing adjustment applies, and why?

Answer

Reduce the lamotrigine target dose by ~50%. Valproate inhibits lamotrigine's hepatic clearance (glucuronidation), raising lamotrigine levels — this increases the risk of the rash/Stevens-Johnson reaction, so a slower titration and lower target dose are used when the two are combined.

LO 020Personality Disorders✓ In your notes

Given a clinical vignette, evaluate therapeutic options for a patient with borderline personality disorder and recurrent self-harm

Answer

Dialectical behavioral therapy (DBT), created by Marsha Linehan specifically for borderline personality disorder, is the appropriate first-line psychotherapy for a patient meeting full BPD criteria with recurrent self-harm and unstable relationships, as confirmed directly by a practice question in the notes. DBT's four skills modules map onto BPD's core dysregulation domains: core mindfulness for cognitive dysregulation, distress tolerance for impulsiveness/self-harm, emotion regulation for labile mood, and interpersonal effectiveness for relationship chaos. No medication is FDA-approved for any personality disorder, so pharmacotherapy is always off-label and symptom-targeted; evidence for pharmacotherapy specifically in BPD is weak, but quetiapine has shown significant improvement on the Zanarini Rating Scale (82% response), and polypharmacy is common in practice even though psychotherapy remains the real mainstay. On a vignette, distinguishing BPD's affective instability from a bipolar mood episode hinges on timing — BPD mood shifts are rapid and reactive to interpersonal triggers rather than lasting days-to-weeks independent of triggers as in bipolar disorder.

🧠
Memory hook · Borderline flips in minutes with a trigger; bipolar shifts in weeks without oneBPD mood swings are rapid + interpersonally triggered; bipolar episodes last days-to-weeks and don't need a trigger. DBT's four modules = MEDI: Mindfulness, Emotion regulation, Distress tolerance, Interpersonal effectiveness.
🧠
Memory hook · No FDA-approved pill for any personalityAll 10 PDs: psychotherapy is primary, meds are off-label symptom patches. The one disorder-specific therapy in the group: DBT for borderline (Linehan). (Quetiapine showed an 82% Zanarini response in BPD — notable, still off-label.)

Pulled from: Personality Disorders · Introduction to Therapy · Mood Disorders

Question 12
A 24-year-old woman meets full criteria for borderline personality disorder, including recurrent self-harm and highly unstable relationships. Which specific psychotherapy modality is most appropriate as first-line treatment?
A. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT)
B. Dialectical behavioral therapy (DBT)
C. Psychoanalysis
D. Exposure and response prevention
Answer: B. DBT was developed specifically for BPD and is the only personality disorder with a dedicated first-line psychotherapy (Section 13). Remember the exam shortcut: DBT is technically a form of CBT — "if DBT is an option, choose it; if not, choose CBT" — but when both are listed and the vignette is BPD, DBT is the more specific and correct answer.
🧠
The exam shortcut: DBT (dialectical behavioral therapy) is specifically for borderline PD; CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) is the mainstay for the other 9 personality disorders. Dr. Smith's exact framing: "DBT is a form of CBT, so if the exam has DBT as an option, choose it; if not, choose CBT." In other words, DBT beats CBT as an answer choice only when the vignette is specifically about BPD — otherwise, default to CBT.

DBT's four modules, each targeting one of BPD's core dysregulation domains: core mindfulness (cognitive dysregulation), distress tolerance (impulsiveness), emotion regulation (labile moods/emotions), interpersonal effectiveness (interpersonal chaos)

Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) ⭐ HY

Created by Marsha Linehan, PhD — for borderline personality disorder
StructureA skills-based, manualized treatment built around 4 modules: emotion regulation, mindfulness, distress tolerance, and interpersonal effectiveness.
OriginLinehan developed DBT partly from her own lived experience with BPD — she has spoken publicly (including in a well-known New York Times profile) about how the treatment reflects what helped her.
Also used forAdapted well beyond BPD to many other conditions, but the BPD connection is the one to remember for exams.
Evidence for pharmacotherapy in BPD specifically is weak, but polypharmacy is extremely common in practice
>50% of BPD patients are on 2 psychotropic medications
>11% are on 5+ psychotropics simultaneously
Quetiapine has shown significant improvement on the Zanarini Rating Scale for BPD — 82% response vs. 48% placebo
APA recommends medication as adjunctive treatment for specific symptom domains: affective instability, impulsivity, psychosis, self-destructive behavior — never as monotherapy for the disorder itself
⚠️
The single most important fact in this entire topic: THERE IS NO FDA-APPROVED MEDICATION TO TREAT ANY PERSONALITY DISORDER — not one, for any of the 10. Any medication used is off-label, targeting symptoms that arise from the disorder (depression, paranoia, irritability, affective instability) rather than the core disorder itself.
💡
For every personality disorder besides BPD, psychotherapy is the primary treatment, sometimes continued alongside symptom-targeted medication. Drugs are explicitly not cost-effective substitutes for behavioral psychotherapy.
Question 6
Which feature most reliably distinguishes borderline personality disorder's affective instability from a bipolar mood episode?
A. BPD mood shifts always last several weeks, just like bipolar episodes
B. BPD mood shifts are rapid and reactive to interpersonal triggers, embedded in a broader pattern of relationship instability and identity disturbance
C. Bipolar disorder is ego-syntonic, while BPD is ego-dystonic
D. Only bipolar disorder can involve self-harm
Answer: B. BPD and bipolar disorder are classically confused in both directions (Section 07) — the key discriminator is that BPD's mood instability is fast (hours), reactive to specific relational triggers (fear of abandonment, a perceived slight), and sits inside a broader personality pattern, rather than existing as an autonomous, sustained mood episode.
🔑 High-Yield Differentiator — Timing, Not Symptoms

Bipolar disorder and borderline personality disorder (BPD) both involve dramatic mood swings, and mixing them up is a classic exam trap and a real clinical pitfall (a lot of BPD gets misdiagnosed as bipolar over a patient's lifetime). The fastest way to split them:

Bipolar DisorderBorderline Personality Disorder
Episode durationWeeks to monthsHours to a few days at most
FrequencyRoughly every couple of years (≥4 episodes/year = rapid cycling, and that's already considered remarkable)Multiple mood swings within a single day or week — far more frequent than "rapid cycling" bipolar
SleepDecreased need for sleep is a core, reliable feature of mania/hypomaniaSleep is typically not disrupted in the same characteristic way

In short: how long does the episode last, and how often does it happen? That question alone resolves most of the confusion.

Borderline PD

Instability in self-image and interpersonal relationships
Name origin"Borderline" of depression and psychosis — patients oscillate near the boundary between mood dysregulation and brief, stress-related psychotic phenomena (see micropsychotic episodes below).
Core pictureImpulsivity that may lead to self-harm (drug abuse, promiscuity, cutting), and relationships that are polarized — black/white, love/hate — in a pattern of extreme idealization followed by devaluation. Drives frantic efforts to avoid real or imagined abandonment, alongside chronic feelings of emptiness.
F > MRoughly 3:1 — the one Cluster B disorder that's female-predominant.
🧠
Para-suicidal behavior — behavior that looks like self-harm/suicide on the surface, but isn't intended to end in death; the intent is to feel physical pain, or to get someone else to notice, acknowledge, and support them. Dr. Smith's memory hook, straight from organic chemistry: para- as in para-dimethylbenzene means "opposite" — para-suicidal is, functionally, the opposite of suicidal, even though it can look identical from the outside.
💡
Cutting (classically wrists or thighs), head-banging, or burning with cigarettes — the goal in the vast majority of cases is not suicide. It's to generate physical pain that distracts from unbearable emotional pain (the same underlying logic as trichotillomania's hair-pulling as anxiety distraction). If a patient with BPD does die by suicide, it's typically accidental — e.g., someone overdoses on pills and calls their boyfriend to be "rescued" as part of the pattern, and if he's delayed by traffic and doesn't arrive in time, death results from a gesture that was never actually intended to be lethal.

LO 021Cross-Cutting Pharm✓ In your notes

Given a clinical vignette, identify complications of psychiatric medications usage including serotonin syndrome and

Answer

Serotonin syndrome can be triggered by any serotonergic medication or combination (not just MAOIs), with onset typically rapid — within 24 hours of a new drug, dose change, or interaction — and severity tracking the degree of CNS serotonin excess (mild, moderate, or severe, each with a typical trigger). The '3 A's' mnemonic captures the presentation: increased Activity (clonus, hyperreflexia, hypertonia, tremor, seizure), Autonomic instability (hyperthermia, diaphoresis, diarrhea), and Altered mental status. The bedside discriminator from neuroleptic malignant syndrome is timing and exam: serotonin syndrome develops over hours with hyperreflexia and clonus after a serotonergic drug, while NMS develops over days with 'lead-pipe' rigidity and hyporeflexia after an antipsychotic. The real risk factor is combining different mechanisms that raise serotonin (e.g., an MAOI with another serotonergic agent) rather than simply stacking drugs from the same mechanism; MDMA's serotonin release can also precipitate the syndrome. Treatment is benzodiazepines and supportive care, adding cyproheptadine if there's no improvement, with prevention resting on a proper washout period (2 weeks after stopping an MAOI) before starting another serotonergic drug.

🧠
Memory hook · Fast & twitchy vs. slow & stiffSerotonin syndrome: hours after a serotonergic change — the 3 A's (↑Activity: clonus/hyperreflexia · Autonomic instability · AMS). Tx: benzos → cyproheptadine. NMS: days after an antipsychotic — lead-pipe rigidity + hyporeflexia + fever + ↑CK. First move: STOP the drug. The danger is crossing mechanisms, not stacking the same one; 2-week MAOI washout.

Q: How do you distinguish serotonin syndrome from neuroleptic malignant syndrome at the bedside?

Answer

Serotonin syndrome develops rapidly (hours) with hyperreflexia and clonus, and follows a serotonergic drug/combination. NMS develops over days with "lead-pipe" rigidity and hyporeflexia, and follows antipsychotic (dopamine-blocking) exposure. Both can cause hyperthermia and autonomic instability, but the reflex findings and time course are the key differentiators.

🔑 First Aid Mnemonic — 3 A's

↑Activity (neuromuscular: clonus, hyperreflexia, hypertonia, tremor, seizure) · Autonomic instability (hyperthermia, diaphoresis, diarrhea) · Altered mental status

Can be triggered by any serotonergic medication or combination — not just MAOIs. Onset is typically rapid (within 24 hours of a new drug/dose/interaction).

🩺 Treatment

Benzodiazepines and supportive care first; cyproheptadine (a 5-HT2 receptor antagonist) if there's no improvement. Prevention: avoid combining serotonergic drugs and observe a proper washout period between them (2 weeks after stopping an MAOI before starting another serotonergic drug).

🔑 The Real Risk Factor Is Crossing Mechanisms, Not Counting Drugs

It's tempting to think "more serotonergic drugs = more risk," but the more precise clinical teaching point is: risk climbs sharply when you combine different mechanisms of raising serotonin, not just more drugs from the same mechanism. Two SSRIs together (both block reuptake) carry less added risk than one SSRI plus one MAOI (reuptake block + degradation block) — because once the reuptake pumps are saturated, adding a second reuptake blocker doesn't meaningfully raise synaptic serotonin further, but blocking a completely different step in the pathway does. Practically: don't stress as much about stacking two SSRIs or two SNRIs, but always pause before combining across classes — especially anything touching an MAOI.

⚠️ Serotonin Syndrome Risk — ANY serotonergic drug

Because MAOIs block 5-HT breakdown, combining with other serotonergic agents (decongestants, stimulants, other antidepressants, MDMA, certain pain meds, certain anesthesia meds) risks serotonin syndrome. See the dedicated section below for full presentation.

⚠️ Serotonin Syndrome & Hyponatremia

MDMA's serotonin release can precipitate serotonin syndrome (agitation, confusion, tachycardia/hypertension, dilated pupils, myoclonus/rigidity, diaphoresis, diarrhea). A presentation that's easy to miss: increased water consumption + polydipsia → hyponatremia — not on most slide summaries, but a real ED presentation. Because synthesis is inhibited and reuptake blocked after release, there's marked intracellular serotonin depletion for ~24h post-dose, which underlies the crash/withdrawal.

LO 022Psychosis & Antipsychotics✓ In your notes

Given a clinical vignette, identify physiology, pharmacology and complications of psychiatric medications in the management of psychotic disorders

Answer

Extrapyramidal symptoms arise from D2 blockade tipping the striatal acetylcholine:dopamine balance toward cholinergic excess in the nigrostriatal tract; efficacy without EPS sits in a narrow window around 78-80% striatal D2 occupancy, with agents like haloperidol 2-5 mg staying in that zone while crossing above it produces motor side effects. The four EPS syndromes follow a timeline, each with a distinct first-line treatment: acute dystonia (hours-days, e.g., torticollis, opisthotonos, treated with IM/IV benztropine or diphenhydramine), akathisia (days-weeks, motor restlessness, treated with propranolol), pseudoparkinsonism (anticholinergics or amantadine), and tardive dyskinesia (after years, orofacial chewing/lip-smacking, managed by stopping the antipsychotic). Neuroleptic malignant syndrome presents as rigidity, diaphoresis, and hyperthermia after repeated antipsychotic dosing (e.g., the 'B-52'), and the essential first step is to stop the antipsychotic. Other complications to recognize on a vignette include lithium toxicity (coarse tremor, diarrhea, headache), clozapine/olanzapine levels dropping when a hospitalized smoker who was CYP1A2-induced resumes smoking after discharge (risking breakthrough psychosis despite perfect compliance), and clozapine/olanzapine's outsized metabolic risk (weight gain, type 2 diabetes) alongside clozapine's unique agranulocytosis risk.

🧠
Memory hook · EPS timeline: ADAPTAcute Dystonia (hours–days) → Akathisia (days–weeks) → Parkinsonism (weeks) → Tardive dyskinesia (years). Treatments rhyme with the clock: benztropine IM → propranolol → anticholinergic/amantadine → stop the drug.

Pulled from: Psychotic Disorders & Antipsychotic Pharmacology

EPS arises from an acetylcholine : dopamine imbalance in the nigrostriatal tract (Section 02) caused by dopamine blockade. Normally dopamine and acetylcholine counterbalance each other in the striatum; blocking D2 receptors tips the seesaw toward relative cholinergic excess.

The ACh : DA seesaw — antipsychotics push it toward cholinergic excess

Relative dopamine deficiency in the nigrostriatal pathway — same final common pathway as Parkinson's disease (loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta) vs. antipsychotic-induced D2 blockade

There is a narrow window between antipsychotic efficacy and excessive side effects. The striatal D2 receptor occupancy threshold to reduce psychosis with minimal EPS is approximately 78–80%; crossing above the EPS threshold produces motor side effects.

Hypothetical thresholds for antipsychotic drug effects — the therapeutic window sits between the ~70% "antipsychotic effect" line and the ~80% "EPS" line

TypeTimelineDescription
Dystonic reactionAcute (hours–days)Sudden, sustained muscle contraction — e.g., torticollis (twisted neck), oculogyric crisis, opisthotonos. Most common in young men on high-potency typicals.
AkathisiaAcute/subacute (days–weeks)Subjective/objective motor restlessness — "can't sit still," constant leg movement.
PseudoparkinsonismAcute/subacute (days–weeks)Bradykinesia, rigidity, resting tremor, masked facies — mimics idiopathic Parkinson's disease.
Tardive dyskinesiaChronic (months–years)Involuntary, repetitive, often choreoathetoid movements — classically orofacial (chewing, lip-smacking, tongue protrusion, "snake-like" movements).
Acute dystonia → IM/IV anticholinergic (benztropine or diphenhydramine) — fast-acting, often dramatic relief
Akathisia → propranolol (beta-blocker) is classically first-line; benzodiazepines also used
Pseudoparkinsonism → anticholinergics (benztropine, trihexyphenidyl) or amantadine
Tardive dyskinesia → withdraw/reduce offending agent, switch to an atypical, consider VMAT2 inhibitors; TD is often not reversible, so prevention matters most
B.1
Which is the most reasonable next step in treatment?
A. Continue both medications at current doses and monitor closely
B. Gradually discontinue both medications over the next 2 weeks
C. Gradually decrease the olanzapine but continue lithium
D. Gradually discontinue the lithium but continue the olanzapine
E. Immediately discontinue both medications and initiate a different mood stabilizer
Answer: C. Olanzapine is a highly sedating "-pine" atypical (Section 14) — appropriate for acute mania/psychosis but not necessarily needed long-term once symptoms resolve. Lithium is the maintenance mood stabilizer and should continue. Taper the sedating agent (olanzapine) while keeping the foundational mood stabilizer, rather than abruptly stopping everything (B, E) or dropping the maintenance drug instead of the sedating one (D).
D.1
Which adverse effect is most likely responsible?
A. Catatonia
B. Parkinsonian rigidity
C. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
D. Serotonin syndrome
E. Neuroleptic-induced dystonia
Answer: C. Rigidity + diaphoresis + hyperthermia (103°F) after repeated antipsychotic (Haldol) dosing is the classic triad pointing to NMS, not isolated dystonia (E, which wouldn't cause fever) or plain parkinsonian rigidity (B, which lacks the autonomic/hyperthermic component). There's no serotonergic agent on board here to suggest serotonin syndrome (D).
D.2
This is best treated by doing which of the following?
A. Change to a low-potency typical antipsychotic
B. Add an anxiolytic
C. Add an antidepressant
D. Add an anticonvulsant
E. Add a beta blocker
F. Stop the antipsychotic
G. Add an anticholinergic
Answer: F. The first and most essential step in NMS is to discontinue the causative antipsychotic and provide supportive care (cooling, IV fluids; dantrolene/bromocriptine in severe cases). Switching to a different (even lower-potency) antipsychotic (A) still blocks dopamine and won't resolve an ongoing NMS episode.
E.1
Which of the following most likely caused his symptoms?
A. Anticholinergic toxicity
B. Lithium toxicity
C. Neuroleptic-induced dystonia
D. Neuroleptic-induced EPS
E. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Answer: B. Coarse tremor + GI upset (diarrhea) + headache is the classic early lithium toxicity picture. The trigger: frequent ibuprofen (an NSAID) reduces renal prostaglandin synthesis → reduced renal blood flow → reduced lithium clearance → rising lithium levels. Docusate is a distractor (a stool softener with no meaningful lithium interaction). This is a classic drug-interaction vignette, distinct from anything on the antipsychotic side.
F.3
How is this treated?
Propranolol
Answer: Propranolol. A beta-blocker is classically first-line for akathisia (Section 16) — distinct from the anticholinergics used for dystonia/pseudoparkinsonism.
G.1
This sign indicates a side effect of antipsychotic medication known as:
A. Restless leg syndrome
B. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
C. Akathisia
D. Tardive dyskinesia
E. Acute dystonia
F. Pseudo-parkinsonism
Answer: D. Orofacial chewing/lip-smacking movements after years of antipsychotic exposure is the hallmark presentation of tardive dyskinesia (Section 16) — the "chronic" EPS syndrome, as opposed to the acute/subacute syndromes (dystonia, akathisia, pseudoparkinsonism).

Smoking causes induction of the CYP1A2 isoenzyme, which principally affects two antipsychotics: clozapine and olanzapine.

Fluvoxamine inhibits CYP1A2 (raising levels); ongoing smoking induces CYP1A2 (lowering levels) — stopping smoking (e.g., during hospitalization) removes that induction and can raise serum levels ~50%

LO 023Eating Disorders✓ In your notes

Given a clinical vignette, identify the best treatment for eating disorders in individuals with multiple psychiatric co-morbidities

Answer

Once a patient is medically stabilized, eating-disorder treatment turns to addressing comorbid diagnoses (depression, anxiety, etc.) alongside therapy, largely CBT; comorbidity is the rule rather than the exception in bulimia, where mood disorders occur in 50-70%, anxiety disorders in 15-65%, substance use disorders in 25%, and personality disorders in 20-80% of patients. Medication choice should do double duty where possible — SSRIs can both increase appetite in anorexia and treat comorbid depression/anxiety, and mirtazapine offers a dual benefit (appetite stimulation plus antidepressant effect) when depression is comorbid — but bupropion carries a US boxed warning and is contraindicated in active or recent bulimia or anorexia because purging-related electrolyte disturbances and dehydration raise seizure risk, and lithium should also be avoided since purging-induced dehydration raises the risk of lithium toxicity. For binge eating disorder specifically, medication (lisdexamfetamine, sertraline, or topiramate) combined with therapy produces better outcomes than either alone.

🧠
Memory hook · Anorexia gets NO drugs; Bulimia gets fluoxetine; Binge gets VyvanseNo FDA-approved med for anorexia (treatment = weight restoration ~1 lb/week, beware refeeding). Bulimia → SSRI ± ondansetron/topiramate. BED → lisdexamfetamine, sertraline, or topiramate. Bupropion is Banned in Both bulimia and anorexia (purging → electrolytes → seizures). Purging dehydration also makes lithium dangerous.

Pulled from: Eating Disorders

Once medically stabilized, treat comorbid diagnoses (depression, anxiety, etc.) and pursue therapy — largely CBT, though the lecturer notes this is an oversimplification of the real therapeutic approach.

  • Mood disorders — 50–70%
  • Anxiety disorders — 15–65%
  • Substance use disorders — 25%
  • Personality disorders — 20–80%

Treat medical abnormalities, reduce binge/purge frequency, treat comorbid diagnoses. Therapy is first-line — CBT primarily, with interpersonal therapy, the Maudsley model, and DBT also used.

☐ US Boxed Warning

Bupropion (Wellbutrin) — Contraindicated in active or recent Bulimia (or Anorexia) Nervosa. Carries a black box warning for increased seizure risk in this population, related to the electrolyte disturbances and dehydration that purging behaviors cause. On an exam, if a stem describes bulimia and asks "which medication is contraindicated," bupropion is almost always the answer.

⚠️ Also Avoid: Lithium

Lithium requires a stable, consistent hydration state to avoid nephrotoxicity. Purging behaviors (especially self-induced vomiting) create a dehydration-prone state that raises the risk of lithium toxicity.

🔑 Key Takeaways
  • BMI is the fastest way to narrow the differential — low points to anorexia, normal/high moves away from it.
  • Ask "what's the goal of the behavior?" — losing weight (anorexia) vs. correcting a binge (bulimia) vs. no correction at all (BED).
  • Therapy (largely CBT) is first-line across all three disorders; medication is adjunctive.
  • Avoid bupropion and lithium in active bulimia/anorexia.
  • The DSM is black-and-white; real patients are gray — "unspecified" is a legitimate clinical category, not a cop-out.
  1. Check the BMI first. Below normal (<18.5) points strongly toward anorexia. Normal-to-high points away from anorexia and toward bulimia or BED.
  2. Identify the driving behavior. Is the primary goal ongoing weight loss (restriction-focused), or correcting/compensating after a binge (bulimia), or a binge with no compensation at all (BED)?
  3. Confirm frequency and duration. Bulimia and BED both need recurrent episodes; bulimia specifically needs ≥1×/week for 3 months, and anorexia's subtype (restricting vs. binge/purge) is defined over the past 3 months.
  4. Rule out exclusionary criteria. Anorexia must be excluded before diagnosing bulimia. If the picture is incomplete or mixed, consider "unspecified."
LO 024Mood & Mood Stabilizers◐ Partly covered

Given a clinical vignette, identify the difference between MDD and persistent depressive disorder and the appropriate treatments

Answer

MDD requires 5 of 9 SIG E CAPS symptoms, including depressed mood or anhedonia, for at least 2 weeks with clinically significant impairment, whereas persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) requires only 3 criteria but sustained for at least 2 years (1 year in youth), producing a milder but longer, higher-functioning picture; a full major depressive episode superimposed on PDD is called 'double depression.' Treatment across depression generally is severity-stratified: mild depression is managed with lifestyle changes and monitoring, moderate depression with therapy or an antidepressant (therapy alone is often sufficient), and severe depression with both together, with augmentation considered. SSRIs are the first-line antidepressant class for most depression, binding the serotonin transporter to block reuptake and increase synaptic serotonin, with the PHQ-9 serving as the fast, validated screener that lets primary care providers manage the roughly 70-80% of psychiatric care that occurs outside specialist visits. CBT remains the default first-line, evidence-based psychotherapy for depression generally.

🧠
Memory hook · SIG E CAPS ×2 weeks; dysthymia ×2 yearsMDE = 5+/9 for ≥2 weeks (must include depressed mood or anhedonia). Persistent depressive disorder = 3 criteria, ≥2 years (1 yr in kids) — milder but longer. MDE on top of PDD = double depression.
◐
Missing from your notesWhether PDD's treatment differs from standard MDD treatment (e.g., longer maintenance therapy) is still not explicitly stated; the new child psychiatry lecture only addresses childhood depression generally (irritability/somatic complaints, SSRIs first-line pharmacologically) and does not distinguish MDD from PDD.

Pulled from: Mood Disorders · Introduction to Therapy

🧸 ELI5 — MDD vs. PDD

MDD is a hard storm — intense, but it passes. PDD is a low, grey overcast sky that just doesn't lift for years. Storms (MDD) can actually happen on top of the overcast sky too — that's called "double depression," and if a full MDE shows up it should make you reconsider whether it's really MDD instead of (or in addition to) PDD.

Chronic depressed mood for most of the day, more days than not, for ≥2 years (1 year in children/adolescents), plus 2+ of: poor appetite/overeating, insomnia/hypersomnia, low energy, low self-esteem, poor concentration, hopelessness. Symptoms never absent for more than 2 months at a time. No MDE during the first 2 years (if present → consider MDD instead). Per lecture: think of it as generally a somewhat milder symptom picture than MDD, just stretched across years instead of weeks.

5+ of 9 SIG E CAPS symptoms for ≥2 weeks, including depressed mood or anhedonia, causing clinically significant distress or impairment. Lifetime prevalence up to 15% (up to 25% in women); annual prevalence ~10%; female:male ratio 2:1. Formally, diagnosis technically requires ruling out that symptoms represent a single vs. recurrent presentation (2+ episodes separated by ≥2 months of normal mood) — but in practice, most people are diagnosed off a single qualifying episode without getting hung up on that technicality.

🩺 Why PHQ-9 Matters More Than It Looks

~70–80% of people who get psychiatric care get it from their primary care provider, not a psychiatrist — and a PCP visit is often 15 minutes, while a full psychiatric intake for MDD can take closer to an hour. The PHQ-9 is a fast, validated screener that lets a time-strapped PCP get most of the way to a diagnosis without conducting a full intake. If it shows up on an exam, it's pointing you toward MDD.

LO 025Neurocognitive & AMS✓ In your notes

Given a clinical vignette, identify the pathobiology and neuroanatomy of limbic circuits that control mood disorders, intrusive and disordered thoughts and dyskinesias

Answer

The basal ganglia form parallel re-entrant cortico-striato-pallido-thalamocortical loops (basal ganglia loops or macrosystems, described by Heimer) that map onto specific clinical phenomena. The motor loop runs motor cortex to putamen to globus pallidus to the VL thalamic nucleus and its disruption produces dyskinesias. The associative loop runs sensory/associative and parietal/DLPFC cortex through the caudate and globus pallidus to the VL/VA thalamic nuclei and its disruption produces disordered and intrusive thoughts. The limbic loop runs anterior cingulate/hippocampal and limbic cortex through the ventral striatum and ventral pallidum to the AN/VA/DM thalamic nuclei and its disruption produces labile emotions and mood disorders. Within the limbic loop, the nucleus accumbens and amygdala anchor opposing functions: dopamine release into the accumbens drives pleasure and behavioral augmentation (reward-seeking), while the amygdala drives fear and restraint responses via norepinephrine, forming the basis for mood-disorder circuitry. This loop model builds on earlier limbic-system concepts such as the Papez circuit and McLean's triune brain, which described a brainstem with base behavioral patterns overlaid by an old-mammalian (limbic) brain and then by neocortex.

🧠
Memory hook · Three loops, three failuresBasal-ganglia re-entrant loops: motor loop breaks → dyskinesias · associative loop breaks → intrusive/disordered thoughts · limbic loop breaks → labile mood. Accumbens dopamine = pleasure/reward; amygdala (NE) = fear/restraint.

Pulled from: Psychiatry Key Drug List 2026 · Neuroanatomy of Psychiatric Disorders

One receptor (D2), four brain pathways, four different outcomes. Block the right one and psychosis improves; the other three blocks are your side-effect chapters. "Major tranquilizers"/"neuroleptics" by their old names.

LO 026Substance Use & Tox◐ Partly covered

Identify the mechanism of action and adverse effects of the drugs of abuse

Answer

Benzodiazepines agonize the benzodiazepine site on the GABA-A ionotropic receptor, increasing chloride influx and hyperpolarizing neurons to decrease excitability, producing 'downer' intoxication (sedation, ataxia, anterograde amnesia, respiratory depression) with over 30% of benzo-related ER visits resulting in a serious medical outcome (70% in patients over 65) and an 'upper' withdrawal picture (anxiety, insomnia, tremulousness, possible seizures). Alcohol acutely potentiates GABA-A and inhibits NMDA receptors, causing anxiolysis/sedation, but chronic use shifts receptor expression toward fewer GABA-A and more NMDA(NR2B) receptors to compensate; removing alcohol unmasks that adaptation as the most dangerous withdrawal syndrome covered, with seizures and delirium tremens carrying the highest death risk of any withdrawal discussed. THC, the primary psychoactive compound in cannabis, is an agonist at the CB1 receptor (a GPCR), producing intoxication with euphoria, paranoid delusions, and conjunctival injection, and withdrawal with irritability, insomnia, and anorexia. PCP is an NMDA/glutamate receptor antagonist whose blockade of excitatory transmission produces anesthesia, delirium, hallucinations, and profound analgesia that lets intoxicated patients sustain severe, unnoticed injuries while behaving belligerently and impulsively. MDMA is chemically related to methamphetamine but acts primarily as a serotonergic agent, reversing SERT to flood the synapse with serotonin, causing euphoria and heightened sensation for 30 minutes to 6 hours alongside nausea, hyperthermia, and rare end-organ damage. Amphetamines block dopamine/norepinephrine reuptake and enhance dopamine/norepinephrine release, with adverse effects including decreased appetite/weight, insomnia, anxiety/agitation, GI upset, dysphoria/mania, tachycardia/hypertension, growth suppression, tics, and headache, and a rebound withdrawal picture (headache, hypersomnia, hyperphagia, depression) on abrupt stopping; naloxone, buprenorphine (partial-agonist ceiling), and methadone (full agonist, QTc risk) are the related opioid-agent options.

🧠
Memory hook · Receptor one-linersBenzos → GABA-A (Cl⁻ in, calm down) · Alcohol → GABA-A agonist + NMDA blocker (chronic use flips the ratio — that's the withdrawal) · THC → CB1 · PCP → NMDA blocker (painless belligerence — they hurt themselves and don't notice) · MDMA → reverses SERT (serotonin flood).
◐
Missing from your notesCocaine's specific mechanism (monoamine reuptake blockade plus local-anesthetic/vasoconstrictive Na+-channel effects) and the intoxication/adverse-effect profile of opioids themselves as drugs of abuse are still not covered; the neuroanatomy lecture discusses general dopamine reward circuitry (accumbens, mesolimbic pathway) but does not describe the pharmacology of specific abused substances.

Pulled from: Addiction & Non-Clinical Drug Use · Anxiety, OCD & Trauma-Related Disorders · Psychiatry Key Drug List 2026

Classic animal work (electrode implanted directly in the VTA, wired to a lever) shows the mechanism starkly: rather than eating or drinking, the animal presses the lever for stimulation — repeatedly, to the exclusion of survival behaviors, until it dies if left unchecked. That is addiction distilled to its circuit: a learned association between an action and a rewarding brain stimulus, strong enough to override every competing drive.

Benzodiazepines

Agonize the benzodiazepine site on the GABA-A ionotropic receptor complex → conformational change in the Cl⁻ channel → more Cl⁻ flows into the neuron → hyperpolarization → decreased neuronal excitability/transmission.

Sedation, fatigue, depression, dizziness, ataxia, paradoxical excitement/agitation, confusion, disorientation, anterograde amnesia, respiratory depression, disinhibition — all classic "downer" intoxication effects.

🧠
Withdrawal from a downer produces upper effects — and vice versa (this exact logic reappears in the antipsychotic pharmacology unit). Benzo withdrawal syndrome: anxiety, insomnia, tremulousness, nausea/vomiting, transient hallucinations, and — critically — seizures are possible with acute withdrawal, so taper slowly. Adverse cognitive effects of ongoing use include difficulty focusing attention, memory impairment, and confusion.
Long-term benzo use carries high socioeconomic costs
>30% of ER visits involving benzos resulted in a serious medical outcome
In patients >65 years, that figure jumps to 70% — elderly patients need less benzo and are more susceptible to adverse effects (especially cognitive impairment)
Risk is greater when combined with opiates or alcohol
Alprazolam (Xanax) is the most-abused benzo in the US, with rising ER-visit rates

Alcohol

Chronic alcohol use shifts receptor expression — fewer GABA-A, more NMDA(NR2B) — setting up the withdrawal rebound

  • Acutely, alcohol potentiates GABA-A and inhibits specific NMDA subtypes → decreased excitability → anxiolysis/sedation.
  • With chronic use, GABA-A expression falls while NMDA (NR2B) expression rises to compensate — restoring excitability in alcohol's presence. Remove the alcohol and that adaptation is unmasked as withdrawal hyperexcitability.
  • Alcohol's rewarding effect may also involve indirect activation of cannabinoid receptors, feeding back to enhance dopaminergic reward signaling.
🍷

Intoxication

  • Emotional lability, slurred speech
  • Ataxia, blackouts, coma
🚨

Withdrawal

  • Anxiety, tremor, insomnia
  • Severe: autonomic hyperactivity, seizures, delirium tremens

Cannabis (THC)

Compounds derived from Cannabis sativa. Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) is the primary psychoactive component — an agonist at cannabinoid receptor type 1 (CB1), a GPCR. Pharmacokinetics vary widely by route/preparation (smoking, vaping, dabbing, edibles all behave differently, and patients will ask you about this directly).

🌿

Intoxication

Euphoria, increased appetite, dry mouth, anxiety, paranoid delusions, perceived time slowing, impaired judgment, social withdrawal, conjunctival injection, hallucinations.

😣

Withdrawal

Irritability, depression, insomnia, nausea, anorexia. Cannabis use disorder is now increasingly recognized as its own diagnosis — historically thought mild given cannabis's large volume of distribution and long elimination half-life, but that literature is genuinely mixed.

PCP (phencyclidine)

Originally developed as a dissociative anesthetic; discontinued for behavioral toxicity. An NMDA antagonist — NMDA/glutamate receptors mediate excitatory transmission and are central to synaptic plasticity and memory, so blocking them produces complex effects: anesthesia, delirium, hallucinations, intense paranoia, agitation, amnesia.

MDMA (ecstasy / molly)

MDMA ("ecstasy"/"molly") is chemically related to methamphetamine but primarily serotonergic: causes serotonin release into the extracellular space, inhibits its synthesis, and blocks its reuptake — a "selective serotonergic neurotoxin" that empties the tank all at once (via reversing SERT). It also has central stimulant effects similar to cocaine/amphetamine plus its own hallucinogenic quality.

Amphetamines & stimulants

Mechanism
Block DA/NE reuptake AND enhance release of DA/NE (amphetamines especially push release).
Side effects
Decreased appetite/weight, insomnia (dose after meals, not at night), anxiety/jitteriness/agitation, GI upset, dysphoria/mania, tachycardia/palpitations/HTN, possible growth suppression (drug holidays help), tics/dyskinesias, headache.
Stopping abruptly
Rebound: headache, hypersomnia, hyperphagia, depression, irritability, poor concentration.
Abuse reality check
Oral ADHD dosing has low abuse potential (vs snorted/IV meth); untreated ADHD raises later drug-abuse risk — treatment lowers it. Watch for feigned ADHD (diversion). FDA: no ER stimulants in children <6 years (weight loss).

LO 027Substance Use & Tox✓ In your notes

Identify the pharmacologic properties of a drug which make it an appropriate agent for medication-assisted treatment of a substance use disorder

Answer

Medications for opioid use disorder use two pharmacologic strategies targeting the mu-opioid receptor: agonist-based (methadone, buprenorphine) or antagonist-based (naltrexone), all most effective when paired with psychotherapy/counseling. Buprenorphine, a high-affinity partial agonist, prevents withdrawal and reduces craving by increasing mesolimbic dopaminergic transmission just enough to relieve dependence; because it already occupies mu-receptors at high affinity, a full agonist added on top (e.g., for surgical pain) needs a much higher dose and remains capped by buprenorphine's ceiling effect. For alcohol use disorder, naltrexone can be started while the patient is still drinking (unlike in opioid use disorder) and is used mainly for craving management, while acamprosate (an NMDA-receptor antagonist plus GABA-A agonist) is dosed three times daily. Disulfiram instead works by aversive conditioning — pairing alcohol with an unpleasant physical reaction so drinking becomes associated with feeling ill.

🧠
Memory hook · Buprenorphine hogs the receptor but never floors the gasHigh-affinity partial agonist → ceiling effect caps euphoria/respiratory depression, and surgical opioids struggle to out-compete it. Methadone = full agonist (watch QTc). Naltrexone = the antagonist option.

Pulled from: Addiction & Non-Clinical Drug Use · Introduction to Therapy

Two pharmacologic strategies, both targeting the μ-opioid receptor — agonist-based (methadone, buprenorphine) or antagonist-based (naltrexone). All are most effective paired with psychotherapy/counseling; accessibility remains a major real-world barrier (accreditation hurdles, enrollment hurdles, inconsistent insurance coverage, social stigma).

Naltrexone

Oral or long-acting injectable

Can start while the patient is still drinking (unlike opioid use disorder). Avoid in patients taking opioids for pain or with hepatic insufficiency. Used mainly for craving management.

Acamprosate

Oral, 3×/day

NMDA-receptor antagonist + GABA-A agonist — mirrors alcohol's own mechanism. Effective, but 3×/day dosing hurts adherence.

Disulfiram ⭐ HY — Aversive Therapy

Aldehyde dehydrogenase inhibitor

Blocks acetaldehyde → acetate, letting acetaldehyde bioaccumulate → intense hangover (flushing, headache, nausea, vomiting, weakness, orthostatic hypotension, respiratory difficulty) if alcohol is consumed. This is negative reinforcement by design — requires informed patient buy-in, since the reaction itself can warrant an ED visit. Rare AE: hepatitis, optic neuritis, peripheral neuropathy.

Q5: Why did buprenorphine/naloxone relieve Mr. A's symptoms and long-term craving, and how long should maintenance continue?

Answer

As a partial agonist, buprenorphine prevents withdrawal symptoms and reduces craving by increasing mesolimbic dopaminergic neurotransmission just enough to relieve dependence without a full-agonist high. It can be used for both detox and long-term maintenance — and because addiction is considered permanent, maintenance is often continued for years, with tapering (as Mr. A begins to consider) approached cautiously and individually.

Q2: How could Mr. A's pain be managed if he needed surgery while on buprenorphine/naloxone?

Answer

Because buprenorphine is a high-affinity partial agonist already occupying μ-receptors, a full agonist given on top would need a much higher dose to achieve analgesia — and even then is capped by buprenorphine's ceiling. In practice this often means an alternative analgesic/anesthetic strategy rather than simply stacking a full agonist on top.

The mirror image of systematic desensitization: pair a noxious/unpleasant stimulus with an undesired behavior to extinguish it. Classic example: disulfiram (Antabuse) + alcohol — drinking while on disulfiram produces an unpleasant physical reaction, so alcohol becomes associated with feeling ill.

Detoxification

Cold turkey vs. taper vs. MOUD — the approach depends entirely on which substance and how dangerous its withdrawal is.

🧩

Treatment

Pharmacologic — aversive therapies (block desired effects/cause hangover), replacement therapy (manage dysphoria/reward), treat comorbid psychiatric disease. Psychosocial — CBT, mutual support (AA/NA), moderation management as early intervention.

LO 028Mood & Mood Stabilizers✓ In your notes

Identify the pharmacological and side-effect profiles of major drugs used to treat both bipolar disorder and epilepsy, focusing on both commonality and criticality

Answer

Among the anticonvulsant mood stabilizers, valproic acid (GABA modulation) causes weight gain, hair loss, sedation, thrombocytopenia, elevated ammonia (hyperammonemic delirium can occur at any point in treatment regardless of dose), rash, and neural tube teratogenicity, with supratherapeutic levels above 100-125. Carbamazepine's defining feature is CYP autoinduction: it induces its own metabolism (and that of oral contraceptives), so a level checked early can look therapeutic before the drug ramps up its own breakdown and the patient relapses weeks later; it also causes SIADH/hyponatremia, is the second most common cause of rash among the mood stabilizers, and is teratogenic. Lamotrigine is the best-tolerated agent (nausea most common effect, weight neutral) but carries a Stevens-Johnson syndrome/TEN risk that rises with fast titration, requiring slow titration and a 50% dose cut when combined with valproate, which slows lamotrigine's clearance. Despite sharing toxicity profiles with their epilepsy indications, valproate and carbamazepine are first-line for acute mania but only third-line/combination options for bipolar depression, while lamotrigine is the reverse -- weak for mania, first-line for bipolar depression.

🧠
Memory hook · Each stabilizer has one signature trapValproate → hyperammonemic delirium (check ammonia at ANY dose) + neural tube defects. Carbamazepine → the cannibal: autoinduces its own metabolism (early 'therapeutic' level, manic again weeks later) + SIADH. Lamotrigine → best tolerated, but titrate slowly or SJS; halve the dose with valproate on board.

Pulled from: Mood Disorders

All have poorly established mechanisms overall — low yield to memorize MOA in depth (think "sodium channels" broadly). What is high yield: each drug's distinct side-effect profile, monitoring needs, and clinical niche. Three of the four have a narrow therapeutic window requiring blood level monitoring.

MOA: Modulates GABA. Side effects: weight gain (can contribute to PCOS), hair loss, sedation, thrombocytopenia, elevated ammonia, rash (less common than lamotrigine), neural tube teratogenicity. Supratherapeutic above 100–125.

Key feature: CYP autoinduction — induces its own metabolism (and that of oral contraceptives). Generally well tolerated: nausea, dizziness, drowsiness. Can cause SIADH (hyponatremia via increased ADH sensitivity). Rash is the second most common cause among mood stabilizers. Teratogenic (neural tube defects). Can help treat certain pain syndromes.

⚠️ Autoinduction — a Classic Trap

Autoinduction means the drug ramps up its own breakdown over time via the CYP system. Clinical trap: start carbamazepine, check a level a week later — it looks great, therapeutic, everything's going well. Come back two weeks later and the patient looks more manic again, even though nothing about the prescription changed. Check the level and it's dropped significantly — carbamazepine induced its own metabolism faster than expected, and the same dose no longer produces the same blood level. The fix isn't "the drug stopped working" — it's recognizing that carbamazepine levels need to be rechecked periodically even on a stable dose, especially early in treatment.

Thought to be the best tolerated mood stabilizer. Nausea is the most common side effect. Weight neutral.

☐ Rash Risk

Stevens-Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis. Risk rises with fast titration — always titrate slowly, and cut the target dose by 50% if combined with valproate (valproate slows lamotrigine clearance).

Relative Therapeutic-Level Scale (mcg/mL, log-ish)

Lithium (~1)
Carbamazepine (~10)
Valproic acid (~100)
