🧸 ELI5 — Reading This Table

Notice the pattern: lithium, valproate, and carbamazepine are the go-to's for mania but are only backup options for bipolar depression. Lamotrigine flips that completely — it's weak for mania but is actually a first-line choice for bipolar depression. Different phases genuinely need different drugs — memorizing "one mood stabilizer treats bipolar" will get you the wrong answer on a phase-specific question.

🩺 Clinical Pearl — Check an Ammonia Level

Valproate can cause a hyperammonemic delirium — a confused, altered patient on valproate should prompt an ammonia level, regardless of whether the dose "seems low." This isn't strictly dose-dependent, and it can happen at any point in treatment. Catching this is a small detail that reads as genuine clinical fluency. (Weight gain and hair loss are also worth knowing as the reasons patients often stop taking valproate on their own.)

LO 029Legal, Ethics & Risk◐ Partly covered

Manage a patient with active, passive, and/or parasuicidal behavior in the outpatient clinic

Answer

Para-suicidal behavior -- behavior that looks like self-harm or a suicide attempt on the surface but is not intended to end in death -- is most classically seen in borderline personality disorder, where cutting, head-banging, or burning is used to generate physical pain that distracts from unbearable emotional pain, or to get someone else to notice, acknowledge, and support the patient. Dialectical behavior therapy, created by Marsha Linehan specifically for borderline personality disorder and built around emotion regulation, mindfulness, distress tolerance, and interpersonal effectiveness modules, is the outpatient treatment tied to managing this population. Involuntary inpatient commitment criteria (danger to self or others, or gravely disabled) versus involuntary outpatient commitment (mentally ill but capable of surviving safely in the community with supports) determine whether active or passive suicidality requires hospitalization or can be managed in the outpatient clinic. The strongest legal protection when managing such a patient outpatient is a regular, documented suicide risk assessment -- a safety contract made without a careful assessment offers no legal protection, and a family's promise to monitor the patient does not transfer the physician's responsibility.

🧠
Memory hook · Borderline flips in minutes with a trigger; bipolar shifts in weeks without oneBPD mood swings are rapid + interpersonally triggered; bipolar episodes last days-to-weeks and don't need a trigger. DBT's four modules = MEDI: Mindfulness, Emotion regulation, Distress tolerance, Interpersonal effectiveness.
🧠
Memory hook · SAD PERSONS, and who dies vs. who triesSex(M) · Age · Depression · Previous attempt (#1 risk factor) · Ethanol · Rational-thought loss · Sickness · Organized plan · No support · Stated intent. Women attempt more; men die more (lethal means). The documented assessment (C-SSRS) is your legal shield — a safety contract without one protects no one.
◐
Missing from your notesA concrete outpatient safety-planning protocol (means restriction, follow-up scheduling, a structured safety plan) is still absent; neither the child psychiatry nor the neuroanatomy lecture addresses outpatient suicide risk management.

Pulled from: Personality Disorders · Introduction & History of Psychiatry · Legal Psychiatric Medicine · Introduction to Therapy · Mood Disorders · Anxiety, OCD & Trauma-Related Disorders

🧠
Para-suicidal behavior — behavior that looks like self-harm/suicide on the surface, but isn't intended to end in death; the intent is to feel physical pain, or to get someone else to notice, acknowledge, and support them. Dr. Smith's memory hook, straight from organic chemistry: para- as in para-dimethylbenzene means "opposite" — para-suicidal is, functionally, the opposite of suicidal, even though it can look identical from the outside.
💡
Cutting (classically wrists or thighs), head-banging, or burning with cigarettes — the goal in the vast majority of cases is not suicide. It's to generate physical pain that distracts from unbearable emotional pain (the same underlying logic as trichotillomania's hair-pulling as anxiety distraction). If a patient with BPD does die by suicide, it's typically accidental — e.g., someone overdoses on pills and calls their boyfriend to be "rescued" as part of the pattern, and if he's delayed by traffic and doesn't arrive in time, death results from a gesture that was never actually intended to be lethal.
Involuntary — Inpatient Criteria*Involuntary — Outpatient Criteria*
Danger to self or othersMentally ill, and capable of surviving safely in the community with supports
Gravely disabledBased on psychiatric history, respondent is in need of treatment to prevent further deterioration
In need of protection or treatment for health/safety because of a mental disorderCurrent mental status negates/limits the ability to voluntarily comply with treatment
🛡️
Your best defense against a suicide-related malpractice claim: regular, documented assessment showing a lack of suicidality — e.g., using a structured tool like the Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale. You are not expected to predict the future — only to act on what was predictable/foreseeable. If the patient gave no indication of suicidality, failing to intervene is not a deviation from the standard of care. The proof of this is documentation of ongoing suicide risk assessment, not any single note.

Contracting for Safety ≠ Protection

A safety contract made in the absence of a careful suicide assessment offers no legal protection. It's the assessment — not the contract — that protects the physician.

Family Promises ≠ Your Responsibility Transferred

A family's promise to monitor a patient does not absolve the physician of responsibility if the patient is suicidal and no assessment/intervention occurred.

Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) ⭐ HY

Created by Marsha Linehan, PhD — for borderline personality disorder
StructureA skills-based, manualized treatment built around 4 modules: emotion regulation, mindfulness, distress tolerance, and interpersonal effectiveness.
OriginLinehan developed DBT partly from her own lived experience with BPD — she has spoken publicly (including in a well-known New York Times profile) about how the treatment reflects what helped her.
Also used forAdapted well beyond BPD to many other conditions, but the BPD connection is the one to remember for exams.
🔑 Gold Standards to Memorize Verbatim

Gold standard for depression: therapy + medication combined. Gold standard for mania: lithium. Severe depression sometimes warrants brief hospitalization even without acute safety risk — not because outpatient treatment can't work, but because an inpatient setting allows faster titration and augmentation of medications than a normal 4–6 week outpatient follow-up cadence would allow.

Question 5
A patient dies by suicide two weeks after a routine outpatient visit at which no suicidal ideation was elicited or documented as absent. The family sues for malpractice. What is most likely to determine the outcome?
A. Whether the psychiatrist could have predicted the suicide with certainty
B. Whether there is documentation of an ongoing, adequate suicide risk assessment showing no indication of suicidality
C. Whether the patient had signed a safety contract
D. Whether the patient's family had agreed to monitor them
Answer: B. Documentation of ongoing assessment is the actual legal defense (Section 07) — physicians aren't required to predict the future, only to act on the foreseeable. A safety contract (C) or family monitoring (D) alone offers no legal protection without a real underlying assessment.

Core Principle

PurposeSeclusion should be used only to protect the immediate physical safety of the patient and staff.
Least restrictive alternative applies here tooIf a patient can be treated as an outpatient, they should not be kept in the hospital. If they can be treated in an open setting, seclusion should not be used.
📋
Example: a 28-year-old woman becomes bitter and angry when her husband of 5 years leaves her for a younger man. One week later she quits her job with no notice and begins drinking heavily; over the following weeks she calls friends reporting passive suicidal ideation and makes several threatening calls to the new boyfriend — note the mixed presentation (anxiety/depression + disturbed conduct) tied directly and proportionally to a real, recent stressor.
LO 030Somatoform, Dissoc. & Sexual✓ In your notes

Provide a differential diagnosis for "regression" in an adult due to past sexual trauma

Answer

Regression is a psychodynamic defense mechanism in which a person reverts to behaviors of an earlier developmental stage already achieved, distinct from fixation (being stuck at a stage never fully progressed past). In an adult with a history of sexual trauma, the differential includes dissociative identity disorder, thought to result from severe early-childhood trauma (often repetitive physical, sexual, or emotional abuse) with dissociation acting as a protective mechanism that lets the mind compartmentalize unbearable experience; dissociative fugue, in which a person is found away from home under a different identity with no memory of how they got there; and depersonalization/derealization disorder, in which a person feels detached from their body or surroundings while retaining insight that the feelings are not literally true. Conversion disorder belongs on the differential too, classically marked by la belle indifference -- an unconcerned affect despite a dramatic neurological complaint (e.g., sudden blindness) unsupported by exam or imaging. Somatoform, factitious, and malingering presentations round out the differential and are split by whether symptom production is unconscious (somatoform) or consciously produced for external gain (malingering) versus the internal/primary gain of the sick role (factitious disorder).

🧠
Memory hook · The three-branch deception treeSymptoms unconscious → somatoform spectrum. Conscious, to live the sick role (internal gain) → factitious. Conscious, for money/court/drugs (external gain) → malingering (not a psychiatric diagnosis). Vignette tells: thick chart, many specialists, normal workups.
🧠
Memory hook · Reality testing is the dissociation/psychosis borderDepersonalization/derealization keeps intact reality testing ('I know this isn't literally true') — that's what separates it from psychosis. Fugue = travel + identity amnesia (a specifier of dissociative amnesia, not its own diagnosis). DID ← severe early childhood trauma.

Pulled from: Introduction to Therapy · Sexual, Somatoform & Dissociative Disorders · Anxiety, OCD & Trauma-Related Disorders

Two commonly confused pairs: repression (unconscious, involuntary) vs. suppression (conscious, deliberate); and fixation (stuck at a stage, never fully progressed) vs. regression (moving backward from a stage already reached).

💡
DID is thought to result from severe trauma during early childhood — usually extreme, repetitive physical, sexual, or emotional abuse. The dissociation is theorized as a protective/coping mechanism that allows the developing mind to compartmentalize unbearable experience.
Topics
3 lecture parts, 1 combined handout
Core Split
Unconscious (somatoform) vs. conscious (factitious/malingering) symptom production
Boards Fact
Malingering = external gain; Factitious = sick role (internal/primary gain)
High-Yield
La belle indifférence · DID alters · Paraphilia vs. paraphilic disorder

Yield check: This handout stitches together three shorter lecture segments that all share a theme: symptoms without a clear organic explanation — whether that's a physical complaint (somatoform spectrum), a break in the continuity of identity/memory/reality (dissociative spectrum), or a pattern of sexual functioning or interest (sexual disorders). The single highest-yield organizing question across the whole handout is: is production of the symptom conscious or unconscious — and if conscious, is the goal external gain (malingering) or the sick role itself (factitious disorder)?

Section 01 · Part I
Question 6
A woman reports recurrently "losing time" — finding herself in unfamiliar places with no memory of how she got there. Her family reports that she sometimes speaks in a markedly different voice and refers to herself by another name. She has a history of severe, repeated childhood abuse. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A. Dissociative amnesia with fugue
B. Dissociative identity disorder
C. Depersonalization/derealization disorder
D. Brief psychotic disorder
Answer: B. Distinct personality states (a different voice, a different name) plus recurrent gaps in recall, on a background of severe early childhood trauma, is the DID picture (Section 07) — distinguished from simple dissociative amnesia by the presence of actual alternate identity states, not just memory gaps alone.
Question 7
A man is found 300 miles from home with no memory of his identity. It's discovered he has been living under a different name for the past two weeks. No substance use or medical cause is identified on workup. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A. Dissociative identity disorder
B. Dissociative amnesia, with dissociative fugue
C. Depersonalization/derealization disorder
D. Malingering
Answer: B. Apparently purposeful travel (or bewildered wandering) associated with amnesia for identity is the definition of the dissociative fugue specifier (Section 08) — coded alongside dissociative amnesia, not as a stand-alone diagnosis.
Question 8
A patient describes feeling, during panic attacks, as though she is "watching herself from outside her body," and says the world sometimes seems "foggy and unreal." She is clear, however, that she knows these feelings are not literally true. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A. Brief psychotic disorder
B. Depersonalization/derealization disorder
C. Dissociative identity disorder
D. Schizotypal personality disorder
Answer: B. Out-of-body-type detachment from self (depersonalization) plus a foggy/unreal perception of the environment (derealization), with reality testing intact (she knows it isn't literally true), is exactly Criterion A + B of depersonalization/derealization disorder (Section 09) — intact reality testing is what rules out a primary psychotic process.
Question 1
A 22-year-old woman develops sudden-onset blindness shortly after witnessing a fatal car accident. Neurological exam, imaging, and ophthalmologic workup are all normal. She describes her vision loss matter-of-factly and seems remarkably unconcerned about being unable to see. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A. Malingering
B. Illness anxiety disorder
C. Conversion disorder
D. Factitious disorder
Answer: C. Sudden loss of a sensory/motor function following an acute stressor, with a normal workup and la belle indifférence — a striking lack of concern about the deficit — is the textbook picture of conversion disorder (Section 02).

Vignette pattern · Somatoform spectrum (unconscious symptom production)

Presenting complaints — dramatic, multiple, and peculiar complaints; extreme anxiety or a profound lack of anxiety about minor medical problems; medical complaints presenting alongside clear psychological issues.
History — often vague; complex medical problems abound; multiple past workups with inconclusive findings; a trail of past or current treatment by many different physicians.
Mental status exam — may show anxiety, or a peculiar indifference to significant medical complaints (echoing la belle indifférence from Section 02).
Physical exam/labs — often inconsistent with the medical complaints, or don't map onto any known physiological mechanism.

Vignette pattern · Factitious disorder & malingering (conscious symptom production)

Presenting complaints — dramatic, peculiar, and changing medical complaints, often with an identifiable environmental incentive for illness lurking in the background.
History — vague/complex medical problems; guardedness about revealing past complaints or assessments; multiple inconclusive past workups; treatment by many physicians; a history of signing out of hospitals against medical advice (AMA); noncompliance with treatment/diagnostics.
Mental status exam — anxiety, peculiar indifference to significant complaints, and (a real tell) extreme familiarity with medical terminology or procedures — often beyond what a layperson would know.
Physical exam/labs — inconsistent with known physiological mechanisms; possible signs of multiple prior surgical procedures.

Psychodynamic psychotherapy

Approach
Help the patient understand how unconscious drives, suppressed experiences, past conflicts, and past relationships are shaping their present.
Limitations
Pays limited attention to current/present-day events; usually a long treatment course; cost can limit access.

Exactly the same principle as psychotic disorders: before diagnosing a primary anxiety disorder, exclude medical and substance causes. Naming convention: "anxiety disorder due to [hyperthyroidism]" or "substance/medication-induced anxiety disorder due to [heroin]." This distinction also matters for realistic, situationally-appropriate fear — e.g., a patient with severe COPD who feels anxious because they genuinely can't breathe isn't having a primary anxiety disorder; that's a rational response to reality (though if the anxiety becomes disproportionate to the medical threat, it could be coded "anxiety disorder due to COPD exacerbation").

LO 031Somatoform, Dissoc. & Sexual✓ In your notes

Provide a differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with what appears to be a somatic delusion

Answer

Delusional disorder (somatic type) is marked by a single fixed, non-bizarre false belief about the body with preserved functioning and organized thought process, and insight retained into every other area of life except the delusion itself — illustrated by the classic "serpent around the brain" patient discussed in this unit. It must be distinguished from the somatoform-spectrum conditions, which involve unconscious symptom production without a true fixed delusion: somatic symptom disorder (multi-system complaints for months to years with excessive, persistent thoughts about the symptoms, sometimes alongside a real medical condition) and illness anxiety disorder. Diagnostic clues favoring a somatoform disorder over a true delusion include a thick chart, multiple past workups with inconsistent findings, and a symptom picture that doesn't fit a single organic disease process. Because psychosis is a symptom rather than a diagnosis, any new somatic delusion should also prompt the standard primary (psychiatric) versus secondary (organic) workup for psychosis.

🧠
Memory hook · Blind but unbotheredSudden neuro deficit + normal workup + la belle indifférence (strangely unconcerned) = conversion disorder. Fear of illness with no symptoms = illness anxiety; months of multi-system symptoms + obsessive worry about them = somatic symptom disorder.

Pulled from: Psychotic Disorders & Antipsychotic Pharmacology · Sexual, Somatoform & Dissociative Disorders · Personality Disorders

🔎
Preserved functioning is the hallmark: delusions are often not overtly bizarre, thought process stays organized, and overall functioning is largely intact except relative to the delusion itself. Patients can appear entirely normal to the world except when the delusion surfaces — which the public may find "odd" but not overtly bizarre. As a result, this is often subclinical for years to decades before presenting to clinical attention.

Somatic Symptom Disorder

PictureA variety of complaints across one or more organ systems, lasting months to years, associated with excessive and persistent thoughts about the symptoms. May genuinely co-occur with real medical conditions — the psychological preoccupation is disproportionate to whatever organic pathology is (or isn't) present.
VideoNone available for this one per the handout.

Illness Anxiety Disorder (Hypochondriasis)

PicturePreoccupation with and fear of having a serious medical illness, despite medical evidence and reassurance to the contrary. Unlike somatic symptom disorder, the somatic symptoms themselves may be minimal or absent — it's the fear/preoccupation that's the disorder.
▶ Illness anxiety disorder case 🔒 UNE

Conversion Disorder

Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder
PictureSudden loss of sensory or motor function — paralysis, blindness, mutism — often following an acute stressor. Classically more common in females, young adults, and adolescents.
Signature findingLa belle indifférence — the patient is aware of the symptom but shows a striking, disproportionate lack of concern about it.
▶ Conversion disorder case 🔒 UNE
Master split
Unconscious production (somatic symptom, illness anxiety, conversion) vs. conscious production (malingering, factitious).
Somatic symptom disorder
Multi-system complaints, months-years, excessive/persistent thoughts about symptoms.
Illness anxiety disorder
Fear of serious illness despite reassurance; minimal actual symptoms.
Conversion disorder
Sudden sensory/motor loss after a stressor; la belle indifférence; F > M, young.
Malingering
External gain; complaints STOP once gain achieved; avoids invasive workups.
Factitious disorder
Sick role = primary gain; WELCOMES invasive procedures; Munchausen = chronic physical form.
Munchausen by proxy
Illness caused in a child/elder by caregiver; mandatory reporting, = abuse.
DID criteria
≥2 distinct personality states + recurrent amnesia gaps; early childhood trauma.
DID alter patterns
Mutually aware / mutually unaware / one aware, not reciprocated.
DID vs. PTSD
Ongoing field debate: is DID distinct, or severe/chronic PTSD with dissociative features?
Dissociative amnesia
Localized/selective vs. generalized; info not permanently lost, just unretrievable.
Dissociative fugue
A SPECIFIER of dissociative amnesia (not separate dx) — purposeful travel/wandering + identity amnesia.
Amnesia/fugue course
Usually adult-onset, rapid onset/resolution, F > M; most recover spontaneously.
Depersonalization
Altered perception of SELF (detachment, out-of-body).
Derealization
Altered perception of ENVIRONMENT (foggy, dreamlike, unreal).
Depersonalization/derealization key
Reality testing INTACT — this is what separates it from psychosis.
Sexual dysfunction classification
DSM-5 lists alphabetically (no agreed sexual-response model) — replaced Masters & Johnson's 4-stage cycle.
Psychogenic vs. physiologic ED
Preserved nocturnal/morning erections → psychogenic. Absent → physiologic.
Paraphilia vs. paraphilic disorder
Paraphilia = atypical interest (ascertained). Disorder = + distress/impairment/harm to others (diagnosed).
8 named paraphilic disorders
Fetishistic, transvestic, pedohebephilic, voyeuristic, exhibitionistic, frotteuristic, sexual sadism, sexual masochism.
Non-consent paraphilias
Voyeuristic, exhibitionistic, frotteuristic — inherently involve a non-consenting party.
Paraphilia treatment
Incorporation therapy, psychotherapy, orgasmic reconditioning, drug therapy (antiandrogens/SSRIs).
Hypersexuality red flags
Brain injury, Klüver-Bucy, Kleine-Levin, dopamine agonists (mesolimbic overactivity) — rule out before assuming psychiatric.

Vignette pattern · Somatoform spectrum

Presenting complaints — dramatic, multiple, and peculiar complaints; extreme anxiety or a profound lack of anxiety about minor medical problems; medical complaints presenting alongside clear psychological issues.
History — often vague; complex medical problems abound; multiple past workups with inconclusive findings; a trail of past or current treatment by many different physicians.
Mental status exam — may show anxiety, or a peculiar indifference to significant medical complaints (echoing la belle indifférence from Section 02).
Physical exam/labs — often inconsistent with the medical complaints, or don't map onto any known physiological mechanism.
🩺
Reading this pattern as a vignette: a patient with a thick chart, a long list of specialists already seen, normal or inconsistent workups, and a symptom picture that doesn't fit any single organic disease process is the classic setup for a somatoform-spectrum diagnosis. The specific disorder then comes down to what kind of complaint dominates (diffuse multi-system complaints → somatic symptom disorder; fear of illness despite reassurance → illness anxiety disorder; a discrete neurological deficit → conversion disorder).
🎙️
The "serpent around the brain" patient — likely a familiar callback: Dr. Smith references a "serpent around brain" patient story for dependent PD in lecture. This is almost certainly the same patient discussed under delusional disorder, somatic type, in the psychotic disorders unit — a woman with a decades-long somatic delusion of a snake coiled around her brain, whose headaches were ultimately traced to undiagnosed opiate withdrawal, and who Dr. Smith followed for 3–4 years afterward. If so, the callback here is to a different facet of the same patient: beyond the somatic delusion itself, her intense, prolonged reliance on her physicians for reassurance and care is a textbook illustration of dependent traits layered on top of (or entangled with) her delusional disorder. Worth confirming against your own lecture notes if you want the exact framing he used.
📌
Boards-relevant nuance: delusional disorder is one of the few DSM-5 conditions with preserved functioning and minimal impairment across most life domains. There is no insight into the delusion itself, though the patient retains insight into the rest of their life — a combination that's fairly unique among psychotic disorders.

LO 032Neurocognitive & AMS◐ Partly covered

Provide a differential diagnosis for altered mental status

Answer

Altered mental status calls for a structured rule-out sequence: first exclude malingering or factitious production of symptoms, then rule out a substance etiology (intoxication, withdrawal, or a medication side effect), and then rule out an underlying general medical condition before attributing the picture to a primary psychiatric illness, since a missed medical or drug cause treated as a psychiatric diagnosis is a recurring exam theme. When AMS is secondary to another condition, treating the underlying cause is the priority. Documented medication/toxin causes include serotonin syndrome (the '3 A's': increased activity, autonomic instability, altered mental status), lithium toxicity at levels above 1.2 (nausea, diarrhea, altered mental status, severe tremor, ataxia, slurred speech, hyperreflexia, polyuria, seizure), and valproate-induced hyperammonemic delirium, which is not strictly dose-dependent and warrants an ammonia level in any confused patient on valproate.

🧠
Memory hook · The universal rule-out ladderFaking? → Substance (intox/withdrawal/med)? → Medical? → only then primary psychiatric. AMS culprits from this course: serotonin syndrome (3 A's), lithium >1.2, valproate hyperammonemia (check ammonia at any dose).
◐
Missing from your notesA systematic organic differential for AMS (infection/sepsis, metabolic derangement, hepatic/renal failure, hypoglycemia, structural CNS lesions, hypoxia) is still not present; the neuroanatomy lecture covers only limbic/basal-ganglia circuitry and monoamine systems, not a clinical AMS workup, and the child psychiatry lecture does not address AMS.

Pulled from: Introduction & History of Psychiatry · Mood Disorders · Psychotic Disorders & Antipsychotic Pharmacology · Addiction & Non-Clinical Drug Use

  1. Rule out Malingering & Factitious DisorderIs the person intentionally producing/feigning symptoms (for external gain, or for the sick role itself)?
  2. Rule out a substance etiologyIntoxication, withdrawal, or a medication side effect mimicking psychiatric illness.
  3. Rule out an etiological medical conditionE.g. thyroid disease, a CNS lesion, a metabolic derangement.
  4. — Only now can you diagnose a primary mental illness —
  5. Determine the specific primary psychiatric disorder(s)Pick from the DSM-5-TR's 365 diagnoses.
  6. Differentiate Adjustment Disorder from residual Other Specified/Unspecified categories
  7. Establish the boundary with no mental disorderDistress that doesn't rise to a diagnosable condition.
🚨
The single most important idea in this whole section: always rule out a drug-induced or general medical cause before diagnosing a primary psychiatric illness. Medical/drug causes are treatable with medical therapy; a missed medical cause treated as "just depression" with antidepressant after antidepressant is a classic, avoidable failure mode.
🔀
Primary psychiatric disorder: one of the 365 DSM-5-TR diagnoses in its own right. Secondary psychiatric disorder: psychiatric symptoms caused by something else entirely — e.g. hypothyroidism-induced depressive disorder. The distinction matters clinically: if it's secondary, treating the underlying medical problem can resolve the "psychiatric" symptoms too.
🔑 First Aid Mnemonic — 3 A's

↑Activity (neuromuscular: clonus, hyperreflexia, hypertonia, tremor, seizure) · Autonomic instability (hyperthermia, diaphoresis, diarrhea) · Altered mental status

☐ Lithium Toxicity — level >1.2

Nausea, diarrhea, altered mental status, severe tremor, ataxia, slurred speech, hyperreflexia, polyuria, seizure. Treatment: stop lithium, hydrate; consider dialysis in severe cases.

🩺 Clinical Pearl — Check an Ammonia Level

Valproate can cause a hyperammonemic delirium — a confused, altered patient on valproate should prompt an ammonia level, regardless of whether the dose "seems low." This isn't strictly dose-dependent, and it can happen at any point in treatment. Catching this is a small detail that reads as genuine clinical fluency. (Weight gain and hair loss are also worth knowing as the reasons patients often stop taking valproate on their own.)

LO 033Somatoform, Dissoc. & Sexual✓ In your notes

Provide a differential diagnosis for the paraphilias relating to sexual deviance

Answer

DSM-5 recognizes 8 named paraphilic disorders defined by their object of sexual attraction: fetishistic (an inanimate object), transvestic (cross-dressing), pedohebephilic (children), voyeuristic (watching unsuspecting others), exhibitionistic (exposing genitals to an unwilling stranger), frotteuristic, and others in the full table. A paraphilia — any intense, persistent sexual interest outside attraction to genital stimulation with phenotypically normal, consenting adult partners — only becomes a paraphilic disorder when it causes the individual distress or impairment, or causes harm to others; voyeuristic, exhibitionistic, and frotteuristic disorders by definition involve a non-consenting party, as does any sexual contact with a child. Less-common named interests without their own DSM-5 category, such as asphyxiophilia (arousal linked to self-induced oxygen restriction, with real accidental-death risk), are coded as other specified paraphilic disorder when they cause distress, impairment, or harm. Treatment ranges from psychotherapy and orgasmic reconditioning to androgen-lowering agents or high-dose SSRIs, which reduce the intensity/frequency of sexual drive rather than cure the underlying interest.

🧠
Memory hook · An interest isn't an illnessParaphilia → paraphilic disorder only with distress, impairment, or harm. Voyeuristic, exhibitionistic, frotteuristic (and anything with children) involve a non-consenting party → disorder by definition. Tx: therapy, orgasmic reconditioning, androgen-lowering agents, high-dose SSRIs.

Exhibitionistic disorderExposing one's genitals to an unwilling stranger

The 8 named paraphilic disorders in DSM-5, with their object of sexual attraction/interest

📌
A paraphilic disorder is a paraphilia that causes distress or impairment to the individual, or harm to others. This distinction matters clinically and diagnostically: you would ascertain a paraphilia based on actions and self-report (e.g., a self-reported sexual attraction to amputees or inanimate objects), but you only diagnose a paraphilic disorder once distress, impairment, or harm to others is actually present. Having an atypical sexual interest is not, by itself, a psychiatric diagnosis under DSM-5's framework — the disorder label requires the added element of distress/impairment/harm.
📖
DSM-5 definition: a paraphilia denotes any intense and persistent sexual interest other than sexual interest in genital stimulation or preparatory fondling with phenotypically normal, consenting adult human partners.
⚖️
Legal note relevant to several of these: voyeuristic, exhibitionistic, and frotteuristic disorders by definition involve a non-consenting other party — as does any sexual contact with a child. These aren't simply private preferences; they involve actual or potential harm to others, which is part of why they clear the "paraphilic disorder" bar regardless of the individual's own reported distress level.

A longer list of less-common named paraphilias that don't have their own dedicated DSM-5 diagnostic category — coded as "other specified paraphilic disorder" when they cause distress, impairment, or harm

💡
Asphyxiophilia — a newer area of discussion in DSM-5, referring to sexual arousal linked to self-induced oxygen restriction; it's clinically significant partly because of the real risk of accidental death, distinct from its classification questions as a paraphilia per se.
💊
Pharmacologic mechanism, in practice: the drug therapy referenced here is typically androgen-lowering treatment (e.g., antiandrogens, GnRH agonists) or high-dose SSRIs — both work by reducing the intensity/frequency of sexual drive and intrusive sexual thoughts, rather than "curing" the underlying paraphilic interest itself. This is most relevant in court-ordered or high-risk treatment settings where reducing the frequency of harmful behavior is the primary clinical/legal goal.
Incorporation therapy — the paraphilic behavior is decreased or modified to more acceptable levels, without aiming for complete abolition
Psychotherapy — talk therapy
Orgasmic reconditioning — a conditioning-based therapy where the person is trained to become aroused and achieve orgasm in a socially acceptable context that bears no resemblance to the paraphilic stimulus
Drug therapy — used when a brain/glandular chemical imbalance is contributing to unwanted, inappropriate sexual behavior; medications may help alter the production or effects of those chemicals

LO 035Child & Adolescent✓ In your notes

Provide a differential diagnosis of anxiety and trauma disorders in children

Answer

In a child with anxiety or trauma symptoms, the DSM-5 differential draws from three chapters split out from the old single "anxiety disorders" chapter: anxiety disorders (separation anxiety disorder, selective mutism, specific phobia, social anxiety disorder, panic disorder, generalized anxiety disorder), OCD and related disorders, and trauma/stressor-related disorders. Separation anxiety disorder affects about 4% of school-age children (F>M, familial pattern, often in close-knit families where a parent's own separation anxiety is "copied" by the child), presenting as excessive fear of separation from attachment figures — illustrated by a 6-year-old boy who worries "bad men" will abduct his mother. Selective mutism presents as a child who behaves and speaks normally at home but refuses to speak in specific settings such as school, as in a 9-year-old who never raises her hand or speaks in class. The underlying model taught for these disorders is serotonin-mediated dysfunction plus limbic system hyperactivity.

🧠
Memory hook · The copied worrySeparation anxiety (~4% of school kids, F>M) often mirrors a parent's own — 'bad men will take mom.' Selective mutism: chatty at home, silent at school. Model for both: serotonin dysfunction + limbic hyperactivity.

Pulled from: Anxiety, OCD & Trauma-Related Disorders

Separation Anxiety Disorder

Excessive fear/anxiety about separation from attachment figures
Epidemiology4% of school-aged children; F > M; familial pattern — often close-knit families where a parent's own undue anxiety about separation gets "copied" by the child. Exposure to traumatic separation is also a predisposing factor.
Diagnostic criteriaExcessive/persistent anxiety about caregivers abandoning them, plus fantastic worries — often producing school refusal, academic difficulty, comorbid depression, and family conflict over separation. Kids may worry harm will befall parents, become reluctant to leave home for fear of never seeing them again, and frequently feign illness to avoid leaving.
CourseSymptoms exacerbate with acute stress, death of a relative, abuse, etc. — always look for a trigger; treating the trigger often resolves the disorder. Symptoms wax and wane.
TreatmentIdentify the trigger and use therapy to help the child understand and cope with it differently. Medication (anxiolytics or antidepressants) may help but only in combination with behavioral psychotherapy and family therapy — serotonergic antidepressants are first-line if medication is used.
▶ Separation anxiety disorder case 🔒 UNE

1. Anxiety Disorders

IncludesSeparation anxiety disorder, selective mutism, specific phobia, social anxiety disorder (social phobia), panic disorder, generalized anxiety disorder.

2. Obsessive-Compulsive & Related Disorders

IncludesOCD, body dysmorphic disorder, hoarding disorder, trichotillomania, excoriation (skin-picking) disorder.

3. Trauma & Stressor-Related Disorders

IncludesReactive attachment disorder, disinhibited social engagement disorder, PTSD, acute stress disorder, adjustment disorders.
Question 1
A 6-year-old boy constantly worries that "bad men" will come to his house and abduct his mother while he's at school. He has recently begun refusing to get on the school bus, and reports hearing his mom "yelling" in her bedroom when she doesn't know he's home. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A. Generalized anxiety disorder
B. Separation anxiety disorder
C. Specific phobia
D. Adjustment disorder with anxiety
E. Panic disorder
Answer: B. The anxiety is specifically about separation from an attachment figure (his mother) and possible harm befalling her — the defining feature of separation anxiety disorder (Section 02), not a diffuse worry (GAD), a discrete object/situation (specific phobia), or an identifiable external stressor (adjustment disorder).
Question 2
Two months after starting at a new school, a 9-year-old girl's teacher reports she never raises her hand and refuses to speak to anyone in class, even when called on directly. At home, she interacts completely normally with family. Psychiatric exam is otherwise unremarkable. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A. Autism spectrum disorder
B. Social anxiety disorder
C. Selective mutism
D. Separation anxiety disorder
Answer: C. Failure to speak in one specific venue (school) despite normal speech elsewhere (home), lasting >1 month, with an otherwise unremarkable exam, is the definition of selective mutism (Section 02) — not autism (no other developmental/social-communication abnormalities are described) and not separation anxiety (no fear of separation from caregivers is described).
Topics
3 DSM-5 chapters + anxiolytic pharm
Core Model
Serotonin dysfunction + limbic hyperactivity
Boards Fact
Acute stress d/o = "brief psychotic disorder" of anxiety (3d–1mo)
High-Yield
LOT benzos · GAD-7 · PTSD A–H criteria

Yield check: DSM-5 split the old "anxiety disorders" chapter into three separate sections — Anxiety Disorders, Obsessive-Compulsive & Related Disorders, and Trauma- & Stressor-Related Disorders. Dr. Smith flags several timeline traps here too — acute stress disorder vs. PTSD (1 month cutoff), and adjustment disorder's "within 3 months / resolves within 6 months" rule — plus the LOT benzodiazepines (lorazepam/oxazepam/temazepam) that skip Phase I hepatic metabolism entirely. These get dedicated callouts below.

Section 01
LO 036Anxiety, OCD & Trauma✓ In your notes

Provide a differential diagnosis of conditions in the anxiety disorder section of the DSM5

Answer

DSM-5's anxiety disorders chapter includes separation anxiety disorder, selective mutism, specific phobia, social anxiety disorder (social phobia), panic disorder, and generalized anxiety disorder — split from a single DSM-IV-TR chapter into three separate chapters (anxiety, OCD-related, and trauma/stressor-related). Panic attacks are not exclusive to panic disorder and occur across GAD, OCD, and social phobia as well, so panic disorder specifically requires frequent, spontaneous attacks plus additional behavioral change, not just an isolated attack (1:2 male:female ratio, 2% prevalence). Agoraphobia (fear of being unable to escape a crowded/open situation) and panic disorder were unlinked in DSM-5 and are now separate, co-occurring diagnoses rather than agoraphobia being a specifier of panic disorder. GAD requires excessive, poorly-controlled worry for >6 months with at least 3 of restlessness, fatigue, poor concentration, irritability, muscle tension, or sleep disturbance (only 1 required if mood is irritable-predominant), with a GAD-7 score ≥10 suggesting a probable diagnosis; GAD affects about 5% of the population (2:3 male:female). Social anxiety disorder (F>M, 2% point/10% lifetime prevalence) can occur alongside avoidant personality traits.

🧠
Memory hook · GAD: 3-of-6 for 6 monthsExcessive worry >6 months + ≥3 of: restlessness, fatigue, poor concentration, irritability, muscle tension, sleep problems (GAD-7 ≥10 supports it). Panic disorder needs recurrent spontaneous attacks + a month of worry/behavior change — an attack alone can happen in any anxiety disorder.

A panic attack isn't exclusive to panic disorder — the same attack phenomenology shows up as a feature of several other conditions.

Panic attacks can occur in panic disorder (frequent, spontaneous), GAD (constant worry + physical symptoms), OCD (excessive repetitive thoughts/behaviors), social phobia (embarrassment/humiliation in social situations), and PTSD (thoughts/experiences of a horrible event)

Literally "fear of the marketplace" — not a fear of crowds itself, but fear of being unable to escape a crowded/open situation, which itself provokes extreme anxiety. A patient with agoraphobia can often tolerate a crowd fine as long as they know they can get out. Per DSM-5, agoraphobia and panic disorder are now unlinked as separate diagnoses (a change from earlier editions) — see Section 05.

📌
Boards-relevant change: in DSM-5, panic disorder and agoraphobia are unlinked — they're now separate diagnoses that can co-occur, rather than agoraphobia being coded as a specifier of panic disorder as in earlier editions.

Full DSM-5 criteria A–J for social anxiety disorder — note criterion I (not better explained by panic disorder, BDD, or autism) and the "performance only" specifier

🎯
Core features: excessive, poorly-controlled anxiety/worry about routine life circumstances, present >6 months, hard for the patient to control, impairing daily function. Requires ≥3 of: restlessness, easily fatigued, poor concentration, irritability, muscle tension, sleep disturbance (only 1 item required in children).

Epidemiology: 1:2 male:female ratio; 2% prevalence. Panic disorder = panic attacks (defined below) plus additional behavioral criteria — a panic attack alone does not equal panic disorder.

Full DSM-5 GAD criteria A–F, including the differential-diagnosis exclusions in criterion F

Question 5
On the GAD-7, what total score threshold suggests a probable diagnosis of GAD warranting further clinical evaluation?
A. ≥5
B. ≥10
C. ≥15
D. ≥20
Answer: B. A GAD-7 score of ≥10 suggests a probable GAD diagnosis warranting confirmatory evaluation (Section 06). 5/10/15 are rough severity anchors for mild/moderate/severe, respectively, once the diagnosis is under consideration.

LO 037Mood & Mood Stabilizers✓ In your notes

Provide a differential diagnosis of hypomania

Answer

The differential for a hypomanic-appearing presentation centers on whether the episode is true hypomania, mania, or part of another cyclical mood pattern. Using DIGFAST (distractibility, impulsivity, grandiosity, flight of ideas, activity increase, decreased sleep need, talkativeness), hypomania requires ≥3 symptoms (4+ if mood is only irritable) lasting only ≥4 days with no significant impairment, no hospitalization, and no psychosis — mapping to Bipolar II (≥1 hypomanic episode plus ≥1 major depressive episode, never a manic episode) or cyclothymic disorder (≥2 years of numerous hypomanic- and depressive-symptom periods that never meet full mania or MDE criteria). Mania requires the same core symptoms but lasting ≥7 days, or requiring hospitalization, or including psychosis, plus significant impairment — a single manic episode reclassifies the patient as Bipolar I even with a well-documented prior history of Bipolar II. Unlike most DSM-5 diagnoses, hypomania is non-impairing by definition, so Bipolar II (like delusional disorder) is one of the few conditions that does not require impairment to diagnose.

🧠
Memory hook · Mania is a 7-day week; hypomania a 4-day workweekDIGFAST ≥3 (4 if only irritable): ≥7 days OR hospital OR psychosis + impairment = mania → Bipolar I (depression not required). ≥4 days, fully functional, no psychosis = hypomania; + ≥1 MDE and never mania = Bipolar II. One manic episode ever → converts to Bipolar I forever.

Pulled from: Mood Disorders · Psychotic Disorders & Antipsychotic Pharmacology

If a manic episode ever occurs, the diagnosis is Bipolar I regardless of prior hypomanic/depressive history.

🌪️

Mania

  • Lasts 7 days
  • OR requires hospitalization
  • OR includes psychosis
  • AND causes significant impairment
🌤️

Hypomania

  • Only has to last 4 days
  • Does not cause significant impairment
  • No psychosis, no hospitalization

Bipolar I (full mania possible) vs. Bipolar II (ceiling = hypomania) over time

🧸 ELI5 — The Upside of Hypomania

Unlike full mania, hypomania doesn't cause significant impairment — and it can even look like a benefit. Think of the stereotypical high-achieving CEO or the physician who's constantly producing research: less need for sleep, more energy, bigger ideas. This is exactly why hypomania and even mania can be hard to treat clinically — patients often don't want the feeling to go away, because subjectively it feels good, even though objectively it's often unsustainable or a warning sign of worse to come.

🧸 ELI5 — Hurricane vs. Tropical Storm

Mania is a hurricane: it can flatten your house (impairment), force an evacuation (hospitalization), or come with a storm surge that distorts reality (psychosis) — and it sticks around for a full week. Hypomania is a tropical storm: strong winds people definitely notice, but it doesn't damage the house, doesn't require an evacuation, and moves through in as little as 4 days.

DisorderRequired episodes
Bipolar I≥1 manic episode (may be preceded/followed by hypomanic or MDEs — not required)
Bipolar II≥1 hypomanic episode + ≥1 MDE, never a manic or mixed episode
Cyclothymic disorder≥2 years of numerous hypomanic-symptom periods + numerous depressive-symptom periods, never meeting full episode criteria, symptom-free gaps never >2 months
🧸 ELI5 — Bipolar I vs. II

Bipolar I is the "I mean it" version: one manic episode is all it takes to earn the diagnosis — depression is optional. Bipolar II needs a two-ingredient recipe: at least one hypomanic episode and at least one major depressive episode, but if a manic episode ever shows up, the diagnosis is immediately promoted to Bipolar I. Hypomania is Bipolar II's ceiling — it can never break through into full mania and stay Bipolar II.

📌
Bipolar II is one of the few DSM-5 disorders that does not require impairment to diagnose (hypomania is non-impairing by definition) — delusional disorder shares this unusual feature (Section 07). Also remember: if psychosis is ever present in a bipolar presentation, or if hospitalization is required, the diagnosis is automatically bipolar I, never bipolar II.

Provide a differential diagnosis of restrictive eating in a young female

Answer

For a young female with restrictive eating, the first differentiating step is BMI: a low BMI (<18.5) points strongly toward anorexia nervosa, while a normal-to-high BMI shifts the differential toward bulimia nervosa or binge eating disorder. The second step is identifying the driving behavior — ongoing weight loss (restriction, seen in anorexia, sometimes layered with binge/purge episodes but still aimed at further weight loss) versus correcting/compensating after a binge (bulimia, which requires recurrent inappropriate compensatory behavior) versus bingeing with no compensatory behavior at all (binge eating disorder). Anorexia itself can present with a binge-eating/purging subtype (low BMI plus occasional binges and diet-pill/laxative/thyroid-supplement misuse) rather than pure restriction. A patient with a BMI of 19 who restricts intake, has missed menstrual cycles, and shows body-image distortion but has never binged or purged doesn't cleanly meet anorexia's BMI cutoff and would be classified as an unspecified/atypical feeding-eating disorder.

🧠
Memory hook · BMI first, behavior secondLow BMI (<18.5) → anorexia. Normal/high BMI → is there compensation? Yes → bulimia, no → binge eating disorder. Anorexia severity is graded by BMI; bulimia severity by compensations per week.

Pulled from: Eating Disorders

  1. Check the BMI first. Below normal (<18.5) points strongly toward anorexia. Normal-to-high points away from anorexia and toward bulimia or BED.
  2. Identify the driving behavior. Is the primary goal ongoing weight loss (restriction-focused), or correcting/compensating after a binge (bulimia), or a binge with no compensation at all (BED)?
  3. Confirm frequency and duration. Bulimia and BED both need recurrent episodes; bulimia specifically needs ≥1×/week for 3 months, and anorexia's subtype (restricting vs. binge/purge) is defined over the past 3 months.
  4. Rule out exclusionary criteria. Anorexia must be excluded before diagnosing bulimia. If the picture is incomplete or mixed, consider "unspecified."
📉

Anorexia — Restrict to Lose

Driving factor is ongoing weight loss. Expect a low-to-very-low BMI. Core behavior is restriction, sometimes layered with binge/purge episodes — but the goal underneath is always further weight loss.

  • BMI: low (specifiers are BMI-defined)
  • Self-view: "I am overweight," despite objective evidence otherwise
🔁

Bulimia — Binge, Then Correct

Driving factor is avoiding weight gain after a binge episode. Expect a normal-to-high BMI. Core behavior is binge → compensate, in a repeating cycle.

  • BMI: normal to elevated
  • Self-worth tied to body shape/weight, without the same degree of "I am overweight" distortion seen in anorexia

Q: This case is deliberately left vague. What single piece of missing information would most help differentiate the diagnosis, and why?

Answer

Vital signs, specifically BMI. BMI is one of the main criteria separating Anorexia (low BMI) from Bulimia/Binge Eating Disorder (normal-to-high BMI). Without it, the ice cream episode could point to binge eating, and the diet pills/laxatives to purging — but there's no way yet to know whether this is a restriction-dominant or binge-dominant picture. We'll revisit this same case with vitals added in the Anorexia and Bulimia sections below.

🔑 Key Takeaways
  • BMI is the fastest way to narrow the differential — low points to anorexia, normal/high moves away from it.
  • Ask "what's the goal of the behavior?" — losing weight (anorexia) vs. correcting a binge (bulimia) vs. no correction at all (BED).
  • Therapy (largely CBT) is first-line across all three disorders; medication is adjunctive.
  • Avoid bupropion and lithium in active bulimia/anorexia.
  • The DSM is black-and-white; real patients are gray — "unspecified" is a legitimate clinical category, not a cop-out.

Q — Case Revisited: Same 24-year-old female. Vitals now added: BP 110/60, Pulse 60, BMI 15.5. She still reports feeling significantly overweight, occasional half-gallon ice cream episodes, and use of diet pills/thyroid supplements/laxatives. What's the diagnosis?

Answer

Anorexia Nervosa, Binge-Eating/Purging Type, Severe. A BMI of 15.5 falls in the severe range (15–15.99). The ice cream episode suggests a binge-eating pattern, and the diet pills/thyroid supplements/laxatives suggest purging-type compensatory behavior — both layered on top of a body-image distortion (feeling overweight at a BMI well below normal). The low BMI is the single biggest clue steering this toward anorexia rather than bulimia.

Q: A patient has a BMI of 19, restricts intake to the point of missing two menstrual cycles, and insists she is overweight despite reassurance. She has never binged or purged. Best-fit diagnosis?

Answer

Likely an unspecified feeding/eating disorder (atypical anorexia pattern). Her behavior and body-image distortion match anorexia nervosa closely, but her BMI (19) is technically above the standard anorexia cutoff (below ~18.5). Clinically and on higher-order exam questions, this "driving factor" reasoning — restriction aimed at continued weight loss — outweighs a BMI that doesn't perfectly fit the textbook cutoff.

🧩 "Unspecified" Eating Disorder

Real presentations don't always fit neatly. A person might show a clear anorexia-pattern (restriction, fear of weight gain, body image distortion) at a BMI of 19 — technically above the anorexia cutoff — or have a binge/purge pattern where it's unclear if the driving factor is more anorexia-like or bulimia-like. Clinically, these get labeled an unspecified feeding/eating disorder rather than forced into a diagnosis that doesn't fully fit.

Anorexia Nervosa, Bulimia Nervosa, and Binge Eating Disorder are all built from combinations of the same three symptom clusters. Learning these three first makes every individual diagnosis below a matter of "which combination, at what BMI, for how long."

LO 039Somatoform, Dissoc. & Sexual✓ In your notes

Provide a differential diagnosis of the somatoform disorders

Answer

The somatoform (somatic symptom and related) disorders are unified by unconscious symptom production, the key branch point that separates them from the consciously-produced conditions malingering and factitious disorder. Somatic symptom disorder presents with multi-system complaints lasting months to years plus excessive, persistent thoughts about the symptoms (which may co-occur with a real medical condition, disproportionate to it); illness anxiety disorder is fear of serious illness despite reassurance and normal workups (minimal actual somatic symptoms); conversion disorder presents as a sudden neurological deficit (e.g., blindness, paralysis) with a normal workup, classically accompanied by la belle indifférence — a strikingly unbothered affect about the deficit. The typical vignette pattern across all of them is a thick chart, multiple specialists already seen, normal or inconsistent workups, and a symptom picture that doesn't fit a single organic disease process. The master decision tree: no conscious deception → a somatoform disorder (the specific one depending on presentation); conscious deception for internal/primary gain (wanting to be sick or cared for — the sick role) → factitious disorder; conscious deception for external/secondary gain (money, drugs, avoiding work or court) → malingering.

🧠
Memory hook · The three-branch deception treeSymptoms unconscious → somatoform spectrum. Conscious, to live the sick role (internal gain) → factitious. Conscious, for money/court/drugs (external gain) → malingering (not a psychiatric diagnosis). Vignette tells: thick chart, many specialists, normal workups.
🧠
Memory hook · Blind but unbotheredSudden neuro deficit + normal workup + la belle indifférence (strangely unconcerned) = conversion disorder. Fear of illness with no symptoms = illness anxiety; months of multi-system symptoms + obsessive worry about them = somatic symptom disorder.

Pulled from: Sexual, Somatoform & Dissociative Disorders

Master split
Unconscious production (somatic symptom, illness anxiety, conversion) vs. conscious production (malingering, factitious).
Somatic symptom disorder
Multi-system complaints, months-years, excessive/persistent thoughts about symptoms.
Illness anxiety disorder
Fear of serious illness despite reassurance; minimal actual symptoms.
Conversion disorder
Sudden sensory/motor loss after a stressor; la belle indifférence; F > M, young.
Malingering
External gain; complaints STOP once gain achieved; avoids invasive workups.
Factitious disorder
Sick role = primary gain; WELCOMES invasive procedures; Munchausen = chronic physical form.
Munchausen by proxy
Illness caused in a child/elder by caregiver; mandatory reporting, = abuse.
DID criteria
≥2 distinct personality states + recurrent amnesia gaps; early childhood trauma.
DID alter patterns
Mutually aware / mutually unaware / one aware, not reciprocated.
DID vs. PTSD
Ongoing field debate: is DID distinct, or severe/chronic PTSD with dissociative features?
Dissociative amnesia
Localized/selective vs. generalized; info not permanently lost, just unretrievable.
Dissociative fugue
A SPECIFIER of dissociative amnesia (not separate dx) — purposeful travel/wandering + identity amnesia.
Amnesia/fugue course
Usually adult-onset, rapid onset/resolution, F > M; most recover spontaneously.
Depersonalization
Altered perception of SELF (detachment, out-of-body).
Derealization
Altered perception of ENVIRONMENT (foggy, dreamlike, unreal).
Depersonalization/derealization key
Reality testing INTACT — this is what separates it from psychosis.
Sexual dysfunction classification
DSM-5 lists alphabetically (no agreed sexual-response model) — replaced Masters & Johnson's 4-stage cycle.
Psychogenic vs. physiologic ED
Preserved nocturnal/morning erections → psychogenic. Absent → physiologic.
Paraphilia vs. paraphilic disorder
Paraphilia = atypical interest (ascertained). Disorder = + distress/impairment/harm to others (diagnosed).
8 named paraphilic disorders
Fetishistic, transvestic, pedohebephilic, voyeuristic, exhibitionistic, frotteuristic, sexual sadism, sexual masochism.
Non-consent paraphilias
Voyeuristic, exhibitionistic, frotteuristic — inherently involve a non-consenting party.
Paraphilia treatment
Incorporation therapy, psychotherapy, orgasmic reconditioning, drug therapy (antiandrogens/SSRIs).
Hypersexuality red flags
Brain injury, Klüver-Bucy, Kleine-Levin, dopamine agonists (mesolimbic overactivity) — rule out before assuming psychiatric.
🧠
One clean decision tree, memorized: (1) Is there a conscious attempt to deceive? If no → somatoform disorder (somatic symptom, illness anxiety, or conversion, depending on presentation). If yes → (2) is the goal psychological/internal (wanting to be sick, cared for, the center of medical attention) or external (money, work avoidance, drugs, legal advantage)? Internal/psychological → factitious disorder. External → malingering.
Unconsciously-ProducedConsciously-Produced
DisordersSomatic symptom disorder, illness anxiety disorder, conversion disorderMalingering, factitious disorder
IntentSymptoms and illness motivation are NOT intentionally producedIntentional production or feigning of symptoms
EpidemiologyMore common in womenVaries by specific disorder (Section 04)

Somatic Symptom Disorder

PictureA variety of complaints across one or more organ systems, lasting months to years, associated with excessive and persistent thoughts about the symptoms. May genuinely co-occur with real medical conditions — the psychological preoccupation is disproportionate to whatever organic pathology is (or isn't) present.
VideoNone available for this one per the handout.

Illness Anxiety Disorder (Hypochondriasis)

PicturePreoccupation with and fear of having a serious medical illness, despite medical evidence and reassurance to the contrary. Unlike somatic symptom disorder, the somatic symptoms themselves may be minimal or absent — it's the fear/preoccupation that's the disorder.
▶ Illness anxiety disorder case 🔒 UNE

Conversion Disorder

Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder
PictureSudden loss of sensory or motor function — paralysis, blindness, mutism — often following an acute stressor. Classically more common in females, young adults, and adolescents.
Signature findingLa belle indifférence — the patient is aware of the symptom but shows a striking, disproportionate lack of concern about it.
▶ Conversion disorder case 🔒 UNE
📌
La belle indifférence, translated: "the beautiful indifference." It's the single most quotable, most testable finding in this section — a patient who has just gone functionally blind or paralyzed, but who seems almost unbothered by it. Note it's a classic association, not a required or universal criterion for conversion disorder — plenty of real patients with conversion disorder are appropriately distressed.
🩺
Reading this pattern as a vignette: a patient with a thick chart, a long list of specialists already seen, normal or inconsistent workups, and a symptom picture that doesn't fit any single organic disease process is the classic setup for a somatoform-spectrum diagnosis. The specific disorder then comes down to what kind of complaint dominates (diffuse multi-system complaints → somatic symptom disorder; fear of illness despite reassurance → illness anxiety disorder; a discrete neurological deficit → conversion disorder).

Malingering

Not itself a psychiatric diagnosis — a V-code / behavior
MotivationDriven by external incentives — the classic "secondary gain": financial compensation, disability payments, avoiding work, avoiding legal consequences, obtaining drugs.
PatternPoor compliance with treatment, follow-up, or diagnostic testing (since genuine treatment isn't actually the goal). The complaints cease once the gain is achieved — a key differentiator from factitious disorder.
▶ Malingering case 🔒 UNE

Factitious Disorder

A true psychiatric diagnosis
MotivationDriven by a desire to assume the sick role and receive medical attention itself — this is primary gain, not an external reward.
Munchausen syndromeThe chronic form, predominantly physical signs/symptoms — a history of multiple hospital stays and a striking willingness to undergo invasive procedures.
Munchausen syndrome by proxyIllness is caused in a child or elderly dependent by their caregiver, so the caregiver can occupy the sick role by proxy. This is a form of child/elder abuse and must be reported to authorities.
▶ "Rebecca" — factitious disorder case 🔒 UNE

Unexplained symptoms → is there a conscious attempt to deceive? No → somatoform disorder. Yes → is the chief goal psychological (1° gain) or external (2° gain)? Psychological → factitious disorder. External → malingering.

LO 041Personality Disorders✓ In your notes

Provide a differential diagnosis of the various personality disorders

Answer

DSM-5 personality disorders sort into three clusters, mnemonic "Weird, Wild, and Worried." Cluster A ("odd/eccentric," genetically linked to schizophrenia) includes paranoid, schizoid, and schizotypal PD, all sharing overlap with the negative symptoms of schizophrenia (social withdrawal, restricted affect) but no true psychosis — schizotypal PD is the member most associated with actual psychotic illness and can coexist with or be mistaken for schizophrenia. Cluster B ("dramatic/erratic," linked to mood and substance use disorders) includes antisocial, borderline, histrionic, and narcissistic PD, plotted on axes of affective instability and impulsivity — borderline is highest on both, histrionic leans toward affective instability, antisocial toward impulsivity, and narcissistic sits lower on both; antisocial PD specifically requires documented conduct disorder before age 15. Cluster C ("anxious/fearful") includes avoidant ("inhibited"), dependent ("insecure"), and obsessive-compulsive PD ("rigid, requiring order"). Borderline PD also belongs on the differential for both psychosis (brief stress-induced micropsychotic and dissociative episodes) and bipolar disorder, distinguished from bipolar by timescale and trigger.

🧠
Memory hook · Weird, Wild, Worried — and their alliterationsCluster A (weird): Accusatory (paranoid), Aloof (schizoid), Awkward (schizotypal) — genetic link to schizophrenia. Cluster B (wild): Bad to the Bone — antisocial (needs conduct disorder before 15), borderline, histrionic, narcissistic. Cluster C (worried): Cowardly (avoidant), Clingy (dependent), Compulsive (OCPD).

Pulled from: Personality Disorders · Introduction to Therapy · Psychotic Disorders & Antipsychotic Pharmacology

All 10 personality disorders share the same general template — an enduring, pervasive, inflexible pattern of inner experience and behavior that deviates from cultural norms, is stable from early adulthood, and causes distress or impairment. They sort into three clusters: Weird, Wild, Worried.

The 10 personality disorders — defining feature vs. discriminator
DisorderDefining featureDiscriminator / board pearl
Cluster A — “Weird” · odd/eccentric · genetic link to schizophrenia · negative-symptom overlap, no true psychosis
ParanoidPervasive distrust and suspiciousness; reads hidden malice into benign remarks, bears grudges, doubts others’ loyalty.No fixed delusions or hallucinations (vs delusional disorder / paranoid schizophrenia).
SchizoidVoluntary detachment — genuine indifference to relationships; solitary, emotionally cold and flat; content alone.Does not want relationships (vs avoidant, who does); no magical thinking or odd perceptions (vs schizotypal).
SchizotypalMagical thinking, ideas of reference, odd perceptions, eccentric speech/appearance; social anxiety from discomfort with interacting itself.The Cluster A member closest to psychosis — can coexist with or be mistaken for schizophrenia; genetically related to it.
Cluster B — “Wild” · dramatic/erratic · genetic link to mood & substance use disorders · plotted on affective-instability × impulsivity axes
AntisocialDisregard for and violation of others’ rights — deceit, aggression, impulsivity, no remorse.Requires documented conduct disorder before age 15; patient must be ≥18. Conduct disorder = “antisocial PD in a child.”
BorderlineInstability of relationships, self-image, and affect plus impulsivity, fear of abandonment, self-harm, splitting.Mood shifts in hours, reactive to interpersonal triggers (vs bipolar: days–weeks, trigger-independent). Brief stress-induced micropsychotic/dissociative episodes. First-line: DBT.
HistrionicExcessive emotionality and attention-seeking; theatrical, seductive, rapidly shifting shallow emotions; needs to be center of attention.Highest on the affective-instability axis; impressionistic speech, easily influenced by others.
NarcissisticGrandiosity, need for admiration, lack of empathy; entitlement, envy.Fragile self-esteem underneath — rage or withdrawal in response to criticism.
Cluster C — “Worried” · anxious/fearful · genetic link to anxiety disorders
AvoidantSocial inhibition from fear of criticism and rejection plus feelings of inadequacy.Wants relationships but avoids them out of low self-image (vs schizoid: no desire; vs schizotypal: discomfort with the act of interacting, not self-image).
DependentExcessive need to be taken care of — submissive, clingy; can’t make decisions or be alone; urgently seeks a new caretaker when a relationship ends.Core fear is separation and self-reliance, not criticism (vs avoidant).
Obsessive-compulsive (OCPD)Preoccupation with order, perfectionism, and control; rigid, inflexible, miserly, work over leisure.Ego-syntonic with no true obsessions or compulsions — vs OCD, which is ego-dystonic with intrusive thoughts and rituals.

All four Cluster B disorders plotted on axes of affective instability (vertical) and impulsivity (horizontal) — borderline sits at the intersection of both being highest; histrionic leans toward affective instability; antisocial leans toward impulsivity; narcissistic sits comparatively lower on both

Cluster A · deep-dive

Schizotypal PD

The Cluster A member most associated with true psychotic illness
Core pictureDifficulty interacting with others driven by discomfort with the act of interacting itself — critically, not from negative self-image (contrast with avoidant PD, Section 10). May demonstrate cognitive distortions, odd speech patterns, and genuinely strange perceptual experiences (believing they can see the future, read minds, sense energy, etc.) that influence behavior.
The headline featureUnusual perceptions — this is the discriminating symptom to focus on. The affect can be inappropriate to context (e.g., unexpectedly cheerful at a somber occasion), and ideas of reference are common (believing the TV or environment is sending them personal messages).
📌
Boards-relevant fact: schizotypal PD is the one personality disorder most associated with true psychotic disorders — it can coexist with schizophrenia, and the symptom overlap means it's sometimes misdiagnosed as (or mistaken for) a primary psychotic illness.

All three Cluster A disorders share an underlying overlap with the negative symptoms of schizophrenia — social withdrawal, reclusiveness, restricted affect

All three Cluster C disorders share an underlying anxious symptomatology — avoidant is "inhibited," dependent is "insecure," OCPD is "rigid, requiring order"

📌
The conduct disorder link is required, not incidental: DSM-5 requires documentation of conduct disorder before age 15 to diagnose antisocial PD — this is one of the only personality disorders with an explicit childhood-diagnosis prerequisite built into the criteria (most PDs are simply never diagnosed in children, but this one specifically requires evidence of it). Conduct disorder is essentially "antisocial PD in a child" — harming animals, lack of remorse, violating others' rights — and typically (though not always documented) precedes the adult diagnosis.
📌
BPD belongs on your differential for psychosis: under acute stress, patients can have brief micropsychotic episodes and dissociative symptoms — doing things during a period of time they later don't remember. This is the literal meaning behind the name "borderline": the patient sits at the boundary between mood dysregulation and transient psychosis.
🧠
Borderline PD vs. Bipolar Disorder — a frequently confused pair, in both directions: always keep bipolar disorder on the differential when BPD is suspected, and vice versa. The key discriminator is timescale and trigger: bipolar mood episodes last days-to-weeks and shift relatively independent of external events; BPD's affective instability is reactive — it shifts rapidly (hours) in direct response to interpersonal triggers (a perceived slight, a fear of abandonment), and is embedded in the broader identity-disturbance/relationship-instability picture rather than existing as a standalone mood episode.

LO 042Child & Adolescent◐ Partly covered

Understand adjunctive medications to be added to stimulant medications in children with ADHD

Answer

Non-stimulant options that can be used alongside or as adjuncts to stimulant medications in pediatric ADHD include atomoxetine (Strattera), a selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor dosed 1-1.4 mg/kg with about 60% response versus 80-90% for stimulants; viloxazine (Qelbree), a 5-HT2C partial agonist/norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor; and the alpha-2 agonists clonidine and guanfacine, which calm hyperactivity/behavior rather than improving attention. The Child & Adolescent Psychiatry lecture's medication table confirms stimulants (methylphenidate ER, dexmethylphenidate ER, mixed amphetamine salts, lisdexamfetamine) as first-line unless contraindicated, with long-acting formulations standard in children and about 80-90% response, and lists alpha-2 agonists as a second medication group in the same ADHD treatment table alongside stimulants.

🧠
Memory hook · Stimulants 80–90% ; atomoxetine 60% ; alpha-2s calm the body, not the focusFirst-line: long-acting stimulants (methylphenidate ER, lisdexamfetamine…) — watch appetite, sleep, ~2–3 cm growth, tics (esp. amphetamines), CV review. Failed stimulants → atomoxetine (NRI, 1–1.4 mg/kg) or viloxazine; guanfacine/clonidine for hyperactivity. Diagnosis needs: >6 months, onset <12, impairment, ≥2 settings.
◐
Missing from your notesAn explicit description of adding a non-stimulant on top of a stimulant for residual symptoms, insomnia, or tics, and any mention of bupropion augmentation, remain absent from both sources.

Pulled from: Psychiatry Key Drug List 2026 · Child & Adolescent Psychiatry

Non-stimulant #1 (Schedule-free)
atomoxetine (Strattera)
  • Selective NE reuptake inhibitor; helps ~60% vs 80–90% for stimulants.
  • For stimulant-averse families, tic disorders, abuse-risk households. Dose by weight: 1–1.4 mg/kg (RS: underdosing = why "it never works").
  • SEs: GI upset, sedation, dizziness, irritability.
Non-stimulant #2
viloxazine (Qelbree)
  • 5-HT2C partial agonist + NE reuptake inhibitor (old European antidepressant, relaunched 2021 for ADHD).
The α2 agonists
clonidine (Kapvay) & guanfacine (Intuniv)
  • Central α2-adrenergic agonists (from HTN world): fix hyperactivity, do NOT improve focus — for patients who can't take stimulants.
  • Onyda XR (2024): first liquid clonidine, nighttime dosing, mono/adjunct.
  • Also: bupropion IR/SR is used off-label for ADHD.
Memory Hook — the non-stimulant ladder
"ATOMs FOCUS, alphas CALM." ATOMoxetine (NRI) actually helps attention (just less often — 60%); clonidine/guanfacine (α2) only quiet the body. And VyvanSe needS Stomach acid (pH<5) — the abuse-proof prodrug.
Mechanism
Block DA/NE reuptake AND enhance release of DA/NE (amphetamines especially push release).
Side effects
Decreased appetite/weight, insomnia (dose after meals, not at night), anxiety/jitteriness/agitation, GI upset, dysphoria/mania, tachycardia/palpitations/HTN, possible growth suppression (drug holidays help), tics/dyskinesias, headache.
Stopping abruptly
Rebound: headache, hypersomnia, hyperphagia, depression, irritability, poor concentration.
Abuse reality check
Oral ADHD dosing has low abuse potential (vs snorted/IV meth); untreated ADHD raises later drug-abuse risk — treatment lowers it. Watch for feigned ADHD (diversion). FDA: no ER stimulants in children <6 years (weight loss).

ADHD is the most common pediatric psychiatric complaint in the lecture, with a strong emphasis on collateral school data and stimulant-first pharmacology.
