LO 043Cross-Cutting Pharm✓ In your notes

Understand CYP 450 interactions (major inducers, inhibitors, substrates) among psychiatric medications, particularly the SSRIs

Answer

CYP450 pharmacology rests on three terms: the substrate (the drug being metabolized), an inhibitor (reduces enzyme activity, raising the substrate's plasma level and increasing toxicity/side-effect risk), and an inducer (increases enzyme activity, lowering the substrate's plasma level and risking loss of efficacy or relapse). Classic teaching cases from these notes: cigarette smoke is a CYP1A2 inducer, so a smoker on clozapine or olanzapine (1A2 substrates) who starts or quits smoking needs monitoring for dropping or rising drug levels; bupropion is a CYP2D6 inhibitor, so adding it to a patient already stable on imipramine (a 2D6 substrate, a TCA) for smoking cessation raised imipramine levels and caused anticholinergic delirium/arrhythmia. Among the SSRIs, fluoxetine is a notably potent CYP2D6 inhibitor with a very long half-life and active metabolite, producing many drug-drug interactions (e.g., raising benzodiazepine levels) — a common source of exam questions. Mastering CYP450 substrate/inhibitor/inducer logic alongside the 6 SSRIs is flagged as fair game for both the course exam and boards.

🧠
Memory hook · Smoke burns away the -PINEsCigarette hydrocarbons induce CYP1A2 → clozaPINE and olanzaPINE levels drop (relapse); quitting in hospital → levels climb (toxicity). 95% of schizophrenia patients smoke — this WILL show up. Fluvoxamine does the opposite (1A2 inhibitor).

Pulled from: Introduction & History of Psychiatry · Psychotic Disorders & Antipsychotic Pharmacology · Anxiety, OCD & Trauma-Related Disorders · Mood Disorders

Substrate + Inhibitor

A drug that reduces enzyme activity → increases plasma level of the substrate → increased side effects & toxicity risk.

Substrate + Inducer

A drug that increases enzyme activity → decreases plasma level of the substrate → loss of efficacy / relapse risk (the handout frames this as "decreased side effects and toxicity," which is true, but the clinically dangerous side of induction is usually treatment failure, not safety).
TermDefinition
SubstrateThe drug (or other substance) being metabolized by the P450 enzyme system — i.e., the drug you're actually giving the patient.
InhibitorA drug/substance that reduces enzyme activity → substrate is metabolized more slowly → plasma level of substrate rises.
InducerA drug/substance that increases enzyme activity → substrate is metabolized faster → plasma level of substrate falls.
⚖ Hardest discrimination: CYP450 Inhibitor vs. Inducer
InhibitorInducer
Effect on enzyme↓ activity↑ activity
Effect on substrate level↑ plasma level↓ plasma level
Clinical riskToxicity / side effectsEfficacy loss / relapse
Case exampleBupropion (2D6) + imipramine → delirium, arrhythmiaSmoking (1A2) + clozapine → psychosis relapse
NH State Hospital — cigarette smoking as a 1A2 inducer Inducer

~95% of patients with schizophrenia smoke cigarettes — still the current statistic, and worth remembering because hydrocarbons in cigarette smoke are a 1A2 inducer. Both clozapine and olanzapine (antipsychotics) are 1A2 substrates.

A patient was hospitalized, titrated onto clozapine, and did well — psychosis cleared and he was discharged. He went home and resumed smoking ~2 packs/day. His psychosis re-emerged (he was found naked in the street, screaming, while smoking) and he was re-hospitalized — despite being fully medication-compliant. The smoking induced faster clozapine metabolism, plasma levels plummeted, and psychosis returned.

Eastport, ME — smoking cessation script triggers anticholinergic delirium Inhibitor

A stable patient on imipramine (a TCA — a 2D6 substrate) was doing well in Dr. Smith's practice. Her PCP started her on bupropion (a 2D6 inhibitor) for smoking cessation, without knowing she was already on imipramine.

Bupropion inhibited 2D6 → imipramine could no longer be metabolized normally → imipramine levels rose to ~10× therapeutic levels. She became confused and delirious with florid anticholinergic symptoms, and developed a cardiac arrhythmia — TCAs carry real cardiotoxicity at supratherapeutic levels. She was admitted to telemetry; bupropion was stopped immediately, and she improved.

C.1
What is the pharmacokinetic mechanism at work here?
A. Smoking induces the CYP3A4 enzyme
B. Olanzapine is a substrate of CYP3A4
C. Smoking is an inducer of CYP1A2
D. Smoking is an inhibitor of 1A2
E. Smoking is an inducer of the 2D6 isoenzyme and olanzapine is a substrate of 2D6
F. Patient is lying and should be re-hospitalized for noncompliance
Answer: C. This is Section 19's smoking/CYP1A2 interaction in action: olanzapine (like clozapine) is metabolized by CYP1A2, which cigarette smoke induces. While hospitalized (not smoking), his CYP1A2 activity normalized, keeping olanzapine levels adequate. Resuming smoking after discharge re-induces CYP1A2 → faster olanzapine metabolism → falling serum levels → breakthrough psychosis despite genuine adherence. No need to suspect noncompliance (F) — the mechanism is fully explained pharmacokinetically.
🤔
Discussion prompt: "Why might this be clinically significant in a patient specifically asking for fluoxetine?" — fluoxetine is both a potent CYP inhibitor and has an extremely long half-life/active metabolite, so a patient requesting it while also on a benzo (or requesting it specifically, by name) raises a flag worth thinking through — both for the interaction itself and for what's driving the specific drug-seeking request.

Sertraline

Most prescribed SSRI

"Longish" half-life, well tolerated.

Fluoxetine

Longest half-life in class (2–4 days)

Inhibits CYP2D6 → many drug–drug interactions. The long half-life is clinically useful — good for patients who won't take medication reliably, since missing a dose barely registers, and can even be dosed once weekly.

Escitalopram

Isomer of citalopram

No meaningful cardiac (QTc) effect — the key differentiator from citalopram.

Citalopram

Dose-dependent QTc risk

The older of the pair; best known for QTc prolongation.

Fluvoxamine

FDA-approved for OCD ONLY

Doesn't carry the general depression indication the rest of the class does — a very testable exception.

Paroxetine

Shortest half-life, "dirty" drug

Inhibits CYP2D6; interacts with a lot of other medications, so many clinicians avoid it when there's a cleaner option.

LO 044Cross-Cutting Pharm◐ Partly covered

Understand how to manage the sexual side-effects commonly seen with antidepressant medications

Answer

Among antidepressant classes, bupropion (an NDRI) is specifically noted as less likely to cause sexual dysfunction than SSRIs, making it a reasonable switch option when sexual side effects are a concern; it belongs to the broader atypical antidepressant group (bupropion, mirtazapine, trazodone, vilazodone, vortioxetine -- mnemonic 'Atypical Bees Make Tasty Vegan Venison'). DSM-5 recognizes substance/medication-induced sexual dysfunction as its own diagnostic category, distinct from primary male/female sexual dysfunctions such as hypoactive desire, erectile, or orgasmic disorder. PDE-5 inhibitors are noted as relevant to the pharmacologic side of sexual functioning, though the notes do not elaborate on their specific use for antidepressant-induced dysfunction. Bupropion can also be used as an add-on to augment another antidepressant (rather than only as a switch) for erectile dysfunction in a patient on an SSRI, though it helps erection specifically and not ejaculation.

🧠
Memory hook · Bupropion: the smoking-cessation drug with a 2D6 tollboothDepressed smoker → bupropion (FDA-approved for MDD + smoking cessation). But it inhibits CYP2D6 — added to a TCA like imipramine it caused anticholinergic delirium. Avoid with seizures or eating disorders; the trade-off gift: minimal sexual side effects.
◐
Missing from your notesDose reduction, scheduled drug holidays, and adding a PDE-5 inhibitor as specific management steps for SSRI/SNRI-induced sexual dysfunction are still not stated in any source, and neither the child psychiatry nor the neuroanatomy lecture addresses this topic.

Pulled from: Mood Disorders · Sexual, Somatoform & Dissociative Disorders · Psychiatry Key Drug List 2026

Bupropion (NDRI)

Inhibits NE + DA reuptake

Structurally close to a stimulant. Side effects: tachycardia, weight loss, ↓seizure threshold (black box warning). Less likely to cause sexual dysfunction. Helps smoking cessation; can be paired with naltrexone for weight loss.

Mirtazapine

Alpha-2 antagonist, 5-HT2/5-HT3 antagonist, H1 antagonist

Side effects: weight gain, sedation, ↑appetite, dry mouth — less likely sexual side effects. Useful when sedation/appetite gain is desirable (underweight, insomnia).

Trazodone

Blocks 5-HT2, alpha-1, H1

Mainly used for insomnia (high doses needed for antidepressant effect). Side effects: sedation, priapism (erection >4h — surgical emergency, from alpha blockade).

Nefazodone

Serotonin blocker

Liver toxicity — rarely prescribed today.

Vilazodone

5-HT reuptake inhibition + 5-HT1A partial agonist

Low yield beyond MOA — not frequently used or tested.

Vortioxetine

5-HT reuptake inhibition + 5-HT1A agonist + 5-HT3 antagonist

Low yield beyond MOA — not frequently used or tested.

NE + dopamine reuptake inhibition — ZERO serotonin effect, unique among ALL antidepressants.

MDD with atypical features: hypersomnia, increased appetite, weight gain, mood reactivity, excessive fatigue, "leaden paralysis".
Also for
Smoking cessation (as Zyban); erectile dysfunction in patients on an SSRI (helps erection, not ejaculation); augmenting another antidepressant; flat/numb affect (it intensifies affect rather than calming).
Side effects
Insomnia, irritability, anxiety, headache, activation — but NO sexual side effects, NO weight gain.
LO 045Psychosis & Antipsychotics✓ In your notes

Understand how to select an antipsychotic based on side-effect profile and patient co- morbidities

Answer

Antipsychotic selection criteria include prior/family history of response, patient's medical status, side-effect profile (potency), dosing complexity/compliance, and cost. Typical (first-generation) antipsychotics are stratified into high, medium, and low potency relative to chlorpromazine, and potency alone predicts the side-effect profile. Among atypicals, key discriminators are: clozapine and olanzapine carry the highest metabolic risk (weight gain, dyslipidemia, T2DM; clozapine uniquely risks agranulocytosis, seizures, and myocarditis) and clozapine is reserved as the superior but last-resort "gold standard" for treatment-resistant schizophrenia; risperidone causes frequent hyperprolactinemia; ziprasidone has low weight gain but notable QTc prolongation; aripiprazole (a D2 partial agonist) sits at the lowest-risk end for metabolic syndrome, prolactin elevation, and QT prolongation, making it favorable for patients with cardiometabolic comorbidities. Haloperidol, despite appearing in bipolar medication reference tables alongside atypicals, remains a first-generation (typical) agent and should not be confused with the second-generation options listed beside it.

🧠
Memory hook · -PINEs pack Pounds; -DONEs Drain prolactinOlanzapine/clozapine/quetiapine → weight, sedation, metabolic syndrome. Risperidone → prolactin; ziprasidone → QTc. Cleanest metabolics: aripiprazole (D2 partial agonist), ziprasidone, lurasidone, cariprazine. Clozapine = last-resort gold standard: agranulocytosis (ANC checks), seizures, myocarditis — and the only drug FDA-approved to cut suicidality in schizophrenia.

Pulled from: Psychotic Disorders & Antipsychotic Pharmacology · Mood Disorders

Complexity of dosing — compliance issues
Medication cost to patient

Typical antipsychotics are stratified into high, medium, and low potency categories relative to the original antipsychotic, chlorpromazine. Dr. Smith's key teaching point: you can predict a typical's side-effect profile from its potency alone — you don't even need to know the drug's name.

Clozapine: absent EPS/hyperprolactinemia, high weight gain/sedation, unique agranulocytosis/seizure risk. Olanzapine: rare EPS, high weight gain/sedation. Risperidone: frequent hyperprolactinemia. Ziprasidone: low weight gain, notable QTc. Aripiprazole: absent hyperprolactinemia, rare weight gain — the cleanest metabolic profile of the group.

Section 21

Cardiovascular risk table — clozapine and olanzapine carry the broadest metabolic risk footprint (weight gain + T2DM + dyslipidemia, clozapine adds myocarditis/pericarditis); quetiapine and risperidone add QT risk; ziprasidone is comparatively metabolically clean but still carries QT risk

Aripiprazole — D2 partial agonist (stabilizes rather than fully blocking dopamine tone)
Ziprasidone — modulates norepinephrine/serotonin in addition to D2/5-HT2A antagonism
Clozapine — serotonergic predominance (5-HT2A:D2 ratio ~10:1); broadest receptor footprint of any agent
🧠
The "PIPs" and the "RIP": the aripiprazole-family partial agonists (aripiprazole, brexpiprazole, cariprazine) round out the atypicals as a mechanistically distinct group (D2 partial agonists rather than full antagonists — Section 19), while clozapine stands apart as the last-resort "gold standard" agent, reserved for treatment-resistant disease because of its unique, tightly-monitored risk profile (Section 22).

Clozapine (Clozaril)

The most effective antipsychotic — and the most heavily regulated
Why "gold standard"Superior efficacy vs. all other agents, including for treatment-resistant schizophrenia (confirmed in CUTLASS Band 2, Section 26) — but a heavy side-effect burden makes it a later-line agent.
Unique side effectsAgranulocytosis (1–2%), seizures (1–5%, dose-related), sialorrhea (drooling), fever, myocarditis/pericarditis (Section 19's Table 1).
Unique lack of side effectsEssentially no EPS and no tardive dyskinesia — the trade-off for its heavy receptor promiscuity elsewhere.
⚠️ Watch for Haloperidol in the Bipolar Drug Table

Haloperidol is a first-generation antipsychotic, even though it shows up listed alongside aripiprazole, olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone, and ziprasidone in bipolar medication reference tables. The lecture's own teaching point: if a question says "a second-generation antipsychotic" is indicated for bipolar disorder, don't reflexively pick haloperidol — any antipsychotic could be effective given dopamine's role in bipolar disorder, but when a question specifically asks for a second-generation agent, haloperidol is the wrong answer.

LO 046Mood & Mood Stabilizers✓ In your notes

Understand the "specifiers" of MDD and how they differ in their presentation

Answer

MDD specifiers describe the "flavor" of a depressive episode: anxious distress (tension, restlessness, poor concentration from worry, fear of losing control), mixed features (manic/hypomanic symptoms during a depressive episode or the reverse, 3+ symptoms most days), rapid cycling, and — noted as applying across both depressive and bipolar episodes — melancholic, atypical, psychotic, catatonia, peripartum, and seasonal patterns. Atypical features are actually the most common subtype despite the name, and are marked by mood reactivity and "gains" (weight/sleep/heaviness) — essentially the opposite polarity of melancholic depression, which "loses" (appetite, pleasure, energy). The seasonal pattern specifier requires episodes and remissions to have a regular seasonal relationship with no off-cycle episodes, which is how it is distinguished from atypical features on exam vignettes.

🧠
Memory hook · Atypical GAINS, melancholic LOSESAtypical features (the most common subtype!): mood reactivity + weight/sleep gains + leaden paralysis. Melancholic: loses appetite, pleasure, energy. Seasonal pattern needs a strict seasonal on/off relationship with no off-season episodes.

Pulled from: Mood Disorders

SpecifierKey features
With anxious distressTension, restlessness, poor concentration from worry, fear of losing control
With mixed featuresManic/hypomanic symptoms during a depressive episode, or depressive symptoms during mania/hypomania — 3+ symptoms, most days of the episode
With rapid cycling4+ mood episodes in the past 12 months
With melancholic featuresLoss of pleasure or non-reactivity to normally pleasurable events + early morning awakening, psychomotor changes, anorexia/weight loss, excessive guilt
With atypical featuresMood reactivity + 2 of: ↑appetite/weight, hypersomnia, leaden paralysis, rejection sensitivity — most common depression subtype
With psychotic featuresDelusions/hallucinations — mood-congruent (fits the episode, e.g. grandiosity in mania) vs. mood-incongruent (doesn't fit)
With catatoniaCatatonic features present for most of the episode

With seasonal patternEpisodes and remissions track a particular season, ≥2 consecutive years
🧸 ELI5 — Typical vs. Atypical, In Plain English

Think of "typical" SIG E CAPS depression as the low-and-slow presentation: sleeping more, eating more or less but generally shutting down. Atypical features flip a couple of those dials the opposite direction — instead of sleeping too much, some people can't sleep at all (insomnia) even though everything else says depression. That reversal is exactly why it's called "atypical," even though statistically it's the most common flavor.

🩺 Clinical Pearl

"Atypical" depression is a bit of a misnomer — it's actually the most common subtype. Mnemonic hook: atypical depression reacts (mood reactivity) and gains (weight/sleep/heaviness) — basically the opposite polarity of melancholic depression, which loses (appetite, pleasure, energy) and doesn't react to good news.

Q: A patient reports her depressive episodes only happen every winter and remit by spring, for the past 3 years. Which specifier applies, and how does this differ from "atypical features"?

Answer

With seasonal pattern — episodes and remissions have a regular seasonal relationship, no off-cycle episodes, over ≥2 years. This is about timing. "Atypical features" is about the symptom profile (mood reactivity, hyperphagia, hypersomnia, leaden paralysis) and can co-occur with a seasonal pattern, but they are separate specifiers.

📎 Note

MDD specifiers are covered in the Depressive Disorders section above (anxious distress, mixed features, rapid cycling, melancholic, atypical, psychotic, catatonia, peripartum, seasonal) — they apply across both depressive and bipolar mood episodes.

These describe the flavor of an episode — high yield for both classroom and boards.

LO 047Psychosis & Antipsychotics✓ In your notes

Understand the 4 major dopamine pathways in the brain, and what dopamine dysregulation in each can portend clinically

Answer

The basic dopamine hypothesis of psychosis: the mesolimbic tract (motivation and reward) is overactive in psychosis and drives positive symptoms, and blockade here produces the therapeutic effect of antipsychotics. The mesocortical tract (cognition and motivation) is underactive in psychosis and drives negative symptoms, so further dopamine blockade there worsens or does not help negative and cognitive symptoms. The nigrostriatal tract governs the extrapyramidal motor system, and dopamine blockade there produces EPS. Antipsychotics block dopamine broadly without discriminating among tracts; typicals block relatively more dopamine than serotonin while atypicals block relatively more serotonin (5-HT2A) than dopamine, which is part of why atypicals carry less EPS but more metabolic risk. The drug list's one-page antipsychotics summary names all four dopamine pathways in one line -- mesolimbic (efficacy/positive symptoms), nigrostriatal (EPS), tuberoinfundibular (prolactin), and mesocortical (negative symptoms, untouched by typicals) -- supplying the previously missing tuberoinfundibular tract and its clinical link to prolactin.

🧠
Memory hook · The 4 M's of dopamineMesolimbic = Madness (overactive → positive sx; blockade = the therapeutic effect) · Mesocortical = Missing (underactive → negative sx; blockade worsens) · Nigrostriatal = Movement (blockade → EPS) · Tuberoinfundibular = Milk (blockade → prolactin).

Pulled from: Psychotic Disorders & Antipsychotic Pharmacology · Psychiatry Key Drug List 2026

TractFunctionEffect of Dopamine Blockade
MesolimbicMotivation & reward; overactive in psychosisReduces positive symptoms (the therapeutic effect)
MesocorticalCognition, motivation; underactive in psychosisWorsens/does not help negative & cognitive symptoms
NigrostriatalExtrapyramidal motor systemProduces EPS (Section 16)
TuberoinfundibularControls prolactin release (dopamine tonically inhibits prolactin)Produces hyperprolactinemia — galactorrhea, amenorrhea, gynecomastia

The basic pathophysiological model of psychosis: an overabundance of dopamine in the mesolimbic tract drives positive symptoms, while an underabundance of dopamine in the mesocortical tract drives negative symptoms. Antipsychotics block dopamine broadly, renormalizing levels — but they don't discriminate between tracts, which is the root of most antipsychotic side effects.

Quick pathway map: mesolimbic = positive symptoms/reward, mesocortical = negative symptoms, nigrostriatal = movement/EPS, tuberoinfundibular = prolactin.

The four dopamine tracts relevant to psychosis and antipsychotic side effects

5 psychosis criteria
Hallucinations, delusions, disorganized speech, disorganized behavior, negative symptoms — need ≥1.
Illusion vs. hallucination
Illusion = misperceived real stimulus. Hallucination = no external stimulus at all.
4 dopamine tracts
Mesolimbic (+ → positive sx), mesocortical (− → negative sx), nigrostriatal (blockade → EPS), tuberoinfundibular (blockade → hyperprolactinemia).
Timeline trio
Brief psychotic: 1 day–1 mo. Schizophreniform: 1–6 mo. Schizophrenia: >6 mo. Identical criteria otherwise.
Schizoaffective
Baseline psychosis + mood episodes, PLUS ≥2 weeks of psychosis alone at some point.
Delusional disorder
Plausible (non-bizarre) fixed delusion; otherwise preserved functioning; no insight into the delusion only.
95%
Percent of patients with psychotic disorders who smoke cigarettes.
Typical vs. atypical
Typical: D > S blockade. Atypical: S > D blockade.
Potency ↔ side effects
High potency = high EPS/low ACH. Low potency = low EPS/high ACH.
PINES vs. DONES
-pines = sedating/metabolic (olanzapine, quetiapine, asenapine). -dones = "watered-down typicals," more EPS (risperidone, ziprasidone, paliperidone, iloperidone).
D2 occupancy window
~70% = antipsychotic effect threshold; ~78–80% = EPS threshold.
EPS timeline
Dystonia (acute) → Akathisia (acute/subacute) → Pseudoparkinsonism (acute/subacute) → Tardive dyskinesia (chronic).
EPS treatment
Dystonia → IM anticholinergic. Akathisia → propranolol. Pseudoparkinsonism → anticholinergic/amantadine. TD → withdraw/reduce/switch agent.
Side-effect-receptor map
Sedation=H1. Hypotension=α1. Dry mouth/retention=M1. EPS=D2 (nigrostriatal). Galactorrhea=D2 (tuberoinfundibular).
Relapse rates
20%/yr oral-medicated vs. ~5%/yr on LAI vs. 70% at 1yr / 90% at 2yr unmedicated.
Antisuicidal drugs
Clozapine (antipsychotics) and lithium (mood stabilizers) are the only two psychiatric drugs with this FDA-recognized property.
Smoking & CYP1A2
Smoking induces CYP1A2 → lowers clozapine/olanzapine levels. Quitting (e.g., hospitalization) can raise levels ~50%.
Clozapine's trade
No EPS/TD, but agranulocytosis (1–2%), seizures, sialorrhea, myocarditis — mandatory ANC/WBC REMS monitoring.
B-52
Benadryl 50mg + Haldol 5mg + Ativan 2mg IM, PRN for acute agitation.
NMS red flags
Rigidity + hyperthermia + diaphoresis after antipsychotic dosing → stop the antipsychotic first.
CATIE/CUTLASS
FGA ≈ SGA for routine use (perphenazine cost-effective); clozapine superior for treatment-resistant disease.
First-line consensus
SGA first episode → SGA/FGA second → clozapine third → clozapine augmentation fourth (nearly universal across guideline bodies).

EPS arises from an acetylcholine : dopamine imbalance in the nigrostriatal tract (Section 02) caused by dopamine blockade. Normally dopamine and acetylcholine counterbalance each other in the striatum; blocking D2 receptors tips the seesaw toward relative cholinergic excess.

The ACh : DA seesaw — antipsychotics push it toward cholinergic excess

Relative dopamine deficiency in the nigrostriatal pathway — same final common pathway as Parkinson's disease (loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta) vs. antipsychotic-induced D2 blockade

Side EffectReceptor / Mechanism
SedationH1 (histamine) antagonism
Orthostatic hypotensionα1-adrenergic antagonism
Dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retentionM1 (muscarinic/anticholinergic) antagonism
Movement syndromes (EPS)D2 antagonism in the nigrostriatal tract
Galactorrhea, amenorrhea, gynecomastiaD2 antagonism in the tuberoinfundibular tract → disinhibited prolactin release
💊
Typical vs. Atypical, in one line: Typicals block more Dopamine than serotonin; atypicals block more Serotonin than dopamine. Serotonin is implicated indirectly, particularly in the mesolimbic pathway — atypicals' extra serotonin blockade is part of why they carry relatively less EPS but more metabolic burden (previewed here, detailed in Sections 12–20).

One receptor (D2), four brain pathways, four different outcomes. Block the right one and psychosis improves; the other three blocks are your side-effect chapters. "Major tranquilizers"/"neuroleptics" by their old names.

LO 048Anxiety, OCD & Trauma✓ In your notes

Understand the acute and chronic pharmacological treatment of the various anxiety disorders

Answer

Across anxiety disorders, an SSRI/SNRI is first-line chronic pharmacotherapy: GAD, panic disorder, agoraphobia, and social phobia all list an SSRI/SNRI (plus buspirone for GAD/agoraphobia) first-line, and OCD specifically requires much higher SSRI doses than used for depression to achieve response. PRN benzodiazepines provide acute control across GAD, panic disorder, adjustment disorder with anxious mood, and acute stress disorder/PTSD, used PRN rather than as chronic scheduled dosing. For comorbid presentations, GAD pairs with a high-potency benzodiazepine, TCA, SSRI, RIMA, or buspirone augmentation; generalized social phobia responds to an SSRI, RIMA, or MAOI, while the circumscribed/performance-only subtype adds a beta-blocker or PRN alprazolam/clonazepam; comorbid PTSD uses an SSRI, MAOI, or TCA, and comorbid OCD uses an SSRI or clomipramine. The exam-reading rule for social anxiety is that chronic/daily exposure calls for serotonergic therapy (SSRI/buspirone) as core treatment while episodic/occasional exposure (e.g., public speaking) can be managed with a beta-blocker or benzodiazepine alone, and PTSD-related nightmares/nighttime hyperarousal are specifically treated with prazosin.

🧠
Memory hook · Daily fear → SSRI; date-night fear → beta-blockerChronic/generalized anxiety or daily social exposure → serotonergic therapy (SSRI/SNRI, buspirone). Episodic performance anxiety → propranolol or PRN benzo. OCD wants higher SSRI doses than depression.

The single most important OCD pharmacology fact: OCD requires much higher SSRI doses than depression to achieve response — reinforcing Section 07's "maximal doses" language. Don't under-dose an SSRI when treating OCD.

  • ▸ Theoretically a TCA or MAOI could be used, but this is uncommon now given side-effect burden
  • ▸ A short-term/PRN benzo, or buspirone (5-HT1A partial agonist, Section 19), can be added to a baseline antidepressant for further anxiety control
  • ▸ Bupropion is an NDRI — the "D" (dopaminergic) component can sometimes cause excitement/anxiety, though not universally; it's occasionally used as an anxiolytic but this isn't common practice
📌
Anxiety is a difficult condition to control with medication alone — concomitant psychotherapy is often necessary for durable improvement.

LO 049Psychosis & Antipsychotics✓ In your notes

Understand the acute management of each type of EPS

Answer

Acute dystonia is treated with an IM/IV anticholinergic (benztropine or diphenhydramine), giving fast-acting, often dramatic relief. Akathisia is classically treated first-line with propranolol (a beta-blocker); benzodiazepines are also used. Pseudoparkinsonism is managed with anticholinergics (benztropine, trihexyphenidyl) or amantadine (a dopamine agonist). These three are acute-to-subacute syndromes (dystonia in hours-days, akathisia and pseudoparkinsonism in days-weeks), in contrast to tardive dyskinesia, which develops only after years of exposure. Young males are classically the highest-risk group for an acute dystonic reaction on first exposure to a high-potency typical, and high-potency typicals (Haldol, Prolixin, Navane) cause the most EPS overall, while clozapine essentially spares EPS entirely.

🧠
Memory hook · EPS timeline: ADAPTAcute Dystonia (hours–days) → Akathisia (days–weeks) → Parkinsonism (weeks) → Tardive dyskinesia (years). Treatments rhyme with the clock: benztropine IM → propranolol → anticholinergic/amantadine → stop the drug.

Pulled from: Psychotic Disorders & Antipsychotic Pharmacology

Acute dystonia → IM/IV anticholinergic (benztropine or diphenhydramine) — fast-acting, often dramatic relief
Akathisia → propranolol (beta-blocker) is classically first-line; benzodiazepines also used
Pseudoparkinsonism → anticholinergics (benztropine, trihexyphenidyl) or amantadine
Tardive dyskinesia → withdraw/reduce offending agent, switch to an atypical, consider VMAT2 inhibitors; TD is often not reversible, so prevention matters most

Antimuscarinics (benztropine, biperiden, orphenadrine, procyclidine, trihexyphenidyl), antihistamine (diphenhydramine), dopamine agonist (amantadine), benzodiazepines, and beta-blocker (propranolol) options for EPS

LO 050Anxiety, OCD & Trauma◐ Partly covered

Understand the acute management of symptoms of a suspected panic attack

Answer

A panic attack is a discrete period of intense fear/discomfort with abrupt onset, peaking within 30 seconds to 5 minutes, with at least 4 of 13 DSM symptoms (palpitations, sweating, trembling, shortness of breath, chest pain, dizziness, among others). Because panic attacks produce real cardiorespiratory symptoms that can be hard to distinguish from genuine organic disease, any acute presentation requires ruling out MI, angina, PE, and arrhythmia before labeling it 'just a panic attack.' The attack is driven by a self-perpetuating cycle -- stress triggers shortness of breath, which triggers anxiety, which speeds breathing, which tires the breathing muscles and increases anxiety further, accelerating the cycle -- so interrupting this loop is central to acute management. Benzodiazepines (e.g., alprazolam, which is FDA-approved for anxiety/panic) are used on a PRN basis for acute panic symptoms rather than as chronic scheduled dosing.

🧠
Memory hook · Rule out the four killers before calling it panicMI, angina, PE, arrhythmia — panic attacks peak in 30 s–5 min with ≥4 of 13 symptoms and mimic all of them. Acute tx: break the breath-anxiety spiral; PRN benzo (alprazolam).
◐
Missing from your notesA concrete non-pharmacologic component (reassurance, breathing/cognitive techniques) and specific alprazolam dosing for an attack in progress are still not detailed anywhere, and neither new source covers acute panic management.

Pulled from: Anxiety, OCD & Trauma-Related Disorders · Psychiatry Key Drug List 2026

💡
Across every indication below, the theme is PRN use, not chronic scheduled dosing: generalized anxiety disorder, panic disorder, acute stress disorder/PTSD, some sleep disorders, and alcohol-/opiate-/cocaine-/amphetamine-induced disorders.
🚨
Critical clinical caution: panic attacks have real cardiorespiratory features (chest pain, SOB, palpitations) that can be difficult to distinguish from genuine organic disease. Always rule out MI, angina, PE, arrhythmia, etc. before labeling something "just a panic attack" and discharging the patient. Duration is also a clue: a true panic attack peaks and resolves within minutes — if symptoms persist 20–30+ minutes, or if the heart rate is extremely high (e.g., ~250 bpm), think medical (e.g., SVT) rather than psychiatric. Patients often misremember the duration as much longer than it actually was because the surge of anxiety distorts their sense of time.

FDA-approved indications, approved dosage range, and equivalent dose for each major benzodiazepine — e.g., alprazolam (anxiety/panic/anxiety-depression), clonazepam (panic disorder/seizures), lorazepam (anxiety/pre-op sedation)

A discrete period of intense fear/discomfort with an abrupt onset, peaking within 30 seconds to 5 minutes, during which the patient experiences ≥4 of 13 DSM symptoms.

The 13 panic-attack symptoms — palpitations, sweating, trembling, SOB, choking, chest pain, nausea, dizziness/faintness, derealization/depersonalization, fear of losing control, fear of dying, paresthesias, chills/hot flushes

To diagnose panic disorder, you need a panic attack plus at least 1 of 3 maladaptive behavioral changes.

DSM-5 panic disorder criteria — persistent concern about additional attacks, worry about implications/consequences, or significant behavior change related to the attacks

A panic attack isn't exclusive to panic disorder — the same attack phenomenology shows up as a feature of several other conditions.

Panic attacks can occur in panic disorder (frequent, spontaneous), GAD (constant worry + physical symptoms), OCD (excessive repetitive thoughts/behaviors), social phobia (embarrassment/humiliation in social situations), and PTSD (thoughts/experiences of a horrible event)

Stress → shortness of breath begins → anxiety starts → breathing becomes faster → breathing muscles tire → anxiety increases → breathing becomes even more rapid → cycle accelerates

Mechanism
Bind the BZ site on GABA-A → potentiate GABA by ↑ FREQUENCY of Cl⁻ channel opening → hyperpolarization → ↓ firing → calm.
Indications
ACUTE/short-term anxiety & panic; sedative-hypnotic; anticonvulsant (status epilepticus → lorazepam, or diazepam PR/IM/IV); detox (ETOH withdrawal / DT prevention → long-acting chlordiazepoxide); muscle relaxant; night terrors; sleepwalking. Bridge role: cover anxiety during the 4–6 weeks an SSRI needs to work.
Why not long-term
Somnolence, psychomotor impairment, impaired memory, and addiction — dependence develops rapidly. Medical Letter: even for anxiety without depression, an SSRI is first choice; benzos = short-term/intermittent, limited benefit in OCD/PTSD.
Toxicity
Additive CNS depression with alcohol; overdose antidote = flumazenil (competitive BZ-receptor antagonist).
Mechanism
Selectively block SERT (serotonin reuptake) at the presynaptic neuron — nothing else. That selectivity is why they're clean.
Indications
MDD, persistent depressive disorder; drug of choice for long-term panic disorder (acute panic → short-acting benzo PRN) and OCD; social anxiety disorder, PTSD, PMDD, trichotillomania. Anxiety/OCD need HIGHER doses than depression
Side effects (10–15% quit — far less than TCAs)
  • GI upset / diarrhea — the #1 reason for discontinuation (transient)
  • Sexual dysfunction — #2 reason: ↓libido, anorgasmia, delayed/retrograde ejaculation. Dose-dependent and NOT transient. Fixes: add sildenafil or bupropion (erection), cyproheptadine/bethanechol (ejaculation).
  • Insomnia (dose in AM or add trazodone), hyperhidrosis, headache, and apathy/decreased spontaneity (not transient).

Understand the acute treatment of EPS in a young male patient

Answer

Young males are classically the highest-risk group for an acute dystonic reaction on first exposure to a high-potency typical antipsychotic, presenting with sudden, sustained muscle contractions such as torticollis, oculogyric crisis, or opisthotonos (sustained arching/twisting). The acute treatment is an IM/IV anticholinergic — benztropine or diphenhydramine — which gives fast-acting, often dramatic relief; in the case-based question, the most appropriate initial treatment for these motor symptoms was 2 mg of benztropine IM.

🧠
Memory hook · Young man, new Haldol, twisted neck → benztropine IMYoung males on a first dose of a high-potency typical are the classic acute-dystonia setup (torticollis, oculogyric crisis, opisthotonos). IM/IV benztropine or diphenhydramine works fast and dramatically.

A.1
Which of the following is the most likely etiology for these findings?
A. Akathisia
B. Catatonia
C. Dystonia
D. Parkinsonism
E. Tardive dyskinesia
Answer: C. Opisthotonos (sustained arching/twisting) is a sustained muscle contraction — the definition of an acute dystonic reaction, classically emerging within hours-to-days of starting a high-potency typical in a young patient (Section 16).
A.2
Which is the most appropriate initial treatment for this patient's motor symptoms?
A. Administer 2 mg of benztropine IM
B. Administer 2 mg of trihexyphenidyl PO
C. Discontinue all antipsychotic medication and observe
D. Switch medication to fluphenazine
E. Switch medication to thiothixene
Answer: A. Acute dystonia needs a fast-acting IM anticholinergic — benztropine IM works within minutes. Oral trihexyphenidyl (B) is too slow for an acute, distressing dystonic reaction. Simply stopping and observing (C) leaves the patient in an acutely uncomfortable, potentially airway-relevant state. Switching to another high-potency typical (D, E — fluphenazine and thiothixene are both high-potency) does nothing to treat the current reaction and would likely reproduce it.

LO 052Legal, Ethics & Risk✓ In your notes

Understand the application of the Tarasoff Doctrine to specific psychiatric cases

Answer

Under Tarasoff, a psychiatrist has a "duty to warn" when they determine a patient poses a serious danger to an identifiable victim; in practice "warn" means contacting the police and letting them handle notifying/protecting the victim, not calling the victim directly. Tarasoff applies when a specific, identifiable victim appears to be in imminent and probable danger from a mentally ill patient's threat, and it is considered ethical to break confidentiality once the treating psychiatrist's clinical judgment supports that risk. Before breaching confidentiality, the psychiatrist should exhaust the least restrictive in-house options first — change medication, involve family, increase visit frequency, then hospitalization — resorting to a warning only if these don't sufficiently protect the potential victim. The doctrine originates from the 1976 California Supreme Court case following the death of Tatiana Tarasoff, killed by a man whose therapist knew of his threats, and it is flagged as the highest-yield of the standard exceptions to confidentiality since protecting an identifiable third party takes precedence over maintaining confidentiality.

🧠
Memory hook · Warn = call the cops, not the targetTarasoff duty fires when an identifiable victim faces imminent danger. Climb the least-restrictive ladder first (meds, family, more visits, hospitalize) — then warn via police. A confessed past crime stays confidential; only future risk breaks the seal.

Pulled from: Legal Psychiatric Medicine

📖
The actual case: in this 1976 California Supreme Court case, the court ruled that mental health professionals have a legal duty to protect identifiable individuals who are being threatened with serious harm by a patient. The case stemmed from the death of Tatiana Tarasoff, who was killed by a man who had told his therapist he intended to harm her.

When Tarasoff Applies

TriggerA specific, identifiable victim appears to be in imminent and probable danger from the threat of a mentally ill patient.
Professional standardPsychiatry holds that it is ethical to break confidentiality when, in the clinical judgment of the treating psychiatrist, the risk of danger is significant. The psychiatrist carries the duty of determining which threats are likely to be acted upon, based on the details of the case and their clinical judgement.
Fantasies ≠ reportableA patient's fantasies alone are not reportable. This assumes the clinician's judgment is that these are not feelings the patient actually intends to act upon.
Specific vs. fantasy — the actual test"I hate all men" or "I could kill my brother, I just hate him" is not reportable — it's global or clearly rhetorical, with no real target or plan. "I'm going to kill my brother with a handgun at 4 p.m. on Friday" is reportable — a named, identifiable victim plus a credible plan and timeframe. When it's genuinely unclear which side of that line a statement falls on, get a second clinician's opinion before deciding not to report.
Tarasoff I
Establishes the "duty to warn" — a psychiatrist who determines a patient poses a serious danger to an identifiable victim has a duty to warn that intended victim. In practice, "warn" means contact the police and let them handle notifying/protecting the victim — you are not expected to call the intended victim yourself.
Tarasoff II
Expands the duty into the broader "duty to protect" — the obligation isn't satisfied by a warning alone; the psychiatrist must take whatever reasonable steps are needed to protect the potential victim. This does not mean physically inserting yourself between patient and victim — it still means notifying the police and documenting that you did.
📋
Before breaching confidentiality — try the least restrictive option first. The psychiatrist should exhaust reasonable in-house options to stabilize the patient and protect the potential victim before resorting to a warning: change medication → involve family → increase visit frequency → hospitalize. Warning/breaching confidentiality is not automatically the first move.

The patient has the right to receive the least restrictive means of treatment that still achieves the requisite clinical effect — this principle underlies Tarasoff management, medication-over-objection (Section 06), and seclusion/restraint (Section 10) alike.

1. Tarasoff Doctrine

TriggerProtecting an identifiable third party from a dangerous patient. Protecting the potential victim takes precedence over maintaining confidentiality.
More detailFull breakdown in Section 04 — this is the highest-yield exception by far.

2. Involuntary Hospitalization

TriggerThe doctor must break confidentiality to testify in court or to record the legal documentation explaining why involuntary hospitalization is necessary.

3. Supervision

TriggerA trainee disclosing patient information to a supervising attending. Allowed specifically for teaching and training purposes.

4. Emergency

TriggerPhysicians may break confidentiality in an emergency to obtain the information needed to treat the patient safely.

5. Incompetence

TriggerIf a patient is declared incompetent, the physician may break confidentiality to discuss the case with the court-appointed guardian.

6. Mandatory Reporting

TriggerState mandatory reporting laws require physicians to report specific circumstances to the appropriate authority — e.g., child abuse, elder abuse, an impaired physician, or certain communicable diseases.
Also coversMalicious wounding (a gunshot or stab wound) → inform law enforcement. Danger to the public (e.g., driving drunk, or a seizure disorder that impairs safe driving) → inform law enforcement and/or the DMV/RMV.
ProtectionMany states grant immunity from liability for an appropriate, good-faith breach of confidentiality made under a mandatory reporting statute.
LO 053Psychosis & Antipsychotics✓ In your notes

Understand the approach to the treatment of extrapyramidal symptoms in a psychotic patient being treated with high-potent antipsychotic medication

Answer

Because there is a narrow window between antipsychotic efficacy and EPS (roughly 78-80% striatal D2 occupancy gives efficacy with minimal EPS, corresponding to about 2-5 mg of Haldol or 100-200 mg of Thorazine), high-potency typicals like haloperidol carry the strongest EPS/akathisia signal of the antipsychotic classes. Management is EPS-type specific: acute dystonia gets an IM/IV anticholinergic (benztropine or diphenhydramine); akathisia is treated first-line with propranolol (a beta-blocker); pseudoparkinsonism responds to anticholinergics or amantadine. Young males on their first exposure to a high-potency typical are the classic highest-risk group for an acute dystonic reaction, and per the drug-induced movement disorder management algorithm, the first step when EPS emerges is to stop the antipsychotic.

🧠
Memory hook · EPS timeline: ADAPTAcute Dystonia (hours–days) → Akathisia (days–weeks) → Parkinsonism (weeks) → Tardive dyskinesia (years). Treatments rhyme with the clock: benztropine IM → propranolol → anticholinergic/amantadine → stop the drug.

Pulled from: Psychotic Disorders & Antipsychotic Pharmacology

Acute dystonia → IM/IV anticholinergic (benztropine or diphenhydramine) — fast-acting, often dramatic relief
Akathisia → propranolol (beta-blocker) is classically first-line; benzodiazepines also used
Pseudoparkinsonism → anticholinergics (benztropine, trihexyphenidyl) or amantadine
Tardive dyskinesia → withdraw/reduce offending agent, switch to an atypical, consider VMAT2 inhibitors; TD is often not reversible, so prevention matters most

There is a narrow window between antipsychotic efficacy and excessive side effects. The striatal D2 receptor occupancy threshold to reduce psychosis with minimal EPS is approximately 78–80%; crossing above the EPS threshold produces motor side effects.

Hypothetical thresholds for antipsychotic drug effects — the therapeutic window sits between the ~70% "antipsychotic effect" line and the ~80% "EPS" line

B. Add an anxiolytic
C. Add an antidepressant
D. Add an anticonvulsant

Answer: F. Per the drug-induced movement disorder management table (Section 16), the initial step for tardive dyskinesia is withdrawal or dose reduction of the offending agent (often with a switch to an atypical). Anticholinergics (G) do not help TD the way they help dystonia/pseudoparkinsonism — TD can worsen or fail to improve with anticholinergics since it isn't driven by the same relative-cholinergic-excess mechanism.

B. Chlorpromazine
C. Olanzapine
D. Haloperidol
E. Clozapine
Answer: D. Haloperidol is the classic high-potency typical with the strongest EPS/akathisia signal among these five options (Section 13/25) — clozapine (E) essentially never causes EPS, and olanzapine (C) is comparatively low-EPS.

LO 054Legal, Ethics & Risk◐ Partly covered

Understand the concept of a risk assessment and how it is performed, as well as the use of the Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale

Answer

Risk assessment and mitigation is described as one of the central, defining day-to-day activities of psychiatric practice, since both depression and bipolar disorder carry increased suicide risk. Regular, documented assessment -- using a structured tool like the Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale -- showing a lack of suicidality is the best defense against a suicide-related malpractice claim; a psychiatrist is not expected to predict the future, only to act on what was foreseeable. A 'contract for safety' made without a careful suicide assessment offers no legal protection -- it is the assessment itself, not the contract, that protects the physician, and a family's promise to monitor the patient does not transfer that responsibility. The SAD PERSONS mnemonic captures risk factors: Sex (male), Age (young or older adult), Depression, Previous attempt (highest risk factor), Ethanol/drug use, Rational thinking loss (psychosis), Sickness, Organized plan, No social support, and Stated future intent -- and women attempt suicide more often while men die by suicide more often due to more lethal means.

🧠
Memory hook · SAD PERSONS, and who dies vs. who triesSex(M) · Age · Depression · Previous attempt (#1 risk factor) · Ethanol · Rational-thought loss · Sickness · Organized plan · No support · Stated intent. Women attempt more; men die more (lethal means). The documented assessment (C-SSRS) is your legal shield — a safety contract without one protects no one.

Pulled from: Legal Psychiatric Medicine · Mood Disorders

🛡️
Your best defense against a suicide-related malpractice claim: regular, documented assessment showing a lack of suicidality — e.g., using a structured tool like the Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale. You are not expected to predict the future — only to act on what was predictable/foreseeable. If the patient gave no indication of suicidality, failing to intervene is not a deviation from the standard of care. The proof of this is documentation of ongoing suicide risk assessment, not any single note.

Depression and bipolar disorder both carry increased suicide risk — this was emphasized on the very first slide of the lecture for a reason. Risk assessment and mitigation is described as one of the central, defining activities of psychiatric practice — not just a topic, but the actual day-to-day work. Risk mitigation breaks down into two categories: risk of an untimely death (suicide), and risk of dangerous behavior more broadly (violence toward others, reckless spending, or other consequential impulsive acts — relevant in mania as well as depression).

Contracting for Safety ≠ Protection

A safety contract made in the absence of a careful suicide assessment offers no legal protection. It's the assessment — not the contract — that protects the physician.

Family Promises ≠ Your Responsibility Transferred

A family's promise to monitor a patient does not absolve the physician of responsibility if the patient is suicidal and no assessment/intervention occurred.
🔑 First Aid Mnemonic — SAD PERSONS are more likely to die from suicide
  • Sex (male)
  • Age (young adult or older adult)
  • Depression
  • Previous attempt — highest risk factor
  • Ethanol or drug use
  • Rational thinking loss (psychosis)
  • Sickness (medical illness)
  • Organized plan
  • No spouse or social support
  • Stated future intent
⚠️ Know the Asymmetry

Women attempt suicide more often; men die by suicide more often (more lethal means — firearms are the most common method in the US, and access to guns increases risk of death). Protective factors: effective treatment of comorbidities, strong social/family/community connectedness, cultural or religious beliefs favoring self-preservation, and good problem-solving skills.

🩺 Four Treatments Specifically Linked to Reduced Suicide Risk

Most psychiatric treatments target symptoms broadly. A small, specific list is called out in the literature as having direct evidence for reducing death by suicide — worth memorizing as its own group because exams like to test exactly this kind of "unique fact":

  • ECT
  • Esketamine
  • Lithium
  • Clozapine (Clozaril)
Question 5
A patient dies by suicide two weeks after a routine outpatient visit at which no suicidal ideation was elicited or documented as absent. The family sues for malpractice. What is most likely to determine the outcome?
A. Whether the psychiatrist could have predicted the suicide with certainty
B. Whether there is documentation of an ongoing, adequate suicide risk assessment showing no indication of suicidality
C. Whether the patient had signed a safety contract
D. Whether the patient's family had agreed to monitor them
Answer: B. Documentation of ongoing assessment is the actual legal defense (Section 07) — physicians aren't required to predict the future, only to act on the foreseeable. A safety contract (C) or family monitoring (D) alone offers no legal protection without a real underlying assessment.
🆘
Just attempted suicide, risk of further self-harm remains high? Next step: involuntarily hospitalize the patient.
LO 055Psychosis & Antipsychotics✓ In your notes

Understand the concept of determining side-effects of typical antipsychotics given the dose (high vs. low) of medication given

Answer

Typical antipsychotics are stratified into high, medium, and low potency relative to chlorpromazine (100 mg reference dose), and potency alone predicts the side-effect profile without needing to know the specific drug. The core trade-off: high potency = high EPS but low anticholinergic (ACH)/histaminic/alpha-1/cardiac burden; low potency = low EPS but high ACH and more histaminic/alpha-1/cardiac side effects; medium potency sits in between on both axes. Numerically, doses like 2-5 mg of Haldol (high potency) or 100-200 mg of Thorazine (low potency) sit in the efficacious, low-EPS zone at the D2-occupancy threshold. Antipsychotic selection criteria include prior response history, family history of response, medical status, this side-effect profile (high vs. low potency), dosing complexity/compliance, and cost.

🧠
Memory hook · The potency see-sawHigh potency (haloperidol, fluphenazine): hands shake — max EPS, minimal anticholinergic. Low potency (chlorpromazine): lazy & dry — sedation, anticholinergic, orthostasis, minimal EPS. Sweet spot: ~78–80% D2 occupancy ≈ Haldol 2–5 mg.

Pulled from: Psychotic Disorders & Antipsychotic Pharmacology

🧠
The core trade-off: High potency = high EPS, low anticholinergic (ACH) burden. Low potency = low EPS, high ACH (and more histaminic/alpha-1/cardiac) burden. Medium potency sits in between on both axes. Of the ~20–25 typicals that exist, only a handful (bolded below) are board-testable.

Typical antipsychotics are stratified into high, medium, and low potency categories relative to the original antipsychotic, chlorpromazine. Dr. Smith's key teaching point: you can predict a typical's side-effect profile from its potency alone — you don't even need to know the drug's name.

*ACH = histaminic, anticholinergic, alpha-1 blocking effect, and cardiac side effects. EPS = tardive dyskinesia, akathisia, parkinsonism, dystonias.

LO 056Cross-Cutting Pharm◐ Partly covered

Understand the concepts of hypertensive crisis, serotonin syndrome, iatrogenic mania, antidepressant withdrawal and neuroleptic malignant syndrome, and how each differ from the others based on a patient presentation

Answer

Serotonin syndrome develops rapidly (within 24 hours of a new serotonergic drug/dose/combination) with the '3 A's' -- increased activity (clonus, hyperreflexia, hypertonia, tremor, seizure), autonomic instability (hyperthermia, diaphoresis, diarrhea), and altered mental status -- triggered by any serotonergic agent (SSRIs, MAOIs, TCAs, venlafaxine, duloxetine, bupropion, mirtazapine, trazodone, meperidine, fentanyl, tramadol, ondansetron, triptans), with risk climbing sharply when different serotonergic mechanisms are combined rather than just adding more drugs of the same class. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome instead develops over days with 'lead-pipe' rigidity and hyporeflexia after antipsychotic use, classically presenting as rigidity, diaphoresis, and hyperthermia, with the first step being to stop the antipsychotic. Hypertensive crisis is an MAOI-specific phenomenon from increased norepinephrine, triggered by tyramine-rich foods (smoked, fermented, aged) or interacting medications, presenting as diastolic BP over 120 mmHg with headache, palpitations, neck stiffness, nausea/vomiting, sweating, dilated pupils, and arrhythmias. Antidepressant discontinuation syndrome follows abrupt cessation or missed doses of any antidepressant class (not just SSRIs), producing flu-like symptoms, dizziness, 'brain zaps,' and irritability.

🧠
Memory hook · Fast & twitchy vs. slow & stiffSerotonin syndrome: hours after a serotonergic change — the 3 A's (↑Activity: clonus/hyperreflexia · Autonomic instability · AMS). Tx: benzos → cyproheptadine. NMS: days after an antipsychotic — lead-pipe rigidity + hyporeflexia + fever + ↑CK. First move: STOP the drug. The danger is crossing mechanisms, not stacking the same one; 2-week MAOI washout.
🧠
Memory hook · The cheese reactionMAOI + tyramine (aged, smoked, fermented) or interacting drugs → hypertensive crisis: diastolic >120, pounding headache, palpitations, stiff neck. Discontinuation syndrome (any antidepressant, stopped abruptly): flu-ish + dizziness + brain zaps.
◐
Missing from your notesAntidepressant-induced (iatrogenic) manic switching is still not addressed by any source, including the two new ones.

Pulled from: Mood Disorders · Psychotic Disorders & Antipsychotic Pharmacology

Q: How do you distinguish serotonin syndrome from neuroleptic malignant syndrome at the bedside?

Answer

Serotonin syndrome develops rapidly (hours) with hyperreflexia and clonus, and follows a serotonergic drug/combination. NMS develops over days with "lead-pipe" rigidity and hyporeflexia, and follows antipsychotic (dopamine-blocking) exposure. Both can cause hyperthermia and autonomic instability, but the reflex findings and time course are the key differentiators.

☐ Hypertensive Crisis

Caused by increased NE and its excitatory effect — triggered by interacting medications or tyramine-rich foods (smoked, fermented, aged). Presentation: diastolic BP >120 mmHg with headache, palpitations, neck stiffness, nausea/vomiting, sweating, dilated pupils, arrhythmias. Treatment: phentolamine.

Q: A patient on venlafaxine develops a headache, palpitations, and diastolic BP of 128 after eating aged cheese and salami at a family dinner. What happened, and what's the mechanism?

Answer

Careful — this scenario is actually the classic MAOI + tyramine hypertensive crisis presentation, not venlafaxine's typical picture. Tyramine displaces NE at the synapse, causing excess sympathetic stimulation. Treatment is phentolamine. (Venlafaxine itself can raise BP at higher doses via NE reuptake inhibition, but the tyramine-food trigger specifically implicates MAOI use.)

D.1
Which adverse effect is most likely responsible?
A. Catatonia
B. Parkinsonian rigidity
C. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
D. Serotonin syndrome
E. Neuroleptic-induced dystonia
Answer: C. Rigidity + diaphoresis + hyperthermia (103°F) after repeated antipsychotic (Haldol) dosing is the classic triad pointing to NMS, not isolated dystonia (E, which wouldn't cause fever) or plain parkinsonian rigidity (B, which lacks the autonomic/hyperthermic component). There's no serotonergic agent on board here to suggest serotonin syndrome (D).
Drugs that can precipitate serotonin syndrome

AnalgesicsMeperidine, fentanyl, tramadol, pentazocine, propoxyphene
Anti-emeticsOndansetron and others
Anti-migraine drugsSumatriptan (triptans)
AntibioticsLinezolid
