Recreated from Robinson DS, Primary Psychiatry, Vol 13 No 8, 2006 (as cited in lecture) — ×-values reflect relative degree of CNS 5-HT excess.

📌
Watch for this vignette pattern: a patient given repeated "B-52" doses who develops rigidity, diaphoresis, and hyperthermia is showing neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS), not simple dystonia or parkinsonism — the fever and diaphoresis are the tip-off. First step is to stop the antipsychotic and provide supportive care/cooling; dantrolene or bromocriptine may be added in severe cases. This exact scenario is Case D in Section 28.
⚠️ Serotonin Syndrome Risk — ANY serotonergic drug

Because MAOIs block 5-HT breakdown, combining with other serotonergic agents (decongestants, stimulants, other antidepressants, MDMA, certain pain meds, certain anesthesia meds) risks serotonin syndrome. See the dedicated section below for full presentation.

☐ Antidepressant Discontinuation Syndrome

A relatively recently-recognized (last ~10 years) but testable phenomenon: a patient who abruptly stops or misses doses of an antidepressant — SSRIs included, not exclusive to any one class — presents with flu-like symptoms, dizziness, "brain zaps," irritability, and sensory disturbances. Management: restart the antidepressant and taper slowly. If restarting isn't appropriate (e.g. concern for serotonin syndrome), manage supportively (hydration, rest) instead. Higher risk with short half-life agents like paroxetine; lower risk with long half-life agents like fluoxetine.

LO 057Legal, Ethics & Risk✓ In your notes

Understand the concepts related to confidentiality as discussed by Dr. Smith

Answer

Confidentiality is the clinician's default obligation not to release information obtained during treatment to third parties, justified because patients would not seek treatment at all without assurance that their disclosures stay protected; physician-patient privilege lets (and obligates) a physician to refuse to testify about what a patient told them, and this obligation continues even after the patient's death. There are six standard, boards-recognized exceptions, the highest-yield being Tarasoff-type duty to protect an identifiable third party from a dangerous patient, plus involuntary hospitalization, and — flagged as a "common test question" — a patient who refuses to change behavior placing identifiable others at risk of HIV infection, where it becomes ethically permissible to notify the at-risk person or involve public health. Obtaining collateral information from family, an attorney, or a previous treater requires the patient's own consent and is not itself an exception, and disclosing to family/friends under HIPAA is likewise allowed only with explicit patient permission or the patient's non-objection when given a reasonable chance to object. A commonly missed point: if a patient discloses a past murder, that alone is not an exception — confidentiality can only be broken for a separately documented, imminent future risk of harm.

🧠
Memory hook · Warn = call the cops, not the targetTarasoff duty fires when an identifiable victim faces imminent danger. Climb the least-restrictive ladder first (meds, family, more visits, hospitalize) — then warn via police. A confessed past crime stays confidential; only future risk breaks the seal.

Pulled from: Legal Psychiatric Medicine

Confidentiality

DefinitionThe clinician's obligation not to release information obtained during treatment to third parties.
Ethical basisThe benefit of confidentiality outweighs the harm — patients would not seek treatment at all without the assurance that what they disclose stays protected. Confidentiality is considered implicit in the treatment setting; it doesn't need to be separately promised each visit.
Release ruleConfidential information may only be released with the patient's authorization or under proper legal compulsion (e.g., a valid court order).

Six standard, boards-recognized situations where breaking confidentiality is permitted or required. Each is a "spot the exception" vignette waiting to happen.

⚖️
Physician-patient privilege: the right (and obligation) of the physician to refuse to testify in a trial or other legal proceeding about anything a patient told them, on the basis that the communication is confidential. This obligation to protect confidentiality continues after the death of the patient — it doesn't expire.
🔪
The "shocker" every class gets wrong: if a patient discloses that they already murdered someone in the past, you cannot tell anyone — not unless there is a separately documented, imminent risk that they will harm someone else in the future. A past act, on its own, is not an exception to confidentiality, no matter how severe. You may be able to justify telling someone ethically, but you cannot do it legally without that future-risk piece — and legal is what protects your license.
👪
Collateral information from family: obtaining information from a patient's family requires the patient's consent — this is not a standard exception to confidentiality. The same is true when disclosing to, or obtaining information from, an attorney or a previous treater: patient permission is required either way.
🩸
Confidentiality and HIV — "Common test question!" If a patient refuses to change behavior that places identifiable others at risk of HIV infection, it is ethically permissible for the psychiatrist to break confidentiality — either notifying the at-risk individual directly or arranging for public health authorities to do so. The nuance to remember: ethically permissible does not automatically mean legally permissible in every jurisdiction, and a lawyer could still litigate the breach. Good practice is to get legal input before breaking confidentiality in this scenario, not after.

1. Tarasoff Doctrine

TriggerProtecting an identifiable third party from a dangerous patient. Protecting the potential victim takes precedence over maintaining confidentiality.
More detailFull breakdown in Section 04 — this is the highest-yield exception by far.

2. Involuntary Hospitalization

TriggerThe doctor must break confidentiality to testify in court or to record the legal documentation explaining why involuntary hospitalization is necessary.

3. Supervision

TriggerA trainee disclosing patient information to a supervising attending. Allowed specifically for teaching and training purposes.

4. Emergency

TriggerPhysicians may break confidentiality in an emergency to obtain the information needed to treat the patient safely.

5. Incompetence

TriggerIf a patient is declared incompetent, the physician may break confidentiality to discuss the case with the court-appointed guardian.

6. Mandatory Reporting

TriggerState mandatory reporting laws require physicians to report specific circumstances to the appropriate authority — e.g., child abuse, elder abuse, an impaired physician, or certain communicable diseases.
Also coversMalicious wounding (a gunshot or stab wound) → inform law enforcement. Danger to the public (e.g., driving drunk, or a seizure disorder that impairs safe driving) → inform law enforcement and/or the DMV/RMV.
ProtectionMany states grant immunity from liability for an appropriate, good-faith breach of confidentiality made under a mandatory reporting statute.
👨‍👩‍👧
Disclosing to friends/family under HIPAA is allowed only when: the patient gives explicit permission, or the patient does not object when given a reasonable opportunity to do so. Absent either, the better move is to support and encourage the patient to disclose themselves.
Topics
Confidentiality, HIPAA, Tarasoff, capacity/competence, malpractice, ethics & forensics terms
Core Tension
Patient confidentiality/autonomy vs. duty to protect identifiable third parties and society
Boards Fact
Almost entirely vignette-based — "which legal/ethical principle applies here?"
High-Yield
Tarasoff I/II · malpractice's 4 D's · M'Naughton Rule · confidentiality exceptions

Yield check: Confidentiality is the default — it's what makes patients willing to disclose in the first place. Nearly everything in this lecture is really a catalog of the narrow, specific situations where the law or ethics code carves out an exception to that default (Tarasoff, mandatory reporting, emergencies, incompetence, supervision). On boards, expect a clinical vignette followed by "what should the physician do?" or "which principle is this?" — so the goal below is being able to instantly recognize which exception or doctrine a given scenario is testing, not memorizing statutes.

Section 01
LO 058Psychotherapy & Theory◐ Partly covered

Understand the defense mechanisms and apply them to a clinical scenario. Focus on identification, displacement, projection, repression, and sublimation)

Answer

A defense mechanism is an unconscious tendency the ego uses to prevent being overwhelmed by conflict (and the resulting anxiety) among the id, ego, and superego, a framework credited largely to Freud but substantially expanded by his daughter, Anna Freud. Denial is refusing to accept an unbearable piece of reality (a patient with concerning symptoms insists nothing is wrong and skips the recommended workup); projection is attributing one's own unacceptable feelings or impulses to someone else (a person who cheated on a test becomes convinced everyone else cheated too); and repression is unconsciously and involuntarily blocking a disturbing memory from awareness entirely, distinct from suppression, which is conscious and deliberate. Sublimation is one of the four mechanisms classified as mature via the mnemonic "Mature adults wear a SASH" (Sublimation, Altruism, Suppression, Humor), making it likelier to be a correct answer than a distractor, and splitting is the cardinal defense of borderline personality disorder. About 26 named defense mechanisms exist in total, with roughly one exam question expected on the topic overall.

🧠
Memory hook · Mature adults wear a SASHThe 4 mature defenses: Sublimation, Altruism, Suppression, Humor. And remember: Suppression is on purpose (conscious); repression happens to you (unconscious). Splitting = borderline's signature.
◐
Missing from your notesDisplacement and identification remain undefined and unexemplified in every source, including the two new ones.

Pulled from: Introduction to Therapy · Introduction & History of Psychiatry

DefenseDefinitionExample
DenialRefusing to accept an unbearable piece of realityA patient with concerning symptoms insists nothing is wrong and skips the recommended workup
ProjectionAttributing one's own unacceptable feelings or impulses to someone elseA person who cheated on a test becomes convinced their classmates are all cheaters
Reaction formationAdopting the opposite attitude to keep an unacceptable emotion out of awarenessSomeone who unconsciously resents a new sibling becomes their most devoted, over-the-top caretaker
Splitting ⭐Categorizing people as all-good or all-bad, with no in-between; a cardinal feature of borderline personality disorder"You're the only doctor here who actually cares — everyone else on this unit is useless"
DisplacementRedirecting an emotion from its true (often threatening) target onto a safer oneSnapping at a spouse after a bad day with a difficult boss
SublimationChanneling an unacceptable impulse into a socially productive outlet (considered a "mature" defense)A person with aggressive impulses becomes a competitive athlete
SuppressionConsciously (deliberately) pushing an uncomfortable thought or feeling out of awareness — the only defense with a conscious componentDeliberately setting aside anxiety about an exam to focus on the lecture in front of you
RationalizationConstructing a more comfortable, logical-sounding explanation for a distressing outcome"I didn't get the promotion because they don't value hard work here anyway"
RegressionReverting to behavior patterns typical of an earlier developmental stage under stressAn older child starts thumb-sucking again after a new sibling arrives
IdentificationUnconsciously patterning one's own behavior after someone more powerful (can be adaptive or maladaptive)A person bullied by a coach becomes an overly harsh coach themselves
IntellectualizationUsing facts and logic to distance oneself from the emotional weight of a situationFocusing on the technical mechanics of a diagnosis instead of its emotional impact
HumorUsing comedy to express or deflect an otherwise uncomfortable feelingA lecturer uncomfortable with a topic inserts jokes throughout the talk
Acting outExpressing an unacceptable emotion through behavior instead of acknowledging the feeling directlyA teenager who feels ignored gets into repeated disciplinary trouble
UndoingTrying to "magically" reverse a past action through a symbolic later behaviorConfessing to and repaying a theft, then going out of one's way to help the person repeatedly afterward
AltruismManaging personal distress by focusing on helping others (a "mature" defense)A person with low self-esteem devotes significant time to volunteering
DissociationMentally separating from distressing real-life events or from one's own thoughts/feelingsHaving no memory of the details surrounding a traumatic event
IdealizationSeeing another person as more competent or powerful than they really areA patient insists their doctor "always knows exactly what to do"
FixationStaying partially stuck at an earlier, more childish stage of development (contrast with regression, which is moving backward from a stage already passed)A college student still sucks her thumb while studying for a stressful exam
Isolation of affectSeparating a distressing fact from the feeling that would normally go with itDescribing a traumatic event in graphic detail with a completely flat, unaffected tone
Passive aggressionExpressing hostility indirectly, through inaction or subtle resistance rather than open confrontationAn employee who resents a manager keeps "forgetting" to complete assigned tasks on time
RepressionInvoluntarily blocking a distressing thought or feeling from conscious awareness entirely (contrast with suppression, which is a deliberate, conscious, temporary version of the same thing)An adult has no memory of attending counseling during a difficult period in childhood
DefenseMaturityDefinitionExample
RepressionLess mature Unconsciously blocking a disturbing wish, thought, or memory from awareness entirely (distinct from suppression, which is conscious). A patient has no memory at all of a traumatic childhood event.
FantasyLess mature Substituting reality with a less disturbing, imagined version of the world. A terminally ill patient states she's sure she'll survive because her long-deceased mother assured her so in a dream.
RegressionLess mature Reverting to an earlier, less mature pattern of behavior under stress. An adult throws a tantrum when frustrated at work.
SplittingLess mature Viewing people/situations as all-good or all-bad, unable to integrate positive and negative qualities together. Classic in BPD. A patient idealizes a new nurse, then suddenly devalues her entirely after one minor disagreement.
DenialLess mature Failure to acknowledge a disturbing aspect of external reality. A patient with a grim prognosis insists he will get better because he "just knows it."
ResistanceLess mature Unconscious opposition to bringing repressed material into conscious awareness — often surfaces in therapy as avoidance of a topic. A patient repeatedly changes the subject whenever therapy approaches a specific childhood memory.
ConversionLess mature Emotional conflict transformed into a physical symptom. A patient who is obviously angry about a subtle insult instead develops sudden gastric distress and denies any feelings beyond concern.
DissociationLess mature Sealing off disturbing thoughts/emotions from consciousness. Hours after a terrible accident, a patient says she has no memory of the event.
Isolation (of affect)Less mature Separating a thought from its attached emotional tone, making it tolerable. Common in extremely stressful moments. Hours after a fatal accident, a patient mechanically discusses the financial/legal paperwork with no visible emotion.
ProjectionLess mature Attributing one's own uncomfortable feelings (often anger/guilt) to other people instead. A patient seeking large financial compensation accuses other patients of "manipulating the system."
UndoingLess mature An act performed to symbolically negate or atone for an unacceptable thought, feeling, or act. A person who had an angry thought about their spouse buys them an elaborate gift that same day.
SymbolizationLess mature One object/idea unconsciously comes to represent another, usually via some similarity. A patient with unresolved anger toward a parent has recurring nightmares about a menacing authority figure.
DisplacementLess mature Emotions tied to an unacceptable object/idea are transferred onto a different, often symbolically-related, object. A patient badly injured in an accident becomes angry at his surgeon over a small scar from the reconstructive procedure.
DistortionLess mature Reshaping one's perception of a disturbing reality to make it more palatable. A patient permanently disabled by his own careless driving views himself as a victim of "bad traffic laws."
Reaction formationLess mature Unacceptable feelings/impulses are transformed into their exact opposite. A person with an unwanted attraction acts with exaggerated hostility toward that person instead.
IntrojectionLess mature Absorbing aspects of another person into one's own self-image, including their negative views. A victim of spousal abuse absorbs her partner's negative opinions of her worth and defends his right to batter her.
Passive-aggressive behaviorLess mature Expressing unconscious anger/aggression through passive failure to meet another person's needs. A resident consistently arrives late to rounds with his attending because he "has so many important tasks."
CompensationLess mature Using skill/competence in one area to counterbalance a self-perceived deficiency in another. A patient with a gait disturbance becomes a self-taught expert on the history of dance.
IdealizationLess mature Unrealistically attributing only excellent qualities to a person or situation. An elderly man fondly but unrealistically describes his hometown as the most wonderful place that ever existed.
IdentificationLess mature Modeling oneself after someone perceived as admirable or powerful. A hospitalized child decides she wants to be a doctor and asks for her own toy stethoscope.
RationalizationLess mature Distorting reality to make an undesirable act or outcome seem more acceptable — often used when a person can't tolerate the real reason. A student who didn't study for an exam blames a "bad test-writer" for the failing grade.
IntellectualizationLess mature Transforming an emotionally disturbing event into a purely cognitive/academic problem. A physician diagnosed with a serious illness becomes consumed with reading every available clinical research report about it.
SublimationMature Channeling an unacceptable impulse into a socially acceptable, often productive, activity. A person with aggressive impulses becomes a competitive athlete in a contact sport.
SuppressionMature The conscious, deliberate postponement of attention to a disturbing thought or feeling — the mature, conscious cousin of repression. A surgeon consciously sets aside worry about a personal problem in order to focus during an operation.
HumorMature Using amusing thoughts or observations to decrease anxiety about a difficult situation. A patient with a severe motor disability tells droll stories about his struggles with airport security.
AltruismMature Decreasing one's own internal fear/anxiety by caring for others facing a similar struggle. A patient with a rare but serious illness devotes himself to leading a support group for others with the same disease.
🔑
Definition: A defense mechanism is a psychological tendency the ego uses to prevent a person from being overwhelmed by conflict (and the resulting anxiety) among the id, ego, and superego. Freud's original framework. Defense mechanisms operate at an unconscious level — you're not aware of them while using them, though you may recognize their use afterward, often through psychotherapy. They're also the reason our own automatic habits sometimes baffle (or drive crazy) the people close to us.

Two commonly confused pairs: repression (unconscious, involuntary) vs. suppression (conscious, deliberate); and fixation (stuck at a stage, never fully progressed) vs. regression (moving backward from a stage already reached).

Credited largely to Freud but substantially expanded by his daughter, Anna Freud. Defense mechanisms exist to protect the ego from being exposed to something too threatening or vulnerable — some are considered more "mature," others more "primitive," though how useful that mature/immature split really is remains debated. These are easy to write test questions about, so they're worth knowing cold.

🧠
Memory Hook: "Mature adults wear a SASH" — Sublimation, Altruism, Suppression, Humor are the four defenses usually classified as "mature." And for splitting: borders split countries — splitting is the cardinal defense of borderline personality disorder.
🧠
Memory Hook — "SASH" for the mature four: Suppression, Altruism, Sublimation, Humor. If you only lock in four terms for this topic, make it these — they're the ones most likely to be the "correct" answer choice rather than a distractor.
🎯
There are technically ~26 named defense mechanisms (more granular lists run to 40–45). Dr. Smith does not require memorizing all of them — some psych courses do, this one doesn't. Expect roughly one question on the exam. Dr. Wolfrum's psychotherapy lecture goes into more depth; wait for the study guide to know exactly which ones you're responsible for. What's worth knowing at this stage: the handful of mature defenses, and roughly what each term means when you see it on boards.
LO 059Assessment & MSE◐ Partly covered

Understand the descriptors used in a mental status exam's thought process and thought content sections as they apply to a psychotic patient

Answer

The Mental Status Exam (MSE) is the complete written narrative of a patient's mental functioning, done alongside or in place of the physical exam within the psychiatric SOAP note, and is distinct from the MMSE (a scored 0-30 cognitive screening test) and MoCA, which are single components rather than the whole exam; its components table lists domains such as physical appearance, arousal/attention (tested with serial sevens), and psychomotor activity alongside thought process and thought content. For a psychotic patient, delusional disorder illustrates a concrete thought-content and thought-process picture: thought process stays organized and functioning is largely intact except in relation to the delusion itself, while thought content is dominated by fixed, non-bizarre false beliefs sorted into subtypes such as persecutory, somatic, and erotomanic. These patients have no insight into the delusion itself but retain insight into the rest of their life, so they can appear entirely normal until the delusion surfaces.

🧠
Memory hook · MSE describes; MMSE scoresThe MSE is the narrative exam (appearance, attention, thought process/content…) inside the psych SOAP note. A number out of 30 means MMSE/MoCA — a single cognitive screen, never the whole MSE. Classic exam trap.
◐
Missing from your notesGeneral psychotic thought-process descriptors (flight of ideas, tangentiality, looseness of association, thought blocking, ideas of reference) remain undefined in every source, including the two new ones.

Pulled from: Introduction & History of Psychiatry · Psychotic Disorders & Antipsychotic Pharmacology

🧩
MSE vs. MMSE vs. MoCA — a very common source of confusion:
  • MSE (Mental Status Exam): the whole written narrative described above — a full description of the patient's mental functioning.
  • MMSE (Mini-Mental State Exam): just one piece of the MSE — a scored (0–30) cognitive screening test.
  • MoCA (Montreal Cognitive Assessment): a specific type of MMSE-style instrument, testing visuospatial/executive function, naming, memory, attention, language, abstraction, delayed recall, and orientation — also scored out of 30.
ComponentWhat you're observingExample bedside tests
Physical appearancePhysical signs of illness, manner of dress, grooming—
Arousal & attentionLevel of arousal; ability to focus/sustain attentionSerial sevens
Psychomotor activityAppropriateness, focal deficits, incoordination, abnormal movementsHandshake
SpeechRate, rhythm, articulation, coherency, vocabularySentence repetition
MoodLevel of psychomotor activity, patient's self-report—
AffectFacial expression, quality, range, intensity—
Memory & other cognitive fxAbility to relate history, understand/communicate, recognize people/objects, plan & execute tasksDigit span; orientation; three objects at 5 min; demographic recall; sentence repetition; comprehension of instructions

Thought contentInformation-related themes, suicidal/homicidal ideation, judgment—
  1. I–IV. Identifying data, source/reliability, chief complaint, present illnessSame as any H&P.
  2. V–IX. Psychiatric, substance use, medical, family, developmental/social historyStandard background — but substance use history carries extra weight here.
  3. X. Review of systems
  4. XI. Mental Status ExaminationThe psychiatry-specific substitution for (or complement to) the physical exam.
  5. XII. Physical examination
  6. XIII–XV. Formulation, DSM-5 diagnoses, treatment planFormulation is where the biopsychosocial synthesis happens (below).

Guiding question: Comment on the psychiatric diagnostic interview — what is the MSE and what are its parts?

Psychiatry documents in a SOAP-note structure, just like every other specialty — but with one substitution: the Mental Status Exam (MSE) is done either alongside or in place of the physical exam. It's a written description detailed enough that another clinician reading only your note can understand the patient's mental state at the time you saw them.

🔎
Preserved functioning is the hallmark: delusions are often not overtly bizarre, thought process stays organized, and overall functioning is largely intact except relative to the delusion itself. Patients can appear entirely normal to the world except when the delusion surfaces — which the public may find "odd" but not overtly bizarre. As a result, this is often subclinical for years to decades before presenting to clinical attention.

A disorder involving delusions — fixed, false beliefs held despite contrary evidence — about relatively plausible events (as opposed to bizarre, physically-impossible content). The test Dr. Smith uses: could this, in principle, actually be true, even if the evidence says it isn't? "Is my body rotting from the inside out?" — implausible but not impossible. "Can I fly, or run 300 mph?" — that would be a different, more bizarre kind of delusion, not typical of this disorder.

SubtypeBelief
PersecutoryBelief that the patient is being persecuted, most often unfairly/unjustly
SomaticBelief that the patient has a serious or unique illness ("My face is made out of air"; "My insides are rotting from the inside-out")
ErotomanicBelief in a secret, often sexual, relationship with another person — often someone of higher stature ("I have a special relationship with [a public figure]")
GrandioseBelief that the patient has a special ability to make something happen that isn't realistically plausible (wishing something into reality, clairvoyance)
JealousBelief that the spouse is cheating, maintained even with ample contrary evidence
MixedA combination of the above subtypes
📌
Boards-relevant nuance: delusional disorder is one of the few DSM-5 conditions with preserved functioning and minimal impairment across most life domains. There is no insight into the delusion itself, though the patient retains insight into the rest of their life — a combination that's fairly unique among psychotic disorders.
🎙️
Dr. Smith's framing, worth internalizing: "Psychosis is a symptom, OK — psychosis is not a diagnosis. Just like depression is not a diagnosis, it's a symptom of a larger diagnosis or disorder." Every patient's psychosis looks a little different — there are common themes (religiosity shows up constantly in delusion content) but you'll rarely see two patients with identical psychotic symptoms. Because so few conditions can produce it, the presence of psychosis is a pertinent positive that dramatically narrows your differential — never ignore it, and never treat it as self-explanatory ("the person's hallucinating, so it's psychiatric") without ruling out secondary causes first (Section 03).
LO 060Anxiety, OCD & Trauma✓ In your notes

Understand the diagnostic criteria of trauma and stressor related disorders in the DSM5

Answer

DSM-5 groups trauma- and stressor-related disorders separately from anxiety disorders, and this chapter includes PTSD, acute stress disorder, and adjustment disorders. Adjustment disorder criteria (A-E) require emotional/behavioral symptoms developing in response to an identifiable stressor within 3 months of its onset (Criterion A), distress clinically out of proportion to the stressor's severity/context and/or significant functional impairment (Criterion B), and that the presentation not meet criteria for another disorder (Criterion C) — and it differs from PTSD/acute stress disorder in that it can follow any identifiable stressor, not necessarily a traumatic or life-threatening one. Acute stress disorder is described as "the anxiety-related equivalent of brief psychotic disorder" — essentially early/acute PTSD sharing the same symptom domains, but on a compressed timeline of 3 days to 1 month post-trauma; symptoms persisting past 1 month convert the diagnosis to PTSD. PTSD itself is defined by DSM-5 criteria A-H, with full detail behind criteria B, C, D, and E.

🧠
Memory hook · The stressor clockAny stressor → symptoms within 3 months = adjustment disorder (gone by 6 months after stressor ends). Traumatic stressor → 3 days–1 month = acute stress disorder; past 1 month = PTSD.
🧠
Memory hook · 3 days to 1 month, then it changes its nameAcute stress disorder = PTSD's symptoms on a compressed clock (3 d–1 mo post-trauma); persist past 1 month → PTSD. Adjustment disorder follows ANY stressor (not necessarily traumatic) within 3 months.

Pulled from: Anxiety, OCD & Trauma-Related Disorders

CriterionRequirement
AEmotional/behavioral symptoms develop in response to an identifiable stressor, within 3 months of its onset
BClinically significant: marked distress out of proportion to the stressor's severity/context, and/or significant functional impairment
CDoesn't meet criteria for another mental disorder and isn't just an exacerbation of a pre-existing one
DDoes not represent normal bereavement
EOnce the stressor (or its consequences) has ended, symptoms do not persist beyond an additional 6 months

Criteria A–E — note the two timing rules in A and E

💡
PTSD is more common in times/places of increased disaster; symptoms often begin immediately after the stressor. Clinical course varies — most cases resolve within 3 months, though some persist a lifetime. Frequently complicated by phobic avoidance, impaired relationships, emotional lability, guilt, self-destructive behavior, and substance abuse.

The full detail behind criteria B, C, D, and E

🧠
The one-line summary: acute stress disorder is "the anxiety-related equivalent of brief psychotic disorder" — essentially "early" or "acute" PTSD. Must last 3 days to 1 month; past 1 month, the diagnosis converts to PTSD. Same underlying symptom domains as PTSD, just on a compressed timeline.

Acute stress disorder = first 30 days post-trauma; most people recover fully in this window; those still symptomatic after 30 days convert to a PTSD diagnosis

Much like PTSD, these are extremely common — Dr. Smith: "please learn this section well." Reclassified from their own DSM-IV-TR chapter into the trauma/stressor-related disorders section in DSM-5.

Question 10
Which of the following best distinguishes adjustment disorder from PTSD/acute stress disorder?
A. Adjustment disorder requires a life-threatening stressor, while PTSD does not
B. Adjustment disorder can follow any identifiable stressor (not necessarily traumatic/life-threatening), while PTSD/ASD specifically require exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence
C. Adjustment disorder has no duration criteria at all
D. PTSD does not require any identifiable stressor
Answer: B. Adjustment disorder's stressor can be almost anything with real functional impact — a divorce, a job loss, a diagnosis (Section 11) — whereas PTSD/ASD require Criterion A trauma exposure specifically. Adjustment disorder does have timing rules (within 3 months of the stressor, resolving within 6 months after it ends) — option C is incorrect.

LO 061Psychotherapy & Theory✓ In your notes

Understand the differences between the Id, Ego and Superego as described by Freud and how they function as a control for human drives

Answer

Freud's structural model divides the psyche into the id (unfiltered, largely sexual or aggressive urges pushing for immediate gratification), the ego (a "primitive control" that introduces enough restraint to function in society, e.g. sitting through a long lecture instead of walking out to get food), and the superego (a more fine-tuned layer of control). Defense mechanisms are unconscious tendencies the ego uses to keep a person from being overwhelmed by the anxiety created by conflict among the id, ego, and superego; Freud originated the concept and his daughter Anna Freud substantially expanded it into a spectrum from more "primitive" to more "mature" defenses. This id-ego-superego framework is specifically the Freudian school within psychodynamic/psychoanalytic theory, distinct from other psychodynamic "flavors" like Jungian theory (individuation, extraversion vs. introversion) or Kleinian theory (object relations).

🧠
Memory hook · Founder → school, in one breathRogers → humanistic (unconditional positive regard) · Freud → psychodynamic (free association, transference) · Beck & Ellis → cognitive · Skinner → behavioral · Linehan → DBT.

Pulled from: Introduction to Therapy · Introduction & History of Psychiatry

Id

The drives

Unfiltered urges Freud framed as largely sexual or aggressive — the raw push to meet a need right now.

Ego

Primitive control

Introduces enough restraint to function in society — e.g., sitting through a long lecture instead of walking out to get food.

Superego

Fine-tuned control

Adds social/moral nuance on top of the ego — e.g., pausing the lecture recording instead of just leaving, in case something important is said.

SchoolKey concepts
FreudianConscious vs. unconscious; the id, ego, and superego
JungianIndividuation; extraversion vs. introversion
Kleinian (Melanie Klein)Child/adolescent analysis; object relations — extended adult-focused theory downward to children
🔑
Definition: A defense mechanism is a psychological tendency the ego uses to prevent a person from being overwhelmed by conflict (and the resulting anxiety) among the id, ego, and superego. Freud's original framework. Defense mechanisms operate at an unconscious level — you're not aware of them while using them, though you may recognize their use afterward, often through psychotherapy. They're also the reason our own automatic habits sometimes baffle (or drive crazy) the people close to us.

Credited largely to Freud but substantially expanded by his daughter, Anna Freud. Defense mechanisms exist to protect the ego from being exposed to something too threatening or vulnerable — some are considered more "mature," others more "primitive," though how useful that mature/immature split really is remains debated. These are easy to write test questions about, so they're worth knowing cold.

Around 1886, Sigmund Freud — trained as an Austrian neurologist — opened a private practice to study psychopathology, building on hypnosis research he'd seen from Charcot. In 1906, Freud's ideas were introduced to the United States via a lecture at Clark University. Freud's real contribution wasn't necessarily originality — he was one of the first to package these ideas into a digestible, "scientific-style" written form, turning hysteria into a testable theory: a cause (often trauma), a mechanism, and a targeted treatment.

LO 062Neurocognitive & AMS✕ Not in your notes

Understand the differential diagnosis of memory impairment, as well as the various forms of dementia

Answer

The only available content states that cognitive disorders -- delirium and later-stage dementia -- can present with psychosis, while early dementia typically does not, and that trazodone is sometimes used off-label as a lower-risk alternative to antipsychotics for agitation or insomnia in dementia patients. The neuroanatomy lecture covers limbic/basal-ganglia circuitry, monoamine control systems, the habenula, and deep brain stimulation, and the child psychiatry lecture covers pediatric diagnoses; neither addresses the differential diagnosis of memory impairment or distinguishes dementia subtypes.

✕
Not covered by any of your sourcesThe differential diagnosis of memory impairment and the distinguishing features among dementia subtypes (Alzheimer's, vascular, Lewy body, frontotemporal), plus a delirium-vs-dementia workup, remain unaddressed in all available sources.

Pulled from: Psychotic Disorders & Antipsychotic Pharmacology

  • ▸ Cognitive disorders — delirium, and later-stage dementia (early dementia does not typically present with psychosis)
  • ▸ Mood disorders — major depressive disorder, severe, with psychotic features; bipolar I disorder, with psychotic features (psychosis occurs only at the peaks/valleys — the manic or depressive episodes — never during euthymia, "the middle part"); psychotic features are either mood-congruent or mood-incongruent
  • ▸ Autistic disorder — disorganized speech/behavior can be mistaken for psychosis
  • ▸ Primary psychotic disorders (Sections 05–07)
  • ▸ Personality disorders — mainly Cluster A, with Cluster C to a lesser degree (and Cluster B least so) can show psychotic-flavored presentations, though it's a manifestation of the personality pathology rather than pure psychosis
💊
Trazodone comment: the lecture flags trazodone as a comparison point in this population — it's sometimes used off-label for agitation/insomnia in dementia as a lower-risk alternative to antipsychotics, though it carries its own risks (orthostasis, priapism) and isn't itself an antipsychotic.
LO 063Psychosis & Antipsychotics✓ In your notes

Understand the differential diagnosis of psychosis, including both primary- and secondary- psychiatric conditions

Answer

New-onset psychosis is worked up along a primary ("psychiatric," a DSM-5 diagnosis in its own right such as schizophrenia) versus secondary ("organic," most often substance-induced or due to a general medical condition) axis, since primary psychotic disorders are, to some degree, diagnoses of exclusion. History clues favoring a primary disorder include past episodes of psychosis, past psychiatric hospitalization, family history of psychotic disorders, prior antipsychotic treatment, marked post-morbid decline in functioning, and heavy smoking (95% of patients with psychotic disorders smoke); an unremarkable physical exam is itself a useful pertinent negative supporting a primary cause. For substance-related psychosis, the rule of thumb is "uppers in intoxication, downers in withdrawal": amphetamine intoxication causes psychosis while amphetamine withdrawal does not, whereas alcohol/benzodiazepine/opiate withdrawal (e.g., delirium tremens) causes psychosis but their intoxication generally does not. Real secondary-psychosis cases include a glioblastoma presenting as psychosis (resolved only by treating the tumor, not antipsychotics alone), a UTI causing visual hallucinations, and tertiary/neurosyphilis, which can stay latent for decades before producing psychosis, notably clustering in nursing-home patients.

🧠
Memory hook · Uppers freak you ON the drug; downers freak you OFF itPsychosis with stimulant intoxication (amphetamines, cocaine) but with depressant withdrawal (alcohol/benzo/opioid — think DTs). Opioids: intox = dry & pinpoint; withdrawal = wet & wide (tearing, runny nose, diarrhea, dilated pupils — 'worst flu ever', miserable but not lethal).
🧠
Memory hook · Psychosis is a symptom until proven a diagnosisRule out malingering → substances → medical causes → THEN primary psychiatric. Uppers cause it in intoxication, downers in withdrawal. Remember the curveballs: glioblastoma, UTI in the elderly, neurosyphilis.

Pulled from: Psychotic Disorders & Antipsychotic Pharmacology · Introduction & History of Psychiatry

Differential diagnosis of new-onset psychosis — Primary ("psychiatric") vs. Secondary ("organic")

🔀
Primary psychiatric disorder: one of the 365 DSM-5-TR diagnoses in its own right. Secondary psychiatric disorder: psychiatric symptoms caused by something else entirely — e.g. hypothyroidism-induced depressive disorder. The distinction matters clinically: if it's secondary, treating the underlying medical problem can resolve the "psychiatric" symptoms too.

Primary Psychotic Disorder

DefinitionPsychosis derived from a condition described in DSM-5 (e.g., schizophrenia).

Secondary Psychotic Disorder

DefinitionMost often substance-induced psychotic disorder, or psychosis due to a general medical condition.
Naming conventione.g., [cocaine]-induced psychotic disorder; psychotic disorder due to [glioblastoma multiforme] — the bracket holds the etiologic drug/condition.

Schizophrenia is, to some degree, a diagnosis of exclusion — organic/substance causes must be eliminated before a primary psychotic disorder is concluded.

Underlying triggers — medications/drugs (left) and medical illnesses (right) that can cause secondary psychosis

🧠
One-line summary for substance-induced psychosis: uppers in intoxication, or downers in withdrawal. Amphetamine intoxication → psychosis; amphetamine withdrawal → no psychosis. Alcohol/benzo/opiate withdrawal (downers) → psychosis (e.g., delirium tremens); their intoxication generally doesn't. Apply it in both directions on an exam question.
  • ▸ Past episodes of psychosis
  • ▸ Past psychiatric hospitalization
  • ▸ Family history of psychotic disorders
  • ▸ Past treatment with antipsychotic medications
  • ▸ Marked post-morbid decline in level of function
  • ▸ Smoking — 95% of patients with psychotic disorders smoke cigarettes ⭐ HY
  • ▸ Potential use of substances that cause psychosis (secondary psychosis)
🩺
Pertinent negatives matter: physical exams in primary psychotic disorders are often unremarkable — the absence of other physical findings is itself diagnostically useful, because it helps rule out secondary/organic causes of psychosis. Also note smooth pursuit eye saccade abnormalities as a described (if non-specific) finding.
Psychotic disorder due to glioblastoma multiforme — a brain tumor presenting with psychosis. Treating the tumor (not an antipsychotic alone) is what resolves the psychiatric picture.
UTI-induced visual hallucinations — a woman shot up her own car because she saw "midgets" inside it refusing to get out. Tox screen negative; work-up revealed a urinary tract infection. Note the tell: a visual hallucination — atypical for primary psychosis (Section 01) — correctly pointed toward a secondary cause.
Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis — an older patient referred as presumed "late-onset schizophrenia." Since genuine new-onset schizophrenia essentially never appears after 45 (Section 05), that label itself was the red flag; targeted testing confirmed autoimmune encephalitis instead.
🎙️
Why syphilis shows up in nursing homes: syphilis can stay latent for decades with no symptoms. A man can carry it silently for years, unknowingly transmit it, and only decades later — once it reaches tertiary/neurosyphilis — does it produce psychosis. That long latency is exactly why it clusters in an elderly nursing-home population.

LO 064Mood & Mood Stabilizers✓ In your notes

Understand the drug-drug interactions common with lithium, including which medications specifically interact with it (i.e., names of diuretics, names of NSAIDs, etc)

Answer

Drugs that increase lithium levels: thiazide diuretics, spironolactone, triamterene, the ACE-inhibitor enalapril, and NSAIDs. Drugs that decrease lithium levels: acetazolamide, theophylline, aminophylline, and caffeine. Metronidazole increases nephrotoxicity risk, neuroleptics may induce neurotoxicity, and antiarrhythmics potentiate cardiac effects. Mechanistically, lithium is reabsorbed at the proximal convoluted tubule on the same sodium channels the kidney uses for salt, so anything that makes the kidney retain more sodium (thiazides, low-salt states, NSAIDs, ACE-inhibitors) raises lithium levels — which is why prescreening and monitoring specifically include checking for co-administered NSAIDs, ACE-inhibitors, and thiazides. Lithium toxicity (level >1.2) presents with nausea, diarrhea, altered mental status, severe tremor, ataxia, slurred speech, hyperreflexia, polyuria, and seizure, and is treated by stopping lithium, hydrating, and considering dialysis in severe cases; dehydration from purging behaviors in bulimia is likewise flagged as a lithium-toxicity risk because lithium requires a stable, consistent hydration state.

🧠
Memory hook · Lithium follows saltReabsorbed on the kidney's sodium channels → anything that makes you keep sodium keeps lithium: thiazides, NSAIDs, ACE-inhibitors, dehydration. Levels: 0.8–1.2 treats · >1.2 toxic (coarse tremor, ataxia, AMS, seizure) · severe → dialysis. LiTHIUM: Low Thyroid, Heart (Ebstein), Insipidus, Unwanted Movements.

Pulled from: Mood Disorders · Eating Disorders

Increases lithium levelsDecreases lithium levelsAffects lithium's toxicity
Thiazide diuretics, spironolactone, triamterene, enalapril (ACE-I), NSAIDsAcetazolamide, theophylline, aminophylline, caffeineMetronidazole ↑nephrotoxicity · Neuroleptics may induce neurotoxicity · Antiarrhythmics potentiate cardiac effects of digoxin/quinidine
🧸 ELI5 — Lithium & the Kidney

Lithium hitches a ride on the same sodium channels the kidney uses to reabsorb salt at the PCT. Anything that makes the kidney hang onto more sodium (thiazides, low-salt states, NSAIDs, ACE-inhibitors) makes it hang onto more lithium too — levels climb. Anything that flushes sodium out (caffeine, theophylline) flushes lithium out with it — levels drop.

Prescreening: CBC, renal function (creatinine, BUN), thyroid function (TSH, free T3/T4), serum HCG in women, ECG, screen for co-administered NSAIDs/ACE-inhibitors/thiazides, and check for preexisting renal disease/CHF/arrhythmia.

☐ Lithium Toxicity — level >1.2

Nausea, diarrhea, altered mental status, severe tremor, ataxia, slurred speech, hyperreflexia, polyuria, seizure. Treatment: stop lithium, hydrate; consider dialysis in severe cases.

🔑 Default Answer, With Four Exceptions

On an exam, if a stem describes bipolar disorder and gives you a plain drug list with no other clues, lithium is the default first-line answer. Four things should make you look elsewhere: (1) pregnancy (Ebstein anomaly), (2) significant renal impairment (lithium is a salt excreted essentially unchanged by the kidney, so impaired renal clearance is a direct problem), (3) cardiac conduction disease such as an existing heart block (lithium can further affect cardiac conduction), and (4) difficult-to-manage thyroid disease (lithium can push a patient hypo- or hyperthyroid).

⚠️ Also Avoid: Lithium

Lithium requires a stable, consistent hydration state to avoid nephrotoxicity. Purging behaviors (especially self-induced vomiting) create a dehydration-prone state that raises the risk of lithium toxicity.

LO 066Psychotherapy & Theory✓ In your notes

Understand the efficacy of psychiatric treatment options including both pharmacologic and non-pharmacologic options, and how to explain the efficacy of therapy vs. medication treatment in psychiatry in plain language to a patient

Answer

For mild-to-moderate depression, anxiety, and especially personality disorders, therapy is often as effective as medication without the side-effect burden, so risk-benefit sometimes clearly favors therapy over a prescription. Early studies found CBT and behavioral treatments superior for depression, but once researchers controlled for "allegiance" (a researcher's own preference for the modality being tested), that superiority mostly disappeared — a reminder that "which therapy won the trial" often reflects tester bias rather than true superiority. Per the "common factors"/Dodo Bird idea, the therapeutic relationship itself and the patient's belief in and fit with the chosen modality matter as much as the specific technique, much like a patient who won't tolerate a medication's side effects; theory also gives the therapist a way to explain the approach to the patient. In practice, depression treatment typically combines lifestyle changes, therapy (e.g., CBT), and medication rather than choosing one exclusively, and for substance use disorders pharmacologic treatment mainly addresses detoxification/withdrawal while psychosocial interventions (CBT, mutual support programs, harm reduction) are what actually drive long-term outcomes.

🧠
Memory hook · The Dodo Bird verdict"Everybody has won and all must have prizes" — no single modality is clearly superior overall; the therapeutic alliance predicts outcome better than the brand of therapy.

Pulled from: Introduction to Therapy · Mood Disorders · Addiction & Non-Clinical Drug Use

⚖️
Med vs. therapy risk-benefit: For mild-to-moderate depression, anxiety, and especially the personality disorders, therapy is often as effective as medication — without the side-effect burden. Risk-benefit sometimes clearly favors therapy over a prescription, which is worth remembering when a patient asks "can't I just take a pill?"
🔬
Research bias watch: Early studies found CBT and behavioral treatments superior for depression — but once researchers controlled for "allegiance" (a researcher's own preference for the modality they're testing), that superiority mostly disappeared. A good reminder that "which therapy won the trial" sometimes says as much about who ran the trial as about the therapy itself.

Beyond the relationship itself, fit matters: the patient has to believe in and accept the chosen modality (much like a patient who won't take a medication with a side effect they can't tolerate). Selecting a theory really requires two things to both be true — the therapist must understand and believe in it, and the patient must also believe it can help them.

  • Provides a roadmap for the treatment
  • Gives the therapist a lens for formulating the case
  • Therapist and theory need to be compatible
  • Gives the therapist a way to explain the approach to the patient
Extra detail: what even counts as "scientific"?

Foundational options: lifestyle changes, therapy (think CBT for depression), and medications — and they're often combined, not either/or.

🩹

Detoxification

Cold turkey vs. taper vs. MOUD — the approach depends entirely on which substance and how dangerous its withdrawal is.

🧩

Treatment

Pharmacologic — aversive therapies (block desired effects/cause hangover), replacement therapy (manage dysphoria/reward), treat comorbid psychiatric disease. Psychosocial — CBT, mutual support (AA/NA), moderation management as early intervention.

  • Harm reduction — any reduction in use, or a patient simply returning after being told you're concerned, is a genuine win.
  • Abstinence — considered by some literature to itself be a behavioral intervention; not functional for every SUD.
  • Psychosocial — CBT, mutual support programs (note: some are faith-based and may not fit every patient).
LO 067Eating Disorders◐ Partly covered

Understand the emergency department workup for acute exacerbation of an eating disorder

Answer

In the emergency department, vital signs -- specifically BMI -- are the single most useful missing piece of information for differentiating an eating-disorder presentation: a low BMI points toward anorexia, while a normal-to-high BMI shifts the differential toward bulimia or binge eating disorder. The recommended approach is to check BMI first, then identify the driving behavior -- ongoing weight loss (anorexia), correcting a binge (bulimia), or binge eating with no compensatory behavior (binge eating disorder). Physical exam clues supporting bulimia specifically include Russell's sign (calluses from self-induced vomiting) and dental decay, since bulimic patients typically present with less severe findings than anorexia at a normal-to-overweight BMI. Workup should also ask about substances misused to aid weight loss or purging, such as stimulants (amphetamines, pseudoephedrine, caffeine) and supratherapeutic thyroid medication taken to induce an artificial hyperthyroid state.

🧠
Memory hook · BMI first, behavior secondLow BMI (<18.5) → anorexia. Normal/high BMI → is there compensation? Yes → bulimia, no → binge eating disorder. Anorexia severity is graded by BMI; bulimia severity by compensations per week.
🧠
Memory hook · The knuckles confess what the patient won'tRussell's sign (knuckle calluses) + dental erosion = self-induced vomiting → bulimia. ED workup: BMI from vitals is the single most useful number; ask about stimulants, laxatives, and sneaky thyroid-pill misuse.
◐
Missing from your notesThe physiologic ED stabilization workup (electrolyte panel, ECG for bradycardia/QT changes, refeeding-syndrome risk, admission criteria) remains unaddressed in every source, including the two new ones.

Pulled from: Eating Disorders

Q: This case is deliberately left vague. What single piece of missing information would most help differentiate the diagnosis, and why?

Answer

Vital signs, specifically BMI. BMI is one of the main criteria separating Anorexia (low BMI) from Bulimia/Binge Eating Disorder (normal-to-high BMI). Without it, the ice cream episode could point to binge eating, and the diet pills/laxatives to purging — but there's no way yet to know whether this is a restriction-dominant or binge-dominant picture. We'll revisit this same case with vitals added in the Anorexia and Bulimia sections below.

  1. Check the BMI first. Below normal (<18.5) points strongly toward anorexia. Normal-to-high points away from anorexia and toward bulimia or BED.
  2. Identify the driving behavior. Is the primary goal ongoing weight loss (restriction-focused), or correcting/compensating after a binge (bulimia), or a binge with no compensation at all (BED)?
  3. Confirm frequency and duration. Bulimia and BED both need recurrent episodes; bulimia specifically needs ≥1×/week for 3 months, and anorexia's subtype (restricting vs. binge/purge) is defined over the past 3 months.
  4. Rule out exclusionary criteria. Anorexia must be excluded before diagnosing bulimia. If the picture is incomplete or mixed, consider "unspecified."
📉

Anorexia — Restrict to Lose

Driving factor is ongoing weight loss. Expect a low-to-very-low BMI. Core behavior is restriction, sometimes layered with binge/purge episodes — but the goal underneath is always further weight loss.

  • BMI: low (specifiers are BMI-defined)
  • Self-view: "I am overweight," despite objective evidence otherwise
🔁

Bulimia — Binge, Then Correct

Driving factor is avoiding weight gain after a binge episode. Expect a normal-to-high BMI. Core behavior is binge → compensate, in a repeating cycle.

  • BMI: normal to elevated
  • Self-worth tied to body shape/weight, without the same degree of "I am overweight" distortion seen in anorexia

Similar workup to anorexia, but findings are typically less severe. Look for Russell's sign and dental decay. Patients with bulimia most often present at a normal-to-overweight BMI — a key distinguishing feature from anorexia.

CategoryExamples / Notes
StimulantsAmphetamines (e.g., Ritalin, Adderall), pseudoephedrine, caffeine — weight loss is a known side effect of increased energy expenditure.
Thyroid medicationsLevothyroxine taken by someone with a normal thyroid induces an artificial hyperthyroid state, which burns extra energy.
Laxatives / EnemasProducts such as Miralax or fleet enemas.
DiureticsLasix is the most commonly tested example.
EmeticsIpecac syrup — historically used to induce vomiting; sale is now restricted and it is rarely abused today.
Weight-loss-indicated drugs used without indicationLipase inhibitors, serotonin modulators, naltrexone/bupropion, GLP-1 receptor agonists — purging-type behavior when used by someone who does not medically qualify for weight-loss treatment.
LO 068Psychosis & Antipsychotics✓ In your notes

Understand the four major dopamine systems in the brain, and what each controls relative to positive, negative, EPS, and related clinical effects

Answer

The dopamine hypothesis of psychosis rests on four dopaminergic tracts. The mesolimbic tract governs motivation and reward and is overactive in psychosis; dopamine blockade here reduces positive symptoms (hallucinations, delusions, disorganized speech/behavior) — the therapeutic effect of antipsychotics. The mesocortical tract governs cognition and motivation and is underactive in psychosis; dopamine blockade here worsens or does not help negative symptoms (affective flattening, alogia, avolition) or cognitive symptoms. The nigrostriatal tract runs the extrapyramidal motor system; blocking D2 receptors here disrupts the normal acetylcholine:dopamine balance in the striatum, tipping it toward relative cholinergic excess and producing extrapyramidal symptoms (dystonia, akathisia, pseudoparkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia). Because antipsychotics block dopamine broadly across all tracts without discrimination, both typical and atypical agents treat positive symptoms (typicals often edging ahead), atypicals work better historically for negative symptoms, and atypicals carry less EPS but more metabolic side effects because they block relatively more serotonin than dopamine compared to typicals.

🧠
Memory hook · The 4 M's of dopamineMesolimbic = Madness (overactive → positive sx; blockade = the therapeutic effect) · Mesocortical = Missing (underactive → negative sx; blockade worsens) · Nigrostriatal = Movement (blockade → EPS) · Tuberoinfundibular = Milk (blockade → prolactin).

Pulled from: Psychotic Disorders & Antipsychotic Pharmacology

TractFunctionEffect of Dopamine Blockade

MesocorticalCognition, motivation; underactive in psychosisWorsens/does not help negative & cognitive symptoms
NigrostriatalExtrapyramidal motor systemProduces EPS (Section 16)

The basic pathophysiological model of psychosis: an overabundance of dopamine in the mesolimbic tract drives positive symptoms, while an underabundance of dopamine in the mesocortical tract drives negative symptoms. Antipsychotics block dopamine broadly, renormalizing levels — but they don't discriminate between tracts, which is the root of most antipsychotic side effects.

Quick pathway map: mesolimbic = positive symptoms/reward, mesocortical = negative symptoms, nigrostriatal = movement/EPS, tuberoinfundibular = prolactin.

The four dopamine tracts relevant to psychosis and antipsychotic side effects

5 psychosis criteria
Hallucinations, delusions, disorganized speech, disorganized behavior, negative symptoms — need ≥1.
Illusion vs. hallucination
Illusion = misperceived real stimulus. Hallucination = no external stimulus at all.
4 dopamine tracts
Mesolimbic (+ → positive sx), mesocortical (− → negative sx), nigrostriatal (blockade → EPS), tuberoinfundibular (blockade → hyperprolactinemia).
Timeline trio
Brief psychotic: 1 day–1 mo. Schizophreniform: 1–6 mo. Schizophrenia: >6 mo. Identical criteria otherwise.
Schizoaffective
Baseline psychosis + mood episodes, PLUS ≥2 weeks of psychosis alone at some point.
Delusional disorder
Plausible (non-bizarre) fixed delusion; otherwise preserved functioning; no insight into the delusion only.
95%
Percent of patients with psychotic disorders who smoke cigarettes.
Typical vs. atypical
Typical: D > S blockade. Atypical: S > D blockade.
Potency ↔ side effects
High potency = high EPS/low ACH. Low potency = low EPS/high ACH.
PINES vs. DONES
-pines = sedating/metabolic (olanzapine, quetiapine, asenapine). -dones = "watered-down typicals," more EPS (risperidone, ziprasidone, paliperidone, iloperidone).
D2 occupancy window
~70% = antipsychotic effect threshold; ~78–80% = EPS threshold.
EPS timeline
Dystonia (acute) → Akathisia (acute/subacute) → Pseudoparkinsonism (acute/subacute) → Tardive dyskinesia (chronic).
EPS treatment
Dystonia → IM anticholinergic. Akathisia → propranolol. Pseudoparkinsonism → anticholinergic/amantadine. TD → withdraw/reduce/switch agent.
Side-effect-receptor map
Sedation=H1. Hypotension=α1. Dry mouth/retention=M1. EPS=D2 (nigrostriatal). Galactorrhea=D2 (tuberoinfundibular).
Relapse rates
20%/yr oral-medicated vs. ~5%/yr on LAI vs. 70% at 1yr / 90% at 2yr unmedicated.
Antisuicidal drugs
Clozapine (antipsychotics) and lithium (mood stabilizers) are the only two psychiatric drugs with this FDA-recognized property.
Smoking & CYP1A2
Smoking induces CYP1A2 → lowers clozapine/olanzapine levels. Quitting (e.g., hospitalization) can raise levels ~50%.
Clozapine's trade
No EPS/TD, but agranulocytosis (1–2%), seizures, sialorrhea, myocarditis — mandatory ANC/WBC REMS monitoring.
B-52
Benadryl 50mg + Haldol 5mg + Ativan 2mg IM, PRN for acute agitation.
NMS red flags
Rigidity + hyperthermia + diaphoresis after antipsychotic dosing → stop the antipsychotic first.
CATIE/CUTLASS
FGA ≈ SGA for routine use (perphenazine cost-effective); clozapine superior for treatment-resistant disease.
First-line consensus
SGA first episode → SGA/FGA second → clozapine third → clozapine augmentation fourth (nearly universal across guideline bodies).

EPS arises from an acetylcholine : dopamine imbalance in the nigrostriatal tract (Section 02) caused by dopamine blockade. Normally dopamine and acetylcholine counterbalance each other in the striatum; blocking D2 receptors tips the seesaw toward relative cholinergic excess.

The ACh : DA seesaw — antipsychotics push it toward cholinergic excess

Relative dopamine deficiency in the nigrostriatal pathway — same final common pathway as Parkinson's disease (loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta) vs. antipsychotic-induced D2 blockade

💊
Typical vs. Atypical, in one line: Typicals block more Dopamine than serotonin; atypicals block more Serotonin than dopamine. Serotonin is implicated indirectly, particularly in the mesolimbic pathway — atypicals' extra serotonin blockade is part of why they carry relatively less EPS but more metabolic burden (previewed here, detailed in Sections 12–20).
Side EffectReceptor / Mechanism
SedationH1 (histamine) antagonism
Orthostatic hypotensionα1-adrenergic antagonism
Dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retentionM1 (muscarinic/anticholinergic) antagonism
Movement syndromes (EPS)D2 antagonism in the nigrostriatal tract
Galactorrhea, amenorrhea, gynecomastiaD2 antagonism in the tuberoinfundibular tract → disinhibited prolactin release

Positive Symptoms

Present in a psychotic patient, absent in a non-psychotic patient (in excess of normal baseline)
ExamplesHallucinations, delusions, disorganized speech, disorganized behavior.
Best respondersStrong/tight D2-binding drugs (typicals, and the "-done" atypicals) — both TAPs and AAPs work, but TAPs are often better specifically for positive symptoms.

Negative Symptoms

Lacking in a non-psychotic person, present in a psychotic person
ExamplesFlat affect, alogia, asociality, avolition.
Best respondersLooser D2-binding, more serotonergic drugs (atypicals) — historically the best (if still limited) option for negative symptoms.
📌
Three-tier takeaway: Positive → typicals & atypicals both work (typicals often edge ahead). Negative → atypicals work best (historically). Cognitive/executive-function symptoms (e.g., learning from one's mistakes) → only atypicals treat these at all.

There is a narrow window between antipsychotic efficacy and excessive side effects. The striatal D2 receptor occupancy threshold to reduce psychosis with minimal EPS is approximately 78–80%; crossing above the EPS threshold produces motor side effects.

Hypothetical thresholds for antipsychotic drug effects — the therapeutic window sits between the ~70% "antipsychotic effect" line and the ~80% "EPS" line

LO 069Personality Disorders✓ In your notes

Understand the general criteria for personality disorders

Answer

Every specific personality disorder is built on top of a shared DSM-5 general personality disorder template, and the 10 disorders are grouped into three clusters. Cluster A ("Weird"/odd-eccentric: paranoid, schizoid, schizotypal) overlaps with negative symptoms of schizophrenia and carries a genetic link to schizophrenia. Cluster B ("Wild"/dramatic-erratic: antisocial, borderline, histrionic, narcissistic) centers on affective instability and impulsivity, with borderline sitting highest on both axes and carrying a genetic link to mood and substance use disorders. Cluster C ("Worried"/anxious-fearful: avoidant, dependent, obsessive-compulsive) shares an underlying anxious symptomatology. Personality disorders are described as among the most difficult psychiatric diagnoses to treat — there is no FDA-approved medication for any of the 10, and dialectical behavioral therapy (DBT), developed for borderline PD, is the one disorder-specific core psychotherapy across the group.

🧠
Memory hook · Weird, Wild, Worried — and their alliterationsCluster A (weird): Accusatory (paranoid), Aloof (schizoid), Awkward (schizotypal) — genetic link to schizophrenia. Cluster B (wild): Bad to the Bone — antisocial (needs conduct disorder before 15), borderline, histrionic, narcissistic. Cluster C (worried): Cowardly (avoidant), Clingy (dependent), Compulsive (OCPD).
🧠
Memory hook · No FDA-approved pill for any personalityAll 10 PDs: psychotherapy is primary, meds are off-label symptom patches. The one disorder-specific therapy in the group: DBT for borderline (Linehan). (Quetiapine showed an 82% Zanarini response in BPD — notable, still off-label.)

LO 070Cross-Cutting Pharm✓ In your notes

Understand the interaction that smoking has on the CYP 450 1A2 isoenzyme, and how that is directly applicable to patient care

Answer

Hydrocarbons in cigarette smoke induce the CYP1A2 isoenzyme, which principally affects two antipsychotics that are CYP1A2 substrates: clozapine and olanzapine (fluvoxamine, by contrast, inhibits CYP1A2 and raises their levels). Because roughly 95% of patients with schizophrenia smoke, this is a highly practical interaction: a patient stabilized on clozapine or olanzapine while hospitalized (not smoking) who resumes smoking after discharge will re-induce CYP1A2, dropping drug levels and risking breakthrough psychosis despite "perfect" medication compliance; conversely, stopping smoking during a hospital stay removes the induction and can raise levels of these drugs toward toxicity. As with any CYP inducer, the clinical risk of smoking's effect on 1A2 is efficacy loss/relapse (falling plasma levels), the opposite of the toxicity risk seen with an enzyme inhibitor.

🧠
Memory hook · Smoke burns away the -PINEsCigarette hydrocarbons induce CYP1A2 → clozaPINE and olanzaPINE levels drop (relapse); quitting in hospital → levels climb (toxicity). 95% of schizophrenia patients smoke — this WILL show up. Fluvoxamine does the opposite (1A2 inhibitor).

Pulled from: Psychotic Disorders & Antipsychotic Pharmacology · Introduction & History of Psychiatry

Smoking causes induction of the CYP1A2 isoenzyme, which principally affects two antipsychotics: clozapine and olanzapine.

Fluvoxamine inhibits CYP1A2 (raising levels); ongoing smoking induces CYP1A2 (lowering levels) — stopping smoking (e.g., during hospitalization) removes that induction and can raise serum levels ~50%

NH State Hospital — cigarette smoking as a 1A2 inducer Inducer

~95% of patients with schizophrenia smoke cigarettes — still the current statistic, and worth remembering because hydrocarbons in cigarette smoke are a 1A2 inducer. Both clozapine and olanzapine (antipsychotics) are 1A2 substrates.

A patient was hospitalized, titrated onto clozapine, and did well — psychosis cleared and he was discharged. He went home and resumed smoking ~2 packs/day. His psychosis re-emerged (he was found naked in the street, screaming, while smoking) and he was re-hospitalized — despite being fully medication-compliant. The smoking induced faster clozapine metabolism, plasma levels plummeted, and psychosis returned.

📌
Why this matters clinically: a patient stabilized on clozapine/olanzapine while hospitalized (not smoking) who then resumes smoking after discharge will re-induce CYP1A2, dropping drug levels — risking breakthrough psychosis despite "perfect" medication compliance. This exact scenario appears as a case question in Section 28.
⚖ Hardest discrimination: CYP450 Inhibitor vs. Inducer
InhibitorInducer
Effect on enzyme↓ activity↑ activity
Effect on substrate level↑ plasma level↓ plasma level
Clinical riskToxicity / side effectsEfficacy loss / relapse
Case exampleBupropion (2D6) + imipramine → delirium, arrhythmiaSmoking (1A2) + clozapine → psychosis relapse
C.1
What is the pharmacokinetic mechanism at work here?
A. Smoking induces the CYP3A4 enzyme
B. Olanzapine is a substrate of CYP3A4
C. Smoking is an inducer of CYP1A2
D. Smoking is an inhibitor of 1A2
E. Smoking is an inducer of the 2D6 isoenzyme and olanzapine is a substrate of 2D6
F. Patient is lying and should be re-hospitalized for noncompliance
Answer: C. This is Section 19's smoking/CYP1A2 interaction in action: olanzapine (like clozapine) is metabolized by CYP1A2, which cigarette smoke induces. While hospitalized (not smoking), his CYP1A2 activity normalized, keeping olanzapine levels adequate. Resuming smoking after discharge re-induces CYP1A2 → faster olanzapine metabolism → falling serum levels → breakthrough psychosis despite genuine adherence. No need to suspect noncompliance (F) — the mechanism is fully explained pharmacokinetically.
Practice Question
A patient stable on clozapine is admitted with re-emergent psychosis despite confirmed medication adherence. Records show he recently resumed heavy cigarette smoking. What's the mechanism?
A. Nicotine directly blocks dopamine receptors, counteracting clozapine's effect.
B. Hydrocarbons in cigarette smoke induce CYP1A2, increasing clozapine's metabolism and lowering its plasma level below the therapeutic threshold.
C. Smoking inhibits CYP1A2, causing clozapine toxicity.
D. Smoking has no pharmacokinetic effect on clozapine; the relapse is unrelated.
Answer: B. Cigarette-smoke hydrocarbons (not nicotine itself) are a CYP1A2 inducer; clozapine and olanzapine are 1A2 substrates, so resumed smoking drops their plasma levels and can precipitate relapse even with perfect adherence.

LO 071Mood & Mood Stabilizers✓ In your notes

Understand the most likely diagnosis of the mood disorders and the treatments associated

Answer

A manic episode requires 3+ DIGFAST symptoms (4+ if mood is only irritable) lasting at least 7 days, or any duration if it requires hospitalization or includes psychosis, plus significant impairment — one such episode is enough to diagnose Bipolar I, and depression is not even required. A hypomanic episode needs the same symptom threshold but only 4+ days, with no psychosis, no hospitalization, and no significant impairment; combined with at least one major depressive episode and no lifetime manic episode, this defines Bipolar II, and if a manic episode ever occurs in a patient with Bipolar II, the diagnosis converts to Bipolar I. Persistent Depressive Disorder is depression that is milder but longer-lasting (mild depressive symptoms for 2+ years). For treatment, acute mania responds to lithium, valproate, and antipsychotics, while acute bipolar depression responds to lithium, carbamazepine, and lamotrigine — valproate does not protect against depressive relapse, being the most sedating of the mood stabilizers.

🧠
Memory hook · Mania is a 7-day week; hypomania a 4-day workweekDIGFAST ≥3 (4 if only irritable): ≥7 days OR hospital OR psychosis + impairment = mania → Bipolar I (depression not required). ≥4 days, fully functional, no psychosis = hypomania; + ≥1 MDE and never mania = Bipolar II. One manic episode ever → converts to Bipolar I forever.
🧠
Memory hook · Opposite jobs: mania drugs vs. depression drugsAcute mania: lithium, valproate, carbamazepine (+ antipsychotics). Bipolar depression: lamotrigine first-line (weak for mania). Lithium is the gold standard — the only agent that covers mania, depression, AND maintenance. Antidepressants only ever ride with a mood stabilizer.

Pulled from: Mood Disorders

If a manic episode ever occurs, the diagnosis is Bipolar I regardless of prior hypomanic/depressive history.

🧸 ELI5 — Bipolar I vs. II

Bipolar I is the "I mean it" version: one manic episode is all it takes to earn the diagnosis — depression is optional. Bipolar II needs a two-ingredient recipe: at least one hypomanic episode and at least one major depressive episode, but if a manic episode ever shows up, the diagnosis is immediately promoted to Bipolar I. Hypomania is Bipolar II's ceiling — it can never break through into full mania and stay Bipolar II.

DisorderBuilt from
Major Depressive Disorder1+ major depressive episode
Persistent Depressive DisorderDepression "light" but long — mild depressive symptoms ≥2 years
Bipolar I1+ manic episode, +/− a depressive episode (depression isn't even required!)
Bipolar II1+ hypomanic episode + 1+ major depressive episode (never a full manic episode)
Cyclothymic disorderHypomania "light" + depression "light," fluctuating for ≥2 years, never meeting full episode criteria
DisorderRequired episodes
Bipolar I≥1 manic episode (may be preceded/followed by hypomanic or MDEs — not required)
Bipolar II≥1 hypomanic episode + ≥1 MDE, never a manic or mixed episode
Cyclothymic disorder≥2 years of numerous hypomanic-symptom periods + numerous depressive-symptom periods, never meeting full episode criteria, symptom-free gaps never >2 months

Bipolar I (full mania possible) vs. Bipolar II (ceiling = hypomania) over time

  • Acute mania: lithium, valproate, and antipsychotics all break a manic episode effectively.
  • Acute depression: lithium, carbamazepine, and lamotrigine all help prevent/treat depressive episodes. Valproate does not — it's the most sedating of the mood stabilizers and doesn't protect against depressive episodes, so relying on it alone for the depressive phase is a mismatch. Antipsychotics are inconsistent here — augmentation (e.g. SSRI + second-generation antipsychotic) is the more common approach for a resistant depressive phase.
  • Maintenance: lithium, carbamazepine, and lamotrigine all have a role.

Q: A patient with a well-documented history of Bipolar II disorder has a manic episode requiring hospitalization. What is the new diagnosis?

Answer

Bipolar I disorder. A single manic episode is sufficient to diagnose Bipolar I, and Bipolar II is defined by the absence of any lifetime manic episode. The occurrence of mania supersedes the prior Bipolar II diagnosis.

MDD and Bipolar: mood episodes are the whole picture, no continuous psychosis. Schizoaffective: continuous psychosis plus episodic mood. Schizophrenia: continuous psychosis, no mood component.

🌪️

Mania

  • Lasts 7 days
  • OR requires hospitalization
  • OR includes psychosis
  • AND causes significant impairment
🌤️

Hypomania

  • Only has to last 4 days
  • Does not cause significant impairment
  • No psychosis, no hospitalization
