LO 072Cross-Cutting Pharm◐ Partly covered

Understand the optimal treatment strategies for major depressive disorder when co-morbid with smoking cigarettes

Answer

For a depressed patient who also smokes, the exam-favored choice is bupropion, since it is FDA-approved for both major depressive disorder and smoking cessation (plus an ADHD indication) -- a classic 'extra clue' pattern used to pick one specific antidepressant once SSRI vs. SNRI has already been settled. A real-practice case illustrates a key hazard of this exact scenario: bupropion is a CYP2D6 inhibitor, so starting it for smoking cessation in a patient already stabilized on a 2D6-substrate drug (the TCA imipramine) raised her imipramine level and precipitated anticholinergic delirium. The teaching point drawn from that case is that medication reconciliation -- checking for other CYP2D6 substrates already on board -- matters before adding bupropion in an already-medicated smoker.

🧠
Memory hook · Bupropion: the smoking-cessation drug with a 2D6 tollboothDepressed smoker → bupropion (FDA-approved for MDD + smoking cessation). But it inhibits CYP2D6 — added to a TCA like imipramine it caused anticholinergic delirium. Avoid with seizures or eating disorders; the trade-off gift: minimal sexual side effects.
◐
Missing from your notesNon-pharmacologic and alternative pharmacologic smoking-cessation options (counseling, nicotine replacement therapy, varenicline) tied to the MDD-plus-smoking scenario are still absent from every source, including the two new ones.

Pulled from: Mood Disorders · Introduction & History of Psychiatry · Psychiatry Key Drug List 2026

🩺 The "Extra Clue" Pattern

Once you've picked SSRI vs. SNRI, exams love adding one more clue to point at a specific drug. Classic example: everything above is true and the patient smokes → answer is bupropion (FDA-approved for both depression and smoking cessation, plus an ADHD indication). Get comfortable scanning the stem for a single extra detail like this — it's almost always the intended differentiator.

Eastport, ME — smoking cessation script triggers anticholinergic delirium Inhibitor

A stable patient on imipramine (a TCA — a 2D6 substrate) was doing well in Dr. Smith's practice. Her PCP started her on bupropion (a 2D6 inhibitor) for smoking cessation, without knowing she was already on imipramine.

Bupropion inhibited 2D6 → imipramine could no longer be metabolized normally → imipramine levels rose to ~10× therapeutic levels. She became confused and delirious with florid anticholinergic symptoms, and developed a cardiac arrhythmia — TCAs carry real cardiotoxicity at supratherapeutic levels. She was admitted to telemetry; bupropion was stopped immediately, and she improved.

💡
This is exactly why medication reconciliation and reading existing notes before prescribing matters — a single uncoordinated addition caused a genuinely dangerous interaction.
Mechanism
NE + dopamine reuptake inhibition — ZERO serotonin effect, unique among ALL antidepressants.
The vignette that screams bupropion
MDD with atypical features: hypersomnia, increased appetite, weight gain, mood reactivity, excessive fatigue, "leaden paralysis".
Also for
Smoking cessation (as Zyban); erectile dysfunction in patients on an SSRI (helps erection, not ejaculation); augmenting another antidepressant; flat/numb affect (it intensifies affect rather than calming).
Side effects
Insomnia, irritability, anxiety, headache, activation — but NO sexual side effects, NO weight gain.
Contraindication
Seizure disorder (esp. documented epilepsy) and eating disorders (esp. anorexia nervosa) — it lowers the seizure threshold.
Major interaction — CYP2D6
Mostly 2D6. Example: add bupropion (2D6 inhibitor) to imipramine (2D6 substrate) → imipramine levels climb → arrhythmia and death. Best prescribed by a psychiatrist.
LO 073Psychotherapy & Theory✓ In your notes

Understand the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic concepts underlying the prescription of SSRI medications

Answer

Pharmacodynamically, SSRIs bind the serotonin transporter (SERT) and block reuptake of serotonin from the synapse, and over time also desensitize the presynaptic autoreceptor, further boosting serotonin release. Because the transporter is blocked immediately but postsynaptic receptors need roughly 4-6 weeks to adapt and upregulate, side effects appear right away while the antidepressant benefit lags behind. Pharmacokinetically, individual SSRIs differ meaningfully: sertraline is the most prescribed, with a 'longish' half-life and good tolerability, while fluoxetine has the longest half-life in the class (2-4 days) and inhibits CYP2D6, creating many drug-drug interactions; fluoxetine's long half-life is clinically useful for patients with unreliable adherence, since a missed dose barely registers. This half-life variability also explains antidepressant discontinuation syndrome — a patient who abruptly stops or misses doses can develop flu-like symptoms, dizziness, 'brain zaps,' and irritability, a risk that is generally lower with longer-half-life agents like fluoxetine.

🧠
Memory hook · Side effects sprint; benefits run a marathonSSRIs block SERT on day one (GI upset, sexual dysfunction start immediately) but postsynaptic receptors need 4–6 weeks to adapt before mood lifts. Fluoxetine = the long goodbye: longest half-life (2–4 days), no discontinuation syndrome, potent 2D6 inhibitor.

Pulled from: Mood Disorders

Sertraline

Most prescribed SSRI

"Longish" half-life, well tolerated.

Fluoxetine

Longest half-life in class (2–4 days)

Inhibits CYP2D6 → many drug–drug interactions. The long half-life is clinically useful — good for patients who won't take medication reliably, since missing a dose barely registers, and can even be dosed once weekly.

Escitalopram

Isomer of citalopram

No meaningful cardiac (QTc) effect — the key differentiator from citalopram.

Citalopram

Dose-dependent QTc risk

The older of the pair; best known for QTc prolongation.

Fluvoxamine

FDA-approved for OCD ONLY

Doesn't carry the general depression indication the rest of the class does — a very testable exception.

Paroxetine

Shortest half-life, "dirty" drug

Inhibits CYP2D6; interacts with a lot of other medications, so many clinicians avoid it when there's a cleaner option.

MOA: Bind the serotonin transporter (SERT), blocking reuptake of serotonin from the synapse. At the cell body, autoreceptor desensitization over time boosts serotonin release too — a dual effect.

🩺 Why Side Effects Show Up Before the Antidepressant Effect

The moment an SSRI is started, the transporter is blocked and serotonin floods the synapse immediately — but the postsynaptic receptors need time (roughly 4–6 weeks) to adapt/upregulate before the person actually feels less depressed. Side effects, though, don't need that adaptation: the flood of serotonin hits GI receptors, sexual-function pathways, and other targets right away, which is why side effects typically appear in the first 1–2 weeks, well before the therapeutic benefit does. This is also why severely depressed patients are sometimes hospitalized — not because outpatient treatment can't work, but because it allows faster dose titration and augmentation than waiting out a 4–6 week outpatient trial. And it's why "I started the antidepressant two weeks ago and don't feel different" is expected, not a treatment failure.

🧸 ELI5 — SSRI Mechanism

Serotonin is a text message between two neurons. Normally, right after it's "read," the sender scoops the message back up (reuptake) so the conversation stops. An SSRI jams the scoop — the message just sits in the gap longer, getting read over and over. That's a Selective Serotonin Reputake Inhibitor.

🔑 Learn the Exceptions, Not the Whole List

Rather than memorizing every FDA indication for every SSRI, learn what's different: fluvoxamine = OCD only. Fluoxetine also carries an FDA approval for bulimia nervosa — an easy, distinctive exam point. Fluoxetine also has the longest track record and broadest approval in children and adolescents — pediatric FDA indications differ from adult ones, so if a question stem involves a child, don't assume adult approvals transfer automatically.

☐ Antidepressant Discontinuation Syndrome

A relatively recently-recognized (last ~10 years) but testable phenomenon: a patient who abruptly stops or misses doses of an antidepressant — SSRIs included, not exclusive to any one class — presents with flu-like symptoms, dizziness, "brain zaps," irritability, and sensory disturbances. Management: restart the antidepressant and taper slowly. If restarting isn't appropriate (e.g. concern for serotonin syndrome), manage supportively (hydration, rest) instead. Higher risk with short half-life agents like paroxetine; lower risk with long half-life agents like fluoxetine.

A classic exam setup gives you one SSRI, one SNRI, one TCA, and one MAOI as options — don't panic. SSRIs and SNRIs are tied as first-line, so the tie-breaker is almost always a comorbidity or side-effect clue hidden in the stem:

🎯

Favor an SSRI when...

  • "Garden variety" depression with no other clues
  • Comorbid anxiety-spectrum disorder — PTSD, OCD, panic, social anxiety
⚡

Favor an SNRI when...

  • Comorbid pain condition (fibromyalgia, neuropathic pain) — the norepinephrine component helps pain
  • Comorbid ADHD-like presentation or need for a mildly stimulating effect

Recreated from Robinson DS, Primary Psychiatry, Vol 13 No 8, 2006 (as cited in lecture) — ×-values reflect relative degree of CNS 5-HT excess.

LO 074Mood & Mood Stabilizers✓ In your notes

Understand the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of lithium

Answer

Lithium is renally excreted and reabsorbed at the proximal convoluted tubule on the same sodium channels the kidney uses for salt, so any state or drug that increases renal sodium retention raises lithium levels (thiazide diuretics, spironolactone, triamterene, ACE-inhibitors, NSAIDs), while acetazolamide, theophylline, aminophylline, and caffeine lower levels. Toxicity (level >1.2) presents with nausea, diarrhea, altered mental status, severe tremor, ataxia, slurred speech, hyperreflexia, polyuria, and seizure, and is managed by stopping lithium, hydrating, and considering dialysis in severe cases. The mnemonic "LiTHIUM" captures its major adverse effects: Low Thyroid (hypothyroidism), Heart (Ebstein anomaly), Insipidus (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus), and Unwanted Movements (tremor), with additional effects of acne, weight gain, and mild hypercalcemia. Lithium is the exam default first-line drug for bipolar disorder, with exceptions for pregnancy (Ebstein anomaly risk, highest in the first trimester when cardiac formation occurs) and significant renal impairment; required prescreening includes CBC, renal function, thyroid function, HCG in women, and ECG.

🧠
Memory hook · Lithium follows saltReabsorbed on the kidney's sodium channels → anything that makes you keep sodium keeps lithium: thiazides, NSAIDs, ACE-inhibitors, dehydration. Levels: 0.8–1.2 treats · >1.2 toxic (coarse tremor, ataxia, AMS, seizure) · severe → dialysis. LiTHIUM: Low Thyroid, Heart (Ebstein), Insipidus, Unwanted Movements.

Pulled from: Mood Disorders

🧸 ELI5 — Lithium & the Kidney

Lithium hitches a ride on the same sodium channels the kidney uses to reabsorb salt at the PCT. Anything that makes the kidney hang onto more sodium (thiazides, low-salt states, NSAIDs, ACE-inhibitors) makes it hang onto more lithium too — levels climb. Anything that flushes sodium out (caffeine, theophylline) flushes lithium out with it — levels drop.

Increases lithium levelsDecreases lithium levelsAffects lithium's toxicity
Thiazide diuretics, spironolactone, triamterene, enalapril (ACE-I), NSAIDsAcetazolamide, theophylline, aminophylline, caffeineMetronidazole ↑nephrotoxicity · Neuroleptics may induce neurotoxicity · Antiarrhythmics potentiate cardiac effects of digoxin/quinidine
☐ Lithium Toxicity — level >1.2

Nausea, diarrhea, altered mental status, severe tremor, ataxia, slurred speech, hyperreflexia, polyuria, seizure. Treatment: stop lithium, hydrate; consider dialysis in severe cases.

Prescreening: CBC, renal function (creatinine, BUN), thyroid function (TSH, free T3/T4), serum HCG in women, ECG, screen for co-administered NSAIDs/ACE-inhibitors/thiazides, and check for preexisting renal disease/CHF/arrhythmia.

🔑 Default Answer, With Four Exceptions

On an exam, if a stem describes bipolar disorder and gives you a plain drug list with no other clues, lithium is the default first-line answer. Four things should make you look elsewhere: (1) pregnancy (Ebstein anomaly), (2) significant renal impairment (lithium is a salt excreted essentially unchanged by the kidney, so impaired renal clearance is a direct problem), (3) cardiac conduction disease such as an existing heart block (lithium can further affect cardiac conduction), and (4) difficult-to-manage thyroid disease (lithium can push a patient hypo- or hyperthyroid).

🔑 First Aid Mnemonic — LiTHIUM

Low Thyroid (hypothyroidism) · Heart (Ebstein anomaly — right atrial enlargement, displaced tricuspid valve) · Insipidus (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus) · Unwanted Movements (tremor)

Lecture additions: fine tremor, hypo- or hyperthyroidism, acne, weight gain, mild hypercalcemia.

  • Lithium: Ebstein anomaly risk is trimester-specific — cardiac formation happens early, so risk is highest in the first trimester. Many clinicians minimize or hold lithium during the first trimester, then resume or increase the dose later in pregnancy once heart formation is complete and risk drops substantially.
  • Valproate, carbamazepine, lamotrigine: neural tube defect risk; folic acid supplementation (typically more than a standard prenatal vitamin provides) can help mitigate this risk.
  • Antipsychotics: most have little to no pregnancy safety data — the exception is clozapine, which actually has accumulated outcome data. Because of this data gap (not necessarily proven danger), antipsychotics are often the preferred bipolar treatment in pregnancy when a mood stabilizer's teratogenic risk is a bigger concern.
  • Antidepressants: no strong teratogenic signal either way. The main concern is neonatal discontinuation/serotonin syndrome in the newborn after birth, from placental transfer — but most patients are kept on their antidepressant throughout pregnancy regardless, because untreated depression carries its own fetal risk.
LO 075Child & Adolescent◐ Partly covered

Understand the pharmacological treatment of ADHD, including stimulants and non- stimulants, in a patient with specific medical co-morbidities

Answer

Amphetamines used for ADHD work through a mixed mechanism of dopamine transporter reversal, reuptake inhibition, and MAO inhibition, and ADHD carries a well-documented 'terrible triad' association with OCD and Tourette disorder. The child psychiatry lecture adds that in children, stimulants -- methylphenidate ER, dexmethylphenidate ER, mixed amphetamine salts, and lisdexamfetamine -- are first-line unless contraindicated, that long-acting formulations are the pediatric standard, and that about 80-90% of children respond to stimulants. It also lists comorbidity-relevant stimulant watch-outs: appetite suppression, sleep effects, GI upset/headache, a growth effect of roughly 2-3 cm, the need for cardiovascular review of systems, and a risk of tics that is called out as especially associated with amphetamines; alpha-2 agonists are named as a non-stimulant medication group used when stimulants are not preferred.

🧠
Memory hook · Stimulants 80–90% ; atomoxetine 60% ; alpha-2s calm the body, not the focusFirst-line: long-acting stimulants (methylphenidate ER, lisdexamfetamine…) — watch appetite, sleep, ~2–3 cm growth, tics (esp. amphetamines), CV review. Failed stimulants → atomoxetine (NRI, 1–1.4 mg/kg) or viloxazine; guanfacine/clonidine for hyperactivity. Diagnosis needs: >6 months, onset <12, impairment, ≥2 settings.
◐
Missing from your notesExplicit guidance on selecting or avoiding a specific ADHD agent in a patient with known cardiac disease, beyond noting that a cardiovascular review of systems is needed before/during stimulant use, remains absent from both sources.

Pulled from: Addiction & Non-Clinical Drug Use · Anxiety, OCD & Trauma-Related Disorders · Psychiatry Key Drug List 2026 · Child & Adolescent Psychiatry

Clinical uses: ADHD, nasal decongestants, antidepressants, diet pills. Mechanism — mixed-acting: tyramine-like reversal of the dopamine transporter (releases DA), cocaine-like reuptake inhibition, and MAO inhibition — three simultaneous ways of flooding the synapse.

📌
The "terrible triad" of psychiatry: OCD has a well-documented association with ADHD and Tourette disorder — worth remembering as a cluster.
The two stimulant families + special members
Family / drugKey membersWhat makes it special
methylphenidateRitalin (IR/LA/SR), Concerta, Metadate, Quillivant XR (liquid), Daytrana (patch); dexmethylphenidate = FocalinDOC by convention in ADHD; dozens of release formats
amphetamine familydextroamphetamine (Dexedrine), mixed salts (Adderall/XR), Dyanavel XR liquidmore release-enhancing; same SE profile

Xelstrymdextroamphetamine patchfirst amphetamine transdermal (ages 6+)
Non-stimulant #1 (Schedule-free)
atomoxetine (Strattera)
  • Selective NE reuptake inhibitor; helps ~60% vs 80–90% for stimulants.
  • For stimulant-averse families, tic disorders, abuse-risk households. Dose by weight: 1–1.4 mg/kg (RS: underdosing = why "it never works").
  • SEs: GI upset, sedation, dizziness, irritability.
Non-stimulant #2
viloxazine (Qelbree)
  • 5-HT2C partial agonist + NE reuptake inhibitor (old European antidepressant, relaunched 2021 for ADHD).
The α2 agonists
clonidine (Kapvay) & guanfacine (Intuniv)
  • Central α2-adrenergic agonists (from HTN world): fix hyperactivity, do NOT improve focus — for patients who can't take stimulants.
  • Onyda XR (2024): first liquid clonidine, nighttime dosing, mono/adjunct.
  • Also: bupropion IR/SR is used off-label for ADHD.
Mechanism
Block DA/NE reuptake AND enhance release of DA/NE (amphetamines especially push release).
Side effects
Decreased appetite/weight, insomnia (dose after meals, not at night), anxiety/jitteriness/agitation, GI upset, dysphoria/mania, tachycardia/palpitations/HTN, possible growth suppression (drug holidays help), tics/dyskinesias, headache.
Stopping abruptly
Rebound: headache, hypersomnia, hyperphagia, depression, irritability, poor concentration.
Abuse reality check
Oral ADHD dosing has low abuse potential (vs snorted/IV meth); untreated ADHD raises later drug-abuse risk — treatment lowers it. Watch for feigned ADHD (diversion). FDA: no ER stimulants in children <6 years (weight loss).
Memory Hook — the non-stimulant ladder
"ATOMs FOCUS, alphas CALM." ATOMoxetine (NRI) actually helps attention (just less often — 60%); clonidine/guanfacine (α2) only quiet the body. And VyvanSe needS Stomach acid (pH<5) — the abuse-proof prodrug.

Two stimulant families (methylphenidate vs amphetamine — many costumes each), then the non-stimulant bench. Stimulants are highly effective; everything else is a negotiated compromise.

ADHD is the most common pediatric psychiatric complaint in the lecture, with a strong emphasis on collateral school data and stimulant-first pharmacology.

Brain circuitry

LO 076Anxiety, OCD & Trauma✓ In your notes

Understand the pharmacological treatment of symptoms in PTSD, and the specific side- effects of these medications

Answer

PTSD has a symptom-cluster-driven pharmacotherapy algorithm: for sleep disturbed by nightmares or nighttime hyperarousal, prazosin (an alpha-1 blocker) is used first — a distinctive, easily-tested use outside its more familiar BPH/hypertension role; for isolated sleep-onset impairment, trazodone is used; an SSRI trial follows, escalating to a second or third SSRI/SNRI/mirtazapine if needed, with an antipsychotic added only if psychosis is present, and augmentation (e.g., quetiapine or clonidine) targeted to the predominant symptom cluster such as hyperarousal. SSRIs bind the serotonin transporter (SERT) and block reuptake, and their side effects — GI distress, sexual dysfunction, SIADH, and serotonin syndrome — appear immediately, well before the 4-6 weeks postsynaptic receptors need to adapt and produce symptomatic benefit. TCAs, an alternative class, bind SERT/NET plus alpha-1, M1, H1, and sodium channels off-target, causing sedation and anticholinergic effects, with tertiary agents like imipramine causing more side effects than smaller secondary agents; bupropion, another atypical option, carries its own black-box seizure-threshold-lowering warning alongside tachycardia and weight loss.

🧠
Memory hook · Nightmares get prazosin; plain insomnia gets trazodonePTSD algorithm: prazosin (α1-blocker) for nightmares/nighttime hyperarousal → trazodone for sleep-onset → SSRI trial → second SSRI/SNRI/mirtazapine → antipsychotic only if psychotic.

Pulled from: Anxiety, OCD & Trauma-Related Disorders · Mood Disorders

Sleep disturbed with nightmares/night-time hyperarousal → prazosin first; sleep-onset impaired → trazodone → SSRI trial → if psychosis is present, add an antipsychotic; if not, try a second/third SSRI/SNRI/mirtazapine → augment based on the predominant symptom cluster (hyperarousal → quetiapine/clonidine; re-experiencing → risperidone/aripiprazole/quetiapine/lamotrigine/topiramate; avoidance → aripiprazole/lamotrigine; all symptoms → prazosin/phenelzine/levetiracetam)

📌
Board-favorite fact: prazosin (an α1-blocker) is specifically used for PTSD-related nightmares and nighttime hyperarousal — a distinctive, easily-tested use outside its more familiar role in BPH/hypertension.
🩺 Why Side Effects Show Up Before the Antidepressant Effect

The moment an SSRI is started, the transporter is blocked and serotonin floods the synapse immediately — but the postsynaptic receptors need time (roughly 4–6 weeks) to adapt/upregulate before the person actually feels less depressed. Side effects, though, don't need that adaptation: the flood of serotonin hits GI receptors, sexual-function pathways, and other targets right away, which is why side effects typically appear in the first 1–2 weeks, well before the therapeutic benefit does. This is also why severely depressed patients are sometimes hospitalized — not because outpatient treatment can't work, but because it allows faster dose titration and augmentation than waiting out a 4–6 week outpatient trial. And it's why "I started the antidepressant two weeks ago and don't feel different" is expected, not a treatment failure.

Side effects to know: GI distress, sexual dysfunction, SIADH, serotonin syndrome (see below).

MOA: Bind the serotonin transporter (SERT), blocking reuptake of serotonin from the synapse. At the cell body, autoreceptor desensitization over time boosts serotonin release too — a dual effect.

MOA: Three-ringed structure binding multiple receptors — mostly SERT and NET, but also alpha-1, M1, H1, and sodium channels. The "off-target" binding likely contributes to benefit, but is also responsible for the long side effect list.

Side effects: Sedation (histamine), anticholinergic effects — tachycardia, dry mouth (muscarinic), hypotension (alpha), QTc prolongation/arrhythmia (multiple targets).

⬆️

Tertiary TCAs — bigger = more side effects

  • Amitriptyline — pain
  • Imipramine — pain, IBS, nocturnal enuresis
  • Clomipramine — OCD, panic disorder
  • Doxepin — bipolar depression, insomnia
⬇️

Secondary TCAs — smaller = fewer side effects

  • Nortriptyline — cyclic vomiting, IBS, pain, migraine, smoking cessation (off-label)
  • Desipramine — ADHD

Bupropion (NDRI)

Inhibits NE + DA reuptake

Structurally close to a stimulant. Side effects: tachycardia, weight loss, ↓seizure threshold (black box warning). Less likely to cause sexual dysfunction. Helps smoking cessation; can be paired with naltrexone for weight loss.

Mirtazapine

Alpha-2 antagonist, 5-HT2/5-HT3 antagonist, H1 antagonist

Side effects: weight gain, sedation, ↑appetite, dry mouth — less likely sexual side effects. Useful when sedation/appetite gain is desirable (underweight, insomnia).

Trazodone

Blocks 5-HT2, alpha-1, H1

Mainly used for insomnia (high doses needed for antidepressant effect). Side effects: sedation, priapism (erection >4h — surgical emergency, from alpha blockade).

Nefazodone

Serotonin blocker

Liver toxicity — rarely prescribed today.

Vilazodone

5-HT reuptake inhibition + 5-HT1A partial agonist

Low yield beyond MOA — not frequently used or tested.

Vortioxetine

5-HT reuptake inhibition + 5-HT1A agonist + 5-HT3 antagonist

Low yield beyond MOA — not frequently used or tested.

Question 6
A veteran with PTSD reports frequent nightmares and marked nighttime hyperarousal that are severely disrupting his sleep. Which medication is most specifically indicated for this symptom cluster?
A. Sertraline
B. Prazosin
C. Quetiapine
D. Diazepam
Answer: B. Prazosin is specifically indicated for PTSD-related nightmares and nighttime hyperarousal — the first branch point in the PTSD treatment algorithm (Section 14). Sertraline (A) treats core PTSD symptoms generally but isn't the targeted answer for this specific symptom cluster.

LO 077Eating Disorders✓ In your notes

Understand the pharmacological treatment of the eating disorders

Answer

For binge eating disorder, lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse) reduces binge frequency, sertraline (an SSRI) is used, and topiramate reduces binge frequency/appetite. For bulimia nervosa, SSRIs/SNRIs are first-line antidepressants, with TCAs/MAOIs as lesser-used alternatives; topiramate also decreases appetite/binge frequency, and ondansetron (an antiemetic) can reduce purging. Bupropion carries a US boxed warning and is contraindicated in active or recent bulimia or anorexia nervosa because of increased seizure risk tied to the electrolyte disturbances and dehydration that purging causes. No medications are FDA-approved for anorexia nervosa; its primary treatment is weight restoration (roughly 1 lb/week), with caution against reintroducing food too aggressively because of refeeding syndrome risk.

🧠
Memory hook · Anorexia gets NO drugs; Bulimia gets fluoxetine; Binge gets VyvanseNo FDA-approved med for anorexia (treatment = weight restoration ~1 lb/week, beware refeeding). Bulimia → SSRI ± ondansetron/topiramate. BED → lisdexamfetamine, sertraline, or topiramate. Bupropion is Banned in Both bulimia and anorexia (purging → electrolytes → seizures). Purging dehydration also makes lithium dangerous.

On an exam, if a stem describes bulimia and asks "which medication is contraindicated," bupropion is almost always the answer.

Weight restoration, generally around 1 lb/week, comes first — but reintroducing food too aggressively risks refeeding syndrome.

LO 078Somatoform, Dissoc. & Sexual✓ In your notes

Understand the presentations of the dissociative disorders and form a differential diagnosis with other disorders which have dissociation as a feature

Answer

DSM-5 recognizes four core dissociative disorders: dissociative identity disorder (disruption of identity into 2+ personality states, thought to arise from severe early childhood trauma), dissociative amnesia (± fugue), and depersonalization/derealization disorder. Dissociative amnesia can be localized, selective, or generalized for identity/life history, lasting hours to years; fugue is a specifier (not a separate diagnosis) involving purposeful travel or wandering with amnesia for identity. In depersonalization/derealization disorder, Criterion B — reality testing stays intact throughout the episode — is the key differentiator from a primary psychotic disorder, since the patient knows the distorted perception isn't literally true. There is genuine board-relevant debate over whether DID is a distinct entity or a severe, chronic form of PTSD with dissociative features, since both share a trauma etiology. Borderline personality disorder also belongs on the differential for dissociation, since under acute stress BPD patients can have brief dissociative symptoms and micropsychotic episodes they later don't remember.

🧠
Memory hook · Reality testing is the dissociation/psychosis borderDepersonalization/derealization keeps intact reality testing ('I know this isn't literally true') — that's what separates it from psychosis. Fugue = travel + identity amnesia (a specifier of dissociative amnesia, not its own diagnosis). DID ← severe early childhood trauma.

Pulled from: Sexual, Somatoform & Dissociative Disorders · Personality Disorders

Dissociative disorders share a common thread: a disruption in the normally integrated functions of consciousness, memory, identity, or perception. DSM-5 recognizes 4 core diagnoses (plus "other specified" and "unspecified" catch-alls):

300.14 Dissociative identity disorder · 300.12 Dissociative amnesia (specify: 300.13 with dissociative fugue) · 300.6 Depersonalization/derealization disorder · plus other specified/unspecified

Dissociative identity disorder — disruption of identity into 2+ distinct personality states (Section 07)
Dissociative amnesia (± fugue) — inability to recall important autobiographical information, sometimes with purposeful travel/wandering (Section 08)
Depersonalization/derealization disorder — persistent or recurrent detachment from self or surroundings, with reality testing intact (Section 09)
⚖️
There is genuine, ongoing debate in the field about whether DID is best understood as its own distinct entity, or whether many presentations currently labeled DID are better conceptualized as a severe, chronic form of PTSD with dissociative features. Both share the trauma etiology and dissociative symptomatology; the distinction matters for how clinicians and researchers frame treatment and prognosis. This is worth knowing exists as a controversy, even without a settled "right answer."
🧠
Three sub-patterns of dissociative amnesia: localized/selective amnesia for a specific event or events, or generalized amnesia for identity and life history. The amnesia may be continuous from a traumatic event to the present, or cover a person's entire life, and can last hours to years. Information isn't permanently lost — it simply can't be retrieved during the episode.
📌
Dissociative fugue — a specifier, not a separate diagnosis (coded 300.13/F44.1 vs. 300.12/F44.0 without it). Defined as apparently purposeful travel or bewildered wandering associated with amnesia for identity or other important autobiographical information — the person doesn't just forget who they are, they may leave home and turn up somewhere else entirely, sometimes having taken on a new identity.

Depersonalization as "the sensation that mind and body have separated" — often described by patients as an out-of-body experience

Side-by-side: depersonalization = altered perception of oneself; derealization = altered perception of the external world

📌
The single most important criterion to remember: Criterion B — reality testing remains intact throughout the episode. The patient knows their perception is distorted; they aren't psychotic, and this is what separates depersonalization/derealization disorder from a primary psychotic disorder despite the surface-level strangeness of the experience.
📌
BPD belongs on your differential for psychosis: under acute stress, patients can have brief micropsychotic episodes and dissociative symptoms — doing things during a period of time they later don't remember. This is the literal meaning behind the name "borderline": the patient sits at the boundary between mood dysregulation and transient psychosis.
💡
DID is thought to result from severe trauma during early childhood — usually extreme, repetitive physical, sexual, or emotional abuse. The dissociation is theorized as a protective/coping mechanism that allows the developing mind to compartmentalize unbearable experience.

LO 079Legal, Ethics & Risk✓ In your notes

Understand the principles of medical malpractice as discussed by Dr. Smith

Answer

To win a psychiatric malpractice claim, a plaintiff must prove all '4 D's': Duty (a doctor-patient relationship existed), Deviation (from the standard of care), Damages (patient suffered injury/harm), and Direct Causation (the deviation directly caused the damages). Deviation alone is not malpractice — prescribing trazodone off-label for agitation deviates from its FDA label but causes no harm, so it doesn't by itself support a claim; deviation only becomes actionable combined with damages and causation. Res ipsa loquitur ('the thing speaks for itself') applies when the deviation is so obvious the 4-D analysis is nearly a formality, as with a surgeon leaving a sponge in a patient who later develops sepsis from it. Common reasons for psychiatric malpractice suits include sexual relationships with patients, patient suicide, negligent or incorrect treatment, medication errors, incorrect diagnosis, boundary violations, negligent supervision, improper commitment, third-party injury (Tarasoff-type), breach of confidentiality, and improper termination of care. The best defense against a suicide-related claim is regular, documented assessment showing a lack of suicidality (e.g., a structured tool like the Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale) — physicians are expected to act on what was foreseeable, not to predict the future.

🧠
Memory hook · Sue me? Prove the 4 D'sDuty + Deviation + Damages + Direct causation — all four, or no malpractice. Off-label ≠ malpractice without harm. Sponge left in the belly = res ipsa loquitur.

Pulled from: Legal Psychiatric Medicine

The 4 D's: Duty → Deviation → Damages → Direct Causation

In a malpractice suit, a patient alleges they were damaged by a physician's negligence. To win, they must prove all four elements.

🚑
Good Samaritan laws and "Duty": if you help a stranger collapse on the sidewalk, there's technically no doctor-patient relationship, so technically no duty — and technically no malpractice suit. In practice, a determined lawyer can still find an angle and sue anyway, so "no duty" isn't an absolute shield, but it's still the correct first checkpoint.
💊
Deviation alone isn't malpractice. Prescribing trazodone off-label for agitation is a deviation from its FDA-labeled indication, but it's a common, benefit-driven practice that causes no harm — so on its own it doesn't support a malpractice claim. Deviation only becomes a problem in combination with the other 3 D's.
🧽
Res ipsa loquitur ("the thing speaks for itself"): when the deviation is so obvious that the whole 4-D analysis is almost a formality. Classic example: a surgeon leaves a sponge inside a patient during surgery, and the patient later develops sepsis traced directly back to that sponge. Duty, deviation, damages, and direct causation are all self-evident from the single fact pattern.
Sexual relationship with a patient
Suicide attempt or completion by a patient
Incorrect or negligent treatment
Medication error or drug reaction
Incorrect diagnosis
Boundary violations
Negligent supervision
Improper commitment
Injury to a third party (Tarasoff-type)
Breach of confidentiality
🛡️
Your best defense against a suicide-related malpractice claim: regular, documented assessment showing a lack of suicidality — e.g., using a structured tool like the Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale. You are not expected to predict the future — only to act on what was predictable/foreseeable. If the patient gave no indication of suicidality, failing to intervene is not a deviation from the standard of care. The proof of this is documentation of ongoing suicide risk assessment, not any single note.
Question 6
Which combination of elements must a plaintiff prove to win a psychiatric malpractice claim?
A. Damages and Direct Causation only
B. Duty, Deviation, Damages, and Direct Causation
C. Mens rea and Actus reus
D. Beneficence and Non-malfeasance
Answer: B. The "4 D's" (Section 07) are all required together — missing any one element defeats the claim.

LO 080Legal, Ethics & Risk◐ Partly covered

Understand the procedure for dealing with suspected child abuse in both an acute and chronic setting

Answer

The only detailed vignette remains a case suggestive of factitious disorder imposed on another (Munchausen syndrome by proxy): a mother repeatedly brings her toddler to the ED for unexplained vomiting and bleeding episodes that occur only while she is alone with the child, and staff note she seems unusually knowledgeable about the child's IV lines and wants the child hospitalized, a presentation that should raise suspicion for caregiver-fabricated illness as a form of abuse. The child psychiatry lecture adds two recognition clues: an affect mismatch, where a child with a caregiver is unexpectedly calm or non-reactive in a situation that should provoke distress, should raise suspicion for abuse; and reactive attachment disorder, seen as an inhibited, hypervigilant, adopted or severely neglected child who has not formed relationships with caregivers (contrasted with disinhibited social engagement disorder), can itself be a marker of severe neglect. On procedure, the lecture states only the general principle that real clinical practice follows local mandatory reporting law and institutional policy whenever abuse or neglect is suspected, and that exam stems should favor immediate safety/reporting over exhaustive investigation.

◐
Missing from your notesNeither source gives the specific acute ED workup (skeletal survey, documentation, photography) or a structured protocol for longitudinal management of chronic abuse.

Pulled from: Sexual, Somatoform & Dissociative Disorders · Child & Adolescent Psychiatry

Question 5
A mother repeatedly brings her toddler to the ED for unexplained episodes of vomiting and bleeding that only occur while the mother is alone with the child. Staff note the mother seems unusually knowledgeable about the child's IV lines and appears to want the child hospitalized. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
A. Discharge the child home with outpatient follow-up
B. Refer the mother for outpatient psychotherapy and reassess in 6 months
C. Report to child protective services / appropriate authorities
D. Confront the mother directly and ask her to stop
Answer: C. This is Munchausen syndrome by proxy (Section 04) — illness induced in a dependent by a caregiver seeking the sick role by proxy. This is a form of child abuse and must be reported to the appropriate authorities; it is not a situation to manage solely through counseling or direct confrontation.
Mandate

In real clinical practice, follow local mandatory reporting law and institutional policy whenever abuse or neglect is suspected. In exam stems, do not over-investigate at the expense of immediate safety/reporting obligations.

Affect mismatch

Unexpected calm can matter

AnKing cue: suspect abuse when a child with a caregiver is not crying or not reacting in a situation where distress would be expected.

Reactive attachment

Severe neglect clue

Adopted child who is inhibited, hypervigilant, and has not formed relationships with caregivers suggests reactive attachment disorder; contrast with disinhibited social engagement disorder.

LO 081Psychotherapy & Theory◐ Partly covered

Understand the psychotherapy options best suited for each of the core anxiety disorders

Answer

For social anxiety disorder, CBT, particularly assertiveness training, is the psychotherapy of choice, paired with serotonergic pharmacotherapy (SSRIs, buspirone) and adjunctive beta-blockers for the circumscribed, performance-only subtype or PRN benzodiazepines; the exam-reading rule is that chronic/daily exposure points to serotonergic therapy as core treatment, while episodic/occasional exposure can be managed with a beta-blocker or benzodiazepine alone. Specific phobia (and agoraphobia) is treated with exposure-based therapy in two forms: systematic desensitization, which gradually pairs the feared stimulus with relaxation training in graded steps (e.g., picture of a spider to plastic spider to dead spider to live spider), and flooding, which uses massive immediate exposure until anxiety extinguishes; a real case of severe bridge/water phobia was treated successfully with systematic desensitization, having the patient's daughter drive her progressively farther onto the bridge each week. More broadly across anxiety disorders, treatment also draws on psychodynamic psychotherapy, support and reassurance, relaxation training, and biofeedback, since anxiety is difficult to control with medication alone and durable improvement typically requires concomitant psychotherapy.

🧠
Memory hook · Ladder vs. cannonballSystematic desensitization = climb the ladder (graded exposure + relaxation: picture spider → plastic spider → real spider). Flooding = cannonball into the deep end (massive exposure until anxiety extinguishes). Social anxiety's therapy of choice: CBT with assertiveness training.
🧠
Memory hook · Daily fear → SSRI; date-night fear → beta-blockerChronic/generalized anxiety or daily social exposure → serotonergic therapy (SSRI/SNRI, buspirone). Episodic performance anxiety → propranolol or PRN benzo. OCD wants higher SSRI doses than depression.
◐
Missing from your notesNeither the drug list nor the two new lectures name a specific psychotherapy modality (CBT, exposure, etc.) for generalized anxiety, panic, or separation anxiety disorder.

Pulled from: Anxiety, OCD & Trauma-Related Disorders · Introduction to Therapy

CBT — particularly assertiveness training
Core pharmacotherapy — SSRIs, buspirone (both serotonergic)
Adjunctive — beta-blockers for circumscribed (performance-only) social phobia; benzodiazepines PRN

Systematic Desensitization

MethodFeared stimuli are gradually paired with relaxation training, in graded steps.
ExampleSpider phobia: picture of a spider → plastic spider → dead spider → live spider.

Flooding

MethodMassive, immediate exposure to the feared stimulus until anxiety extinguishes.
ExampleSpider phobia: place the patient directly into a large tank filled with live spiders.
🔍
Example case — the twist: a patient with a severe fear of water/bridges (couldn't cross the one bridge connecting her island town to the mainland — hadn't left in 20 years) was treated with systematic desensitization (her daughter drove her progressively farther onto the bridge each week) and eventually succeeded. Years into therapy it emerged the "phobia" was secondary to childhood sexual abuse in a house that sat directly along the only road to that bridge — her mind had displaced the trauma onto the bridge/water rather than the house. Lesson: what presents as an isolated specific phobia can actually be a disguised PTSD/trauma presentation — dig below the surface, especially when a fear seems oddly specific and geographically anchored.

Psychotherapy

ModalitiesSupport and reassurance, psychodynamic and cognitive-behavioral psychotherapies, relaxation training, biofeedback.

Psychopharmacology

PrerequisiteA precise diagnosis is needed before medications are utilized — treatment is disorder-specific, not "anxiety" as a monolith.

Remove the etiologic stressor where possible, plus CBT or psychodynamic psychotherapy; supportive psychotherapy also helps. Focus is on improving coping skills, strengthening defense mechanisms, or changing how the person relates to the stressor. Medication can help adjunctively (anxiety, secondary insomnia, depressive symptoms).

  • Gain a basic understanding of the history of psychotherapy.
  • Understand the theoretical basis for the major therapies.
  • Compare the different approaches to therapy and the patient populations each is best suited for.
📌
Anxiety is a difficult condition to control with medication alone — concomitant psychotherapy is often necessary for durable improvement.

Interpersonal Therapy (IPT)

Focused squarely on relationships
ApproachA structured, time-limited therapy focused on improving current interpersonal relationships and communication skills — less exploratory than psychodynamic work, more here-and-now than CBT's focus on thought content.
Worth knowingDistinct from the humanistic modalities above — IPT is manualized and diagnosis-focused (often depression), not a general relational philosophy.
📌
Exam-reading strategy: if the question is about chronic/daily exposure (e.g., a professor lecturing every day), the answer is serotonergic (SSRI/buspirone) as core therapy. If it's about episodic/occasional exposure (e.g., public speaking once every few months), a beta-blocker or benzo alone can be the answer. Both can be used together, but read carefully — questions often list both a serotonergic and an episodic option and are testing whether you can tell which one the stem is actually asking about.
LO 082Cross-Cutting Pharm◐ Partly covered

Understand the rationale of prescribing psychopharmacological medications in the pregnant female in each trimester

Answer

Lithium's Ebstein anomaly risk is trimester-specific: cardiac formation happens early, so risk is highest in the first trimester, and many clinicians minimize or hold lithium then, resuming or increasing the dose later in pregnancy once heart formation is complete and risk has dropped; pregnancy is one of four exceptions that override lithium as the default exam answer for bipolar disorder, and prescreening before starting it includes a serum HCG in women. Valproic acid carries its own teratogenic signal, neural tube defects, and likewise requires a serum HCG check in women before starting. Benzodiazepines carry pregnancy category D and X, with the greatest risk of malformation, growth retardation, and functional deficits concentrated between 2 and 8 weeks gestation, a risk profile the lecture compares to drinking alcohol during pregnancy. Pregnancy category letters generally function as a simplified stand-in for risk-benefit data, A/B is reassuring, C means insufficient information, and D means documented harm, and most psychiatric medications fall into category C simply because pregnant patients are rarely included in trials.

🧠
Memory hook · First trimester: the heart forms, so hold the lithiumLithium → Ebstein anomaly (risk highest in T1; many hold it, resume later). Valproate/carbamazepine → neural tube defects. Benzos → worst at weeks 2–8. Most psych meds are category C only because nobody trials pregnant patients.
◐
Missing from your notesNo source gives SSRI first-trimester cardiac-defect signals or third-trimester neonatal adaptation/persistent pulmonary hypertension concerns; pregnancy-specific content is still limited to lithium's Ebstein anomaly and valproate's neural tube defect risk.

Pulled from: Mood Disorders · Anxiety, OCD & Trauma-Related Disorders

  • Lithium: Ebstein anomaly risk is trimester-specific — cardiac formation happens early, so risk is highest in the first trimester. Many clinicians minimize or hold lithium during the first trimester, then resume or increase the dose later in pregnancy once heart formation is complete and risk drops substantially.
  • Valproate, carbamazepine, lamotrigine: neural tube defect risk; folic acid supplementation (typically more than a standard prenatal vitamin provides) can help mitigate this risk.
  • Antipsychotics: most have little to no pregnancy safety data — the exception is clozapine, which actually has accumulated outcome data. Because of this data gap (not necessarily proven danger), antipsychotics are often the preferred bipolar treatment in pregnancy when a mood stabilizer's teratogenic risk is a bigger concern.
  • Antidepressants: no strong teratogenic signal either way. The main concern is neonatal discontinuation/serotonin syndrome in the newborn after birth, from placental transfer — but most patients are kept on their antidepressant throughout pregnancy regardless, because untreated depression carries its own fetal risk.

Benzodiazepines

🤰
Pregnancy: Category D and X. Greatest malformation/growth-retardation/functional-deficit risk is between 2 and 8 weeks gestation. Often compared to the risk profile of drinking alcohol during pregnancy.

Valproate — mechanism & side effects

MOA: Modulates GABA. Side effects: weight gain (can contribute to PCOS), hair loss, sedation, thrombocytopenia, elevated ammonia, rash (less common than lamotrigine), neural tube teratogenicity. Supratherapeutic above 100–125.

Pregnancy category letters are a simplified stand-in for risk-benefit data: think of them like school grades — A/B is reassuring, C means "we don't have enough information either way," and D means known harm has been documented. Most psychiatric medications land in category C simply because pregnant patients are rarely included in trials, not necessarily because they're dangerous. Because untreated severe depression or mania in pregnancy is itself harmful to the fetus, the goal is an informed risk-benefit conversation, not automatic avoidance of all medication.

🔑 Default Answer, With Four Exceptions

On an exam, if a stem describes bipolar disorder and gives you a plain drug list with no other clues, lithium is the default first-line answer. Four things should make you look elsewhere: (1) pregnancy (Ebstein anomaly), (2) significant renal impairment (lithium is a salt excreted essentially unchanged by the kidney, so impaired renal clearance is a direct problem), (3) cardiac conduction disease such as an existing heart block (lithium can further affect cardiac conduction), and (4) difficult-to-manage thyroid disease (lithium can push a patient hypo- or hyperthyroid).

Lithium — prescreening labs

Prescreening: CBC, renal function (creatinine, BUN), thyroid function (TSH, free T3/T4), serum HCG in women, ECG, screen for co-administered NSAIDs/ACE-inhibitors/thiazides, and check for preexisting renal disease/CHF/arrhythmia.

Valproate — prescreening labs

Prescreening: WBC with differential and platelets, serum HCG in women, liver function tests.

Carbamazepine

Because it's such a "dirty drug" that interacts with many other medications, be especially cautious prescribing it to patients who are young, otherwise healthy, and — critically — anyone capable of becoming pregnant: carbamazepine's induction of hepatic metabolism makes standard oral contraceptives unreliable, so a non-hormonally-interacting method (e.g. an IUD) is usually recommended instead.

LO 083Psychosis & Antipsychotics✓ In your notes

Understand the receptor dynamics and binding profiles of the various classes of antipsychotic medications

Answer

Typical (first-generation) antipsychotics block dopamine (D2) more than serotonin, while atypical (second-generation) agents block serotonin (5-HT2A) more than dopamine; this extra serotonergic blockade is what distinguishes the atypicals, though all antipsychotics fundamentally block post-synaptic D2 receptors. Within the atypicals, receptor profiles vary further: aripiprazole is a D2 partial agonist that stabilizes rather than fully blocks dopamine tone, ziprasidone additionally modulates norepinephrine/serotonin, and clozapine has serotonergic predominance with a roughly 10:1 5-HT2A:D2 ratio and the broadest receptor footprint of any agent. Striatal D2 occupancy of about 78-80% is the threshold for antipsychotic efficacy with minimal EPS (2-5 mg Haldol or 100-200 mg Thorazine sits in this zone); crossing above it produces motor side effects, and some atypicals never reach that occupancy at clinical doses because of looser D2 binding, which is why they cause less EPS. Each drug's receptor-blocking pattern predicts its adverse-effect signature — e.g., clozapine's absent EPS/hyperprolactinemia versus high weight gain/sedation and unique agranulocytosis/seizure risk, risperidone's frequent hyperprolactinemia, and ziprasidone's notable QTc. Typical antipsychotics are further stratified into high, medium, and low potency relative to chlorpromazine, and potency alone predicts the side-effect profile — high-potency agents like haloperidol carry the strongest EPS/akathisia signal.

🧠
Memory hook · The potency see-sawHigh potency (haloperidol, fluphenazine): hands shake — max EPS, minimal anticholinergic. Low potency (chlorpromazine): lazy & dry — sedation, anticholinergic, orthostasis, minimal EPS. Sweet spot: ~78–80% D2 occupancy ≈ Haldol 2–5 mg.

Pulled from: Psychotic Disorders & Antipsychotic Pharmacology

Typical (First-Generation)

Also calledNeuroleptics.

Atypical (Second-Generation)

MechanismBlock serotonin (5-HT2A) > dopamine — this extra serotonin antagonism is why they carry relatively less EPS but more metabolic risk.
GroupingOrganized by chemical-class suffix and by the "PINES/DONES" memory scheme (Section 14).
Aripiprazole — D2 partial agonist (stabilizes rather than fully blocking dopamine tone)
Ziprasidone — modulates norepinephrine/serotonin in addition to D2/5-HT2A antagonism
Clozapine — serotonergic predominance (5-HT2A:D2 ratio ~10:1); broadest receptor footprint of any agent

At their core, all antipsychotics block post-synaptic dopamine (D2) receptors, reducing dopamine signaling. The typical/atypical split is really a split in how selectively they do this and what else they bind.

There is a narrow window between antipsychotic efficacy and excessive side effects. The striatal D2 receptor occupancy threshold to reduce psychosis with minimal EPS is approximately 78–80%; crossing above the EPS threshold produces motor side effects.

Hypothetical thresholds for antipsychotic drug effects — the therapeutic window sits between the ~70% "antipsychotic effect" line and the ~80% "EPS" line

📌
Visually anchored dose: 2–5 mg of Haldol, or 100–200 mg of Thorazine, sits in this efficacious/low-EPS zone. Some atypicals never exceed ~78% D2 occupancy at clinical doses because of looser D2 binding — hence little EPS.

Clozapine: absent EPS/hyperprolactinemia, high weight gain/sedation, unique agranulocytosis/seizure risk. Olanzapine: rare EPS, high weight gain/sedation. Risperidone: frequent hyperprolactinemia. Ziprasidone: low weight gain, notable QTc. Aripiprazole: absent hyperprolactinemia, rare weight gain — the cleanest metabolic profile of the group.

LO 084Mood & Mood Stabilizers✓ In your notes

Understand the risks of the medication prescribed for mood disorders, and their medical risk of toxicity if overdosed on

Answer

Lithium toxicity presents classically with coarse tremor, diarrhea, and headache, as in a patient on lithium plus risperidone with concurrent NSAID use. Lithium also carries a pregnancy-specific risk of Ebstein anomaly that is highest in the first trimester when cardiac formation occurs, so clinicians often minimize or hold the dose then and resume once heart formation is complete. Antidepressants such as fluoxetine used in bipolar disorder carry their own risk of worsening depression, precipitating mania, and increasing suicidality in children. More generally, when another drug inhibits the enzyme metabolizing a mood-disorder medication, its plasma level rises and toxicity risk increases, while an enzyme inducer lowers the level and risks relapse. The drug list supplies dedicated TCA overdose-lethality data (the '3 C's' — Cardiotoxicity, Coma, Convulsions — with QRS widening on EKG, arrhythmias, one week's supply being potentially lethal, and the need for baseline/serial EKGs, worsened by CYP2D6 inhibitors like bupropion raising TCA levels) and valproate overdose data (fatal hepatotoxicity requiring LFT monitoring, pancreatitis, and a toxic level range above 40–150).

🧠
Memory hook · TCA overdose: the 3 C's, and one week can killConvulsions, Coma, Cardiotoxicity (Na-channel block → wide QRS → torsades). A single week's supply is potentially lethal — get the EKG. 2D6 inhibitors (bupropion, fluoxetine) push TCA levels up.

Pulled from: Psychotic Disorders & Antipsychotic Pharmacology · Mood Disorders · Introduction & History of Psychiatry · Psychiatry Key Drug List 2026

E.1
Which of the following most likely caused his symptoms?
A. Anticholinergic toxicity
B. Lithium toxicity
C. Neuroleptic-induced dystonia
D. Neuroleptic-induced EPS
E. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Answer: B. Coarse tremor + GI upset (diarrhea) + headache is the classic early lithium toxicity picture. The trigger: frequent ibuprofen (an NSAID) reduces renal prostaglandin synthesis → reduced renal blood flow → reduced lithium clearance → rising lithium levels. Docusate is a distractor (a stool softener with no meaningful lithium interaction). This is a classic drug-interaction vignette, distinct from anything on the antipsychotic side.
  • Lithium: Ebstein anomaly risk is trimester-specific — cardiac formation happens early, so risk is highest in the first trimester. Many clinicians minimize or hold lithium during the first trimester, then resume or increase the dose later in pregnancy once heart formation is complete and risk drops substantially.
  • Valproate, carbamazepine, lamotrigine: neural tube defect risk; folic acid supplementation (typically more than a standard prenatal vitamin provides) can help mitigate this risk.
  • Antipsychotics: most have little to no pregnancy safety data — the exception is clozapine, which actually has accumulated outcome data. Because of this data gap (not necessarily proven danger), antipsychotics are often the preferred bipolar treatment in pregnancy when a mood stabilizer's teratogenic risk is a bigger concern.
  • Antidepressants: no strong teratogenic signal either way. The main concern is neonatal discontinuation/serotonin syndrome in the newborn after birth, from placental transfer — but most patients are kept on their antidepressant throughout pregnancy regardless, because untreated depression carries its own fetal risk.
⚠️ Antidepressant Caution in Bipolar

Fluoxetine's own bipolar-context side effect profile flags worsening of depression and manic episodes in bipolar patients, plus increased suicidality in children — antidepressants in bipolar disorder are generally used cautiously and typically alongside a mood stabilizer, never as unopposed monotherapy. The one FDA-approved exception is a fluoxetine + olanzapine combination — but that's a maintenance-phase indication, not a treatment for acute mania. You would not start an acutely manic patient on fluoxetine.

Substrate + Inhibitor

A drug that reduces enzyme activity → increases plasma level of the substrate → increased side effects & toxicity risk.

Substrate + Inducer

A drug that increases enzyme activity → decreases plasma level of the substrate → loss of efficacy / relapse risk (the handout frames this as "decreased side effects and toxicity," which is true, but the clinically dangerous side of induction is usually treatment failure, not safety).
Black Box — fatal in overdose
Cardiotoxic in OD: arrhythmias kill — look for QRS prolongation on EKG. Toxicity = the three C's: Cardiotoxicity, Coma, Convulsions. ONE WEEK'S worth of medication is lethal — prescribe with extreme caution to suicidal patients. Get a baseline EKG before starting and serially with dose changes.
Deadliest fact?
TCAs
3 C's: Cardiotoxicity, Coma, Convulsions. QRS widens on EKG; ONE WEEK of pills is lethal; baseline + serial EKGs; 2D6 inhibitors raise levels.
Deadliest fact?
valproate
Fatal hepatotoxicity + pancreatitis + neural tube defects. Levels 40–150; LFTs + CBC; birth control mandatory conversation.
The co-star
valproic acid (Depakote)
  • MOA: ↑ GABA availability (anticonvulsant). Mania efficacy ≈ lithium; also epilepsy, migraine prophylaxis.
  • SEs: somnolence, dizziness, GI upset, diplopia, ataxia, rash, weight gain, alopecia, prolonged bleeding, PCOS (esp. women w/ epilepsy).
  • ⛔ Rare FATAL HEPATOTOXICITY (monitor LFTs), pancreatitis, NEURAL TUBE DEFECTS (spina bifida — birth control!); monitor CBC (granulo-/thrombocytopenia).
  • Levels: 40–150 mcg/mL, serially.
Major interaction — CYP2D6
Mostly 2D6. Example: add bupropion (2D6 inhibitor) to imipramine (2D6 substrate) → imipramine levels climb → arrhythmia and death. Best prescribed by a psychiatrist.
Mechanism
Block reuptake of both NE and serotonin into the presynaptic neuron → more transmitter stays in the cleft. (For chronic pain, it's the NE blockade that matters — RS.)
Place in therapy
2nd/3rd-line for MDD after SSRI/SNRI/NDRI trials — because of side effects and overdose lethality, not weak efficacy. 25–30% of patients quit due to intolerable side effects.
Special niches (board favorites)
  • Chronic pain (trigeminal neuralgia, diabetic neuropathy) → desipramine (most noradrenergic)
  • Bedwetting (enuresis) → imipramine
  • OCD → clomipramine (most serotonergic)
Monitoring
Blood levels are obtainable — useful for malabsorption (short-gut) or suspected noncompliance.
LO 085Mood & Mood Stabilizers✓ In your notes

Understand the side-effect profile of lithium

Answer

Lithium's core side effects are captured by the mnemonic LiTHIUM: Low thyroid (hypothyroidism), Heart (Ebstein anomaly — right atrial enlargement, displaced tricuspid valve — with highest risk in the first trimester of pregnancy), Insipidus (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus), and Unwanted Movements (tremor). Lithium toxicity (level >1.2) presents with nausea, diarrhea, altered mental status, severe tremor, ataxia, slurred speech, hyperreflexia, polyuria, and seizure; treatment is to stop lithium and hydrate, with dialysis considered in severe cases. Because lithium is reabsorbed via the same renal sodium channels used for salt, thiazide diuretics, spironolactone, triamterene, ACE-inhibitors, and NSAIDs raise lithium levels, while acetazolamide, theophylline, and caffeine lower them, and metronidazole/neuroleptics can worsen neuro/nephrotoxicity. Lithium should generally be avoided in unstable-hydration states, such as bulimia with purging (dehydration raises nephrotoxicity risk), and clinicians favor alternatives in pregnancy (Ebstein anomaly) or significant renal impairment.

🧠
Memory hook · Lithium follows saltReabsorbed on the kidney's sodium channels → anything that makes you keep sodium keeps lithium: thiazides, NSAIDs, ACE-inhibitors, dehydration. Levels: 0.8–1.2 treats · >1.2 toxic (coarse tremor, ataxia, AMS, seizure) · severe → dialysis. LiTHIUM: Low Thyroid, Heart (Ebstein), Insipidus, Unwanted Movements.

Pulled from: Mood Disorders · Eating Disorders · Psychotic Disorders & Antipsychotic Pharmacology

🔑 First Aid Mnemonic — LiTHIUM

Low Thyroid (hypothyroidism) · Heart (Ebstein anomaly — right atrial enlargement, displaced tricuspid valve) · Insipidus (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus) · Unwanted Movements (tremor)

☐ Lithium Toxicity — level >1.2

Nausea, diarrhea, altered mental status, severe tremor, ataxia, slurred speech, hyperreflexia, polyuria, seizure. Treatment: stop lithium, hydrate; consider dialysis in severe cases.

🧸 ELI5 — Lithium & the Kidney

Lithium hitches a ride on the same sodium channels the kidney uses to reabsorb salt at the PCT. Anything that makes the kidney hang onto more sodium (thiazides, low-salt states, NSAIDs, ACE-inhibitors) makes it hang onto more lithium too — levels climb. Anything that flushes sodium out (caffeine, theophylline) flushes lithium out with it — levels drop.

Increases lithium levelsDecreases lithium levelsAffects lithium's toxicity
Thiazide diuretics, spironolactone, triamterene, enalapril (ACE-I), NSAIDsAcetazolamide, theophylline, aminophylline, caffeineMetronidazole ↑nephrotoxicity · Neuroleptics may induce neurotoxicity · Antiarrhythmics potentiate cardiac effects of digoxin/quinidine
🔑 Default Answer, With Four Exceptions

On an exam, if a stem describes bipolar disorder and gives you a plain drug list with no other clues, lithium is the default first-line answer. Four things should make you look elsewhere: (1) pregnancy (Ebstein anomaly), (2) significant renal impairment (lithium is a salt excreted essentially unchanged by the kidney, so impaired renal clearance is a direct problem), (3) cardiac conduction disease such as an existing heart block (lithium can further affect cardiac conduction), and (4) difficult-to-manage thyroid disease (lithium can push a patient hypo- or hyperthyroid).

⚠️ Also Avoid: Lithium

Lithium requires a stable, consistent hydration state to avoid nephrotoxicity. Purging behaviors (especially self-induced vomiting) create a dehydration-prone state that raises the risk of lithium toxicity.

LO 086Psychosis & Antipsychotics✓ In your notes

Understand the side-effect profiles of antipsychotic medications

Answer

Across the atypical antipsychotics, side-effect risk varies systematically by domain: aripiprazole, ziprasidone, cariprazine, and lurasidone carry the lowest metabolic-syndrome risk while clozapine and olanzapine carry the highest; lurasidone and aripiprazole have the lowest QT-prolongation risk while ziprasidone is highest among atypicals; aripiprazole has the lowest prolactin-elevation risk. Receptor-linked adverse effects are drug-specific: clozapine has absent EPS/hyperprolactinemia but high weight gain/sedation plus unique agranulocytosis and seizure risk; olanzapine has rare EPS but high weight gain/sedation; risperidone causes frequent hyperprolactinemia; ziprasidone has low weight gain but notable QTc; aripiprazole has absent hyperprolactinemia and rare weight gain. The '-PINE' drugs (olanzapine, quetiapine, asenapine) are largely sedating and more implicated in metabolic syndrome than the '-DONE' drugs (risperidone, ziprasidone, paliperidone, iloperidone). Clozapine, despite superior efficacy, is reserved as a later-line agent because of its heavy side-effect burden, and high-potency typicals like haloperidol carry the strongest EPS/akathisia signal, including acute dystonia (e.g., dysarthria and a twisted neck/opisthotonos).

🧠
Memory hook · -PINEs pack Pounds; -DONEs Drain prolactinOlanzapine/clozapine/quetiapine → weight, sedation, metabolic syndrome. Risperidone → prolactin; ziprasidone → QTc. Cleanest metabolics: aripiprazole (D2 partial agonist), ziprasidone, lurasidone, cariprazine. Clozapine = last-resort gold standard: agranulocytosis (ANC checks), seizures, myocarditis — and the only drug FDA-approved to cut suicidality in schizophrenia.

Clozapine: absent EPS/hyperprolactinemia, high weight gain/sedation, unique agranulocytosis/seizure risk. Olanzapine: rare EPS, high weight gain/sedation. Risperidone: frequent hyperprolactinemia. Ziprasidone: low weight gain, notable QTc. Aripiprazole: absent hyperprolactinemia, rare weight gain — the cleanest metabolic profile of the group.

🧠
Pattern-spotting: Aripiprazole shows up on the "lowest risk" end of almost every row — consistent with its unique partial-agonist mechanism (Section 19) and its reputation as the most metabolically/EPS-friendly atypical. Clozapine anchors the "highest risk" end for sedation, orthostasis, weight gain, and metabolic syndrome — the cost of its unmatched efficacy.

The "-PINE" Drugs

Olanzapine, Quetiapine, Asenapine
PersonalityLargely very sedating medications.
Signature riskImplicated more than the "-done" drugs in metabolic syndrome (weight gain, dyslipidemia, T2DM).

The "-DONE" Drugs

Risperidone, Ziprasidone, Paliperidone, Iloperidone
PersonalityThink of these as "watered-down typicals" — similar effects/side effects to typicals, just to a lesser extent.

Clozapine (Clozaril)

The most effective antipsychotic — and the most heavily regulated

Answer: D. Haloperidol is the classic high-potency typical with the strongest EPS/akathisia signal among these five options (Section 13/25) — clozapine (E) essentially never causes EPS, and olanzapine (C) is comparatively low-EPS.
📋
A 23-year-old white male with an exacerbation of schizophrenia develops the onset of dysarthria and a twisted neck (opisthotonos) shortly after starting a course of haloperidol, a high-potency typical antipsychotic.
D.2
This is best treated by doing which of the following?
A. Change to a low-potency typical antipsychotic
B. Add an anxiolytic
C. Add an antidepressant
D. Add an anticonvulsant
E. Add a beta blocker
F. Stop the antipsychotic
G. Add an anticholinergic
Answer: F. The first and most essential step in NMS is to discontinue the causative antipsychotic and provide supportive care (cooling, IV fluids; dantrolene/bromocriptine in severe cases). Switching to a different (even lower-potency) antipsychotic (A) still blocks dopamine and won't resolve an ongoing NMS episode.

LO 087Cross-Cutting Pharm✓ In your notes

Understand the side-effect profiles of major psychiatric medications, and be able to identify which medication out of a list is causative of specific side-effects

Answer

Each antidepressant class has a recognizable side-effect signature useful for identifying the causative drug from a list: SSRIs cause GI distress, sexual dysfunction, SIADH, and serotonin syndrome; TCAs cause sedation and anticholinergic effects and are dangerous in overdose via sodium-channel blockade causing QRS/QTc widening that can progress to torsades (mnemonic: Convulsions, Coma, Cardiotoxicity); MAOIs risk a tyramine- or drug-triggered hypertensive crisis (diastolic BP >120 with headache, palpitations, sweating) and serotonin syndrome when combined with other serotonergic agents; and bupropion causes tachycardia, weight loss, and a lowered seizure threshold (black box warning). A condition-matching rule of thumb also helps distinguish agents: avoid SNRIs in uncontrolled hypertension because of their norepinephrine effect, and avoid bupropion with a seizure risk or bulimia history. Antidepressants as a class also carry a black box warning for increased suicidality in children, adolescents, and young adults, and abruptly stopping any antidepressant can trigger a discontinuation syndrome of flu-like symptoms, dizziness, and "brain zaps." The drug list fills the missing mood-stabilizer and antipsychotic side-effect-to-drug mapping: the PINE/DONE/PIP/RIP suffix rule and potency see-saw let a student pin weight gain/metabolic syndrome to olanzapine or quetiapine (PINEs), EPS/prolactin elevation to risperidone or haloperidol (DONEs/high-potency typicals), and agranulocytosis/seizures/myocarditis to clozapine, alongside mood-stabilizer signatures (lithium tremor/DI/hypothyroidism, valproate hepatotoxicity/pancreatitis, carbamazepine agranulocytosis/hyponatremia, lamotrigine Stevens-Johnson syndrome).

🧠
Memory hook · Name the culprit by its signatureSSRI → GI, sexual dysfunction, SIADH · TCA → sedating, anticholinergic, deadly OD · MAOI → cheese crisis · bupropion → tachycardia, weight loss, seizures. -PINEs pack on Pounds (metabolic) · -DONEs Drain prolactin & prolong QT · clozapine → agranulocytosis/seizures/myocarditis · lamotrigine → SJS.

Pulled from: Mood Disorders · Psychiatry Key Drug List 2026

ConditionWhat to do
Uncontrolled hypertensionAvoid SNRIs — the norepinephrine component can push blood pressure into a hypertensive crisis
Seizure risk / bulimia historyAvoid bupropion — black box warning for lowering seizure threshold, specifically flagged in bulimia patients
Orthostatic hypotension risk (e.g. elderly)Be cautious with TCAs — alpha-1 blockade is a classic cause
Cardiac conduction concerns / prolonged QTcCitalopram is the antidepressant most specifically flagged for QTc; escitalopram is the safer alternative
Renal impairmentConsider how the drug is cleared/processed; adjust accordingly
On NSAIDs or other bleeding riskAny serotonergic drug (SSRI/SNRI/TCA/MAOI) + NSAID = increased bleeding risk, since serotonin has a role in platelet activity — this combination is a classic "don't miss" interaction
Overweight/obeseAvoid mirtazapine (weight gain) and generally TCAs; bupropion is the one antidepressant that can help with weight loss instead

Side effects to know: GI distress, sexual dysfunction, SIADH, serotonin syndrome (see below).

MOA: Three-ringed structure binding multiple receptors — mostly SERT and NET, but also alpha-1, M1, H1, and sodium channels. The "off-target" binding likely contributes to benefit, but is also responsible for the long side effect list.

Side effects: Sedation (histamine), anticholinergic effects — tachycardia, dry mouth (muscarinic), hypotension (alpha), QTc prolongation/arrhythmia (multiple targets).

☐ Overdose Danger

A one-week supply of a TCA can be lethal in overdose — sodium channel blockade causes QRS/QTc widening that can progress to torsades de pointes.

🔑 First Aid Mnemonic — Tri-CyCliC's

Convulsions, Coma, Cardiotoxicity (arrhythmia from Na⁺ channel inhibition) — plus respiratory depression and hyperpyrexia. Treatment: NaHCO₃ to prevent arrhythmia.

☐ Hypertensive Crisis

Caused by increased NE and its excitatory effect — triggered by interacting medications or tyramine-rich foods (smoked, fermented, aged). Presentation: diastolic BP >120 mmHg with headache, palpitations, neck stiffness, nausea/vomiting, sweating, dilated pupils, arrhythmias. Treatment: phentolamine.

⚠️ Serotonin Syndrome Risk — ANY serotonergic drug

Because MAOIs block 5-HT breakdown, combining with other serotonergic agents (decongestants, stimulants, other antidepressants, MDMA, certain pain meds, certain anesthesia meds) risks serotonin syndrome. See the dedicated section below for full presentation.

Bupropion (NDRI)

Inhibits NE + DA reuptake

Structurally close to a stimulant. Side effects: tachycardia, weight loss, ↓seizure threshold (black box warning). Less likely to cause sexual dysfunction. Helps smoking cessation; can be paired with naltrexone for weight loss.

Mirtazapine

Alpha-2 antagonist, 5-HT2/5-HT3 antagonist, H1 antagonist

Side effects: weight gain, sedation, ↑appetite, dry mouth — less likely sexual side effects. Useful when sedation/appetite gain is desirable (underweight, insomnia).

Trazodone

Blocks 5-HT2, alpha-1, H1

Mainly used for insomnia (high doses needed for antidepressant effect). Side effects: sedation, priapism (erection >4h — surgical emergency, from alpha blockade).

Nefazodone

Serotonin blocker

Liver toxicity — rarely prescribed today.

Vilazodone

5-HT reuptake inhibition + 5-HT1A partial agonist

Low yield beyond MOA — not frequently used or tested.

Vortioxetine

5-HT reuptake inhibition + 5-HT1A agonist + 5-HT3 antagonist

Low yield beyond MOA — not frequently used or tested.

☐ Antidepressant Discontinuation Syndrome

A relatively recently-recognized (last ~10 years) but testable phenomenon: a patient who abruptly stops or misses doses of an antidepressant — SSRIs included, not exclusive to any one class — presents with flu-like symptoms, dizziness, "brain zaps," irritability, and sensory disturbances. Management: restart the antidepressant and taper slowly. If restarting isn't appropriate (e.g. concern for serotonin syndrome), manage supportively (hydration, rest) instead. Higher risk with short half-life agents like paroxetine; lower risk with long half-life agents like fluoxetine.

☐ Class-Wide Black Box Warning

Antidepressants as a class carry a black box warning for increased suicidality — this applies to children, adolescents, and young adults broadly, not just one specific drug. Worth keeping in mind any time you're weighing starting antidepressant therapy in a younger patient.

Memory Hook — the suffix rule (RS)
-PINE → weight gain, diabetes, metabolic syndrome, sedation  ·  -DONE → EPS, prolactin, NMS  ·  -PIP- → akathisia but overall well tolerated (kid-friendly)  ·  -RIP- → metabolically neutral, "watered-down DONE." Watch Dr. Smith's video: "The PINES, the DONES, two PIPs, and a RIP". Also: NMS + EPS = DONEs; metabolic catastrophe = PINEs.
Memory Hook — the potency see-saw
HIGH potency (haloperidol, fluphenazine) = high EPS/NMS/prolactin, low anticholinergic/sedation/hypotension. LOW potency (chlorpromazine) = the reverse: high anticholinergic + sedation + α-block hypotension, low EPS. The see-saw never balances: what you gain on one side you pay on the other. (Rare for both: agranulocytosis, broken thermoregulation → heat stroke/hypothermia.)
