Mechanism
Not fully clear; best evidence: alters intracellular second messengers — notably inhibits inositol triphosphate (IP3) → stabilized neuronal activity.
Indications
Classic euphoric mania; blocks relapse into acute mania. ANTISUICIDAL in bipolar patients (baseline suicide risk ≥15%) — yet lethal in overdose. "Quite a quandary."
Acute side effects
Nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, FINE hand tremor, sedation, muscle weakness, edema, weight gain, dry mouth.
Chronic side effects learn the bolded ones
  • Polyuria/polydipsia → nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (ADH antagonist; reversible)
  • Hypothyroidism + goiter (autoimmune; ♀ > ♂)
  • Acne · psoriasis · leukocytosis (reversible)
  • Teratogenesis — EBSTEIN ANOMALY (1st-trimester organogenesis) boards
Toxicity (narrow window!)
Lethargy, ataxia, slurred speech, tinnitus, severe N/V, COARSE tremor (fine = therapeutic, coarse = toxic), arrhythmias, hypotension, seizures, delirium, coma, death.
Levels & labs
Therapeutic 0.8–1.2 (some say 1.5) mEq/L; toxicity often >1.8 but possible lower. Before starting + serially: Na⁺, Ca²⁺, K⁺, Cr, urinalysis, CBC, EKG, thyroid panel w/ TSH.
The co-star
valproic acid (Depakote)
  • MOA: ↑ GABA availability (anticonvulsant). Mania efficacy ≈ lithium; also epilepsy, migraine prophylaxis.
  • SEs: somnolence, dizziness, GI upset, diplopia, ataxia, rash, weight gain, alopecia, prolonged bleeding, PCOS (esp. women w/ epilepsy).
  • ⛔ Rare FATAL HEPATOTOXICITY (monitor LFTs), pancreatitis, NEURAL TUBE DEFECTS (spina bifida — birth control!); monitor CBC (granulo-/thrombocytopenia).
  • Levels: 40–150 mcg/mL, serially.
The interaction machine
carbamazepine (Tegretol)
  • For mania when Li/valproate fail or aren't tolerated; less used than either.
  • SEs: drowsiness, dizziness, blurred vision, N/V, rash, hyponatremia.
  • ⛔ Leukopenia/AGRANULOCYTOSIS — monitor CBC + levels.
  • Inactivates OCPs; CYP3A4 inducer AND AUTOinducer — chews itself up → dose must rise early or symptoms resurge.
  • Cousin: oxcarbazepine (Trileptal) — same idea minus the interactions; RS prefers it in psych patients.
The slow-motion drug
lamotrigine (Lamictal)
  • MOA: ↓ glutamate release → membrane stabilization. Loved for bipolar depressive episodes.
  • Transient SEs: photosensitivity, headache, GI upset, dizziness, ataxia.
  • ⛔ STEVENS-JOHNSON SYNDROME (~1/1,200): titrate 25 mg every TWO weeks; rash starts on mucosa → stop immediately; off ≥1 week at >25 mg → restart titration from 25 mg.
  • Valproate doubles lamotrigine levels → titrate TWICE as slowly — THE lamotrigine DDI. know it
LO 088Mood & Mood Stabilizers◐ Partly covered

Understand the side-effects of lithium, and how they are each treated

Answer

Lithium's core chronic side effects, per the LiTHIUM mnemonic and lecture additions, are hypothyroidism (or hyperthyroidism), Ebstein anomaly, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, fine tremor, acne, weight gain, and mild hypercalcemia. Overall lithium toxicity (level >1.2, presenting with nausea, diarrhea, altered mental status, severe tremor, ataxia, slurred speech, hyperreflexia, polyuria, and seizure) is treated by stopping lithium and hydrating the patient, with dialysis considered in severe cases. Because lithium is reabsorbed via the same renal sodium channels as salt at the proximal tubule, thiazide diuretics, spironolactone, triamterene, ACE-inhibitors like enalapril, and NSAIDs raise lithium levels, while acetazolamide, theophylline, aminophylline, and caffeine lower them, and metronidazole specifically increases nephrotoxicity risk. Prescreening before starting lithium includes CBC, renal function, thyroid function, serum HCG, and ECG, and lithium is avoided as first-line in pregnancy (Ebstein anomaly risk) or significant renal impairment; the drug list adds precise toxicity thresholds (therapeutic 0.8-1.2, toxic above 1.8) and the mechanistic note that lithium is renally handled like sodium, which explains the diabetes-insipidus and Ebstein-anomaly risks.

🧠
Memory hook · Lithium follows saltReabsorbed on the kidney's sodium channels → anything that makes you keep sodium keeps lithium: thiazides, NSAIDs, ACE-inhibitors, dehydration. Levels: 0.8–1.2 treats · >1.2 toxic (coarse tremor, ataxia, AMS, seizure) · severe → dialysis. LiTHIUM: Low Thyroid, Heart (Ebstein), Insipidus, Unwanted Movements.

Missing from your notesSpecific treatments for lithium's individual chronic side effects (hypothyroidism, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, tremor) remain absent from every source.

Pulled from: Mood Disorders · Eating Disorders · Psychiatry Key Drug List 2026

☐ Lithium Toxicity — level >1.2

Nausea, diarrhea, altered mental status, severe tremor, ataxia, slurred speech, hyperreflexia, polyuria, seizure. Treatment: stop lithium, hydrate; consider dialysis in severe cases.

🔑 First Aid Mnemonic — LiTHIUM

Low Thyroid (hypothyroidism) · Heart (Ebstein anomaly — right atrial enlargement, displaced tricuspid valve) · Insipidus (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus) · Unwanted Movements (tremor)

Lecture additions: fine tremor, hypo- or hyperthyroidism, acne, weight gain, mild hypercalcemia.

Increases lithium levelsDecreases lithium levelsAffects lithium's toxicity
Thiazide diuretics, spironolactone, triamterene, enalapril (ACE-I), NSAIDsAcetazolamide, theophylline, aminophylline, caffeineMetronidazole ↑nephrotoxicity · Neuroleptics may induce neurotoxicity · Antiarrhythmics potentiate cardiac effects of digoxin/quinidine
🧸 ELI5 — Lithium & the Kidney

Lithium hitches a ride on the same sodium channels the kidney uses to reabsorb salt at the PCT. Anything that makes the kidney hang onto more sodium (thiazides, low-salt states, NSAIDs, ACE-inhibitors) makes it hang onto more lithium too — levels climb. Anything that flushes sodium out (caffeine, theophylline) flushes lithium out with it — levels drop.

🔑 Default Answer, With Four Exceptions

On an exam, if a stem describes bipolar disorder and gives you a plain drug list with no other clues, lithium is the default first-line answer. Four things should make you look elsewhere: (1) pregnancy (Ebstein anomaly), (2) significant renal impairment (lithium is a salt excreted essentially unchanged by the kidney, so impaired renal clearance is a direct problem), (3) cardiac conduction disease such as an existing heart block (lithium can further affect cardiac conduction), and (4) difficult-to-manage thyroid disease (lithium can push a patient hypo- or hyperthyroid).

Prescreening: CBC, renal function (creatinine, BUN), thyroid function (TSH, free T3/T4), serum HCG in women, ECG, screen for co-administered NSAIDs/ACE-inhibitors/thiazides, and check for preexisting renal disease/CHF/arrhythmia.

⚠️ Also Avoid: Lithium

Lithium requires a stable, consistent hydration state to avoid nephrotoxicity. Purging behaviors (especially self-induced vomiting) create a dehydration-prone state that raises the risk of lithium toxicity.

Deadliest fact?
lithium
Narrow window: 0.8–1.2 therapeutic, >1.8 toxic. Coarse tremor = toxicity. Antisuicidal yet lethal in OD. Ebstein anomaly in 1st trimester. Kidney (DI) + thyroid labs.
Memory Hook — "LITHIUM hits kidney & thyroid"
Lithium is a small cation the kidney handles like sodium — so it wrecks the kidney's water handling (DI) and rides Na⁺ balance (dehydration/thiazides → toxicity). Ebstein: “Lithium floats the tricuspid down” — atrialized right ventricle. Fine→coarse tremor = your built-in level meter.
Mechanism
Not fully clear; best evidence: alters intracellular second messengers — notably inhibits inositol triphosphate (IP3) → stabilized neuronal activity.
Indications
Classic euphoric mania; blocks relapse into acute mania. ANTISUICIDAL in bipolar patients (baseline suicide risk ≥15%) — yet lethal in overdose. "Quite a quandary."

Nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, FINE hand tremor, sedation, muscle weakness, edema, weight gain, dry mouth.
Chronic side effects learn the bolded ones
  • Polyuria/polydipsia → nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (ADH antagonist; reversible)
  • Hypothyroidism + goiter (autoimmune; ♀ > ♂)
  • Acne · psoriasis · leukocytosis (reversible)
  • Teratogenesis — EBSTEIN ANOMALY (1st-trimester organogenesis) boards
Toxicity (narrow window!)
Lethargy, ataxia, slurred speech, tinnitus, severe N/V, COARSE tremor (fine = therapeutic, coarse = toxic), arrhythmias, hypotension, seizures, delirium, coma, death.

Therapeutic 0.8–1.2 (some say 1.5) mEq/L; toxicity often >1.8 but possible lower. Before starting + serially: Na⁺, Ca²⁺, K⁺, Cr, urinalysis, CBC, EKG, thyroid panel w/ TSH.
LO 089Mood & Mood Stabilizers✓ In your notes

Understand the treatment and assessment of a borderline personality disordered patient, including treatment planning, understanding that these patients are often misdiagnosed as having bipolar disorder

Answer

Borderline personality disorder is frequently misdiagnosed as bipolar disorder because both involve dramatic mood swings, but the key differentiator is timing rather than symptom content: bipolar mood episodes last days to weeks and shift relatively independently of triggers, whereas BPD's affective instability is rapid, reactive to interpersonal triggers, and embedded in a broader pattern of unstable relationships and self-image. BPD sits in Cluster B (dramatic/erratic, with a genetic link to mood and substance use disorders) alongside antisocial, histrionic, and narcissistic personality disorders. Unlike every other personality disorder, where psychotherapy (typically CBT) is primary and there is no FDA-approved medication for any of the ten, BPD is the treatment exception: dialectical behavior therapy (DBT), created by Marsha Linehan specifically for BPD, is first-line and built around four skills modules -- core mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation, and interpersonal effectiveness -- mapped onto BPD's core dysregulation domains, with the exam shortcut being "choose DBT if it's an option, otherwise CBT." Pharmacotherapy evidence in BPD is weak but polypharmacy is still common, with quetiapine showing a notable (82%) response rate on the Zanarini Rating Scale for BPD. In treatment planning around self-harm risk, a safety contract made without a careful, documented suicide assessment offers no legal protection -- it is the assessment itself, not the contract, that protects the physician.

🧠
Memory hook · Borderline flips in minutes with a trigger; bipolar shifts in weeks without oneBPD mood swings are rapid + interpersonally triggered; bipolar episodes last days-to-weeks and don't need a trigger. DBT's four modules = MEDI: Mindfulness, Emotion regulation, Distress tolerance, Interpersonal effectiveness.

Pulled from: Introduction to Therapy · Personality Disorders · Mood Disorders · Legal Psychiatric Medicine

Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) ⭐ HY

Created by Marsha Linehan, PhD — for borderline personality disorder
StructureA skills-based, manualized treatment built around 4 modules: emotion regulation, mindfulness, distress tolerance, and interpersonal effectiveness.
OriginLinehan developed DBT partly from her own lived experience with BPD — she has spoken publicly (including in a well-known New York Times profile) about how the treatment reflects what helped her.
Also used forAdapted well beyond BPD to many other conditions, but the BPD connection is the one to remember for exams.
🧠
The exam shortcut: DBT (dialectical behavioral therapy) is specifically for borderline PD; CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) is the mainstay for the other 9 personality disorders. Dr. Smith's exact framing: "DBT is a form of CBT, so if the exam has DBT as an option, choose it; if not, choose CBT." In other words, DBT beats CBT as an answer choice only when the vignette is specifically about BPD — otherwise, default to CBT.

DBT's four modules, each targeting one of BPD's core dysregulation domains: core mindfulness (cognitive dysregulation), distress tolerance (impulsiveness), emotion regulation (labile moods/emotions), interpersonal effectiveness (interpersonal chaos)

⚠️
The single most important fact in this entire topic: THERE IS NO FDA-APPROVED MEDICATION TO TREAT ANY PERSONALITY DISORDER — not one, for any of the 10. Any medication used is off-label, targeting symptoms that arise from the disorder (depression, paranoia, irritability, affective instability) rather than the core disorder itself.
Evidence for pharmacotherapy in BPD specifically is weak, but polypharmacy is extremely common in practice
>50% of BPD patients are on 2 psychotropic medications
>11% are on 5+ psychotropics simultaneously
Quetiapine has shown significant improvement on the Zanarini Rating Scale for BPD — 82% response vs. 48% placebo
APA recommends medication as adjunctive treatment for specific symptom domains: affective instability, impulsivity, psychosis, self-destructive behavior — never as monotherapy for the disorder itself
Question 6
Which feature most reliably distinguishes borderline personality disorder's affective instability from a bipolar mood episode?
A. BPD mood shifts always last several weeks, just like bipolar episodes
B. BPD mood shifts are rapid and reactive to interpersonal triggers, embedded in a broader pattern of relationship instability and identity disturbance
C. Bipolar disorder is ego-syntonic, while BPD is ego-dystonic
D. Only bipolar disorder can involve self-harm
Answer: B. BPD and bipolar disorder are classically confused in both directions (Section 07) — the key discriminator is that BPD's mood instability is fast (hours), reactive to specific relational triggers (fear of abandonment, a perceived slight), and sits inside a broader personality pattern, rather than existing as an autonomous, sustained mood episode.

Cluster A — "Weird"

Odd/eccentric · genetic link to schizophrenia

Paranoid, Schizoid, Schizotypal — poor social relationships, no true psychosis.

Cluster B — "Wild"

Dramatic/erratic · genetic link to mood & substance use disorders

Antisocial, Borderline, Histrionic, Narcissistic — Borderline is the one paired with DBT and with splitting.

Cluster C — "Worried"

Anxious/fearful · genetic link to anxiety disorders

Avoidant, Obsessive-compulsive (personality type), Dependent.

🔑 High-Yield Differentiator — Timing, Not Symptoms

Bipolar disorder and borderline personality disorder (BPD) both involve dramatic mood swings, and mixing them up is a classic exam trap and a real clinical pitfall (a lot of BPD gets misdiagnosed as bipolar over a patient's lifetime). The fastest way to split them:

Bipolar DisorderBorderline Personality Disorder
Episode durationWeeks to monthsHours to a few days at most
FrequencyRoughly every couple of years (≥4 episodes/year = rapid cycling, and that's already considered remarkable)Multiple mood swings within a single day or week — far more frequent than "rapid cycling" bipolar
SleepDecreased need for sleep is a core, reliable feature of mania/hypomaniaSleep is typically not disrupted in the same characteristic way

In short: how long does the episode last, and how often does it happen? That question alone resolves most of the confusion.

Contracting for Safety ≠ Protection

A safety contract made in the absence of a careful suicide assessment offers no legal protection. It's the assessment — not the contract — that protects the physician.

Family Promises ≠ Your Responsibility Transferred

A family's promise to monitor a patient does not absolve the physician of responsibility if the patient is suicidal and no assessment/intervention occurred.

Cluster A — "Weird, Wacky"

Odd & eccentric
MembersParanoid, Schizoid, Schizotypal

Cluster B — "Wild"

Dramatic, emotional, erratic
MembersAntisocial, Borderline, Histrionic, Narcissistic

Cluster C — "Worried"

Anxious & fearful
MembersDependent, Obsessive-Compulsive, Avoidant

Borderline PD

Instability in self-image and interpersonal relationships
Name origin"Borderline" of depression and psychosis — patients oscillate near the boundary between mood dysregulation and brief, stress-related psychotic phenomena (see micropsychotic episodes below).
Core pictureImpulsivity that may lead to self-harm (drug abuse, promiscuity, cutting), and relationships that are polarized — black/white, love/hate — in a pattern of extreme idealization followed by devaluation. Drives frantic efforts to avoid real or imagined abandonment, alongside chronic feelings of emptiness.
F > MRoughly 3:1 — the one Cluster B disorder that's female-predominant.
📌
BPD belongs on your differential for psychosis: under acute stress, patients can have brief micropsychotic episodes and dissociative symptoms — doing things during a period of time they later don't remember. This is the literal meaning behind the name "borderline": the patient sits at the boundary between mood dysregulation and transient psychosis.

LO 090Legal, Ethics & Risk✓ In your notes

Understand the treatment of acute depression in a patient with active or past suicidal ideation

Answer

The gold standard for depression is therapy plus medication combined, and severe depression sometimes warrants brief hospitalization even without acute safety risk. Suicide risk is stratified with the SAD PERSONS mnemonic (Sex-male, Age, Depression, Previous attempt as the single highest-risk factor, Ethanol/drug use, Rational thinking loss/psychosis, Sickness, Organized plan, No social support, Stated future intent); women attempt suicide more often while men die by suicide more often via more lethal means, and protective factors include effective treatment of comorbidities and strong social/family connectedness. For depression with active suicidality specifically, electroconvulsive therapy is indicated as the gold standard for affective disorders, used for severe/refractory depression, peripartum depression, depression with psychotic features, catatonia, and acute suicidality, after baseline labs, EKG, and head imaging. Legally, a safety contract made without a careful, documented suicide assessment offers no protection to the physician -- it is the assessment itself, not the contract, that matters in a malpractice claim, and a family's promise to monitor the patient does not transfer that responsibility.

🧠
Memory hook · SAD PERSONS, and who dies vs. who triesSex(M) · Age · Depression · Previous attempt (#1 risk factor) · Ethanol · Rational-thought loss · Sickness · Organized plan · No support · Stated intent. Women attempt more; men die more (lethal means). The documented assessment (C-SSRS) is your legal shield — a safety contract without one protects no one.
🧠
Memory hook · ECT: the gold standard nobody remembersIndicated for severe/refractory depression, acute suicidality, psychotic depression, catatonia, peripartum depression. Overall depression gold standard = therapy + medication together.

Pulled from: Mood Disorders · Legal Psychiatric Medicine

ECT

First used 1939 · Gold standard for affective disorders

Indicated for severe/refractory depression, peripartum depression, psychotic features, catatonia, acute suicidality. Screening: basic labs, EKG, head imaging. Induces a seizure, changing neurotransmitter state and possibly improving plasticity. Adverse effects: disorientation, headache, partial antero-/retrograde amnesia (usually resolves in 6 months). No absolute contraindications — safe in pregnancy and older adults.

Esketamine / Ketamine

NMDA receptor antagonist; also opioid receptor & AMPA (glutamate)

Indicated for treatment-resistant, severe unipolar MDD without psychotic features, after failure/declined other indicated treatments. Adverse effects: dissociation, psychotomimetic effects, ↑ systolic/diastolic BP and pulse (usually resolve quickly). Liable to abuse/addiction/diversion; associated with neurotoxicity and bladder dysfunction with chronic misuse.

TMS

Transcranial magnetic stimulation

Magnetic frequency applied to specific brain regions to induce change. Non-invasive, but requires frequent treatments.

DBS

Deep brain stimulation

Implanted electrode targeting a specific brain region. Invasive, implanted device.

VNS

Vagal nerve stimulation

Pulse generator, most commonly on the left vagal nerve. Invasive; unclear efficacy for depression. Lecture flagged TMS/DBS/VNS as "not high yield" overall — know they exist and roughly what they are, don't over-invest.

🔑 Gold Standards to Memorize Verbatim

Gold standard for depression: therapy + medication combined. Gold standard for mania: lithium. Severe depression sometimes warrants brief hospitalization even without acute safety risk — not because outpatient treatment can't work, but because an inpatient setting allows faster titration and augmentation of medications than a normal 4–6 week outpatient follow-up cadence would allow.

🔑 First Aid Mnemonic — SAD PERSONS are more likely to die from suicide
  • Sex (male)
  • Age (young adult or older adult)
  • Depression
  • Previous attempt — highest risk factor
  • Ethanol or drug use
  • Rational thinking loss (psychosis)
  • Sickness (medical illness)
  • Organized plan
  • No spouse or social support
  • Stated future intent
⚠️ Know the Asymmetry

Women attempt suicide more often; men die by suicide more often (more lethal means — firearms are the most common method in the US, and access to guns increases risk of death). Protective factors: effective treatment of comorbidities, strong social/family/community connectedness, cultural or religious beliefs favoring self-preservation, and good problem-solving skills.

🩺 Four Treatments Specifically Linked to Reduced Suicide Risk

Most psychiatric treatments target symptoms broadly. A small, specific list is called out in the literature as having direct evidence for reducing death by suicide — worth memorizing as its own group because exams like to test exactly this kind of "unique fact":

  • ECT
  • Esketamine
  • Lithium
  • Clozapine (Clozaril)

Depression and bipolar disorder both carry increased suicide risk — this was emphasized on the very first slide of the lecture for a reason. Risk assessment and mitigation is described as one of the central, defining activities of psychiatric practice — not just a topic, but the actual day-to-day work. Risk mitigation breaks down into two categories: risk of an untimely death (suicide), and risk of dangerous behavior more broadly (violence toward others, reckless spending, or other consequential impulsive acts — relevant in mania as well as depression).

Walking Through a New Depression Presentation

Presentation: A 25-year-old presents with 2 weeks of insomnia, suicidal ideation, social withdrawal, poor self-care, and decreased energy — a first episode, no major recent life stressor.

What else do you want to know? Family history of depression, current medications/substances (to rule out a substance-induced cause), and medical history. In this vignette the patient was recently diagnosed with a thyroid disorder — on an exam, the SIG E CAPS picture is usually still enough to call this MDD even with that medical comorbidity in the background, though clinically you'd want to investigate further before settling on a primary psychiatric diagnosis. Always ask about safety planning — is there a plan to self-harm, and is anything currently keeping the patient safe? This is one of the most consistently tested (and clinically vital) questions in the whole system.

Treatment ladder, step by step:

  1. SSRI or SNRI first. Decide between them using comorbidities: a pain syndrome or ADHD-like presentation nudges toward an SNRI; a "garden variety" presentation stays with an SSRI. Mechanism for both: block the transporter, flood the synapse with the relevant neurotransmitter(s) — takes several weeks to show full effect.
  2. If the SSRI/SNRI doesn't help → move to a TCA. Mechanism: multiple rings binding many receptors, more side effects, and true overdose danger.
  3. If the TCA causes an intolerable side effect (say, excessive sedation) → the "Others" category — bupropion, mirtazapine, trazodone — chosen based on which side-effect profile fits the patient and any specific indication (e.g. smoking cessation for bupropion).
  4. If that still doesn't work → an MAOI, reserved this late in the sequence because of the dietary restrictions and interaction burden.
  5. If pharmacotherapy across all classes fails → ECT first, then TMS and/or ketamine/esketamine.

Contracting for Safety ≠ Protection

A safety contract made in the absence of a careful suicide assessment offers no legal protection. It's the assessment — not the contract — that protects the physician.

Family Promises ≠ Your Responsibility Transferred

A family's promise to monitor a patient does not absolve the physician of responsibility if the patient is suicidal and no assessment/intervention occurred.
Question 5
A patient dies by suicide two weeks after a routine outpatient visit at which no suicidal ideation was elicited or documented as absent. The family sues for malpractice. What is most likely to determine the outcome?
A. Whether the psychiatrist could have predicted the suicide with certainty
B. Whether there is documentation of an ongoing, adequate suicide risk assessment showing no indication of suicidality
C. Whether the patient had signed a safety contract
D. Whether the patient's family had agreed to monitor them
Answer: B. Documentation of ongoing assessment is the actual legal defense (Section 07) — physicians aren't required to predict the future, only to act on the foreseeable. A safety contract (C) or family monitoring (D) alone offers no legal protection without a real underlying assessment.
🆘
Just attempted suicide, risk of further self-harm remains high? Next step: involuntarily hospitalize the patient.
LO 091Substance Use & Tox✓ In your notes

Understand the treatment of acute substance intoxication in the emergency setting, including which benzos are safe to use in acute alcohol withdrawal protocols in patients with liver impairment

Answer

The three "LOT" benzodiazepines - lorazepam, oxazepam, and temazepam - undergo direct Phase II glucuronidation without hepatic Phase I oxidation, making them the safest benzodiazepines for alcohol withdrawal in patients with liver impairment (or in the elderly), since there is no oxidative step for age- or disease-related hepatic decline to disrupt. Alcohol withdrawal is treated aggressively because it carries the highest death risk of any withdrawal syndrome, via seizures and delirium tremens, progressing from anxiety/tremor/insomnia to autonomic hyperactivity, seizures, and DTs. Clonidine can blunt the sympathetic surge of withdrawal but is not adequate monotherapy because it does not prevent withdrawal seizures, so standard management instead uses a taper or long-acting, cross-tolerant benzodiazepines.

🧠
Memory hook · Liver's bad? Use the parking LOTLorazepam, Oxazepam, Temazepam skip Phase I hepatic oxidation (straight to glucuronidation) — the safe benzos in liver failure and the elderly.

Pulled from: Anxiety, OCD & Trauma-Related Disorders · Addiction & Non-Clinical Drug Use

📌
LOT drugs undergo Phase II glucuronidation directly, skipping Phase I oxidation entirely — no extensive hepatic metabolism. This makes them the ideal benzos for elderly patients or those with liver impairment, since there's no oxidative step to be disrupted by age- or disease-related hepatic decline.
Question 1
An elderly patient with mild hepatic impairment needs a benzodiazepine for severe anxiety. Which agent is the safest choice given his liver function?
A. Diazepam
B. Alprazolam
C. Lorazepam
D. Chlordiazepoxide
Answer: C. Lorazepam is one of the "LOT" benzodiazepines (Lorazepam, Oxazepam, Temazepam) that undergo direct Phase II glucuronidation rather than hepatic Phase I oxidation — making them the preferred choice in liver impairment or in elderly patients generally (Section 16).
⚠️ Alcohol Withdrawal Is the Most Dangerous Withdrawal in This Lecture

Relative to opioids, stimulants, or nicotine, alcohol withdrawal carries the highest risk of death — via seizures and delirium tremens. This is why alcohol detox is managed so much more aggressively than, say, opioid withdrawal.

🍷

Intoxication

  • Emotional lability, slurred speech
  • Ataxia, blackouts, coma
🚨

Withdrawal

  • Anxiety, tremor, insomnia
  • Severe: autonomic hyperactivity, seizures, delirium tremens

Clonidine ⭐ HY

α2-adrenergic agonist

Inhibits noradrenergic outflow, blunting the sympathetic surge common to withdrawal from most drugs of abuse — including partially blocking opioid withdrawal symptoms and easing nicotine withdrawal. Not a monotherapy: does not adequately prevent withdrawal seizures, so it is not recommended alone for CNS depressant (alcohol/benzo/barbiturate) withdrawal.

  1. Taper — gradually decrease the dose to ease withdrawal symptoms; often used as a harm-reduction bridge in patients not yet ready for full treatment (nicotine patches/lozenges, methadone for opioids, cross-tolerant benzodiazepines for alcohol).
  2. Long-acting, cross-tolerant substitutes — a drug in the same class with a longer half-life smooths the withdrawal course (e.g., long-acting benzodiazepines for alcohol withdrawal).
  3. Symptomatic support — an α2-adrenergic agonist (clonidine) blunts the sympathetic hyperactivity common to nearly every withdrawal syndrome.
🧠
Withdrawal from a downer produces upper effects — and vice versa (this exact logic reappears in the antipsychotic pharmacology unit). Benzo withdrawal syndrome: anxiety, insomnia, tremulousness, nausea/vomiting, transient hallucinations, and — critically — seizures are possible with acute withdrawal, so taper slowly. Adverse cognitive effects of ongoing use include difficulty focusing attention, memory impairment, and confusion.

High-yield timeline: minor symptoms first, then hallucinosis/seizures around 24–48h, DTs peak ~day 2 and can last up to a week

LO 092Child & Adolescent◐ Partly covered

Understand the treatment of ADHD in a child who has failed trials of stimulants, including side-effects, contraindications, and unique warnings of subsequent medication options to be tried, focusing especially on non-stimulant medications

Answer

For a child who has failed stimulant trials, second-line non-stimulant options include atomoxetine (Strattera), a selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor dosed 1-1.4 mg/kg that helps about 60% of patients versus an 80-90% response rate for stimulants, with GI upset, sedation, dizziness, and irritability as its side effects; viloxazine (Qelbree), a 5-HT2C partial agonist with added norepinephrine reuptake inhibition; and the alpha-2 agonists clonidine and guanfacine, which calm hyperactivity and bodily symptoms but do not improve attention itself. The child psychiatry lecture's ADHD medication table separately lists alpha-2 agonists as a distinct class alongside first-line long-acting stimulants (methylphenidate ER, dexmethylphenidate ER, mixed amphetamine salts, lisdexamfetamine), and notes that stimulants, while effective in about 80-90% of children, can cause appetite suppression, sleep effects, GI/headache symptoms, a growth effect of roughly 2-3 cm, cardiovascular effects warranting a review of systems, and possible tics especially with amphetamines; the lecture also stresses that a full ADHD diagnosis (not just failure to listen) requires symptom duration, onset before age 12, functional impairment, and symptoms in at least two settings before medication decisions are made.

🧠
Memory hook · Stimulants 80–90% ; atomoxetine 60% ; alpha-2s calm the body, not the focusFirst-line: long-acting stimulants (methylphenidate ER, lisdexamfetamine…) — watch appetite, sleep, ~2–3 cm growth, tics (esp. amphetamines), CV review. Failed stimulants → atomoxetine (NRI, 1–1.4 mg/kg) or viloxazine; guanfacine/clonidine for hyperactivity. Diagnosis needs: >6 months, onset <12, impairment, ≥2 settings.

Board cue

Do not diagnose ADHD from "doesn't listen" alone. AnKing flags this as inattention, not hearing loss, but the full diagnosis needs duration, age, impairment, and at least two settings.

LO 093Neurocognitive & AMS◐ Partly covered

Understand the treatment of agitation and sequela secondary to dementia-related conditions

Answer

Antipsychotics carry an FDA boxed warning for increased mortality (roughly 1.6-1.7x over a 10-week trial, about 4.5% vs. placebo) when used for dementia-related psychosis in elderly patients, and trazodone is noted as a sometimes-used, lower-risk off-label alternative for agitation/insomnia in dementia, though it carries its own risks (orthostasis, priapism) and is not itself an antipsychotic; the drug list separately names risperidone as a specific atypical antipsychotic used for dementia-related agitation in the elderly. For acute agitation generally, the "B-52" PRN IM cocktail (Benadryl 50mg + Haldol 5mg + Ativan 2mg) combines a benzodiazepine and antipsychotic to rapidly control psychotic/manic agitation, with the diphenhydramine component pre-empting EPS; IM olanzapine is an alternative monotherapy, but should not be combined with a benzodiazepine within 2 hours due to additive cardiorespiratory depression. Clinicians should recognize escalating verbal (louder, oppositional, foul language) and behavioral (inability to sit still, fierce eye contact, fist-making, jaw tensing) warning signs before agitation peaks, and watch for repeated antipsychotic dosing producing rigidity, diaphoresis, and hyperthermia, which signals NMS rather than simple dystonia or parkinsonism.

🧠
Memory hook · Antipsychotics in dementia carry a boxed warning≈1.6–1.7× mortality in elderly dementia-related psychosis. Lower-risk moves: trazodone off-label (orthostasis, priapism), risperidone when an antipsychotic is truly needed. IM olanzapine: never within 2 h of a benzo (cardiorespiratory depression).
◐
Missing from your notesNon-pharmacologic first-line measures, explicit lower-anticholinergic-burden reasoning, and geriatric dosing adjustments for dementia-related agitation are still absent; the neuroanatomy lecture does not cover dementia at all.

Pulled from: Psychotic Disorders & Antipsychotic Pharmacology · Anxiety, OCD & Trauma-Related Disorders · Psychiatry Key Drug List 2026

⚠️
Boxed Warning — Increased Mortality in Elderly Patients with Dementia-Related Psychosis. Elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis treated with antipsychotics (largely atypicals, in the pivotal trials) have a 1.6–1.7× increased risk of death vs. placebo over a 10-week trial window (~4.5% vs. ~2.6% mortality). Deaths were mostly cardiovascular (heart failure, sudden death) or infectious (pneumonia). No antipsychotic is FDA-approved for dementia-related psychosis — this is an off-label, risk-laden use.
💊
Trazodone comment: the lecture flags trazodone as a comparison point in this population — it's sometimes used off-label for agitation/insomnia in dementia as a lower-risk alternative to antipsychotics, though it carries its own risks (orthostasis, priapism) and isn't itself an antipsychotic.

What Is a "B-52"? ⭐ HY

A PRN IM "cocktail" for acute psychotic agitation
RecipeBenadryl 50 mg + Haldol 5 mg + Ativan 2 mg, given IM.
RationaleCombining a benzodiazepine + antipsychotic works fastest for decreasing psychotic aggression and acute manic symptoms; the Benadryl/Cogentin component pre-empts acute dystonia from the Haldol.
UsePRN only — not a scheduled/standing combination.

Other acute-agitation options

  • ▸ Chlorpromazine / diphenhydramine combination
  • ▸ Olanzapine IM — effective monotherapy alternative (note: avoid combining IM olanzapine with a benzodiazepine within 2 hours, per Section 18, due to additive cardiorespiratory depression risk)
  • ▸ Other de-escalation and pharmacologic strategies per clinical context
📌
Watch for this vignette pattern: a patient given repeated "B-52" doses who develops rigidity, diaphoresis, and hyperthermia is showing neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS), not simple dystonia or parkinsonism — the fever and diaphoresis are the tip-off. First step is to stop the antipsychotic and provide supportive care/cooling; dantrolene or bromocriptine may be added in severe cases. This exact scenario is Case D in Section 28.

Verbal (becoming louder, demanding/menacing content, foul language, oppositional tone, put-downs) and behavioral (inability to sit still, fierce eye contact, making fists, muscle tightness, tensing jaws) warning signs

The "cocktail"/"B-52": Haldol + Ativan + Cogentin or Benadryl, so named for the classic 50mg Benadryl + 5mg Haldol + 2mg Ativan combination

Clinical uses of benzodiazepines

Psychosis & mania — benzos + antipsychotics help manage agitation
Sleep disorders — some benzos (e.g., temazepam) help, also useful for parasomnias; "Z-drugs" are a related non-benzo option
Substance-induced disorders — benzos reduce anxiety during cocaine/hallucinogen/amphetamine intoxication, and reduce agitation during withdrawal from alcohol, anxiolytics, sedative-hypnotics, cocaine, amphetamines
Epilepsy — benzos (diazepam rectal/IM, clonazepam) treat seizures and status epilepticus
MSK disorders — e.g., dystonia; benzos help with muscle stiffness/relaxation
Uncomfortable procedures — MRI, endoscopy, etc.: PRN benzo prophylaxis
DONE · high potency
risperidone (Risperdal)
  • Uses: schizophrenia, bipolar I/mania, Tourette, autism behavioral dysregulation, dementia in the elderly.
  • At high doses behaves like a high-potency typical: EPS, akathisia, ↑prolactin (gynecomastia, amenorrhea, galactorrhea).
  • Forms: PO, M-tab, Consta (2-wk LAI, fading), Perseris (4-wk SQ, 2019), Uzedy ER-SQ — 2026: also approved for bipolar I maintenance (mono or + Li/valproate).

LO 094Substance Use & Tox◐ Partly covered

Understand the treatment of alcohol withdrawal in the setting of medical co-morbidities, and stat the various alcohol withdrawal protocols, such as CIWA, and the drugs which are hepatically metabolized

Answer

Alcohol withdrawal carries the highest death risk of any withdrawal syndrome, via seizures and delirium tremens, with a high-yield timeline of minor symptoms first, then hallucinosis/seizures around 24-48 hours, and DTs peaking around day 2 and lasting up to a week. Detoxification uses long-acting benzodiazepines with cross-reactivity at GABA-A (diazepam, lorazepam, chlordiazepoxide), dosed either on a fixed schedule or symptom-triggered; for patients with hepatic impairment, the "LOT" benzodiazepines (lorazepam, oxazepam, temazepam) are preferred because they undergo direct Phase II glucuronidation rather than Phase I hepatic oxidation. Clonidine, an alpha-2 agonist, blunts the sympathetic/autonomic surge of withdrawal but is not adequate monotherapy because it does not prevent withdrawal seizures. Comorbidity mapping shows alcohol touches nearly every psychiatric diagnostic category (psychotic, bipolar, depressive, anxiety, OCD-related, sleep, sexual dysfunction, delirium, neurocognitive) with both intoxication and withdrawal specifiers.

🧠
Memory hook · Shakes by breakfast, seizures by tomorrow, DTs by day 2Alcohol withdrawal timeline: tremor/anxiety first → hallucinosis & seizures at 24–48 h → delirium tremens peaks around day 2 (can last a week). It's the only withdrawal that kills — treat with long-acting benzos (diazepam, chlordiazepoxide); clonidine alone never prevents the seizures.

⚠️ Alcohol Withdrawal Is the Most Dangerous Withdrawal in This Lecture

Relative to opioids, stimulants, or nicotine, alcohol withdrawal carries the highest risk of death — via seizures and delirium tremens. This is why alcohol detox is managed so much more aggressively than, say, opioid withdrawal.

High-yield timeline: minor symptoms first, then hallucinosis/seizures around 24–48h, DTs peak ~day 2 and can last up to a week

Long-acting benzodiazepines (diazepam, lorazepam, chlordiazepoxide) are preferred — their cross-reactivity at GABA-A smooths the taper and their active metabolites give a lower chance of recurrent withdrawal or seizures. Two dosing strategies: symptom-triggered (dose only once significant symptoms appear) vs. front-loaded (proactively substitute sedation regardless of symptoms, then taper).

Clonidine ⭐ HY

α2-adrenergic agonist

Inhibits noradrenergic outflow, blunting the sympathetic surge common to withdrawal from most drugs of abuse — including partially blocking opioid withdrawal symptoms and easing nicotine withdrawal. Not a monotherapy: does not adequately prevent withdrawal seizures, so it is not recommended alone for CNS depressant (alcohol/benzo/barbiturate) withdrawal.

Q: Why is clonidine not recommended as monotherapy for withdrawal from CNS depressants (alcohol, benzodiazepines, barbiturates)?

Answer

Clonidine blunts sympathetic outflow but does not adequately prevent withdrawal seizures — a life-threatening feature specific to depressant withdrawal (via GABA-A/NMDA rebound) that an α2-agonist doesn't address.

  1. Taper — gradually decrease the dose to ease withdrawal symptoms; often used as a harm-reduction bridge in patients not yet ready for full treatment (nicotine patches/lozenges, methadone for opioids, cross-tolerant benzodiazepines for alcohol).
  2. Long-acting, cross-tolerant substitutes — a drug in the same class with a longer half-life smooths the withdrawal course (e.g., long-acting benzodiazepines for alcohol withdrawal).
  3. Symptomatic support — an α2-adrenergic agonist (clonidine) blunts the sympathetic hyperactivity common to nearly every withdrawal syndrome.

  • Severe: autonomic hyperactivity, seizures, delirium tremens

LO 095Psychosis & Antipsychotics✓ In your notes

Understand the treatment of side-effects resulting from the use of antipsychotic medications based upon their mechanisms of action and the underlying pathophysiology of schizophrenia. Be sure to note contraindications and second-line therapies when first-line therapies are not indicated

Answer

Antipsychotic side effects map directly onto which receptors each agent blocks off-target: D2 blockade above the ~78-80% striatal occupancy threshold produces EPS, and the class runs on a "match the receptor to the side effect" framework (H1, M1, alpha-1, etc.). Clozapine and olanzapine carry the broadest metabolic risk footprint (weight gain, T2DM, dyslipidemia; clozapine adds myocarditis, agranulocytosis, and dose-related seizure risk), while aripiprazole (a D2 partial agonist) and ziprasidone are comparatively metabolically clean, though ziprasidone still carries QT risk and risperidone causes frequent hyperprolactinemia. High-potency typicals like haloperidol carry the strongest EPS/akathisia signal; when a drug-induced movement disorder occurs, the first step is to stop the antipsychotic rather than add an anticholinergic or switch potency. Clozapine is reserved as the second-line/escalation option because it is uniquely superior for treatment-resistant disease and is the only antipsychotic FDA-approved to reduce recurrent suicidal behavior in schizophrenia/schizoaffective disorder, despite its higher side-effect burden.

🧠
Memory hook · -PINEs pack Pounds; -DONEs Drain prolactinOlanzapine/clozapine/quetiapine → weight, sedation, metabolic syndrome. Risperidone → prolactin; ziprasidone → QTc. Cleanest metabolics: aripiprazole (D2 partial agonist), ziprasidone, lurasidone, cariprazine. Clozapine = last-resort gold standard: agranulocytosis (ANC checks), seizures, myocarditis — and the only drug FDA-approved to cut suicidality in schizophrenia.

Pulled from: Psychotic Disorders & Antipsychotic Pharmacology

A classic "match the receptor to the side effect" framework — every antipsychotic side effect maps back to a specific receptor being blocked somewhere it isn't wanted:

Clozapine: absent EPS/hyperprolactinemia, high weight gain/sedation, unique agranulocytosis/seizure risk. Olanzapine: rare EPS, high weight gain/sedation. Risperidone: frequent hyperprolactinemia. Ziprasidone: low weight gain, notable QTc. Aripiprazole: absent hyperprolactinemia, rare weight gain — the cleanest metabolic profile of the group.

Section 21

There is a narrow window between antipsychotic efficacy and excessive side effects. The striatal D2 receptor occupancy threshold to reduce psychosis with minimal EPS is approximately 78–80%; crossing above the EPS threshold produces motor side effects.

Hypothetical thresholds for antipsychotic drug effects — the therapeutic window sits between the ~70% "antipsychotic effect" line and the ~80% "EPS" line

Cardiovascular risk table — clozapine and olanzapine carry the broadest metabolic risk footprint (weight gain + T2DM + dyslipidemia, clozapine adds myocarditis/pericarditis); quetiapine and risperidone add QT risk; ziprasidone is comparatively metabolically clean but still carries QT risk

Risk of hyperglycemia/weight gain/hyperlipidemia (metabolic syndrome): lowest → Abilify, Geodon, Latuda < Asenapine, Fanapt, Invega, Risperdal, Seroquel < highest → Zyprexa, Clozaril. Diabetes risk in psychiatric patients runs 2–4× the general population baseline; 2004 consensus guidance says switch to Geodon or Abilify if diabetes/weight gain develops.

Aripiprazole — D2 partial agonist (stabilizes rather than fully blocking dopamine tone)
Ziprasidone — modulates norepinephrine/serotonin in addition to D2/5-HT2A antagonism
Clozapine — serotonergic predominance (5-HT2A:D2 ratio ~10:1); broadest receptor footprint of any agent
F.2
The antipsychotic agent this patient is most likely taking is:
A. Risperidone
B. Chlorpromazine
C. Olanzapine
D. Haloperidol
E. Clozapine
Answer: D. Haloperidol is the classic high-potency typical with the strongest EPS/akathisia signal among these five options (Section 13/25) — clozapine (E) essentially never causes EPS, and olanzapine (C) is comparatively low-EPS.
G.2
This side effect is best treated by initially:
A. Change to a low-potency typical antipsychotic
B. Add an anxiolytic
C. Add an antidepressant
D. Add an anticonvulsant
E. Add a beta blocker
F. Stop the antipsychotic
G. Add an anticholinergic
Answer: F. Per the drug-induced movement disorder management table (Section 16), the initial step for tardive dyskinesia is withdrawal or dose reduction of the offending agent (often with a switch to an atypical). Anticholinergics (G) do not help TD the way they help dystonia/pseudoparkinsonism — TD can worsen or fail to improve with anticholinergics since it isn't driven by the same relative-cholinergic-excess mechanism.

Antisuicidal Property

AnswerClozapine is the only antipsychotic FDA-approved to reduce the risk of recurrent suicidal behavior in schizophrenia/schizoaffective disorder.
QuizThe only other psychiatric drug with demonstrated antisuicidal properties is lithium.

"Susie Q"

AnswerQuetiapine (Seroquel) — nicknamed "Susie Q." Frequently prescribed off-label for sleep due to its H1-antihistamine sedation, which is not an evidence-based or recommended use given its metabolic and anticholinergic-adjacent risk profile.

LO 096Mood & Mood Stabilizers✓ In your notes

Understand the treatment protocols for bipolar I and II disorder, as well as the concept of a drug-induced bipolar disorder and how to manage that

Answer

Bipolar I requires only a single manic episode (depression optional), while Bipolar II requires at least one hypomanic plus one major depressive episode - if a manic episode ever occurs, even in a patient with an established Bipolar II history, the diagnosis converts to Bipolar I. Lithium, valproate, and carbamazepine are first-line for acute mania/mixed episodes but only backup for bipolar depression, whereas lamotrigine is weak for mania but first-line for bipolar depression; lithium is the gold standard overall because it is the only agent effective across mania, depression, and maintenance. Second-generation antipsychotics carry FDA approval across bipolar mania, depression, and maintenance, often combined with a mood stabilizer, and antidepressants must be used cautiously (alongside a mood stabilizer) because they can worsen depression or precipitate mania. A classic drug-induced/"unmasked" bipolar presentation is a patient started on an antidepressant for a depressive episode who returns manic roughly 3-6 weeks later; new mania should also prompt screening for organic/substance causes (steroids, stimulants, levodopa, cocaine, hyperthyroidism, Cushing disease, MS, stroke, CNS infection) before concluding it is primary bipolar disorder.

🧠
Memory hook · Opposite jobs: mania drugs vs. depression drugsAcute mania: lithium, valproate, carbamazepine (+ antipsychotics). Bipolar depression: lamotrigine first-line (weak for mania). Lithium is the gold standard — the only agent that covers mania, depression, AND maintenance. Antidepressants only ever ride with a mood stabilizer.

Pulled from: Mood Disorders · Psychotic Disorders & Antipsychotic Pharmacology

🧸 ELI5 — Bipolar I vs. II

Bipolar I is the "I mean it" version: one manic episode is all it takes to earn the diagnosis — depression is optional. Bipolar II needs a two-ingredient recipe: at least one hypomanic episode and at least one major depressive episode, but if a manic episode ever shows up, the diagnosis is immediately promoted to Bipolar I. Hypomania is Bipolar II's ceiling — it can never break through into full mania and stay Bipolar II.

Q: A patient with a well-documented history of Bipolar II disorder has a manic episode requiring hospitalization. What is the new diagnosis?

Answer

Bipolar I disorder. A single manic episode is sufficient to diagnose Bipolar I, and Bipolar II is defined by the absence of any lifetime manic episode. The occurrence of mania supersedes the prior Bipolar II diagnosis.

Bipolar I (full mania possible) vs. Bipolar II (ceiling = hypomania) over time

🧸 ELI5 — Reading This Table

Notice the pattern: lithium, valproate, and carbamazepine are the go-to's for mania but are only backup options for bipolar depression. Lamotrigine flips that completely — it's weak for mania but is actually a first-line choice for bipolar depression. Different phases genuinely need different drugs — memorizing "one mood stabilizer treats bipolar" will get you the wrong answer on a phase-specific question.

🔑 Why Lithium Is "The" Gold Standard

Lithium is the only agent effective across all three domains — mania, depression, and maintenance — which is exactly why it's considered the gold standard for bipolar disorder as a whole, not just for breaking an acute manic episode.

⚠️ Antidepressant Caution in Bipolar

Fluoxetine's own bipolar-context side effect profile flags worsening of depression and manic episodes in bipolar patients, plus increased suicidality in children — antidepressants in bipolar disorder are generally used cautiously and typically alongside a mood stabilizer, never as unopposed monotherapy. The one FDA-approved exception is a fluoxetine + olanzapine combination — but that's a maintenance-phase indication, not a treatment for acute mania. You would not start an acutely manic patient on fluoxetine.

"Unmasking" a Bipolar Disorder with an Antidepressant

Presentation: A patient presents with a depressive episode and is started on an antidepressant, as is standard practice. Several weeks later (roughly 3–6 weeks), they return looking manic.

What happened? This is a classic "unmasking" scenario — the patient likely had an underlying, not-yet-diagnosed bipolar disorder the whole time. Since <5% of bipolar patients present with mania as their very first episode, a first depressive episode can't rule bipolar disorder out, and an antidepressant can push a susceptible patient into their first manic (or hypomanic) episode.

Bipolar I or Bipolar II? Judge by extremity, not just presence of symptoms. Example given in lecture: if the patient is shopping more than usual and can comfortably afford it, that impulsivity looks more like hypomania. If the patient buys three cars and a Lamborghini and bankrupts themselves, that degree of impaired judgment and consequence is mania — pushing the diagnosis to Bipolar I.

How do you know it's "real" bipolar and not just a substance-induced mood disorder? There's no perfect test — it's a clinical judgment call. The strongest supporting clue is the typical pattern: most people with bipolar disorder present with a depressive episode first, and the age of first manic-episode onset for that small subset clusters in the 18–20 range, consistent with the overall epidemiology of the disorder.

⚠️ Rule Out First

Before diagnosing a primary manic/hypomanic episode, screen for organic causes: medications (steroids, amphetamines, levodopa, corticosteroids), substances (cocaine, hallucinogens, caffeine), and medical conditions (Cushing disease, hyperthyroidism, MS, stroke, CNS infection). This is the same "rule out substance/medical cause first" logic that applies to every mood disorder.

Many atypicals carry FDA-approved indications well beyond schizophrenia — acute bipolar mania, bipolar depression, bipolar maintenance, pediatric bipolar/schizophrenia, irritability in autism, and adjunctive therapy for MDD.

FDA-approved indications beyond psychosis (as of 10/2015) — note aripiprazole's uniquely broad label (bipolar, pediatric bipolar/schizophrenia, autism irritability, MDD adjunct) and quetiapine's bipolar depression approval

LO 097Mood & Mood Stabilizers✓ In your notes

Understand the unique pharmacology properties of each class of antidepressants and the associated side effects

Answer

SSRIs block the serotonin transporter (SERT); side effects (GI distress, sexual dysfunction, SIADH) appear immediately because the transporter is blocked right away, while the antidepressant effect takes roughly 4-6 weeks as postsynaptic receptors adapt/upregulate. TCAs bind SERT/NET plus alpha-1, M1, H1, and sodium channels, producing sedation (histamine) and anticholinergic effects and making them risky in overdose via cardiac sodium-channel effects; tertiary TCAs (amitriptyline, imipramine, clomipramine, doxepin) cause more side effects than secondary TCAs (nortriptyline). Among the atypical antidepressants, bupropion (an NDRI) inhibits NE and DA reuptake, causes tachycardia, weight loss, and lowers seizure threshold (black box warning), but is less likely to cause sexual dysfunction and helps with smoking cessation; mirtazapine is an alpha-2 antagonist.

🧠
Memory hook · Side effects sprint; benefits run a marathonSSRIs block SERT on day one (GI upset, sexual dysfunction start immediately) but postsynaptic receptors need 4–6 weeks to adapt before mood lifts. Fluoxetine = the long goodbye: longest half-life (2–4 days), no discontinuation syndrome, potent 2D6 inhibitor.

Pulled from: Mood Disorders

🩺 Why Side Effects Show Up Before the Antidepressant Effect

The moment an SSRI is started, the transporter is blocked and serotonin floods the synapse immediately — but the postsynaptic receptors need time (roughly 4–6 weeks) to adapt/upregulate before the person actually feels less depressed. Side effects, though, don't need that adaptation: the flood of serotonin hits GI receptors, sexual-function pathways, and other targets right away, which is why side effects typically appear in the first 1–2 weeks, well before the therapeutic benefit does. This is also why severely depressed patients are sometimes hospitalized — not because outpatient treatment can't work, but because it allows faster dose titration and augmentation than waiting out a 4–6 week outpatient trial. And it's why "I started the antidepressant two weeks ago and don't feel different" is expected, not a treatment failure.

MOA: Three-ringed structure binding multiple receptors — mostly SERT and NET, but also alpha-1, M1, H1, and sodium channels. The "off-target" binding likely contributes to benefit, but is also responsible for the long side effect list.

Side effects: Sedation (histamine), anticholinergic effects — tachycardia, dry mouth (muscarinic), hypotension (alpha), QTc prolongation/arrhythmia (multiple targets).

⬆️

Tertiary TCAs — bigger = more side effects

  • Amitriptyline — pain
  • Imipramine — pain, IBS, nocturnal enuresis
  • Clomipramine — OCD, panic disorder
  • Doxepin — bipolar depression, insomnia
⬇️

Secondary TCAs — smaller = fewer side effects

  • Nortriptyline — cyclic vomiting, IBS, pain, migraine, smoking cessation (off-label)
  • Desipramine — ADHD

Bupropion (NDRI)

Inhibits NE + DA reuptake

Structurally close to a stimulant. Side effects: tachycardia, weight loss, ↓seizure threshold (black box warning). Less likely to cause sexual dysfunction. Helps smoking cessation; can be paired with naltrexone for weight loss.

Mirtazapine

Alpha-2 antagonist, 5-HT2/5-HT3 antagonist, H1 antagonist

Side effects: weight gain, sedation, ↑appetite, dry mouth — less likely sexual side effects. Useful when sedation/appetite gain is desirable (underweight, insomnia).

Trazodone

Blocks 5-HT2, alpha-1, H1

Mainly used for insomnia (high doses needed for antidepressant effect). Side effects: sedation, priapism (erection >4h — surgical emergency, from alpha blockade).

Nefazodone

Serotonin blocker

Liver toxicity — rarely prescribed today.

Vilazodone

5-HT reuptake inhibition + 5-HT1A partial agonist

Low yield beyond MOA — not frequently used or tested.

Vortioxetine

5-HT reuptake inhibition + 5-HT1A agonist + 5-HT3 antagonist

Low yield beyond MOA — not frequently used or tested.

Side effects to know: GI distress, sexual dysfunction, SIADH, serotonin syndrome (see below).

LO 098Mood & Mood Stabilizers✓ In your notes

Understand the various adjustment disorders, as well as the timeline for this condition and a differential diagnosis for an adjustment disorder

Answer

Adjustment disorders are the most commonly encountered psychiatric disorders overall (up to 50% of stroke/post-CABG patients and 43% of pediatric ER visits), and DSM-5 reclassified them from their own DSM-IV-TR chapter into the trauma/stressor-related disorders section. They sit on a continuum between normal adjustment and a fully diagnosable, sustained mental disorder, and are subtyped as with depressed mood, with anxiety, with mixed anxiety and depressed mood, with disturbance of conduct, with mixed disturbance of emotions and conduct, or unspecified. The key differential point versus PTSD/acute stress disorder is that adjustment disorder can follow any identifiable stressor (not necessarily traumatic/life-threatening), whereas PTSD/ASD require a traumatic stressor; acute stress disorder itself lasts 3 days to 1 month post-trauma and converts to PTSD if symptoms persist beyond a month, which is the timeline that distinguishes these related diagnoses.

🧠
Memory hook · The stressor clockAny stressor → symptoms within 3 months = adjustment disorder (gone by 6 months after stressor ends). Traumatic stressor → 3 days–1 month = acute stress disorder; past 1 month = PTSD.
🧠
Memory hook · 3 days to 1 month, then it changes its nameAcute stress disorder = PTSD's symptoms on a compressed clock (3 d–1 mo post-trauma); persist past 1 month → PTSD. Adjustment disorder follows ANY stressor (not necessarily traumatic) within 3 months.

Pulled from: Anxiety, OCD & Trauma-Related Disorders

📌
Prevalence superlative: adjustment disorders are the most commonly encountered psychiatric disorders of all.

Much like PTSD, these are extremely common — Dr. Smith: "please learn this section well." Reclassified from their own DSM-IV-TR chapter into the trauma/stressor-related disorders section in DSM-5.

Adjustment disorder sits on a continuum — between normal adjustment and a fully diagnosable, sustained mental disorder

With depressed mood · with anxiety · with mixed anxiety and depressed mood · with disturbance of conduct · with mixed disturbance of emotions and conduct · unspecified

Prevalence by setting — notably 50% in stroke/post-CABG patients and up to 43% of pediatric ER visits

Question 10
Which of the following best distinguishes adjustment disorder from PTSD/acute stress disorder?
A. Adjustment disorder requires a life-threatening stressor, while PTSD does not
B. Adjustment disorder can follow any identifiable stressor (not necessarily traumatic/life-threatening), while PTSD/ASD specifically require exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence
C. Adjustment disorder has no duration criteria at all
D. PTSD does not require any identifiable stressor
Answer: B. Adjustment disorder's stressor can be almost anything with real functional impact — a divorce, a job loss, a diagnosis (Section 11) — whereas PTSD/ASD require Criterion A trauma exposure specifically. Adjustment disorder does have timing rules (within 3 months of the stressor, resolving within 6 months after it ends) — option C is incorrect.
🧠
The one-line summary: acute stress disorder is "the anxiety-related equivalent of brief psychotic disorder" — essentially "early" or "acute" PTSD. Must last 3 days to 1 month; past 1 month, the diagnosis converts to PTSD. Same underlying symptom domains as PTSD, just on a compressed timeline.
Question 9
A woman develops classic PTSD-type symptoms (intrusive memories, avoidance, hyperarousal) beginning 2 weeks after witnessing a mass shooting. Given the timeline, what is the correct diagnosis?
A. Post-traumatic stress disorder
B. Acute stress disorder
C. Adjustment disorder with anxiety
D. Brief psychotic disorder
Answer: B. Symptoms within the 3-day-to-1-month window are, by definition, acute stress disorder — "the anxiety-related equivalent of brief psychotic disorder" (Section 11). Only if symptoms persist beyond 1 month does the diagnosis convert to PTSD.

Criteria A–E — note the two timing rules in A and E

LO 099Anxiety, OCD & Trauma✓ In your notes

Understand the workup and differential diagnosis of primary and secondary causes which may include a panic attack - like presentation

Answer

Panic attacks are not exclusive to panic disorder - the same attack phenomenology occurs in GAD, OCD, social phobia, and other conditions - so a panic attack alone does not equal panic disorder, which additionally requires at least one of three maladaptive behavioral changes (persistent concern about more attacks, worry about implications, or significant behavior change). Because panic attacks produce real cardiorespiratory symptoms (chest pain, SOB, palpitations) that can mimic organic disease, the workup must rule out MI, angina, PE, and arrhythmia before labeling something "just a panic attack." A broader secondary-cause table follows the same rule-out-organic-first principle used across psychiatry, covering cardiovascular/respiratory causes (arrhythmias, COPD, mitral valve prolapse, hyperventilation), endocrine causes (hyperthyroidism, hypoglycemia, pheochromocytoma, Cushing's), and others. A panic attack itself is a discrete period of intense fear/discomfort peaking within 30 seconds to 5 minutes with at least 4 of 13 characteristic DSM symptoms.

🧠
Memory hook · Rule out the four killers before calling it panicMI, angina, PE, arrhythmia — panic attacks peak in 30 s–5 min with ≥4 of 13 symptoms and mimic all of them. Acute tx: break the breath-anxiety spiral; PRN benzo (alprazolam).

Pulled from: Anxiety, OCD & Trauma-Related Disorders

A panic attack isn't exclusive to panic disorder — the same attack phenomenology shows up as a feature of several other conditions.

Panic attacks can occur in panic disorder (frequent, spontaneous), GAD (constant worry + physical symptoms), OCD (excessive repetitive thoughts/behaviors), social phobia (embarrassment/humiliation in social situations), and PTSD (thoughts/experiences of a horrible event)

🚨
Critical clinical caution: panic attacks have real cardiorespiratory features (chest pain, SOB, palpitations) that can be difficult to distinguish from genuine organic disease. Always rule out MI, angina, PE, arrhythmia, etc. before labeling something "just a panic attack" and discharging the patient. Duration is also a clue: a true panic attack peaks and resolves within minutes — if symptoms persist 20–30+ minutes, or if the heart rate is extremely high (e.g., ~250 bpm), think medical (e.g., SVT) rather than psychiatric. Patients often misremember the duration as much longer than it actually was because the surge of anxiety distorts their sense of time.
CategoryExamples
Cardiovascular/respiratoryArrhythmias, COPD, hyperdynamic β-adrenergic state, hypertension, hyperventilation, mitral valve prolapse (high correlation to panic), MI, angina, pulmonary embolus
EndocrineCushing's disease, hyperthyroidism, hypothyroidism, hypoglycemia, pheochromocytoma
GIColitis, IBS, peptic ulcer, ulcerative colitis
PsychiatricDepression, mania, psychosis/schizophrenia, delirium/dementia
MiscellaneousEpilepsy, migraine, pain, pernicious anemia, porphyria
CNS depressant-relatedAlcohol/anxiolytic/narcotic withdrawal, nicotine withdrawal
Prescription stimulant-typeAlbuterol, amphetamines, corticosteroids, levothyroxine, methylphenidate, digitalis toxicity
Non-prescriptionCaffeine, ephedrine, pseudoephedrine, phenylephrine, anticholinergic toxicity

To diagnose panic disorder, you need a panic attack plus at least 1 of 3 maladaptive behavioral changes.

DSM-5 panic disorder criteria — persistent concern about additional attacks, worry about implications/consequences, or significant behavior change related to the attacks

A discrete period of intense fear/discomfort with an abrupt onset, peaking within 30 seconds to 5 minutes, during which the patient experiences ≥4 of 13 DSM symptoms.

The 13 panic-attack symptoms — palpitations, sweating, trembling, SOB, choking, chest pain, nausea, dizziness/faintness, derealization/depersonalization, fear of losing control, fear of dying, paresthesias, chills/hot flushes

Exactly the same principle as psychotic disorders: before diagnosing a primary anxiety disorder, exclude medical and substance causes. Naming convention: "anxiety disorder due to [hyperthyroidism]" or "substance/medication-induced anxiety disorder due to [heroin]." This distinction also matters for realistic, situationally-appropriate fear — e.g., a patient with severe COPD who feels anxious because they genuinely can't breathe isn't having a primary anxiety disorder; that's a rational response to reality (though if the anxiety becomes disproportionate to the medical threat, it could be coded "anxiety disorder due to COPD exacerbation").

Common medical disorders (left) and drugs (right) associated with anxiety/insomnia symptoms

📋
Video case: patient describes going to the ED "feeling like I was dying from a heart attack" — sweating, trouble catching his breath, heart "pounding" and feeling like it would "explode out of my chest," a sensation he likens to being alone in the woods and feeling chased. EKG was normal; the episode lasted ~12–15 minutes. This meets criteria for a panic attack (≥4 of 13 symptoms, duration in the normal range) — but without evidence yet of the added behavioral-change criterion, it's a panic attack, not necessarily panic disorder.

Epidemiology: 1:2 male:female ratio; 2% prevalence. Panic disorder = panic attacks (defined below) plus additional behavioral criteria — a panic attack alone does not equal panic disorder.

LO 100Child & Adolescent◐ Partly covered

Understand the workup of a patient with suspected ADHD to rule out medical co-morbidities such as the seizure spectrum disorders

Answer

The general diagnostic principle applied throughout psychiatry is to rule out an intentional/malingered cause, a substance etiology (intoxication, withdrawal, medication side effect), and an underlying general medical condition before concluding a primary psychiatric diagnosis such as ADHD. The child psychiatry lecture reinforces that ADHD requires several inattentive or hyperactive/impulsive symptoms for more than 6 months, onset before age 12, functional impairment, and symptoms in at least two settings (home, school, friends), and specifically warns not to diagnose ADHD from "doesn't listen" alone, but it does not address seizure-spectrum screening.

🧠
Memory hook · The universal rule-out ladderFaking? → Substance (intox/withdrawal/med)? → Medical? → only then primary psychiatric. AMS culprits from this course: serotonin syndrome (3 A's), lithium >1.2, valproate hyperammonemia (check ammonia at any dose).
🧠
Memory hook · Stimulants 80–90% ; atomoxetine 60% ; alpha-2s calm the body, not the focusFirst-line: long-acting stimulants (methylphenidate ER, lisdexamfetamine…) — watch appetite, sleep, ~2–3 cm growth, tics (esp. amphetamines), CV review. Failed stimulants → atomoxetine (NRI, 1–1.4 mg/kg) or viloxazine; guanfacine/clonidine for hyperactivity. Diagnosis needs: >6 months, onset <12, impairment, ≥2 settings.
◐
Missing from your notesNo source discusses EEG, seizure-spectrum screening, or absence-seizure mimics of inattention in the ADHD workup.

Pulled from: Introduction & History of Psychiatry

  1. Rule out Malingering & Factitious DisorderIs the person intentionally producing/feigning symptoms (for external gain, or for the sick role itself)?
  2. Rule out a substance etiologyIntoxication, withdrawal, or a medication side effect mimicking psychiatric illness.
  3. Rule out an etiological medical conditionE.g. thyroid disease, a CNS lesion, a metabolic derangement.
  4. — Only now can you diagnose a primary mental illness —
  5. Determine the specific primary psychiatric disorder(s)Pick from the DSM-5-TR's 365 diagnoses.
  6. Differentiate Adjustment Disorder from residual Other Specified/Unspecified categories
  7. Establish the boundary with no mental disorderDistress that doesn't rise to a diagnosable condition.
🚨
The single most important idea in this whole section: always rule out a drug-induced or general medical cause before diagnosing a primary psychiatric illness. Medical/drug causes are treatable with medical therapy; a missed medical cause treated as "just depression" with antidepressant after antidepressant is a classic, avoidable failure mode.

Understand what rating scales are used for which childhood psychiatric disorders

Answer

For ADHD, home-and-school collateral rating scales are used: Vanderbilt parent and teacher forms, the Conners scale, and the ADHD Rating Scale, reflecting the requirement that symptoms be documented across at least two settings. For autism spectrum disorder, screening tools include M-CHAT-R/F, ESAT, ITC, POSI, and SCQ, applied per current AAP/CDC guidance at general developmental screening (9, 18, and 30 months) and autism-specific screening (18 and 24 months); the ADOS is the gold-standard formal evaluation tool but is not required for a clinical diagnosis of ASD, which remains a clinical diagnosis based on persistent deficits in social communication/reciprocity and restricted/repetitive behavior.

🧠
Memory hook · Two settings → two VanderbiltsADHD scales: Vanderbilt (parent + teacher), Conners, ADHD-RS — because symptoms must show in ≥2 settings. Autism: M-CHAT-R/F screening (18 & 24 mo); ADOS is the gold-standard eval but NOT required — ASD stays a clinical diagnosis.

Missing from your notesNo scale for childhood depression (e.g., CDRS) or OCD (e.g., CY-BOCS) is named in either source.

Collateral

Home plus school

Use Vanderbilt parent/teacher forms, Conners, ADHD Rating Scale, and direct school history when possible.

ASD domainCore criteriaClinical cluesTests/treatment Social communication Persistent deficits in reciprocity, nonverbal communication, and relationships. Poor eye contact, limited back-and-forth conversation, reduced sharing of interests, difficulty with peers. Screen with M-CHAT-R/F, ESAT, ITC, POSI, SCQ; ADOS is gold-standard formal evaluation but not required for clinical diagnosis. Practice Question
An 11-year-old has restricted interests, poor eye contact, and repetitive object manipulation. Which testing statement is best?
A. ADOS is required before autism can be diagnosed clinically.
B. ADOS is a gold-standard formal evaluation, but ASD remains a clinical diagnosis.
C. M-CHAT is the formal adult diagnostic test.
Answer: B. ADOS can support evaluation, especially in trained/research settings, but the diagnosis is clinical.
Screening

Current AAP/CDC guidance supports developmental screening at 9, 18, and 30 months and autism-specific screening at 18 and 24 months. AnKing reinforces the 18-month and 2-year autism screen.

LO 102Cross-Cutting Pharm✓ In your notes

Understand which antidepressant medications can be used together (synergistic) and which would warrant caution or be contraindicated

Answer

Two or more antidepressants combined, or an antidepressant plus a second-generation antipsychotic (or plus a mood stabilizer, or thyroid augmentation), are standard augmentation strategies for treatment-resistant depression and are generally considered acceptable combinations. Combining agents across different serotonin-raising mechanisms (SSRIs, SNRIs, MAOIs, TCAs, tramadol, triptans, linezolid, and others) risks serotonin syndrome - the real danger is crossing mechanisms, not simply stacking more serotonergic drugs. MAOIs carry a separate tyramine-interaction risk (hypertensive crisis from aged cheese, cured meats) that is distinct from serotonin syndrome and requires careful washout when switching to or from other antidepressants. Bupropion is contraindicated in patients with active or recent bulimia or anorexia nervosa due to a black-box seizure-risk warning tied to purging-related electrolyte disturbances.

🧠
Memory hook · Fast & twitchy vs. slow & stiffSerotonin syndrome: hours after a serotonergic change — the 3 A's (↑Activity: clonus/hyperreflexia · Autonomic instability · AMS). Tx: benzos → cyproheptadine. NMS: days after an antipsychotic — lead-pipe rigidity + hyporeflexia + fever + ↑CK. First move: STOP the drug. The danger is crossing mechanisms, not stacking the same one; 2-week MAOI washout.

Pulled from: Mood Disorders · Eating Disorders · Anxiety, OCD & Trauma-Related Disorders

🩺 Augmentation Options (Treatment-Resistant Depression)

Treatment-resistant = no benefit from multiple adequate medication trials. Augmentation strategies: 2 antidepressants combined, antidepressant + second-generation antipsychotic, antidepressant + mood stabilizer, or antidepressant + thyroid augmentation.

Q: A patient has failed three adequate antidepressant trials. Her psychiatrist adds low-dose second-generation antipsychotic to her current SSRI. What is this strategy called, and name two alternative augmentation strategies.

Answer

This is augmentation for treatment-resistant depression. Alternatives: combining two antidepressants, antidepressant + mood stabilizer, antidepressant + thyroid hormone, or moving to an interventional approach like ECT or ketamine/esketamine.

Q: A patient on venlafaxine develops a headache, palpitations, and diastolic BP of 128 after eating aged cheese and salami at a family dinner. What happened, and what's the mechanism?

Answer

Careful — this scenario is actually the classic MAOI + tyramine hypertensive crisis presentation, not venlafaxine's typical picture. Tyramine displaces NE at the synapse, causing excess sympathetic stimulation. Treatment is phentolamine. (Venlafaxine itself can raise BP at higher doses via NE reuptake inhibition, but the tyramine-food trigger specifically implicates MAOI use.)

☐ US Boxed Warning

Bupropion (Wellbutrin) — Contraindicated in active or recent Bulimia (or Anorexia) Nervosa. Carries a black box warning for increased seizure risk in this population, related to the electrolyte disturbances and dehydration that purging behaviors cause. On an exam, if a stem describes bulimia and asks "which medication is contraindicated," bupropion is almost always the answer.

LO 103Child & Adolescent✓ In your notes

Understanding common first-line medications in childhood depression

Answer

The general depression treatment framework by severity uses lifestyle changes and monitoring for mild disease, therapy or an antidepressant for moderate disease, and combined therapy plus an antidepressant for severe disease, with therapy plus medication considered the overall gold standard for depression. Antidepressants as a class carry an FDA black box warning for increased suicidality that applies broadly to children, adolescents, and young adults rather than to one specific drug, which must be weighed any time antidepressant therapy is started in a younger patient. The drug list names fluoxetine (Prozac) explicitly as the drug of choice ('DOC') in childhood depression/anxiety, citing its ~2-week half-life, weekly-dosing option for poor compliance, and absence of a discontinuation syndrome, directly supplying the missing FDA-recognized pediatric first-line antidepressant.

🧠
Memory hook · Kids' depression = fluoxetine, full stopThe DOC for childhood depression/anxiety: ~2-week half-life forgives missed doses, no discontinuation syndrome. All antidepressants carry the black-box suicidality warning in youth — counsel, don't avoid.

Pulled from: Mood Disorders · Psychiatry Key Drug List 2026

☐ Class-Wide Black Box Warning

Antidepressants as a class carry a black box warning for increased suicidality — this applies to children, adolescents, and young adults broadly, not just one specific drug. Worth keeping in mind any time you're weighing starting antidepressant therapy in a younger patient.

🔑 Gold Standards to Memorize Verbatim

Gold standard for depression: therapy + medication combined. Gold standard for mania: lithium. Severe depression sometimes warrants brief hospitalization even without acute safety risk — not because outpatient treatment can't work, but because an inpatient setting allows faster titration and augmentation of medications than a normal 4–6 week outpatient follow-up cadence would allow.

Black Box — pediatric suicidality (know the nuance)
BBW: increased suicidality in children. But when the 2007 warning slowed prescribing, adolescent suicidality went UP; with renewed SSRI use it is no longer increasing. Most psychiatrists consider them safe in children — monitor every depressed patient for SI regardless of treatment.
