Understanding one of the giants of Child Psychiatry's stages of development

Answer

Freud's psychosexual development theory proposes fixed childhood stages tied to an erogenous zone at each age: oral (birth-1 year, mouth - fixation produces behaviors like nail-biting, smoking, or overeating) and anal (1-3 years, bowel/bladder - retentive fixation produces obsessive neatness, expulsive fixation produces recklessness and disorganization), among further stages. The framework was the historical entry point for explaining psychosexual and personality development and still underlies some diagnostic terminology in use today (e.g., "anal-retentive"), though it has been largely superseded as a clinical model and is considered lower-yield for modern exams than descriptive DSM-5 criteria.

🧠
Memory hook · Old Age People Love GrapesOral (0–1: nail-biting, smoking, overeating fixations) → Anal (1–3: retentive = neat-freak, expulsive = reckless) → Phallic → Latency → Genital.

Pulled from: Sexual, Somatoform & Dissociative Disorders · Introduction to Therapy

StageAge RangeErogenous ZoneFixation Consequences
OralBirth – 1 yearMouthAggressive: chewing gum, biting pencil ends. Passive: smoking, overeating, oral sexual practices.
Anal1–3 yearsBowel & bladderRetentive: obsessively organized or excessively neat. Expulsive: reckless, careless, defiant, disorganized.
Phallic3–6 yearsGenitaliaOedipus complex (boys) / Electra complex (girls); theorized site of superego development.
Latency6 – pubertyDormant sexual feelingsSexual unfulfillment.
GenitalPuberty – deathSexual interests matureFrigidity, impotence, unsatisfactory relationships.

The historical entry point for how sexual disorders were originally conceptualized — largely superseded as a clinical framework, but still worth knowing as background, and it still explains some of the older diagnostic terminology you'll encounter (e.g., "anal-retentive" from Section 12 of the personality disorders unit traces directly back to this model).

The 5 psychosexual stages, their erogenous zones, and the theorized consequences of getting "fixated" at each one

Freud's developmental stages (oral, anal, etc.) are also historically important but lower-yield for modern exams — good to recognize, not worth memorizing in depth.

SchoolKey concepts
FreudianConscious vs. unconscious; the id, ego, and superego
JungianIndividuation; extraversion vs. introversion
Kleinian (Melanie Klein)Child/adolescent analysis; object relations — extended adult-focused theory downward to children

Understanding the difference between Oppositional Defiant Disorder and Conduct Disorder

Answer

Oppositional defiant disorder centers on a pattern of angry/irritable mood, argumentative/defiant behavior, or vindictiveness, requiring at least 4 such symptoms occurring at least once weekly for at least 6 months, with severity graded by number of settings involved (mild = one setting, moderate = two, severe = three or more); first-line management is parent management training/CBT (using antecedent-behavior-consequence skills) and treating any comorbid ADHD. Conduct disorder is a more severe escalation defined by persistent violation of the basic rights of others or of major age-appropriate societal rules, spanning aggression, destruction of property, theft/deceit, and serious rule violations. Both conditions frequently co-occur with ADHD, learning disabilities, anxiety, and tic disorders, and treating comorbid ADHD can reduce disruptive symptoms in some children.

🧠
Memory hook · ODD argues with adults; CD violates their rightsODD: ≥4 angry/defiant/vindictive symptoms, ≥1×/week, ≥6 months; severity = # of settings (1/2/3+). Tx: parent management training + treat the ADHD. CD: aggression, property destruction, theft/deceit, serious rule-breaking — and the required childhood prequel to antisocial PD.
◐
Missing from your notesConduct disorder's own severity grading and childhood-onset versus adolescent-onset specifiers are not given in the retrieved text.

Pulled from: Child & Adolescent Psychiatry

Vignette #4 - "I do not have to do that"

ODD centers on angry/irritable mood, argumentative/defiant behavior, or vindictiveness. Conduct disorder escalates into violation of rights or major rules: aggression, destruction, theft/deceit, and serious rule violations.

DisorderCore ruleSeverity/timingManagement Oppositional defiant disorder At least 4 symptoms from angry/irritable mood, argumentative/defiant behavior, or vindictiveness. At least once weekly for at least 6 months; mild = one setting, moderate = two, severe = three or more. Parent management training and CBT; treat comorbid ADHD. AnKing: PTBM/PMT uses antecedent-behavior-consequence skills. Conduct disorder Persistent violation of basic rights or major age-appropriate societal norms. Aggression to people/animals, destruction of property, deceitfulness/theft, serious rule violations. Behavioral/parent interventions; medication only targets outbursts, not the diagnosis itself. Tourette disorder Multiple motor tics plus at least one vocal tic, not necessarily concurrently. Waxing/waning but present for more than 1 year; onset before 18. Lecture: HRT/CBT/behavioral therapy, alpha-2 agonists first, then atypical then typical antipsychotics. AnKing board add-on: VMAT-2 inhibitors such as tetrabenazine may be preferred in some question banks. Persistent motor or vocal tic disorder Motor tics OR vocal tics, but not both. More than 1 year with onset before age 18. Treat if impairing; otherwise education/reassurance plus behavioral therapy.

These conditions often overlap with ADHD, but their diagnostic anchors are different: mood/defiance for ODD, rights violations for conduct disorder, and motor/vocal tic pattern for Tourette syndrome.

Comorbidity

ADHD, learning disabilities, anxiety, ODD, and tic disorders commonly travel together. Treating ADHD can reduce disruptive symptoms in some children.

🧠 Mnemonic Wall

Every memory hook from the objective sections, collected in one place for a final-night cram. Each hook also lives beside the answer it belongs to.

Substance Use & Tox

N-A-D for alcohol use disorderNaltrexone kills the Need (craving — can start while still drinking) · Acamprosate keeps Abstinence (NMDA antagonist + GABA-A agonist, 3×/day) · Disulfiram is the Deterrent (blocks aldehyde dehydrogenase → instant hangover).
The B-52 bomberAgitation cocktail = Benadryl 50 mg + Haldol 5 mg + Ativan 2 mg IM. The Benadryl on board is what pre-empts acute dystonia. Repeated dosing → watch for NMS (rigid + sweaty + hot → STOP the antipsychotic).
Shakes by breakfast, seizures by tomorrow, DTs by day 2Alcohol withdrawal timeline: tremor/anxiety first → hallucinosis & seizures at 24–48 h → delirium tremens peaks around day 2 (can last a week). It's the only withdrawal that kills — treat with long-acting benzos (diazepam, chlordiazepoxide); clonidine alone never prevents the seizures.
Liver's bad? Use the parking LOTLorazepam, Oxazepam, Temazepam skip Phase I hepatic oxidation (straight to glucuronidation) — the safe benzos in liver failure and the elderly.
Uppers freak you ON the drug; downers freak you OFF itPsychosis with stimulant intoxication (amphetamines, cocaine) but with depressant withdrawal (alcohol/benzo/opioid — think DTs). Opioids: intox = dry & pinpoint; withdrawal = wet & wide (tearing, runny nose, diarrhea, dilated pupils — 'worst flu ever', miserable but not lethal).
Narcan wears off before the opioid doesNaloxone's half-life is shorter than most opioids → redose or watch for re-sedation. Its main adverse effect: it precipitates acute withdrawal. Serotonin syndrome antidote ladder: benzos + supportive care → add cyproheptadine (5-HT2 antagonist) if no improvement.
Buprenorphine hogs the receptor but never floors the gasHigh-affinity partial agonist → ceiling effect caps euphoria/respiratory depression, and surgical opioids struggle to out-compete it. Methadone = full agonist (watch QTc). Naltrexone = the antagonist option.
Receptor one-linersBenzos → GABA-A (Cl⁻ in, calm down) · Alcohol → GABA-A agonist + NMDA blocker (chronic use flips the ratio — that's the withdrawal) · THC → CB1 · PCP → NMDA blocker (painless belligerence — they hurt themselves and don't notice) · MDMA → reverses SERT (serotonin flood).

Psychotherapy & Theory

The 10-second therapy pickerBPD → DBT · trauma → EMDR · relationship problems → IPT · acute crisis / medically ill → supportive · everything else → CBT. Dr. Smith's rule: if DBT is an answer choice and the vignette is borderline, pick DBT; otherwise CBT.
Founder → school, in one breathRogers → humanistic (unconditional positive regard) · Freud → psychodynamic (free association, transference) · Beck & Ellis → cognitive · Skinner → behavioral · Linehan → DBT.
Mature adults wear a SASHThe 4 mature defenses: Sublimation, Altruism, Suppression, Humor. And remember: Suppression is on purpose (conscious); repression happens to you (unconscious). Splitting = borderline's signature.
Side effects sprint; benefits run a marathonSSRIs block SERT on day one (GI upset, sexual dysfunction start immediately) but postsynaptic receptors need 4–6 weeks to adapt before mood lifts. Fluoxetine = the long goodbye: longest half-life (2–4 days), no discontinuation syndrome, potent 2D6 inhibitor.
The Dodo Bird verdict"Everybody has won and all must have prizes" — no single modality is clearly superior overall; the therapeutic alliance predicts outcome better than the brand of therapy.
Ladder vs. cannonballSystematic desensitization = climb the ladder (graded exposure + relaxation: picture spider → plastic spider → real spider). Flooding = cannonball into the deep end (massive exposure until anxiety extinguishes). Social anxiety's therapy of choice: CBT with assertiveness training.

Eating Disorders

BMI first, behavior secondLow BMI (<18.5) → anorexia. Normal/high BMI → is there compensation? Yes → bulimia, no → binge eating disorder. Anorexia severity is graded by BMI; bulimia severity by compensations per week.
Anorexia gets NO drugs; Bulimia gets fluoxetine; Binge gets VyvanseNo FDA-approved med for anorexia (treatment = weight restoration ~1 lb/week, beware refeeding). Bulimia → SSRI ± ondansetron/topiramate. BED → lisdexamfetamine, sertraline, or topiramate. Bupropion is Banned in Both bulimia and anorexia (purging → electrolytes → seizures). Purging dehydration also makes lithium dangerous.
The knuckles confess what the patient won'tRussell's sign (knuckle calluses) + dental erosion = self-induced vomiting → bulimia. ED workup: BMI from vitals is the single most useful number; ask about stimulants, laxatives, and sneaky thyroid-pill misuse.

Somatoform, Dissoc. & Sexual

The three-branch deception treeSymptoms unconscious → somatoform spectrum. Conscious, to live the sick role (internal gain) → factitious. Conscious, for money/court/drugs (external gain) → malingering (not a psychiatric diagnosis). Vignette tells: thick chart, many specialists, normal workups.
Blind but unbotheredSudden neuro deficit + normal workup + la belle indifférence (strangely unconcerned) = conversion disorder. Fear of illness with no symptoms = illness anxiety; months of multi-system symptoms + obsessive worry about them = somatic symptom disorder.
Reality testing is the dissociation/psychosis borderDepersonalization/derealization keeps intact reality testing ('I know this isn't literally true') — that's what separates it from psychosis. Fugue = travel + identity amnesia (a specifier of dissociative amnesia, not its own diagnosis). DID ← severe early childhood trauma.
An interest isn't an illnessParaphilia → paraphilic disorder only with distress, impairment, or harm. Voyeuristic, exhibitionistic, frotteuristic (and anything with children) involve a non-consenting party → disorder by definition. Tx: therapy, orgasmic reconditioning, androgen-lowering agents, high-dose SSRIs.

Assessment & MSE

MSE describes; MMSE scoresThe MSE is the narrative exam (appearance, attention, thought process/content…) inside the psych SOAP note. A number out of 30 means MMSE/MoCA — a single cognitive screen, never the whole MSE. Classic exam trap.

Mood & Mood Stabilizers

Mania is a 7-day week; hypomania a 4-day workweekDIGFAST ≥3 (4 if only irritable): ≥7 days OR hospital OR psychosis + impairment = mania → Bipolar I (depression not required). ≥4 days, fully functional, no psychosis = hypomania; + ≥1 MDE and never mania = Bipolar II. One manic episode ever → converts to Bipolar I forever.
SIG E CAPS ×2 weeks; dysthymia ×2 yearsMDE = 5+/9 for ≥2 weeks (must include depressed mood or anhedonia). Persistent depressive disorder = 3 criteria, ≥2 years (1 yr in kids) — milder but longer. MDE on top of PDD = double depression.
Manic at week 3–6? You unmasked bipolarAntidepressant started → returns manic ~3–6 weeks later = unmasking, needs full DIGFAST episode criteria. Serotonin toxicity instead shows up in <24 h with clonus + hyperreflexia + autonomic storm — a neuro exam, not a mood change.
Lithium follows saltReabsorbed on the kidney's sodium channels → anything that makes you keep sodium keeps lithium: thiazides, NSAIDs, ACE-inhibitors, dehydration. Levels: 0.8–1.2 treats · >1.2 toxic (coarse tremor, ataxia, AMS, seizure) · severe → dialysis. LiTHIUM: Low Thyroid, Heart (Ebstein), Insipidus, Unwanted Movements.
Each stabilizer has one signature trapValproate → hyperammonemic delirium (check ammonia at ANY dose) + neural tube defects. Carbamazepine → the cannibal: autoinduces its own metabolism (early 'therapeutic' level, manic again weeks later) + SIADH. Lamotrigine → best tolerated, but titrate slowly or SJS; halve the dose with valproate on board.
Opposite jobs: mania drugs vs. depression drugsAcute mania: lithium, valproate, carbamazepine (+ antipsychotics). Bipolar depression: lamotrigine first-line (weak for mania). Lithium is the gold standard — the only agent that covers mania, depression, AND maintenance. Antidepressants only ever ride with a mood stabilizer.
Atypical GAINS, melancholic LOSESAtypical features (the most common subtype!): mood reactivity + weight/sleep gains + leaden paralysis. Melancholic: loses appetite, pleasure, energy. Seasonal pattern needs a strict seasonal on/off relationship with no off-season episodes.
Borderline flips in minutes with a trigger; bipolar shifts in weeks without oneBPD mood swings are rapid + interpersonally triggered; bipolar episodes last days-to-weeks and don't need a trigger. DBT's four modules = MEDI: Mindfulness, Emotion regulation, Distress tolerance, Interpersonal effectiveness.
TCA overdose: the 3 C's, and one week can killConvulsions, Coma, Cardiotoxicity (Na-channel block → wide QRS → torsades). A single week's supply is potentially lethal — get the EKG. 2D6 inhibitors (bupropion, fluoxetine) push TCA levels up.
The stressor clockAny stressor → symptoms within 3 months = adjustment disorder (gone by 6 months after stressor ends). Traumatic stressor → 3 days–1 month = acute stress disorder; past 1 month = PTSD.

Personality Disorders

Weird, Wild, Worried — and their alliterationsCluster A (weird): Accusatory (paranoid), Aloof (schizoid), Awkward (schizotypal) — genetic link to schizophrenia. Cluster B (wild): Bad to the Bone — antisocial (needs conduct disorder before 15), borderline, histrionic, narcissistic. Cluster C (worried): Cowardly (avoidant), Clingy (dependent), Compulsive (OCPD).
No FDA-approved pill for any personalityAll 10 PDs: psychotherapy is primary, meds are off-label symptom patches. The one disorder-specific therapy in the group: DBT for borderline (Linehan). (Quetiapine showed an 82% Zanarini response in BPD — notable, still off-label.)

Cross-Cutting Pharm

Fast & twitchy vs. slow & stiffSerotonin syndrome: hours after a serotonergic change — the 3 A's (↑Activity: clonus/hyperreflexia · Autonomic instability · AMS). Tx: benzos → cyproheptadine. NMS: days after an antipsychotic — lead-pipe rigidity + hyporeflexia + fever + ↑CK. First move: STOP the drug. The danger is crossing mechanisms, not stacking the same one; 2-week MAOI washout.
The cheese reactionMAOI + tyramine (aged, smoked, fermented) or interacting drugs → hypertensive crisis: diastolic >120, pounding headache, palpitations, stiff neck. Discontinuation syndrome (any antidepressant, stopped abruptly): flu-ish + dizziness + brain zaps.
Smoke burns away the -PINEsCigarette hydrocarbons induce CYP1A2 → clozaPINE and olanzaPINE levels drop (relapse); quitting in hospital → levels climb (toxicity). 95% of schizophrenia patients smoke — this WILL show up. Fluvoxamine does the opposite (1A2 inhibitor).
Bupropion: the smoking-cessation drug with a 2D6 tollboothDepressed smoker → bupropion (FDA-approved for MDD + smoking cessation). But it inhibits CYP2D6 — added to a TCA like imipramine it caused anticholinergic delirium. Avoid with seizures or eating disorders; the trade-off gift: minimal sexual side effects.
Name the culprit by its signatureSSRI → GI, sexual dysfunction, SIADH · TCA → sedating, anticholinergic, deadly OD · MAOI → cheese crisis · bupropion → tachycardia, weight loss, seizures. -PINEs pack on Pounds (metabolic) · -DONEs Drain prolactin & prolong QT · clozapine → agranulocytosis/seizures/myocarditis · lamotrigine → SJS.
First trimester: the heart forms, so hold the lithiumLithium → Ebstein anomaly (risk highest in T1; many hold it, resume later). Valproate/carbamazepine → neural tube defects. Benzos → worst at weeks 2–8. Most psych meds are category C only because nobody trials pregnant patients.

Psychosis & Antipsychotics

The 4 M's of dopamineMesolimbic = Madness (overactive → positive sx; blockade = the therapeutic effect) · Mesocortical = Missing (underactive → negative sx; blockade worsens) · Nigrostriatal = Movement (blockade → EPS) · Tuberoinfundibular = Milk (blockade → prolactin).
EPS timeline: ADAPTAcute Dystonia (hours–days) → Akathisia (days–weeks) → Parkinsonism (weeks) → Tardive dyskinesia (years). Treatments rhyme with the clock: benztropine IM → propranolol → anticholinergic/amantadine → stop the drug.
Young man, new Haldol, twisted neck → benztropine IMYoung males on a first dose of a high-potency typical are the classic acute-dystonia setup (torticollis, oculogyric crisis, opisthotonos). IM/IV benztropine or diphenhydramine works fast and dramatically.
The potency see-sawHigh potency (haloperidol, fluphenazine): hands shake — max EPS, minimal anticholinergic. Low potency (chlorpromazine): lazy & dry — sedation, anticholinergic, orthostasis, minimal EPS. Sweet spot: ~78–80% D2 occupancy ≈ Haldol 2–5 mg.
-PINEs pack Pounds; -DONEs Drain prolactinOlanzapine/clozapine/quetiapine → weight, sedation, metabolic syndrome. Risperidone → prolactin; ziprasidone → QTc. Cleanest metabolics: aripiprazole (D2 partial agonist), ziprasidone, lurasidone, cariprazine. Clozapine = last-resort gold standard: agranulocytosis (ANC checks), seizures, myocarditis — and the only drug FDA-approved to cut suicidality in schizophrenia.
Psychosis is a symptom until proven a diagnosisRule out malingering → substances → medical causes → THEN primary psychiatric. Uppers cause it in intoxication, downers in withdrawal. Remember the curveballs: glioblastoma, UTI in the elderly, neurosyphilis.

Neurocognitive & AMS

The universal rule-out ladderFaking? → Substance (intox/withdrawal/med)? → Medical? → only then primary psychiatric. AMS culprits from this course: serotonin syndrome (3 A's), lithium >1.2, valproate hyperammonemia (check ammonia at any dose).
Antipsychotics in dementia carry a boxed warning≈1.6–1.7× mortality in elderly dementia-related psychosis. Lower-risk moves: trazodone off-label (orthostasis, priapism), risperidone when an antipsychotic is truly needed. IM olanzapine: never within 2 h of a benzo (cardiorespiratory depression).
Three loops, three failuresBasal-ganglia re-entrant loops: motor loop breaks → dyskinesias · associative loop breaks → intrusive/disordered thoughts · limbic loop breaks → labile mood. Accumbens dopamine = pleasure/reward; amygdala (NE) = fear/restraint.

Legal, Ethics & Risk

Warn = call the cops, not the targetTarasoff duty fires when an identifiable victim faces imminent danger. Climb the least-restrictive ladder first (meds, family, more visits, hospitalize) — then warn via police. A confessed past crime stays confidential; only future risk breaks the seal.
Sue me? Prove the 4 D'sDuty + Deviation + Damages + Direct causation — all four, or no malpractice. Off-label ≠ malpractice without harm. Sponge left in the belly = res ipsa loquitur.
SAD PERSONS, and who dies vs. who triesSex(M) · Age · Depression · Previous attempt (#1 risk factor) · Ethanol · Rational-thought loss · Sickness · Organized plan · No support · Stated intent. Women attempt more; men die more (lethal means). The documented assessment (C-SSRS) is your legal shield — a safety contract without one protects no one.
ECT: the gold standard nobody remembersIndicated for severe/refractory depression, acute suicidality, psychotic depression, catatonia, peripartum depression. Overall depression gold standard = therapy + medication together.

Child & Adolescent

Stimulants 80–90% ; atomoxetine 60% ; alpha-2s calm the body, not the focusFirst-line: long-acting stimulants (methylphenidate ER, lisdexamfetamine…) — watch appetite, sleep, ~2–3 cm growth, tics (esp. amphetamines), CV review. Failed stimulants → atomoxetine (NRI, 1–1.4 mg/kg) or viloxazine; guanfacine/clonidine for hyperactivity. Diagnosis needs: >6 months, onset <12, impairment, ≥2 settings.
Kids' depression = fluoxetine, full stopThe DOC for childhood depression/anxiety: ~2-week half-life forgives missed doses, no discontinuation syndrome. All antidepressants carry the black-box suicidality warning in youth — counsel, don't avoid.
Two settings → two VanderbiltsADHD scales: Vanderbilt (parent + teacher), Conners, ADHD-RS — because symptoms must show in ≥2 settings. Autism: M-CHAT-R/F screening (18 & 24 mo); ADOS is the gold-standard eval but NOT required — ASD stays a clinical diagnosis.
ODD argues with adults; CD violates their rightsODD: ≥4 angry/defiant/vindictive symptoms, ≥1×/week, ≥6 months; severity = # of settings (1/2/3+). Tx: parent management training + treat the ADHD. CD: aggression, property destruction, theft/deceit, serious rule-breaking — and the required childhood prequel to antisocial PD.
Old Age People Love GrapesOral (0–1: nail-biting, smoking, overeating fixations) → Anal (1–3: retentive = neat-freak, expulsive = reckless) → Phallic → Latency → Genital.
The copied worrySeparation anxiety (~4% of school kids, F>M) often mirrors a parent's own — 'bad men will take mom.' Selective mutism: chatty at home, silent at school. Model for both: serotonin dysfunction + limbic hyperactivity.

Anxiety, OCD & Trauma

GAD: 3-of-6 for 6 monthsExcessive worry >6 months + ≥3 of: restlessness, fatigue, poor concentration, irritability, muscle tension, sleep problems (GAD-7 ≥10 supports it). Panic disorder needs recurrent spontaneous attacks + a month of worry/behavior change — an attack alone can happen in any anxiety disorder.
Daily fear → SSRI; date-night fear → beta-blockerChronic/generalized anxiety or daily social exposure → serotonergic therapy (SSRI/SNRI, buspirone). Episodic performance anxiety → propranolol or PRN benzo. OCD wants higher SSRI doses than depression.
Rule out the four killers before calling it panicMI, angina, PE, arrhythmia — panic attacks peak in 30 s–5 min with ≥4 of 13 symptoms and mimic all of them. Acute tx: break the breath-anxiety spiral; PRN benzo (alprazolam).
Nightmares get prazosin; plain insomnia gets trazodonePTSD algorithm: prazosin (α1-blocker) for nightmares/nighttime hyperarousal → trazodone for sleep-onset → SSRI trial → second SSRI/SNRI/mirtazapine → antipsychotic only if psychotic.
3 days to 1 month, then it changes its nameAcute stress disorder = PTSD's symptoms on a compressed clock (3 d–1 mo post-trauma); persist past 1 month → PTSD. Adjustment disorder follows ANY stressor (not necessarily traumatic) within 3 months.

New vignette-style questions written from the answers above, grouped by topic. Click an answer choice to check yourself — the correct answer and explanation stay hidden until you commit. (The older questions inside each objective now work the same way.)

Substance Use & Tox0/7 answered

Substance Use & Tox · Q1
A 52-year-old man with alcohol use disorder wants medication to reduce cravings but says he is "not ready to quit yet." Which agent can be started while he is still drinking?
A. Acamprosate, dosed three times daily from day one
B. Chlordiazepoxide on a fixed outpatient taper
C. Naltrexone, oral or long-acting injectable
D. Disulfiram, titrated up slowly while intake continues
Answer: C. Naltrexone manages craving and — unlike its use in opioid use disorder — can be started while the patient is still drinking. Disulfiram requires abstinence and informed buy-in (drinking on it causes the acetaldehyde reaction); acamprosate supports relapse prevention after quitting; chlordiazepoxide is a detox drug, not an anti-craving agent.
Substance Use & Tox · Q2
A 47-year-old with cirrhosis is admitted for alcohol withdrawal. Which benzodiazepine is the safest choice?
A. Chlordiazepoxide, the classic detox standard
B. Diazepam, for its long-acting active metabolites
C. Lorazepam, which skips Phase I oxidation
D. Clorazepate, a long-acting prodrug option
Answer: C. The LOT drugs — Lorazepam, Oxazepam, Temazepam — undergo direct Phase II glucuronidation with no hepatic Phase I oxidation, making them safest in liver impairment and the elderly. Diazepam and chlordiazepoxide depend on hepatic oxidation and active metabolites.
Substance Use & Tox · Q3
A patient maintained on buprenorphine needs post-operative pain control and requires unusually high doses of full opioid agonists. Which property of buprenorphine explains this?
A. Induction of CYP3A4 speeds the metabolism of other opioids
B. Irreversible covalent binding that destroys mu receptors
C. High-affinity partial mu agonism with a ceiling effect
D. Pure mu-receptor antagonism identical to naltrexone
Answer: C. Buprenorphine binds the mu receptor with high affinity but only partial agonism — full agonists must out-compete it, and its ceiling caps the achievable effect. That same profile is what makes it safe and effective as MOUD.
Substance Use & Tox · Q4
A 24-year-old is brought in agitated and belligerent, with prominent analgesia — he walked on a fractured ankle without noticing. The most likely intoxicant acts at which receptor?
A. Mu-opioid receptor, as an agonist
B. GABA-A receptor, as a positive modulator
C. NMDA glutamate receptor, as an antagonist
D. CB1 receptor, as a full agonist
Answer: C. Belligerence plus analgesia masking serious injury is the classic PCP picture; PCP is an NMDA/glutamate receptor antagonist. THC works at CB1, benzos/alcohol at GABA-A.
Substance Use & Tox · Q5
A patient in opioid withdrawal has dilated pupils, lacrimation, rhinorrhea, and diarrhea, and describes "the worst flu ever." Which statement about this syndrome is most accurate?
A. It is life-threatening and warrants ICU-level monitoring
B. It should be reversed immediately with naloxone
C. It typically produces frank psychosis and hallucinations
D. It is miserable but rarely dangerous, unlike alcohol withdrawal
Answer: D. Opioid withdrawal is the mirror image of intoxication — wet, wide-pupiled, and wretched — but not deadly. Alcohol (and benzo/barbiturate) withdrawal is the killer, via seizures and DTs. Naloxone would precipitate withdrawal, not treat it.
Substance Use & Tox · Q6
Why is clonidine alone inadequate as monotherapy for alcohol withdrawal?
A. It blunts the sympathetic surge but does not prevent seizures
B. It cannot be administered by any non-IV route
C. It dangerously raises blood pressure during withdrawal
D. It carries too much intrinsic abuse potential to use safely
Answer: A. Clonidine (alpha-2 agonist) covers autonomic symptoms of opioid or nicotine withdrawal, but CNS-depressant withdrawal needs GABA-A cross-tolerant coverage (long-acting benzos) to prevent seizures.
Substance Use & Tox · Q7
A patient on disulfiram drinks a beer and develops flushing, headache, vomiting, and orthostatic hypotension. Which enzymatic step is blocked?
A. Alcohol dehydrogenase converting ethanol to acetaldehyde
B. CYP2E1-mediated microsomal oxidation of ethanol
C. Aldehyde dehydrogenase converting acetaldehyde to acetate
D. Hepatic glucuronidation of ethanol metabolites
Answer: C. Disulfiram blocks the second step — aldehyde dehydrogenase — so acetaldehyde accumulates and produces the intense hangover reaction. One-step block, worth being able to draw.

Psychotherapy & Theory0/6 answered

Psychotherapy & Theory · Q1
A vignette describes a patient with borderline personality disorder. Both CBT and DBT appear as answer choices. Per the course rule, which do you pick?
A. Psychoanalysis, since BPD stems from early conflict
B. IPT, because BPD is fundamentally an interpersonal illness
C. DBT — the more specific answer when the vignette is BPD
D. CBT, since it is the evidence-based mainstay for all ten PDs
Answer: C. Dr. Smith's exact framing: DBT is a form of CBT — "if DBT is an option, choose it; if not, choose CBT." DBT beats CBT only when the vignette is specifically borderline; CBT covers the other nine PDs.
Psychotherapy & Theory · Q2
A therapist uses unconditional positive regard and reflection. Which founder and school?
A. Freud — psychodynamic therapy
B. Rogers — humanistic therapy
C. Beck — cognitive therapy
D. Skinner — behavioral therapy
Answer: B. Rogers → humanistic (unconditional positive regard, reflection). Freud → psychodynamic (free association, dream analysis, transference); Beck & Ellis → cognitive; Skinner → behavioral.
Psychotherapy & Theory · Q3
Research repeatedly fails to show that any one psychotherapy modality is clearly superior. What best predicts outcome instead?
A. Whether the chosen therapy follows a written manual
B. The therapeutic alliance and the patient's buy-in
C. The number of years of formal therapist training
D. Weekly session frequency and treatment duration
Answer: B. The 'dodo bird verdict': common factors — especially the patient-therapist alliance and the patient's belief in the approach — outperform the specific modality. Early CBT superiority largely vanished once researcher 'allegiance' was controlled.
Psychotherapy & Theory · Q4
A medical student furious at an attending goes home and channels the energy into a brutal gym session and extra studying. Which defense mechanism, and at what maturity level?
A. Acting out, an immature-level defense
B. Displacement, a neurotic-level defense
C. Reaction formation, a neurotic defense
D. Sublimation, a mature-level defense
Answer: D. Channeling an unacceptable impulse into a productive activity is sublimation — one of the four mature 'SASH' defenses (Sublimation, Altruism, Suppression, Humor). Displacement would redirect the anger at a safer target, like snapping at a roommate.
Psychotherapy & Theory · Q5
One patient consciously postpones thinking about her biopsy until after her son's wedding. Another, after a traumatic code, has no memory of the event at all. Which pair of defenses is this?
A. Suppression (conscious), then repression (unconscious)
B. Repression in both cases, at different intensities
C. Suppression first, followed by simple denial
D. Denial first, followed by dissociative amnesia
Answer: A. Suppression is deliberate and conscious (and counts as mature); repression is involuntary and unconscious. That contrast is the classic test pairing.
Psychotherapy & Theory · Q6
EMDR is built on which underlying model of pathology?
A. Distorted core beliefs that maintain a depressive spiral
B. Secondary gain that quietly reinforces illness behavior
C. Fight-or-flight responses misattributed to trauma reminders
D. Unresolved intrapsychic conflict from early childhood
Answer: C. EMDR (kin to systematic desensitization) pairs trauma recall with an external stimulus (the light bar) to decouple the trauma memory from its physiologic fight-or-flight response.

Eating Disorders0/5 answered

Eating Disorders · Q1
A 19-year-old woman, BMI 17.2, restricts intake and uses laxatives after occasional binges. Diagnosis?
A. Bulimia nervosa, purging type
B. Unspecified feeding or eating disorder
C. Anorexia nervosa, binge-eating/purging type
D. Binge eating disorder with compensatory features
Answer: C. BMI decides first: at a low BMI (<18.5) the diagnosis is anorexia even when binge/purge behavior is present — the subtype captures it. Bulimia lives at normal-to-high BMI.
Eating Disorders · Q2
Which medication is contraindicated in a patient with bulimia nervosa, and why?
A. Fluoxetine, because of dose-related serotonin syndrome
B. Topiramate, because it promotes further weight loss
C. Ondansetron, because it masks ongoing purging behavior
D. Bupropion, from purging-related electrolyte seizure risk
Answer: D. Bupropion carries a boxed warning: contraindicated in active/recent bulimia or anorexia because purging-driven electrolyte shifts and dehydration lower the seizure threshold. Fluoxetine is actually the bulimia drug of choice; lithium is also avoided (dehydration → toxicity).
Eating Disorders · Q3
First-line pharmacotherapy for binge eating disorder includes which agent?
A. Olanzapine, for appetite and mood stabilization
B. Mirtazapine, for its appetite-stimulating effect
C. Naltrexone, to blunt the reward of bingeing
D. Lisdexamfetamine, which reduces binge frequency
Answer: D. BED: lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse) reduces binge frequency; sertraline and topiramate are the other named options — and medication plus therapy beats either alone.
Eating Disorders · Q4
What is the primary treatment for anorexia nervosa?
A. High-dose fluoxetine with adjunctive nutritional counseling
B. Topiramate titrated alongside family-based therapy
C. Lisdexamfetamine plus structured meal support programs
D. Weight restoration around 1 lb/week, watching for refeeding
Answer: D. No medication is FDA-approved for anorexia. Treatment is gradual weight restoration — too-aggressive refeeding risks refeeding syndrome. SSRIs may help appetite/comorbidities but are adjuncts.
Eating Disorders · Q5
A normal-BMI college student presents with parotid swelling, dental erosion, and calluses on her knuckles. What behavior do these findings betray?
A. Chronic high-dose laxative misuse
B. Covert stimulant misuse for weight
C. Recurrent self-induced vomiting
D. Long-standing dietary restriction
Answer: C. Russell's sign (knuckle calluses) plus dental decay = recurrent self-induced vomiting → bulimia, which presents at normal-to-high BMI with subtler findings than anorexia.

Somatoform, Dissoc. & Sexual0/5 answered

Somatoform, Dissoc. & Sexual · Q1
A patient presents with sudden blindness, a completely normal workup, and a strikingly calm attitude about it. Diagnosis and the classic descriptor?
A. Factitious disorder, seeking the sick role
B. Conversion disorder, with la belle indifférence
C. Malingering, driven by external secondary gain
D. Illness anxiety disorder, with health preoccupation
Answer: B. Neurological-type deficit + normal workup + odd unconcern = conversion disorder with la belle indifférence. Symptom production is unconscious — that separates it from malingering and factitious disorder.
Somatoform, Dissoc. & Sexual · Q2
A nurse repeatedly induces hypoglycemia in herself with insulin to be admitted, with no financial or legal benefit. A prisoner feigns hallucinations before sentencing. Which pair is correct?
A. Factitious disorder; malingering
B. Malingering; factitious disorder
C. Somatic symptom disorder; factitious disorder
D. Conversion disorder; malingering
Answer: A. Conscious production + internal gain (the sick role) = factitious disorder. Conscious production + external gain (avoiding sentencing) = malingering — which is not a psychiatric diagnosis.
Somatoform, Dissoc. & Sexual · Q3
Which criterion most reliably separates depersonalization/derealization disorder from a primary psychotic disorder?
A. The complete absence of any hallucinations
B. A documented history of childhood trauma
C. Reality testing stays intact through the episode
D. Continuous symptoms lasting longer than six months
Answer: C. Criterion B: the patient knows the detachment isn't literally true. Once reality testing is lost, think psychosis instead.
Somatoform, Dissoc. & Sexual · Q4
A man is sexually aroused by watching unsuspecting strangers undress. When does this become a DSM-5 disorder?
A. It already is one — it involves a non-consenting party
B. Never, because paraphilias are interests, not disorders
C. Only once he is arrested or otherwise faces legal action
D. Only if the pattern persists beyond twelve months
Answer: A. Voyeuristic, exhibitionistic, and frotteuristic patterns (and any sexual contact with children) involve non-consenting people, so acting on them is disordered by definition. Other paraphilias need distress, impairment, or harm to qualify.
Somatoform, Dissoc. & Sexual · Q5
A somatic-type delusional disorder patient differs from a somatic symptom disorder patient in that the delusional patient…
A. reports symptoms in several organ systems for years
B. accumulates a thick chart across many specialists
C. improves substantially with repeated reassurance
D. holds one fixed false belief, functioning otherwise intact
Answer: D. Delusional disorder (somatic type): a single fixed, non-bizarre false belief — think the 'serpent around the brain' patient — with organized thought and preserved functioning everywhere but the delusion. The somatoform patient shows the thick-chart, many-workups pattern without a fixed delusion.

Assessment & MSE0/3 answered

Assessment & MSE · Q1
A note reads "MSE: 26/30." What error has the writer made?
A. They used the MoCA cutoff, which is actually 25
B. They performed an exam reserved for psychiatrists
C. They scored the MMSE/MoCA; the MSE is a narrative
D. None — the mental status exam is scored out of 30
Answer: C. The MSE is the full written narrative of mental functioning inside the psychiatric SOAP note; a number out of 30 belongs to the MMSE (or MoCA), a single cognitive screen. This mix-up is a favorite exam trap.
Assessment & MSE · Q2
Serial sevens primarily test which MSE domain?
A. Thought process and organization
B. Fund of knowledge and intellect
C. Arousal, attention, and concentration
D. Insight into the current illness
Answer: C. Serial sevens (100 − 7, repeatedly) probes attention/concentration. Thought process describes organization (linear, circumstantial, tangential…), not arithmetic.
Assessment & MSE · Q3
A delusional disorder patient's MSE is most likely to show…
A. global cognitive impairment across all domains
B. disorganized thought process with loose associations
C. flight of ideas with pressured, rapid speech
D. organized process; content with a fixed false belief
Answer: D. In delusional disorder, thought PROCESS stays organized and functioning intact — the pathology lives in thought CONTENT (persecutory, somatic, erotomanic subtypes), with insight lost only for the delusion itself.

Mood & Mood Stabilizers0/8 answered

Mood & Mood Stabilizers · Q1
A patient has had 5 days of elevated mood, decreased need for sleep, pressured speech, and grandiosity — fully functional at work, no psychosis. He once had a 2-week depressive episode. Diagnosis?
A. MDD with mixed features
B. Bipolar II disorder
C. Bipolar I disorder
D. Cyclothymic disorder
Answer: B. ≥4 days of DIGFAST symptoms with no marked impairment, no hospitalization, no psychosis = hypomania; plus ≥1 major depressive episode and no lifetime mania = Bipolar II. Seven days, hospitalization, or psychosis would make it mania → Bipolar I.
Mood & Mood Stabilizers · Q2
The same patient later has a 10-day episode with psychotic grandiosity requiring hospitalization. What happens to his diagnosis?
A. It converts permanently to Bipolar I disorder
B. It remains Bipolar II, now with psychotic features
C. It becomes schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type
D. It becomes cyclothymia with a superimposed episode
Answer: A. One true manic episode — ever — makes it Bipolar I, regardless of a well-documented Bipolar II history. Depression isn't even required for Bipolar I.
Mood & Mood Stabilizers · Q3
Psychosis occurring ONLY during mood episodes vs. a 2-week run of psychosis without mood symptoms distinguishes…
A. Bipolar I disorder from Bipolar II disorder
B. brief psychotic disorder from schizophreniform disorder
C. mood disorder with psychosis from schizoaffective disorder
D. major depression from persistent depressive disorder
Answer: C. Schizoaffective disorder requires ≥2 weeks of psychosis in the absence of mood symptoms — which never happens in a mood disorder with psychotic features, where psychosis is confined to the episode.
Mood & Mood Stabilizers · Q4
A stable patient on lithium starts ibuprofen for knee pain and a thiazide for blood pressure. Two weeks later: coarse tremor, ataxia, confusion. Mechanism?
A. Renal sodium retention increased lithium reabsorption
B. Thiazide-induced hypokalemia potentiated lithium
C. CYP2D6 inhibition slowed hepatic clearance of lithium
D. Both drugs displaced lithium from albumin binding
Answer: A. Lithium is handled like sodium at the proximal tubule. NSAIDs, thiazides, ACE inhibitors, spironolactone, and dehydration all make the kidney keep sodium — and lithium with it. Level >1.2 = toxicity; stop the drug, hydrate, dialyze if severe.
Mood & Mood Stabilizers · Q5
Which agent is FIRST-LINE for bipolar depression?
A. Lamotrigine, though it is weak for mania
B. Haloperidol, bridging until lithium works
C. Carbamazepine, for rapid-cycling patterns
D. Valproate, the most sedating stabilizer
Answer: A. Lamotrigine is weak for mania but first-line for bipolar depression — the mirror image of valproate/carbamazepine (first-line mania, backup depression). Lithium alone covers all phases, which is why it's the gold standard.
Mood & Mood Stabilizers · Q6
A patient on carbamazepine had a therapeutic level at week 2 but relapses into mania at week 8 with a low level and perfect adherence. Why?
A. The initial serum assay was a laboratory error
B. Carbamazepine binds dietary protein and went unabsorbed
C. He is genetically an ultra-rapid CYP2D6 metabolizer
D. Carbamazepine autoinduced its own hepatic metabolism
Answer: D. Carbamazepine's hallmark trap: it induces its own CYP metabolism (and OCPs'), so an early 'therapeutic' level falls as induction ramps up. It also causes SIADH/hyponatremia and is a leading rash cause.
Mood & Mood Stabilizers · Q7
An altered, confused patient on valproate has a NORMAL valproate level. Best next test?
A. Urgent EEG for seizures
B. Thyroid function panel
C. Serum ammonia level
D. Repeat trough lithium level
Answer: C. Valproate-induced hyperammonemic delirium is not dose-dependent — check ammonia in any confused patient on valproate regardless of level. Also remember hepatotoxicity/pancreatitis and neural tube teratogenicity.
Mood & Mood Stabilizers · Q8
A depressed patient started on sertraline returns 4 weeks later with decreased sleep need, spending sprees, and pressured speech for 8 days. Best characterization?
A. Serotonin toxicity from dose accumulation
B. Persistent MDD with anxious distress features
C. Antidepressant unmasking of bipolar disorder
D. An expected early activation response to SSRIs
Answer: C. Mania emerging ~3–6 weeks after starting an antidepressant, meeting full DIGFAST criteria, is the classic 'unmasking' switch. Serotonin toxicity would arrive within 24 hours with clonus, hyperreflexia, and autonomic instability — a neuro picture, not a mood one.

Personality Disorders0/4 answered

Personality Disorders · Q1
Which cluster pairing is correct?
A. Cluster A: antisocial and borderline — the 'wild' cluster
B. Cluster C: paranoid and schizoid — the 'worried' cluster
C. Cluster A: avoidant and dependent — the 'weird' cluster
D. Cluster B: antisocial, borderline, histrionic, narcissistic
Answer: D. Weird (A): paranoid, schizoid, schizotypal — genetic link to schizophrenia. Wild (B): antisocial, borderline, histrionic, narcissistic — linked to mood/substance disorders. Worried (C): avoidant, dependent, obsessive-compulsive.
Personality Disorders · Q2
A diagnosis of antisocial personality disorder requires which historical element?
A. An elevated score on a psychopathy checklist
B. Evidence of conduct disorder before age 15
C. A documented comorbid substance use disorder
D. At least one juvenile felony-level conviction
Answer: B. ASPD specifically requires documented conduct disorder before age 15 — the childhood prequel. No other PD has an age-anchored prerequisite like this.
Personality Disorders · Q3
How many personality disorders have an FDA-approved medication?
A. All ten, via off-label pathways
B. One — quetiapine for BPD
C. Two — BPD and schizotypal
D. Zero of the ten
Answer: D. None. All pharmacotherapy in PDs is off-label and symptom-targeted (quetiapine's 82% Zanarini response in BPD is notable but still off-label). Psychotherapy is primary — DBT for borderline, CBT for the rest.
Personality Disorders · Q4
A patient has rapid mood shifts within hours, always after perceived abandonment, plus chronic emptiness and self-harm. What most distinguishes this from bipolar disorder?
A. The prominence of impulsivity in the picture
B. Shifts are rapid and interpersonally triggered
C. The presence of brief psychotic-like symptoms
D. A strongly positive family mood-disorder history
Answer: B. The BPD/bipolar discriminator is timing and trigger: BPD affect flips in minutes-to-hours around interpersonal events; bipolar episodes last days-to-weeks and move independently of triggers. BPD can also show brief stress-induced micropsychotic/dissociative episodes.

Cross-Cutting Pharm0/6 answered

Cross-Cutting Pharm · Q1
A patient on an MAOI takes tramadol post-operatively and within hours develops hyperthermia, clonus, hyperreflexia, and diarrhea. Diagnosis and first-line treatment?
A. NMS — stop the drug and give dantrolene
B. Malignant hyperthermia — dantrolene protocol
C. Hypertensive crisis — IV phentolamine now
D. Serotonin syndrome — benzodiazepines and support
Answer: D. Rapid onset (<24 h) + hyperreflexia/clonus + autonomic instability after combining serotonergic mechanisms = serotonin syndrome (the 3 A's). Benzos + supportive care first; add cyproheptadine (5-HT2 antagonist) if no improvement.
Cross-Cutting Pharm · Q2
Which presentation points to NMS rather than serotonin syndrome?
A. Onset over days, lead-pipe rigidity, hyporeflexia
B. Onset within hours, with hyperreflexia and clonus
C. Flu-like misery and brain zaps after stopping paroxetine
D. Diastolic pressure over 120 after eating aged cheese
Answer: A. NMS: days, stiff, hyporeflexic, antipsychotic on board — first step is stopping the drug. The cheese scenario is MAOI hypertensive crisis; brain zaps are antidepressant discontinuation.
Cross-Cutting Pharm · Q3
A schizophrenia patient stabilized on clozapine in the hospital (where he couldn't smoke) resumes 2 packs/day after discharge. What happens and why?
A. His agranulocytosis risk roughly doubles from the smoke
B. Nothing changes — nicotine does not touch CYP450 enzymes
C. Levels rise toward toxicity — smoking inhibits CYP1A2
D. Levels fall and he risks relapse — smoke induces CYP1A2
Answer: D. Smoke (the hydrocarbons, not nicotine) induces CYP1A2, dropping levels of the 1A2 substrates clozapine and olanzapine → breakthrough psychosis despite perfect adherence. Quitting in hospital runs the same movie backward, toward toxicity.
Cross-Cutting Pharm · Q4
A woman stable on imipramine starts bupropion for smoking cessation and develops delirium and arrhythmia. Mechanism?
A. Bupropion inhibited CYP2D6, raising imipramine levels
B. Serotonin syndrome from combining two potent SSRIs
C. Displacement of imipramine from protein-binding sites
D. Additive dopamine reuptake blockade from both agents
Answer: A. Bupropion is a CYP2D6 inhibitor; imipramine is a 2D6 substrate (a TCA). The result was anticholinergic delirium and cardiotoxicity. Always med-rec for 2D6 substrates before adding bupropion — fluoxetine carries the same 2D6 risk.
Cross-Cutting Pharm · Q5
Which SSRI has the longest half-life, an active metabolite, and the fewest discontinuation symptoms?
A. Fluoxetine
B. Paroxetine
C. Sertraline
D. Escitalopram
Answer: A. Fluoxetine: 2–4 day half-life, active metabolite, potent 2D6 inhibition (many interactions) — but its slow fade makes it forgiving of missed doses and the DOC for spotty adherence (and for kids). Short-half-life paroxetine is the discontinuation-syndrome poster child; the fix for that withdrawal is simply resuming the drug.
Cross-Cutting Pharm · Q6
For treatment-resistant depression, which combination strategy is considered standard and acceptable?
A. A TCA plus an MAOI with no washout period
B. An MAOI layered directly onto an existing SSRI
C. Two different MAOIs at half their usual doses
D. An antidepressant plus an atypical antipsychotic
Answer: D. Augmentation with an SGA, a second antidepressant of a different class, a mood stabilizer, or thyroid hormone is standard. Crossing serotonin-raising mechanisms (MAOI + SSRI/tramadol/linezolid…) is the serotonin-syndrome recipe; MAOIs need a 2-week washout.

Psychosis & Antipsychotics0/7 answered

Psychosis & Antipsychotics · Q1
Match the dopamine tract to the consequence of blocking it: which pairing is WRONG?
A. Nigrostriatal — extrapyramidal motor symptoms
B. Tuberoinfundibular — elevated serum prolactin
C. Mesocortical — improvement of negative symptoms
D. Mesolimbic — fewer positive symptoms (the drug effect)
Answer: C. The mesocortical tract is already UNDERactive in psychosis — further blockade worsens (or fails to help) negative and cognitive symptoms. That's the wrong pairing; the other three are the core dopamine-hypothesis map.
Psychosis & Antipsychotics · Q2
A 22-year-old man given his first dose of haloperidol develops a twisted neck and eyes rolled upward 6 hours later. Best immediate treatment?
A. IV dantrolene
B. Stop everything and observe
C. Oral propranolol
D. IM benztropine
Answer: D. Young male + first exposure to a high-potency typical + hours = acute dystonia (torticollis, oculogyric crisis). IM/IV benztropine or diphenhydramine gives fast, dramatic relief. Propranolol is for akathisia.
Psychosis & Antipsychotics · Q3
Three weeks into risperidone therapy a patient cannot sit still, pacing constantly with an inner sense of restlessness. First-line treatment?
A. Propranolol
B. Benztropine
C. More risperidone
D. Amantadine
Answer: A. Akathisia (days–weeks) → beta-blocker (propranolol) first-line; benzos second. Anticholinergics are for dystonia and pseudoparkinsonism; a dose increase makes akathisia worse.
Psychosis & Antipsychotics · Q4
After 8 years on fluphenazine, a patient develops repetitive lip-smacking and chewing motions. Best management?
A. Stop or switch the offending antipsychotic
B. Add propranolol and reassess in a month
C. Raise the dose to suppress the movements
D. Add scheduled benztropine to the regimen
Answer: A. Orofacial chewing after years = tardive dyskinesia — managed by stopping the offending antipsychotic (anticholinergics don't help and can worsen it). ADAPT: hours dystonia, days akathisia, weeks parkinsonism, years TD.
Psychosis & Antipsychotics · Q5
Which antipsychotic is the best fit for a patient with obesity, diabetes, and a borderline QTc?
A. Aripiprazole
B. Ziprasidone
C. Olanzapine
D. Clozapine
Answer: A. Aripiprazole (D2 partial agonist) sits at the low-risk end for metabolic syndrome, prolactin, AND QT. The -PINEs (olanzapine/clozapine) are the metabolic offenders; ziprasidone is metabolically clean but QTc-heaviest among atypicals.
Psychosis & Antipsychotics · Q6
Clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia despite superior efficacy. Which monitoring/risk set belongs to it?
A. Serial drug levels to track its autoinduction
B. ANC monitoring, plus seizure and myocarditis risk
C. Weekly EKGs for progressive QTc prolongation
D. Monthly liver panels for cumulative hepatotoxicity
Answer: B. Clozapine: agranulocytosis (ANC checks), dose-related seizures, myocarditis, maximal metabolic burden — and it is the only antipsychotic FDA-approved to reduce recurrent suicidal behavior in schizophrenia/schizoaffective disorder.
Psychosis & Antipsychotics · Q7
Why does ~78–80% striatal D2 occupancy matter?
A. It is the sweet spot of efficacy without motor effects
B. It is the occupancy required to elevate prolactin
C. Occupancy below that level precipitates overt NMS
D. It is the threshold above which agranulocytosis appears
Answer: A. Efficacy lives in a narrow window around 78–80% D2 occupancy (≈ haloperidol 2–5 mg or chlorpromazine 100–200 mg). Cross above it and EPS emerges; some atypicals never reach it (looser D2 binding), which is why they spare EPS.

Neurocognitive & AMS0/3 answered

Neurocognitive & AMS · Q1
An agitated 82-year-old with dementia-related psychosis is considered for antipsychotic therapy. What must the family be told?
A. Electroconvulsive therapy is contraindicated at her age
B. Benzodiazepines are the safer first-line alternative
C. These agents hold FDA approval for exactly this use
D. Antipsychotics carry a boxed elderly-mortality warning
Answer: D. The boxed warning (~1.6–1.7× mortality, ≈4.5% vs placebo over 10-week trials) applies to antipsychotic use in dementia-related psychosis. Trazodone is a sometimes-used lower-risk off-label alternative (watch orthostasis/priapism); risperidone is the named atypical when one is truly needed.
Neurocognitive & AMS · Q2
Before diagnosing a primary psychiatric cause of altered mental status, what is the required rule-out order?
A. Any order is acceptable if all three are covered
B. Malingering, then substances, then medical disease
C. Substances, then psychiatric illness, then medical
D. Medical disease, then substances, then malingering
Answer: B. Rule out intentional production, then substances (intoxication/withdrawal/medication), then medical disease, THEN call it psychiatric. The missed-organic-cause vignette (UTI, glioblastoma, neurosyphilis, lithium >1.2, valproate hyperammonemia) is a recurring exam theme.
Neurocognitive & AMS · Q3
Disruption of the basal ganglia ASSOCIATIVE loop produces which clinical picture?
A. Choreiform dyskinesias and motor overflow
B. Labile emotions and disordered mood states
C. Isolated hemiballismus of the limbs
D. Disordered and intrusive thought patterns
Answer: D. Three loops, three failures: motor loop → dyskinesias; associative loop (caudate/DLPFC) → intrusive, disordered thought; limbic loop (ventral striatum) → labile mood. Accumbens dopamine = reward; amygdala NE = fear/restraint.

Legal, Ethics & Risk0/5 answered

Legal, Ethics & Risk · Q1
Your patient credibly threatens to kill his ex-partner, whom he names. After exhausting clinical options, what does Tarasoff obligate you to do?
A. Maintain confidentiality, since threats are protected
B. Call the ex-partner yourself and deliver the warning
C. Contact police to protect and notify the named victim
D. Terminate care and document the discharge carefully
Answer: C. Duty to warn/protect an identifiable victim in imminent danger — operationalized by contacting police, not by calling the victim yourself. First climb the least-restrictive ladder: adjust meds, involve family, increase visits, hospitalize.
Legal, Ethics & Risk · Q2
A patient tells you he killed someone ten years ago. He expresses no current violent intent. Can you report it?
A. Only if the patient repeats the confession in writing
B. Yes, but the disclosure may go only to the victim's family
C. Yes — a homicide disclosure always breaks confidentiality
D. No — only documented future risk breaks confidentiality
Answer: D. Commonly missed: past acts stay confidential (and privilege survives the patient's death). Exceptions require separately documented future risk — Tarasoff-type danger, involuntary hospitalization, or the classic HIV-partner-notification scenario.
Legal, Ethics & Risk · Q3
Which set proves malpractice?
A. Any clear deviation from the standard of care by itself
B. A bad clinical outcome followed by a filed lawsuit
C. Any off-label prescription that a patient complains of
D. Duty, deviation, damages, and direct causation together
Answer: D. All 4 D's are required. Off-label trazodone for agitation deviates from the label but causes no harm — no claim. Res ipsa loquitur ('the sponge speaks for itself') is the shortcut when deviation is self-evident.
Legal, Ethics & Risk · Q4
What actually protects a psychiatrist legally when an outpatient with depression dies by suicide?
A. The family's written promise to watch the patient
B. Proof that an antidepressant had been prescribed
C. A safety contract signed and dated by the patient
D. Regular documented risk assessments (e.g., C-SSRS)
Answer: D. A safety contract without a careful assessment offers zero legal protection, and family monitoring doesn't transfer responsibility. Physicians must act on the foreseeable, not predict the future — the documented assessment is the shield.
Legal, Ethics & Risk · Q5
Highest single risk factor in the SAD PERSONS framework?
A. Ethanol misuse
B. Male sex
C. No social support
D. A previous attempt
Answer: D. Previous attempt is the #1 predictor. And know the epidemiology pairing: women attempt more often; men die more often (more lethal means).

Child & Adolescent0/5 answered

Child & Adolescent · Q1
An 8-year-old failed adequate trials of two stimulants. Which next-step medication is a selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor with roughly 60% response?
A. Viloxazine
B. Guanfacine
C. Atomoxetine
D. Fluoxetine
Answer: C. Atomoxetine (Strattera): selective NRI, 1–1.4 mg/kg, ~60% response vs 80–90% for stimulants; side effects include GI upset, sedation, irritability. Viloxazine is the 5-HT2C partial agonist/NRI; guanfacine/clonidine (alpha-2) calm hyperactivity but don't improve attention.
Child & Adolescent · Q2
Before diagnosing ADHD, which requirement is essential?
A. Symptoms in two or more settings, onset before age 12
B. A Vanderbilt form completed by the child themselves
C. An EEG excluding seizure-spectrum disorders first
D. A documented failed trial of behavioral therapy
Answer: A. ADHD needs duration (>6 months), early onset (<12), functional impairment, and cross-setting symptoms — 'doesn't listen at home' alone never qualifies. Hence Vanderbilt forms from BOTH parent and teacher.
Child & Adolescent · Q3
First-line antidepressant in childhood depression, and the property that makes it forgiving?
A. Venlafaxine — dual action at two monoamine sites
B. Sertraline — the shortest washout in its class
C. Fluoxetine — ~2-week half-life, no discontinuation
D. Paroxetine — sedation that steadies sleep early on
Answer: C. Fluoxetine is the named DOC in childhood depression/anxiety: the very long half-life forgives missed doses (weekly-dosing option exists) and avoids discontinuation syndrome. Remember the class-wide black-box suicidality warning in youth.
Child & Adolescent · Q4
A 10-year-old argues with adults, deliberately annoys others, and is vindictive weekly for 8 months — at home only. A 15-year-old tortures animals, sets fires, and steals with confrontation. Which pair?
A. ADHD; oppositional defiant disorder
B. Adjustment disorder; early ASPD
C. Conduct disorder; severe ODD
D. Mild ODD; conduct disorder
Answer: D. ODD: ≥4 angry/defiant/vindictive symptoms, ≥once weekly, ≥6 months; severity by settings (one setting = mild). CD: violating others' basic rights (aggression, destruction, theft) — and the required precursor if ASPD is ever to be diagnosed after 18.
Child & Adolescent · Q5
Which autism screening statement is correct?
A. Vanderbilt parent and teacher forms screen for autism
B. M-CHAT-R/F screens at 18 and 24 months; ASD is clinical
C. A formal ADOS evaluation is required for the diagnosis
D. Autism-specific screening formally begins at age five
Answer: B. AAP/CDC: general developmental screening at 9/18/30 months, autism-specific (M-CHAT-R/F) at 18 and 24 months. ADOS is the formal gold-standard tool but is NOT required — the diagnosis is clinical.

Anxiety, OCD & Trauma0/6 answered

Anxiety, OCD & Trauma · Q1
A 30-year-old worries uncontrollably about work, health, and family for 8 months, with muscle tension, poor sleep, and irritability. Diagnosis and chronic first-line pharmacotherapy?
A. OCD — a standard depression-range dose of an SSRI
B. Adjustment disorder — supportive care without medication
C. GAD — an SSRI or SNRI, with buspirone as an option
D. Panic disorder — scheduled alprazolam three times daily
Answer: C. GAD = excessive, poorly controlled worry >6 months + ≥3 of 6 somatic/cognitive symptoms (GAD-7 ≥10 supports). Chronic treatment is serotonergic (SSRI/SNRI, buspirone); benzos are PRN acute cover, not maintenance.
Anxiety, OCD & Trauma · Q2
A resident gets crippling anxiety only when presenting at grand rounds, a few times a year. Best pharmacologic approach?
A. PRN propranolol or a benzo before speaking
B. Daily buspirone titrated to a steady state
C. Clomipramine reserved for refractory cases
D. Daily sertraline through the academic year
Answer: A. The exam-reading rule for social anxiety: chronic/daily exposure → serotonergic core treatment; episodic/performance-only exposure → PRN beta-blocker or benzo. CBT with assertiveness training is the therapy of choice.
Anxiety, OCD & Trauma · Q3
Which statement about panic attacks vs. panic disorder is correct?
A. Attacks occur across disorders; panic disorder needs more
B. Panic disorder requires agoraphobia as a specifier
C. A typical panic attack builds slowly over 2–3 hours
D. Any single panic attack establishes panic disorder
Answer: A. Attacks peak in 30 s–5 min with ≥4 of 13 symptoms and occur in GAD, OCD, and social phobia too; panic disorder needs recurrent spontaneous attacks plus a month of worry or behavior change. DSM-5 also unlinked agoraphobia — now a separate, co-occurring diagnosis. Always rule out MI, angina, PE, arrhythmia first.
Anxiety, OCD & Trauma · Q4
Two weeks after a serious car crash, a patient has intrusive memories, hypervigilance, and avoidance. At week 7, symptoms persist unchanged. The diagnosis at week 2, and at week 7?
A. A normal reaction at both points
B. Adjustment disorder, then GAD
C. PTSD initially, then chronic PTSD
D. Acute stress disorder, then PTSD
Answer: D. 3 days–1 month post-trauma = acute stress disorder ('early PTSD' on a compressed clock). Past 1 month, the same picture converts to PTSD. Adjustment disorder is for non-traumatic stressors within 3 months.
Anxiety, OCD & Trauma · Q5
A veteran with PTSD has nightmares and wakes drenched in sweat. First medication for this symptom cluster?
A. Quetiapine
B. Prazosin
C. Trazodone
D. Alprazolam
Answer: B. Prazosin (alpha-1 blocker) is the specific first move for nightmares/nighttime hyperarousal — a distinctive, easily-tested use. Trazodone covers plain sleep-onset insomnia; SSRIs are the daytime backbone; antipsychotics only if psychosis.
Anxiety, OCD & Trauma · Q6
What makes OCD pharmacotherapy different from depression pharmacotherapy with the same drugs?
A. Response arrives within the first week of dosing
B. OCD requires substantially higher SSRI doses
C. TCAs of every kind are contraindicated in OCD
D. MAOIs move up to first-line status in OCD
Answer: B. OCD responds to SSRIs (or clomipramine) but needs much higher doses than depression. Combine with exposure-and-response-prevention psychotherapy.

⭐ Master High-Yield Summary

Every high-yield card from all thirteen sources, regrouped by exam topic — 131 cards across 12 themes. Each card names the source it came from.

Mood & Mood Stabilizers

Episode Durations

  • Manic: ≥7d, OR hospitalization/psychosis — AND impairment
  • Hypomanic: ≥4d, NO psychosis/marked impairment
  • MDE: ≥2wk, 5+/9 SIG E CAPS (mood or anhedonia required)
  • PDD: ≥2yr (1yr peds), 3+ milder symptoms
  • Cyclothymic: ≥2yr hypomania-lite + depression-lite, never full episode

Mood Disorders

Mnemonics

  • DIGFAST (mania): Distractibility, Impulsivity, Grandiosity, Flight of ideas, Activity↑, Sleep need↓, Talkativeness
  • SIG E CAPS (depression): Sleep, Interest↓, Guilt, Energy↓, Concentration↓, Appetite, Psychomotor, Suicidality
  • SAD PERSONS: Sex(M), Age, Depression, Prior attempt (#1 risk factor), EtOH/drug, Rational thought loss, Sickness, Organized plan, No support, Stated intent

Mood Disorders

Disorders at a Glance

  • MDD = 1+ MDE
  • PDD = chronic mild depression ≥2yr
  • Bipolar I = 1+ manic episode (depression not required)
  • Bipolar II = hypomania + MDE, never a manic episode
  • Cyclothymic = hypomania-lite + depression-lite ≥2yr

Mood Disorders

Bipolar vs. Borderline PD

  • Bipolar: episodes last weeks–months, recur ~every couple years, ↓sleep need is core
  • BPD: swings hours–days, multiple times per day/week, sleep not disrupted the same way

Mood Disorders

Depression Treatment Ladder

  • Mild: lifestyle changes ± app-based therapy
  • Moderate: therapy or antidepressant
  • Severe: therapy and antidepressant
  • Resistant: augment (2 antidepressants / +SGA / +mood stabilizer / +thyroid) → ECT → ketamine/esketamine, TMS

Mood Disorders

Antidepressant Line of Therapy

  • 1st: SSRI = SNRI (tied)
  • 2nd: TCA
  • 3rd: "Others" — bupropion, mirtazapine, trazodone
  • 4th: MAOI

Mood Disorders

Gold Standards & Key Facts

  • Gold standard for depression = therapy + medication
  • Gold standard for mania = lithium
  • 4 treatments proven to ↓ suicide: ECT, esketamine, lithium, clozapine
  • Recurrence risk climbs every episode → duration: 1st ep. ≥1yr, 2nd ep. 2–3yr, 3rd ep. lifetime

Mood Disorders

Bipolar Treatment by Phase

  • Mania: lithium, valproate, carbamazepine, 2nd-gen antipsychotic — all 1st-line
  • Depression: lamotrigine 1st-line; lithium/carbamazepine also help; valproate does not
  • Maintenance: lithium (best evidence), carbamazepine, lamotrigine
  • Fluoxetine+olanzapine = only FDA-approved antidepressant combo, maintenance only (not acute mania)
  • 2nd-gen antipsychotics used: aripiprazole, olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone, ziprasidone — haloperidol is 1st-gen despite appearing in med tables; don't pick it if a question specifically asks for "2nd-generation"

Mood Disorders

Interventional / Procedural Options

  • ECT: gold standard, safe in pregnancy/elderly, no absolute contraindications
  • Ketamine (IV) / Esketamine (intranasal): treatment-resistant depression w/o psychotic features
  • TMS: non-invasive, no anesthesia, ~5x/week — lower yield than ECT/ketamine

Mood Disorders

Antidepressants — Named Drugs

  • SSRI: Sertraline (most Rx'd, well tolerated) · Fluoxetine (longest t½, 2D6 inhibitor, also FDA for bulimia) · Escitalopram (no QTc effect) · Citalopram (QTc risk — older) · Fluvoxamine (OCD only) · Paroxetine (shortest t½, "dirty" — many interactions)
  • SNRI: Venlafaxine (dose-dependent, low=SSRI-like/high=NE, ↑BP) · Desvenlafaxine (NE-specific metabolite) · Duloxetine (+ neuropathic pain/fibromyalgia)
  • TCA — tertiary (more SE): Amitriptyline (pain) · Imipramine (pain/IBS/enuresis) · Clomipramine (OCD/panic) · Doxepin (bipolar depression/insomnia)
  • TCA — secondary (fewer SE): Nortriptyline (cyclic vomiting/IBS/pain/migraine/smoking cessation) · Desipramine (ADHD)
  • MAOI: Tranylcypromine · Phenelzine · Isocarboxazid · Selegiline (patch, MAO-B selective, less strict diet)
  • Others: Bupropion — NDRI, smoking cessation, ↓seizure threshold (black box) · Mirtazapine — alpha-2 antagonist, wt gain/sedation · Trazodone — mainly insomnia, priapism · Vilazodone/Vortioxetine — newer, low yield beyond MOA

Mood Disorders

Serotonin Syndrome vs. NMS

  • 5-HT syndrome: hours, hyperreflexia/clonus, autonomic instability, cross-mechanism combos = highest risk
  • NMS: days, "lead-pipe" rigidity, hyporeflexia, high fever, follows antipsychotics

Mood Disorders

Quick Pick by Scenario

  • Depression + pain → SNRI or TCA
  • Depression + smoker → Bupropion
  • Depression + insomnia/↓appetite → Mirtazapine
  • OCD → Fluvoxamine (SSRI) or Clomipramine (TCA)
  • Acute mania, hospitalized → Lithium
  • Bipolar depression → Lamotrigine
